en: In the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* with the commentary of Aparārka, the second chapter on judicial procedure (*vyavahārādhyāya*).
[In this regard, the section on the common matrices of legal procedure (sādhāraṇavyavahāramātṛkāprakaraṇa).

(1)] [595] Now, in the first chapter, various kinds of duties pertaining to the social classes (varṇas) have been stated. And therein, relying upon the instruction for the administration of justice (vyavahāradarśana) which will be explained among the duties of the king (rājadharmas),...
"He should personally examine legal cases every day, surrounded by his court assessors (*sabhyas*).

Since the duty (*dharma*) has been enjoined here, he now begins another chapter to provide instruction on that very examination of legal cases, complete with its entire collection of constituent parts (*aṅga*). In that regard, one might object: "The procedure for legal cases was already taught in the first chapter, whereas here [the procedure] concerns its constituent parts; therefore, this should not be stated. This need not be said, because the determination of the procedure for legal cases occurs right here as a subordinate part (*aṅga*). As it has been said: "When both [texts] are heard, the more extensive [one prevails]."
Free from anger and greed, the king should examine legal cases together with learned Brāhmaṇas, in accordance with the treatises on Dharma. (2.1)

The king, who protects the people, should—accompanied by learned Brahmins who know the meaning of the treatises on legal procedure (*vyavahāraśāstra*)—examine and investigate the legal disputes (*vyavahāra*), which consist of the statements and replies of the plaintiff and defendant, by means of evidence such as written documents and witnesses; he must do so while abandoning the host of defects in judicial deliberation, such as anger, greed, and the like. Although the avoidance of anger and other such passions is already implied by the requirement to follow the *dharmaśāstras*, the specific mention of avoiding anger and so forth is made for the sake of emphasis, for one possessed of anger and the like is not able to establish the law. Therefore, just like the collection of evidence such as written documents and witnesses prescribed in the *dharmaśāstras*, freedom from anger and the like is the primary instrument for the king in the administration of justice. Anger (*krodha*) is the desire to strike; by this, hatred is indicated. Greed (*lobha*) is the longing for another's wealth in the form of bribes and the like. Ignorance and negligence should also be understood here as things to be avoided. Although the term "legal procedure" (*vyavahāra*) also denotes the activities of the members of the court and the presiding judge, [the king’s role remains paramount].
This fourfold judicial procedure is taught for use in legal disputes.

Thus, here the four feet of legal procedure (*vyavahārapāda*), consisting of the plaint (*bhāṣā*), the reply (*uttara*), the means of proof (*pramāṇa*), and the decision (*nirṇaya*), will be explained. Among these, the foot of decision is well known as the activity of the assessors and the presiding judge (*sabhāpati*). Nevertheless, with respect to the king, only the activity of the plaintiff and defendant can be enjoined as something to be observed; however, the activity of the king is not something to be observed, but rather something to be performed. Therefore, in this context, by the word "legal procedure" (*vyavahāra*), only the activity of the plaintiff and defendant must be intended. Alternatively, even the foot of decision is carried out by the assessors, while the king, acting as the examiner, is the one who observes it; thus, the explanation of the term "foot of legal procedure" even with the intention of referring to all four feet is not improper. To define the essential nature of legal procedure, Kātyāyana says:
In this extensive exposition of Nyāya, which is to be accomplished through effort and is divided into that termed Dharma and so forth,
"legal procedure" (vyavahāra) is said to be that debate (vāda) which has the matter to be proven as its root.

The meaning of this is as follows: "Dharmākhya" means that which declares the Dharma (dharma). "Nyāyavistāra" means the expansion of legal reasoning (nyāya-prapañca). When that has been interrupted—that is, when it has been abolished by the opposing party—and consequently, when [the matter] must be accomplished through effort consisting in the presentation of evidence such as written documents and witnesses, the dispute between the two litigants is called *vyavahāra* (legal procedure). For this very reason, Yama says: "The king, assisted by his ministers, should duly examine the cases of two parties in dispute, remaining free from passion and hatred."

The plural number in the word *vyavahārān* (legal procedures) is for the purpose of including legal procedures that are divided eighteenfold according to their distinct subject matters. For this very reason, Manu stated that the subject matter of legal procedure is eighteenfold: "Of these, the first is the non-payment of debt, followed by deposits, sale without ownership, joint undertakings, and the non-delivery of what has been given."
Non-payment of wages, breach of contract,
rescission of purchase and sale, and disputes between owners and herdsmen;
The law concerning boundary disputes, verbal and physical assault,
theft, violence, and the abduction of women;
The division of the duties of women and men, gambling, and betting—
these are the eighteen titles of law established here for judicial procedure.
In these matters, for men who are mostly engaged in disputes, one should make a final determination of the case by resorting to the eternal Dharma.

[597] "Pada" means place or subject matter; Nārada states that there are one hundred and eight of these, such as the non-payment of debts and so forth, when their internal subdivisions are intended to be expressed.
Another division of these very [mantras] is remembered as one hundred and eight;
due to the differences in ritual actions for human beings, it is said to have a hundred branches.
He [the Blessed One] has likewise stated other modes of conventional usage:
"It is proclaimed as having four feet, four bases, and four means;
it is beneficial in four ways, pervasive in four ways, and accomplishes four things."
"It has eight limbs, eighteen points, and likewise a hundred branches;
it has three origins, two applications, two doors, and likewise two destinations.
Thus he explains these very categories himself.
Dharma, judicial procedure, established custom, and royal edict—
this four-legged system of legal procedure is such that each subsequent one supersedes the preceding.
To the question "How is this so?", he says:
In that regard, *dharma* resides in the assembly (*sabhyāḥ*), while legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) resides in the witnesses;
customary practice (*caritra*) resides in the written records, and royal decree (*śāsana*) resides in the king's command.

Because the members of the court (*sabhyāḥ*) are the sole authority, it is said that "Dharma resides in the court. Since legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) depends on witnesses for its determination, it is said that "legal procedure resides in the witnesses. Custom (*caritra*) refers to the laws of regions, times, and families; it resides in written records (*pustakaraṇa* / *likhitakaraṇa*). Indeed, written records of the laws of regions and so forth are authoritative. Punishment (*śāsana*), which consists of the suppression of the wicked, resides in the royal edict (*rājājñā*), because it is dependent upon it. Among these—Dharma and the others—the subsequent one is stronger than the preceding. For example: when members of the castes (*varṇin*) have committed an offense, the punishment in the form of death would be obtained from the testimony of witnesses according to the truth; however, if the witnesses state a falsehood in accordance with the rule, "For where there is the death penalty for the castes," then by means of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), the punishment in the form of death is set aside. Legal procedure is also sublated by custom (*caritra*), as follows: even when the enjoyment of another man by an Ābhīra woman has been established by witnesses and the corresponding punishment has been reached through legal procedure, it is set aside by written records obtained from the royal palace. For it is thus written therein: "Even if Ābhīra women commit adultery, no punishment is to be taken. Custom is also sublated by royal edict. For example: although it is written as a regional law (*deśadharma*) that "the king’s officer must not enter the house of a Brāhmaṇa or similar person," and even though such a house is established [as protected], the king’s officer enters that house by royal command and takes away thieves and the like who are therein. Now he explains the phrase "having four authorities" (*catuḥsādhanatva*) and so forth.
Because he accomplishes [his goals] through the means beginning with conciliation (*sāma*), he is called the "one who employs the four means.
And because he protects the four stages of life (*āśrama*), he is the "one who benefits the four."
Because it pervades the doer, the witnesses, the members of the court, and the king itself, part by part, it is therefore remembered as "four-pervading" (caturvyāpin).
The fruit of merit and demerit pervades the agent and the others quarter by quarter, according to whether they have perceived [the act] correctly or incorrectly. Thus it has been said:
"One quarter reaches the agent; one quarter reaches the witness;
one quarter reaches all the members of the court; and one quarter reaches the king."
Because he brings about these four— dharma, wealth, fame, and likewise social standing—
he is proclaimed as "the achiever of the four."
The order of the world and the affection of the people; the king, his own men, the courtiers, the treatise, the astrologer, the scribe,
gold, fire, and water— this is declared to be the eightfold limb [of royal administration].

The accountant is useful for calculating the amount of wealth that has become the subject of dispute; the scribe for recording the statements [of the parties]; and fire and other elements for the purpose of oaths. Thus, they constitute limbs of legal procedure. Because it proceeds from three causes—lust, anger, and greed—it is proclaimed to have three origins; therefore, this triad is the cause of disputes.
A lawsuit, moreover, should be understood as being of two kinds: based on suspicion and based on facts.
Suspicion arises from association with the wicked, while facts are established through the discovery of stolen goods (*hoḍha*).

Since it is possible for even the wicked to engage in legal proceedings, doubt or suspicion arises. "Discovery of stolen goods" refers to the sight of evidence such as plundered property, or direct visual observation. Thus, in matters such as the non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*), a lawsuit may proceed both on the basis of proof and on the basis of suspicion; hence there is a "twofold nature of the accusation. An "accusation" (*abhiyoga*) is an allegation.
Because it is connected to two sides, it is described as having "two doors":
the first side is the *pakṣa* (the plaintiff's statement), and the counter-side is its reply (*uttara*).

The door is the engagement in the commencement of an action; it is declared to have two courses because it follows both reality and deception. Reality (bhūta) is that which is conjoined with the true meaning, while deception (chala) is that which is stated through negligence. [599]

In the root verse, by the phrase "the king shall examine the legal proceedings" (*vyavahārān*), the term *vyavahāra* is used to denote what is synonymous with "investigation" (*parīkṣā*). Thus says Nārada: "However, by the king especially, while protecting his own duty, the goodness or badness [of the parties] must be investigated due to the diversity of human minds."
The unrefined appear like the refined, and the refined appear like the unrefined;
various such states are observed, therefore careful investigation is appropriate.

Although the role of presiding over legal proceedings is attributed to Brāhmaṇas, they do not possess the authority [to decide cases]; rather, that belongs solely to kings, because it is recorded in tradition that the fruit of such action accrues to them. Thus says Nārada:
"A king who, being composed, personally examines legal cases in this manner, spreads his radiant glory here and attains the same world as Śakra."

Therefore, it has been stated that just as the officiating priests possess the status of agents (*kartṛtva*) in a sacrifice, so too do Brahmins possess it in the administration of justice according to the *Dharmaśāstra*. Kātyāyana declares the sin incurred by failing to perform this duty: "A king's own arbitrary action—when the [legal] word exists—is detrimental to heaven, destructive to the world, brings fear from enemy armies, and destroys longevity and progeny."
Therefore, the king should settle legal matters in accordance with the scriptures;
however, in the absence of scriptural texts for all cases, he should decide them according to local custom.
Bṛhaspati:
A legal decision must not be made by relying on the scriptures alone;
when an inquiry is devoid of reasoning, the destruction of dharma arises.
A thief may become a non-thief, and a virtuous man an unvirtuous one, according to legal proceedings;
without investigation, even Māṇḍavya was reduced to the status of a thief.

Gautama, following the word "king," states: "His means of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) consists of the Veda, the Dharmaśāstras, the auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*), the Upavedas, and the Purāṇa. That by which a matter is transacted—that is, determined—is the means of legal procedure, such as the Veda and so forth. Likewise: "In the pursuit of justice, reasoning (*tarka*) must be employed. Having deliberated by means of it, one should lead the case to its proper place. In the event of conflicting opinions, having referred back to those who are elders among the knowers of the three Vedas, one should reach a final conclusion. In this way, the king’s highest good (*niḥśreyasa*) is attained here. When there is mutual disagreement among investigators, one should refer back to and learn the principles of justice from those who are elders among the knowers of the three Vedas—those who have correctly mastered the fourteen branches of knowledge—and thereby bring the legal procedure to its conclusion or completion. In this manner, the king attains his highest good, which is the fruit described in the scriptures. And the fruit has been stated by Nārada:
For a self-disciplined king who adjudicates legal cases according to dharma,
seven virtues arise, just as the seven flames arise from fire.
“Dharma, wealth, fame, standing in the world, support, great respect from the subjects, and an eternal place in heaven.
In this context, “support” (upagraha) means the acquisition of allies. On this point, Manu says:
But when the king desires to examine legal cases, he should enter the court modestly, accompanied by Brahmins as well as ministers who are experts in counsel.
Seated there or even standing, with his right hand raised and wearing modest dress and ornaments, he should examine the legal cases of the litigants.

Those who know the mantras are those who know the *arthaśāstra*. Therefore, while examining a legal dispute (*vyavahāra*), one should follow that *arthaśāstra* which is not in conflict with the *dharmaśāstra*. To this effect, Nārada says:
"Examining the course of legal proceedings skillfully, in a manner consistent with the paths of both the *dharmaśāstra* and the *arthaśāstra*, he should lead [the case]."
Bṛhaspati said to the assembly:
"The assembly is declared to be of four kinds: the established, the unestablished, the sealed, and likewise the adjudicated; and the members of the assembly are of the same types."
Established in cities and villages, yet unestablished among the fickle;
sealed, supervised by officials, joined with royal authority, and governed.
The king, the appointed assessors, the legal code, the calculator, the scribe,
gold, fire, water, and one’s own men— these indeed are the ten constituent elements of proof.
Furthermore, the specific function of each of these ten has been declared separately:
the king is the presiding speaker and the ruler; the courtier is the examiner of the case.
Smṛti declares that a verdict shall pronounce victory, punishment,
as well as an oath involving gold, fire, or water for thirsty persons.
The accountant shall calculate the matter, and the scribe shall record the legal procedure;
his own attendants shall summon the defendant, the members of the court, and the witnesses.
He should always ensure that the plaintiff and the defendant are kept under guard by bail-bonds;
this is the tenfold administration of justice upon which a king should rely.

A person of refined intellect should examine legal cases; that assembly is equal to a sacrificial rite when it consists of seven, five, or even three members who are knowers of the world, the Vedas, their auxiliary sciences, and the Dharma.

That assembly hall where the foremost of Brahmins are seated is like a sacrificial ground itself. The status of the members of the court—whether they are few or many—should be understood according to the requirements of the case. *Ālagnaka* refers to sureties. Kātyāyana states the time for legal proceedings:
"That which occurs after the third part of the day, following the eighth part from the beginning of the day..."
That time for legal proceedings has been observed by the wise in the treatises.
The judges who oversee legal proceedings must be appointed by the king; for they have no authority to act on their own initiative or by force. (2.1)
And so, he states what qualities those members should possess:
"The king should appoint as members of the court those who are perfected in learning and study, who know the Dharma, who speak the truth, and who are impartial toward both enemy and friend. (2.2)

*Śruta* is the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedic sentences, acquired from a teacher through Mīmāṃsā and the Vedāṅgas—namely Kalpa, Nirukta, and Vyākaraṇa. *Adhyayana* (study) is well known. Those who are endowed with these two are called *upeta*. Those who know *dharma* are those who know the *Dharmaśāstras*. Regarding the *Dharmaśāstras*, Pitāmaha says:
"The four Vedas together with their auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*), Mīmāṃsā, the Smṛtis, as well as these Dharmaśāstras, the Purāṇa, and the Nyāyadarśana."

The king should appoint as members of the court those whose nature is to speak the truth, who provide impartial instruction toward both friend and foe due to the absence of passion and hatred, and who are to be won over by honor and gifts. They are called *sabhāsadas* because they sit (*sīdanti*) in the court (*sabhā*). These should be Brāhmaṇas learned in many scriptures; in their absence, such Kṣatriyas; and in their absence, such Vaiśyas. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says: "Members of the court should be the best of the twice-born—free from greed, wealthy, knowers of the Dharma, speakers of truth, and proficient in all the scriptures."

He who studies only a single treatise will not know how to reach a definitive conclusion regarding legal affairs; therefore, kings should ensure that those well-versed in many scriptures are employed as the highest authorities in disputes.
Where there may be no learned Brāhmaṇa, one should employ a Kṣatriya;
or a Vaiśya who knows the treatises on Dharma; but one should avoid a Śūdra with great effort.
Therefore, whatever task has been performed by others in an unjust manner should be understood as invalid—
even if they were authorized— whether by divine chance or according to the scriptures.
Manu says: It would be better for a king to have one who merely calls himself a Brāhmaṇa and subsists by his birth alone,
than to have a Śūdra as an expounder of dharma.
But the kingdom of that king for whom a Śūdra performs the discernment of dharma perishes, like a cow looking on while standing in the mud. —
Vyāsa.
If a king should neglect the twice-born and conduct affairs with the śūdras,
his kingdom will become agitated, and his army and treasury will perish.
Bṛhaspati: Those who are ignorant of local customs, atheists, those devoid of scriptural knowledge,
the insane, the angry, the greedy, and the afflicted— these should not be questioned in a legal determination.

Manu says: "But when the law-code is not understood, or is poorly understood through a lack of discrimination, there is always great fault for one who speaks in the assembly regarding matters of dharma."
The king should appoint as astrologer and scribe two men who are pure, skilled in calculation, conversant with the true nature of words and lineages, and proficient in various scripts.

In matters of investigation, protection, and the testimony of plaintiffs and defendants, one who speaks the truth must be appointed as a representative of the court, dependent upon the members of the assembly. (2.2)

He states the rule for the presiding judge: "But when the king, due to the burden of business, cannot personally oversee legal cases, he must appoint a Brāhmaṇa who knows all the laws, together with the members of the court. (2.3)

If there is any other matter more important than the administration of justice, the king—who, due to being occupied with that matter, is unable to oversee legal proceedings—must appoint a Brāhmaṇa who knows all the *dharma* scriptures to preside over the administration of justice along with the previously mentioned Brāhmaṇas. Furthermore, even a Kṣatriya Brāhmaṇa known as a *prāḍvivāka* (judge) may himself oversee legal proceedings; indeed, he too must be appointed. As Nārada says:
"Placing the *Dharmaśāstra* before him and abiding by the opinion of the *prāḍvivāka*, let him, with a concentrated mind, examine the legal cases in their proper order."

If the king personally examines legal cases, he is the presiding judge (*prāḍvivāka*) as well as the approver; otherwise, he is merely the observer of the legal proceedings. For this very reason, the elder Bṛhaspati says:

"The king should examine the cases, or else a twice-born man acting as the presiding judge, having placed the constituent elements of justice at the forefront and remaining established in the doctrine of truth and the scriptures."
In a legal dispute, he asks the question as well as the counter-question;
because he speaks first with kind words, he is therefore known as the *prāḍvivāka*.
The Śruti declares that he who asks the question concerning a matter based on legal procedure is called *prāṭ*;
and he who adjudicates therein is traditionally known as the *prāḍvivāka*.
Nārada said: Just as a physician would extract a splinter from the body by means of an instrument, so should the judge extract the splinter through legal procedure. [603]
Gautama: "Among all things, truthfulness is weightier than the judge. || 2.3 ||
Furthermore:
"If members of the court, through passion, greed, or fear, act contrary to the rules of memory and so forth, they shall each be fined double the amount of the fine for the dispute. (2.4)

It has been stated that if those members, under the influence of passion (*rāga*) and so forth, issue a decision in a dispute that contradicts the *Smṛti* scriptures, then they are each to be fined double the amount of the wealth that was the subject of the dispute. Here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), conduct contrary to good custom (*sadācāra*) and reasoning (*nyāya*) is included. Furthermore, the mention of "passion and so forth" is not a qualification of the cause for punishment—namely, the act of deviating from the *Smṛti*—because that would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), just as in the case of the two-fold nature of the oblation (*havis*). Consequently, since it serves as an illustration, even an act contrary to the *Smṛti* caused by delusion (*moha*) and other such factors becomes a ground for a specific fine. For this very reason, Nārada states that ignorance is equivalent to greed (*lobha*) and the like, which are grounds for severe punishment.

"He who speaks otherwise [than the truth], whether out of passion, ignorance, or greed, should be known as an unseated member of the court (asabhya) rather than a seated member (sabhyo). One should severely punish that sinner. This prescription of punishment applies specifically to disputes concerning property. However, in other types of litigation, such as those involving verbal abuse and the like, it should be understood that different punishments apply. For this very reason, Viṣṇu states: "The forfeiture of all property shall be the penalty for false witnesses, and likewise for members of the court who live on bribes. Here too, the mention of "taking bribes" is intended as an illustration. Therefore, Vṛddha-Bṛhaspati says:
Those members who speak unjustly, as well as those who live on bribes and those who deceive the trusting— all of them must be expelled.

As for the statement that "one should be fined one thousand for greed, but for delusion, the first *sāhasa*," and so forth— which speaks of greed and delusion as causes for unequal punishment— that refers to witnesses (*sākṣin*), not to members of the court (*sabhyas*). For this very reason, Kātyāyana prescribes a double fine for a member of the court who is devoid of correct knowledge.
Having correctly understood the determination of the matter, the member of the court should then speak;
otherwise, he must not speak at all, for the speaker shall be subject to a double fine.
Likewise, he states that ignorance is an equal cause for the improper judgment of an assembly member, whether through affection—which is a synonym for passion—or through greed:

"Whether out of affection, or from ignorance, or from delusion, or even from greed—if a member of the assembly speaks otherwise [than the truth], he is to be punished; such a person is declared to be non-member (asabhya)."
But that which has been lost due to the fault of the court members must then be paid by those members;
thus, once the matter of the litigants has been settled, one should not reopen it for reconsideration.
Likewise:
"But if the judge should converse in secret with a litigant regarding a matter that has not yet been decided,
then both the judge and the court members shall undoubtedly be punished."
Nārada: One who has not been appointed must not speak at all in a legal proceeding;
but one who has been appointed must speak words that are impartial.
Whether appointed or unappointed, one who knows the treatises is fit to speak;
he who lives by the treatises speaks the divine word.
Bṛhaspati: Whether appointed or unappointed, one who knows the treatises is qualified to speak; whatever he declares in the assembly is the Dharma—of this there is no doubt.

For example: "He who, having abandoned greed, hatred, and the like, makes a firm resolve regarding his duty according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, shall obtain the fruit of sacrifice."
Kātyāyana, regarding the king’s adherence [to duty], states:
"But the members of the court must not overlook one who has acted unrighteously;
by overlooking him, they, along with the king, go headlong to hell."
Those members of the assembly who follow one who intends to act unjustly share in that guilt; therefore, they must admonish the king.
Manu says:
The king becomes free from sin, and the members of the court are released;
the guilt goes to the perpetrator if one who deserves censure is censured.
One should either not enter an assembly or speak what is correct;
by not speaking or by speaking falsely, a man becomes a sinner.
Kātyāyana says:

Where the members of the court have reached a decision by transgressing the treatises on logic (*nyāyaśāstra*), there dharma, being struck down by adharma, destroys [the world]; of this there is no doubt.
Where dharma is slain by adharma, and truth by falsehood, while the members look on, there the members of the assembly are themselves slain.
The genitive case in *prekṣamāṇānām* is used in the sense of disregard. Vyāsa says:
"That is no assembly where there are no elders; those are no elders who do not speak of dharma.
That is no dharma where there is no truth; that is no truth which is pierced by deceit."
But those members of the assembly who, having entered the court, sit in silence and deep thought, and do not speak as required, they are all speakers of untruth. (2.4)
He states the reason for observing the lineage of the wind:
"One who has not been overcome by others through a path devoid of mindfulness and proper conduct."
For when one reports that matter to the king, it indeed becomes a legal case. || 2.5 ||

When one who has been assailed by others through a path or means devoid of the *smṛti* scriptures and the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) reports to the king, saying, "I have been wronged by this person according to this unjust method," that report constitutes a ground for legal procedure (*vyavahārapada*). "Ground" (*pada*) means a position, a basis, or a cause. The plural number in the word "by others" (*paraiḥ*) is used for the sake of illustration; by it, one who is assailed by one, two, or many is indicated. Since the report is established as the cause for the administration of justice, the king must not conduct a trial without a report. Thus says Manu: [Manu 8.43] "A king should not, on his own initiative, initiate a lawsuit against anyone; nor should he suppress a lawsuit brought before him. [Manu 8.44] "But when a lawsuit is brought before him by either party, he should investigate it in accordance with the law, having seated himself upon the throne of justice. [Manu 8.45] "The king should investigate lawsuits brought by others through the four means of proof: witnesses, documents, possession, and divine ordeal. [Manu 8.46] "In the absence of witnesses, he should examine the case by means of inference based on the facts; and even in the absence of inference, he should investigate by means of divine ordeal. [Manu 8.47] "He should never suppress a lawsuit brought by another; for by suppressing a lawsuit, the king incurs the sin of the perpetrator. [Manu 8.48] "By suppressing a lawsuit concerning debt, deposits, theft, violence, adultery, verbal abuse, assault, and the non-payment of wages, the king becomes liable for the guilt of the perpetrator. [Manu 8.49] "In cases involving a woman, a Brahmin, or a minor, or where the evidence is contradictory, the king should investigate the matter ex officio, even without a complaint. [Manu 8.50] "In cases where a woman, a child, a fool, an aged man, a sick person, a blind person, or a deaf person is oppressed, the king should act of his own accord. [Manu 8.51] "And in cases involving heretics, outcasts, or those who have committed crimes against the state, the king should investigate the matter ex officio, even without a complaint. [Manu 8.52] "For the king is the guardian of those who have no protector, and the lord of all creatures; therefore, he should protect them from oppression. [Manu 8.53] "The king should always investigate lawsuits brought by others, whether they concern debts, deposits, theft, violence, or other matters. [Manu 8.54] "He should investigate a lawsuit brought by another through witnesses, documents, possession, and divine ordeal, in accordance with the law. [Manu 8.55] "In the absence of witnesses, he should investigate by means of inference; and in the absence of inference, he should investigate by means of divine ordeal. [Manu 8.56] "He should never suppress a lawsuit brought by another; for by suppressing a lawsuit, the king incurs the sin of the perpetrator. [Manu 8.57] "By suppressing a lawsuit concerning debt, deposits, theft, violence, adultery, verbal abuse, assault, or the non-payment of wages, the king becomes liable for the guilt of the perpetrator. [Manu 8.58] "In cases involving a woman, a Brahmin, a minor, or where the evidence is contradictory, the king should investigate the matter ex officio, even without a complaint. [Manu 8.59] "In cases where a woman, a child, a fool, an aged man, a sick person, a blind person, or a deaf person is oppressed, the king should act of his own accord.
