The king himself, nor his official, should initiate a legal case;
nor should he ever swallow up a claim brought forward by another.
One should not suppress or deny the matter. On this point, Kātyāyana says:

"By whom, in what, when, and for what reason?"—having thus entered the court, the member of the assembly (sabhyā) shall question the plaintiff who has come to the court: "By which person, in regard to what matter, at what time, and for what cause have you been wronged?"
One who is armed, without an upper garment, with disheveled hair, seated upon a seat, wearing a garland,
or speaking while holding a staff in the left hand, shall incur punishment.

The meaning is this: if, when questioned, he speaks his reply while bearing arms, without his upper garment, with disheveled hair, seated upon a seat, moving something with his left hand, or wearing a garland on his head, then he is to be punished. Likewise: "At the proper time, he should question the seeker of justice who stands before him with a bowed head:
'What is your business? What is your grievance? Do not fear; speak, O man!'"

When he has been thus questioned, the king, together with the members of the assembly and the Brahmins, should deliberate upon what he says; if it is found to be just, then he should proceed further to summon him.
One should cast a seal (mudrā) into it, or one should command a man [to do so].
Likewise:
"He who commits violence or does not give what is due to one who begs,
because of his immoral conduct, may be dragged away by the king's command."
Bṛhaspati: Whether one brings a charge against another based on truth or even out of suspicion, the king should cause that very person to be summoned by means of a seal or by a messenger. [606]
Likewise:
[He should avoid those] who are mentally unfit, children, the elderly, or those distressed by irregular conditions;
those overwhelmed by urgent business, those in the grip of calamity, those occupied with royal affairs, or those distracted by festivals.

A king should not summon servants who are engaged in religious duties, those who are dependent on others for their livelihood, those of deceitful appearance, or those who are intoxicated, insane, or heedless.

"Unfit" means afflicted by illness. "Difficult terrain" refers to rugged ground or being bound in fetters and the like. "Preoccupied with duties" means one who is constantly distracted by the performance of obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika-karma*). "One whose business is pressing" refers to one for whom the destruction of more important matters would occur if [the summons] were to arrive at that time. "Calamity" (*vyasana*) refers to such things as separation from loved ones. "Festival" (*utsava*) refers to a public occasion such as the *Kaumudī* festival, or a private event such as a wedding. If there is a reason for not coming that persists over a long period, then, having been summoned, he may dispatch another person to determine the legal proceedings. For this very reason, it is said: "Neither a brother, nor a father, nor a son, nor an appointed agent [may represent him]."
One who speaks for the sake of another, speaking falsely in legal proceedings, shall be punished.
Likewise:
"A young woman of noble birth who has lost her husband, a woman who has given birth,
and a maiden of the highest caste— all these are declared to have their kinsmen as their masters."

Therefore, the meaning is that only their own kinsmen should be invited. Regarding those who are to be invited, he says: "Those whose husbands are dependent on them, wanton women, courtesans, those who have no family, and those who are outcastes—it is appropriate to invite these."

The king [should do so]—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. And this is merely an illustration; by it, the wives of cowherds, vintners, and others are also included, since they too may be authors of legal proceedings (*vyavahāra*). Where success cannot be achieved except by summoning forest-dwellers and the like, there he should summon even them. As it has been said:
"Having ascertained the nature of the lawsuit, even those who are forest-dwellers, renunciants, and so forth—the king, protecting them, should summon them in matters of great importance."
Likewise:
"He who, being subject to restraint, violates that restraint, deserves punishment;
but he who restrains one who is not subject to restraint shall be punished by the king—this is the settled rule."

When one who has been summoned arrives, the summoner must issue a prohibition against that person who is subject to such prohibition—namely, a ban on other activities such as eating and so forth. Nārada states those who are not subject to prohibition:
"In cases such as crossing a river, traversing a wilderness, or being beset by calamities in difficult terrain, one who departs before the prohibition has been completed does not commit an offense."
One who desires to marry, one afflicted by disease, one wishing to sacrifice, one situated in calamity, one attacked by another, and likewise one occupied with royal business.
Cowherds [should be employed] during the grazing of cattle; farmers at the time of sowing;
artisans also at their respective times; and soldiers during war.

A messenger, one who has not yet attained legal capacity, one intent on giving a gift, one observing a vow, and those in a precarious situation— these should not be obstructed, nor should the king summon them.
Having understood the place and the time, as well as the strength and weakness of the tasks at hand,
the king should gradually cause even those who are incapable of calculation and the like to be brought before him by means of vehicles.

By means of vehicles such as palanquins and the like; Nārada says: One should restrain a person who does not abide by the matter to be discussed and who departs from those words for the sake of the lawsuit, until the appearance of the summons.

Based on the etymological derivation that "one is summoned by this," a royal official is called an *āhvāna*. Regarding restraint (*āsedha*), he states: "Restraint is fourfold: restraint of place, restraint by time, as well as restraint from travel and from occupation. This fourfold restraint must not be violated by one who has not been formally enjoined."

Restriction of place is as follows: "One must not stay here in this house or similar location. Restriction of time, however, is: "You must not eat today," and so forth. Prohibition of departure is the prevention of travel. Prohibition of action is the forbidding of agriculture and other such activities. He who violates a restriction while it is still in force during the period of restriction shall be punished; otherwise, by acting contrary to the injunction, the one who imposed the restriction shall become liable for a fine.

The one to be disciplined is the one to be punished; that is to say, one who acts otherwise than required, or one who imprisons someone who should not be imprisoned. Kātyāyana states: "But if one who is capable should disregard the king's command when summoned, the king shall inflict upon him punishment according to the procedure prescribed by law."
For a minor offense, he shall be fined fifty; for a middling one, at least one hundred;
and for serious matters, he shall always be fined at least five hundred.
This number refers to copper coins (tāmrika-paṇas).
When the mission has been accomplished by the envoy, the leader should cause food to be provided;
likewise, the place, the time, the age, and the capacity [of the recipient] must be taken into account regarding the meal.
Those who know the Dharma understand that this applies everywhere to one who is not the actual perpetrator;
furthermore, the judge must require a surety from the litigant.
When the defendant has arrived and is capable of standing trial, yet there is no surety available for the plaintiff who is fit to bring the suit; [608]
Having guarded him until the end of the day, he should give the messenger his wages.
Regarding the first task for one who examines legal proceedings, he says:

"In the presence of the defendant, the claimant shall cause a written document to be prepared exactly as it was stated, marked with the year, the month, the fortnight, the names, the caste, and other identifying characteristics. (2.6)

In a legal proceeding, whatever manner in which a claimant (plaintiff) has presented his case regarding the subject matter of the law, that very same manner—marked by the year and other details—must be caused to be written down by the king before the defendant (respondent). The manner of presentation is as follows: "This much gold of mine was taken as a loan by such-and-such a debtor of such-and-such a caste on such-and-such a lunar day, in such-and-such a fortnight, in such-and-such a month, in such-and-such a year"; or else, it is marked by the name, caste, and other characteristics of the property that is the subject of the dispute. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), brokenness, wholeness, number, quantity, and the like are included. Otherwise, a dispute concerning an object devoid of number and other such attributes would be inadmissible. On this point, Kātyāyana says:
Having recorded the time, the year, the month, the fortnight, and likewise the lunar day;
as well as the hour, the gift to be given, the district, the location, the caste, the physical appearance, and the age.

He [should know] the object to be accomplished, the means of proof, the substance, the number, and likewise the name of himself; and he should know the names of the kings in their proper order, as well as their residence and the name of the object to be accomplished.
One should set forth the names of the ancestors in order, as well as the afflicter and the giver,
other signs of forgiveness, and the specific party, and then formulate the claim.

Among those [documents], only those which are useful for presenting evidence that either supports or contradicts [a claim] should be written down in a given case; not all of them, because they would serve no purpose. In that regard, the year, month, and so forth are useful in disputes concerning interest, marriage, and the like, as well as in disputes regarding prior or subsequent timing. Names, caste, and so forth are useful in disputes such as theft. In the same way, other factors should be inferred accordingly. The place, the time, the location, and likewise the layout;
the caste, the name, the residence, the measurement, and the name of the field.
In disputes concerning immovable property, one should record these ten things: the paternal and ancestral lineage, and the proclamation of former kings.

"Place" (*deśa*) refers to a district or country. By means of that, the immovable object which is the subject of dispute is to be qualified. The same applies to the subsequent items as well. [609] "Time" (*kāla*) here refers to the time of purchase, sale, acceptance, and so forth. "Location" (*sthāna*) refers to the settlement such as a village, or its circularity, length, and so on. "Species" (*jāti*) refers to the origin, such as rice; the meaning is that the field and so forth are to be characterized by that. Alternatively, "species" refers to the caste of the donor and others, such as Brahmin and so forth. "Name" (*saṃjñā*) is the appellation or a mark, such as a tree and so forth. "Neighborhood" (*adhivāsa*) is the group of owners of the fields situated nearby. "Measure" (*pramāṇa*) is the dimension, such as *nivartana* and so forth, or the boundaries and so on. The rest is well known. A plaint (*bhāṣā*) of the aforementioned form should be written down and accepted by the judges, but not one that is contrary to this. Thus it has been said:
A thesis that is devoid of place and time, lacking in substance and number, and deficient in the measure of what is to be proven, is considered unacceptable.

One who is unacceptable should be rejected by those who investigate. This is the intended meaning: an inquiry that serves the purpose of reaching a definitive conclusion is to be adopted by prudent persons. And legal proceedings such as the non-payment of debt have the acquisition of wealth as their purpose. However, wealth devoid of the aforementioned characteristics cannot be paid even by a defeated defendant, nor can it be received by the other party. One should avoid a semblance of a plaint (*pakṣābhāsa*) that is unestablished, unassailable, useless, purposeless, impossible to prove, or contradictory.

An unestablished [plaint] is, for example: "My hare's horn has been stolen by him. An unassailable and untroubled [plaint] is, for example: "He is conducting his affairs in his own house by means of the light of our lamp. A meaningless and inexpressible [plaint] is, for example: "Kaca-tata-pa. A purposeless [plaint] is, for example: "He is reciting while praising [us] in the vicinity of our house. An impossible [plaint], one whose proof is unattainable, is, for example: "I was mocked by Devadatta with a wink of the eye"; for this matter is not within the scope of witnesses because of its brevity of time, nor is it within the scope of ordeals because of its insignificance, and no other means of proof is possible at all. A contradictory [plaint] is one that opposes the interests of the city, the kingdom, or the king. A plaintiff should avoid and not put forward such a plaint; even if it is put forward, the king shall not accept it. — Kātyāyana.
A plaint that is opposed by the city and the kingdom, one that has been rejected by the king,
or one that is confused by multiple points, does not succeed.

"Contrary to city and kingdom" means contrary to the customs of the city and kingdom; "avoided by the king" means prohibited [by him], such as [an edict stating]: "No one shall conduct transactions using coins in our kingdom," and so forth. That case among the titles of law, such as debt and the rest, in which there is a confusion of several [issues] is "mixed with multiple titles," for example: "My gold was taken by this man; a thousand *drammas* were deposited by me in his hand; this man, who is not the owner, sold my cow; and he struck me with a staff.
A legal matter in which many assertions are determined in the lawsuits [is likewise considered mixed].
Even that the king might accept out of a desire to know the truth. [610]

When a single legal matter, such as the non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*) and so forth, cannot be established without multiple assertions (*pratijñā*), that case is to be accepted; for, since there is no confusion of subject matters (*saṃkīrṇaviṣayatva*), it is indeed admissible. For example: "In Vārāṇasī, this man took from me a hundred gold pieces in the form of a debt; furthermore, in another year, he took this many garments; and after that, at other times and in other places, he took goats, cows, and grain. Alternatively, the meaning is this: when there are multiple assertions concerning various subjects of legal procedure—such as the non-payment of debt, deposits (*nikṣepa*), and sale without ownership (*asvāmivikraya*)—which all relate to a single objective consisting of the recovery of wealth, the king may certainly accept that case, provided that he presents evidence separately for each of the individual assertions. Thus says Nārada:
A legal proceeding between one person on one side and many— whether women or servants—
is declared by those who know the Dharma to be inadmissible.
Between teacher and pupil, father and son, husband and wife, and master and servant— when these are assembled together, no legal dispute exists.

A lawsuit involving one person against many, whether individually or simultaneously, shall not be admitted. However, it may indeed be admitted even against many, whether acting collectively or successively. A lawsuit brought by women—excluding those such as female cowherds, female vintners, and the like—as well as by servants, slaves, and others, shall not be admitted; rather, the matter must be transacted with their respective masters. When disciples have been punished by a teacher in accordance with the scriptures, a lawsuit between them and the teacher regarding the severity of that punishment shall not be admitted. The same applies to sons and others in relation to their fathers and others. As stated by Manu: *naikaḥ pratyarthibhir bahubhiḥ saha vyavaharet | na ca bahava ekena saha, anyatra strī-go-paśu-śauṇḍikebhyaḥ ||* *preṣyair dāsaiś ca kartavyaḥ svāmibhis teṣu vai saha | guruṇā śāsitāḥ śiṣyāḥ putraiś caiva ca dāpitāḥ ||* *yadi tatkāryam ātiṣṭhan vipratipadyeta vā punaḥ | na tatra kāryo vimardo guruṇā śāsite kṛte ||* *tathā pitrā ca putreṇa bhāryayā svāminā tathā | nyūnādhikavisaṃvāde kartavyo na tu vigrahaḥ ||* (MDh 8.65–67) Thus, no conflict should be pursued when the teacher has already administered the correction. Likewise, no dispute should be raised by sons and others against their parents and others regarding matters of deficiency or excess.
A wife, a son, a slave, a pupil, and a uterine brother—
when they have committed an offense, they may be beaten with a rope or a split bamboo cane.
But one should never strike the back of the body, nor the head;
for striking otherwise than this, one incurs the guilt of a thief.

Sin is that which results from punishment. Likewise, because the property of a husband and wife is held in common, a dispute regarding their joint wealth should not be admitted as a suit. Furthermore, a dispute should not be admitted on the suspicion that "she might provoke a quarrel with her husband and thereby suffer loss. Bṛhaspati says:
Those who know the nature of a legal plea recognize a valid *pakṣa* (plaint) as being free from defects of the claim, supported by evidence, certain, and established by worldly consensus.

For one who causes the initial plaint to be written down in a manner that is devoid of truth, logic, and proper action; which concerns an impossible matter or the like; and which is confused, a loss of the lawsuit arises.

A defect of the proposition (*pratijñādoṣa*) is as follows: contradiction with means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as "fire is not hot"; contradiction with the world (*lokavirodha*), such as "the moon is not the moon" (*aśaśī candraḥ*); contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*), such as "my mother is barren," or "my father is a celibate from childhood," and so forth. [Kātyāyana said: Falsehood is untruth. One should cut down the excessive portions of the matter and fill out those that are deficient;
one should record it on the ground for as long as the matter has been fully described.
Likewise:
The judge shall cause the plaintiff's case, as stated by himself, to be written down with chalk on a board;
thereafter, it is refined upon the leaf (the document).

Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the state of being free from adventitious conditions such as fear and the like. Nārada says: "The plaintiff (*arthin*) shall cause the defendant (*pratyarthin*) to submit a written response before the latter has had an opportunity to present his own case; this should be done for as long as the matter intended to be expressed remains to be set forth."
Bṛhaspati: When the plaintiff, due to lack of confidence, does not venture to speak,
time should be granted to him in accordance with his capacity and the requirements of the case.

The plaintiff is the one who speaks first. Where both parties have the status of both plaintiff and defendant due to a difference in the matters to be proven, and it is required to determine who shall speak first, Bṛhaspati says: "When the plaintiff and the defendant approach with a desire for priority, the trial should be conducted according to the order of the castes, while taking into account the relative suffering."
Regarding the judicial examination where multiple pairs of plaintiff and defendant may appear simultaneously, Manu has declared the rule for the sequence [of cases]:
"Having considered both the matter and its opposite, as well as merit and demerit alone,
he should examine all the legal affairs of the litigants according to the order of their castes."
Kātyāyana says: In that case, the plaintiff should speak first, and the defendant immediately thereafter;
when both have spoken, the members of the court shall deliberate, and after that, the judge shall deliver his judgment.
The determination of the subsequent proceedings after the speech has been delivered, as distinguished by the subject matter of the plaintiff and others, has been stated therein. Nārada says:
"To him whose suffering is greater or whose case is more urgent, the right of priority in speaking should be granted; not to one who failed to present it first."
Bṛhaspati says:
The plaintiff's case is of four kinds, and likewise the defendant's case;
the decision is declared to be fourfold, though some record it as being eightfold.

Accusation based on suspicion, the truth, a request regarding the matter at hand, and a renewed legal proceeding once a case has been concluded—these are to be known as the four kinds of plaints. (2.6)

[612] The reply to the meaning of what was heard should be written in the presence of the plaintiff. By whomsoever the meaning of the plaint has been heard—that defendant’s reply must be written in the presence of the plaintiff. On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
Once the prima facie case has been determined— distinguished by its subject matter and the object of apprehension—
and has been formally stated and stabilized, one should then cause the reply to be written down.
Nārada says: When such a plea has been formulated by the plaintiff, the defendant should then provide an answer connected to that plea.
Those who know [the art of debate] recognize a reply as being comprehensive, essential, free from doubt, unconfused, and not requiring further explanation.

That which pervades the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that which encompasses the thesis by way of negating it. "Essential" (*sāra*) means firm. "Undoubted" (*asaṃdigdha*) means unambiguous. "Unconfused" (*anākula*) means not contradictory in its preceding and succeeding parts. "Not requiring further explanation" (*avyākhyāgamya*) means being free from ellipsis, disjointed construction, syntactic separation, assumption of unstated meanings, or alteration of the sense. He states the divisions of the reply (*uttara*): "The reply is fourfold: through false understanding, or through counter-attack (*pratyavaskandana*), or through the establishment of a prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*), or through the formal procedure (*vidhi*)."
Kātyāyana says: But when another, having heard the meaning of what was spoken, objects to it—
either in terms of the meaning or the words— that reply should be known as false.
False rejoinders are of four kinds, as that same author has stated:
"This is false; I do not recognize it; at that time I was absent;
and I was unborn at that time"—thus the false rejoinder is fourfold.

The first type of false rejoinder (*mithyottara*) is "This is false. The second is "I do not recognize [it]. The third is "At that time and in that place, I was not present. The fourth is "At that time, I had not yet been born"; this means "I do not recognize" or "I do not remember. He states the nature of the rejoinder of admission (*saṃpratipattyuttara*): "Admission is declared to be the truthful statement regarding the point to be proven (*sādhya*)."

When the defendant admits that the plaintiff’s proposition is true, it is a *saṃpratipatti* (admission). In the case of an admission, the legal proceeding ends precisely with that reply. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati states that in such cases the lawsuit consists of two stages:

"In the case of a *mithyā* (denial) reply, the lawsuit has four stages; likewise in the case of a *pratyavaskandana* (counter-claim); but in cases of admissions (*saṃpratipatti*), the lawsuit should be known to have two stages. [613]

The plaint (*bhāṣā*), the reply (*uttara*), the means of proof (*pramāṇa*), and the decision (*nirṇaya*): these are the four stages (*pāda*) of a legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*). However, in the case of a mutual admission (*saṃpratipatti*), there are only two stages, consisting of the plaint and the reply. Nārada defines the characteristic of the counter-attack (*pratyavaskandana*): "If the defendant, having accepted the matter as it has been written by the plaintiff, states a reason [for his own defense], that is known as a counter-attack."
He [Yājñavalkya] himself states the definition of *prāṅnyāya* (defeat by prior judgment):
"If one who has been defeated according to established custom is made to write a plea again, he is a defendant previously defeated; that is called *prāṅnyāya*."

*Ācāra* means legal procedure (*vyavahāra*). It is considered "defeated" (*avasanna*) when it has been overcome. A reply possesses the status of being a valid *uttara* only when the various types of replies—such as the "false" (*mithyā*) and others—are mutually distinct, and not when they are mixed. As Kātyāyana says:

"When there is truth regarding one part of the claim, a plea of justification (*kāraṇa*) regarding another part, and a denial (*mithyā*) regarding yet another part, that is no valid reply because of its confusion (*saṃkara*)."
He states the reason for its being unsurpassed:
"Furthermore, there could not be a single action in a dispute between two disputants;
nor would there be the establishment of the object for both, nor could there be two actions in one [place]."

Proof consists of evidence such as witnesses and the like; this belongs to the plaintiff (*pūrvavādin*) in the case of a plea of denial (*mithyottara*), and to the defendant (*uttaravādin*) in the case of a plea of counter-claim (*pratyavaskanda*). In that regard, if there were a valid response (*samyaguttara*) when the plea of denial and the plea of counter-claim are combined, then proof would accrue to both litigants. That is contradictory. Furthermore, if it is a plea of denial, then proof belongs only to the plaintiff and not to the defendant; and this is contradictory within a single legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*). Or, even if the proof for both were not contradictory, the establishment of the objectives of both would still be contradicted. For instance—the plaintiff establishes his own claim, such as "He owes me a hundred gold pieces," by means of writing and other evidence; the opponent likewise [establishes] "It need not be paid. In that case, there is no establishment of the objective for either party due to their mutual contradiction. Moreover, when the plea of counter-claim and the plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*) are combined into a valid response, two types of proof would accrue to one litigant. To explain: because of the nature of the plea of counter-claim, some form of evidence must be produced regarding the cause, such as whether something was received or given; whereas, in the case of a plea of prior judgment, the evidence consists of the document of victory (*jitapatra*) and so forth. And the validity of two types of evidence cannot coexist because of the difference in the objects to be proven (*prameya*); for once the matter to be established is accomplished by one piece of evidence, the other becomes useless. Therefore, a combined response is indeed a valid response. Vyāsa says:
If both a false plea and a plea based on a special cause should occur in one case,
or if a true plea occurs along with another, which reply should be accepted therein?
Between two false pleas or two defenses,
that which concerns a more extensive subject matter, or in which the fruit of the legal action may be realized, should be accepted as the defense.
In that case, the answer should be understood as unambiguous; otherwise, it would be the opposite.

The meaning of this is as follows: in one case, at the time of the reply, the defendant (uttaravādī) states both a false denial (*mithyottara*) and a plea of justification (*kāraṇa*). For example, when the plaintiff has stated, "My cow was stolen by him at this time; that cow of mine is in his house," the other replies: "This is false; rather, she was born in our own house. Likewise, when questioned, "This man is a thief, because Devadatta’s lost cow is found in his house," he replies: "It is true that Devadatta’s cow is in our house, but I am not a thief, because she came to our house together with our own herd of cattle. In such a case, only the portion constituting the plea of justification (*pratyavaskanda*) should be accepted as the formal reply. Alternatively, that reply which, once its point is established, establishes a second matter by implication—that is, the reply with the broader scope—should be accepted. Or, that part in which the result of proof (*pramāṇaphala*), whether avoidance (*hāna*) or acceptance (*upādāna*), is possible, should be accepted. Therefore, one must state a distinct variety [of reply] that is unmixed, and not a mixed one. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says:
If, having first accepted a reason,
one should state another, more weighty reason contained within the counter-argument, then that [latter] is established, and not the other.
Bṛhaspati: The rule regarding the defendant has been declared for the purpose of establishing the relevant facts;
now that which is to be accepted from each of the four types [of evidence] shall be stated.
One should not characterize that which is other than the subject at hand, that which is neutral, deficient, excessive, irrelevant, devoid of the essence of what is to be said, doubtful, or contrary.

Kātyāyana states: Any other [reply] that is ambiguous, different from the subject matter, too little, or too much; or that which, while pervading only a portion of the plaintiff's claim, does not do so in the same way—such a reply is not valid.

An answer that consists of disjointed words, is non-comprehensive, has a hidden meaning, is confused, relies on scriptural citations for its explanation, or is devoid of substance, does not lead to the accomplishment of one's own purpose.

Among these, an ambiguous response (*saṃdigdha*) is, for example: when asked, "Does this man owe me a hundred gold pieces? one replies, "A hundred gold pieces or a hundred coins. A response concerning something other than the subject at hand (*prakṛtād anyat*) is, for example: when told, "You owe me a hundred gold pieces," one says, "I do not strike you. An insufficient response (*aty-alpa*) is, for example: when accused of a debt of a hundred, saying, "Truly, I owe ten. Alternatively, it is the communication of multiple intended meanings by means of particles such as *ca* (and) and so forth; or an excessively long statement (*atibhūri*) when a very small matter is to be expressed, which contains an unseizable meaning. A response that covers only a portion of the claim (*pakṣaikadeśavyāpi*) but refutes only a portion of the plaintiff's case (*pūrvapakṣaikadeśe nirākāraka*) is, for example: when an accusation has been made regarding various items such as cattle and gold, one says, "I do not owe the gold"—this being a disjointed phrase with a remote syntactic connection (*vyavahitānvaya*). A non-pervasive response (*avyāpi*) refutes the plaintiff's case as qualified by a specific place or time, but not in its essential nature; for example, when accused that "in the month of Caitra, in Ujjayinī, this man took my hundred gold pieces," one says, "I did not take them in Ujjayinī in the month of Caitra. One does not say, "I did not take them at all. An obscure response (*nigūḍhārtha*) uses words whose meaning is not well-known; for example, denoting a cow by the word *arjunī*, or the earth by the word *kāśyapī*. A confused response (*ākula*) is one where the preceding and following parts are contradictory. A response requiring interpretation (*vyākhyāgamya*) is one that becomes intelligible only through the force of complex compounds, ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), or grammatical transformation (*vipariṇāma*). A weak response (*asāra*) is one that is not firm, where the thought arises in everyone immediately upon hearing it: "This is not possible. — Bṛhaspati.
However, he who does not give a reply according to the facts in the first half of the trial must be compelled to pay in the presence [of witnesses] by means of conciliation and other such methods.
Affectionate speech is conciliation; sowing dissension is the display of fear;
the seizure of wealth is punishment, as are beating and imprisonment.
But he who, even when urged by both parties, does not give an answer,
becomes defeated once seven nights have passed and deserves punishment.
By both means, gentle and harsh; likewise:

those who are insane, intoxicated, or driven mad, those defiled by mortal sins, and those who are mentally deficient, very old, or children—these should be known as those for whom no legal response is required.
Kātyāyana says: One should provide a reply according to the facts, and if the defendant does not do so, one should compel him to pay by means of conciliation,
sowing dissension, and other such methods, until that matter has been fully resolved.
Whether due to delusion or through deceit, whatever was not stated by the proponent but is included within the reply should be accepted by both parties as well.

This is the meaning: whatever was not stated by the plaintiff due to confusion or other causes, yet is included within the reply and is mentioned while the reply is being delivered, must be accepted as part of the reply of the defendant. The "action-stage" (*kriyāpāda*) constitutes the reply. Regarding the conclusion of the reply, Kātyāyana says:
"When both [sides] have been written down and the determination of the case has begun, he who speaks of something not previously stated therein is defeated on account of that matter."
Then the plaintiff shall immediately cause to be written the proof of the matter he has asserted. (2.7)
When that is established, one attains success; otherwise, the opposite occurs.
This four-footed procedure has been demonstrated regarding legal disputes. (2.8)

[616] Therefore, after the writing of the plaint (*uttara-lekhana*), the plaintiff (*arthin*), who is the proponent of the initial claim (*pūrvavādī*), must immediately at that very time write down the proof (*sādhana*)—that is, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—for the matter he has asserted. Upon the establishment of that proof, he attains success, characterized by victory. Conversely, if the proof is not established, the opposite occurs: he incurs defeat. Such is the meaning. And so says Nārada:
"The essence of legal proceedings is declared to be the plaint (*pratijñā*)."
In that case, the proponent is defeated, while the opponent becomes the winner.

The meaning is that one should emerge victorious from the claim. This four-footed, four-part judicial procedure (*vyavahāra*) or operation has been described by us in all disputes. Among these, the first foot of the procedure is stated by the rule: "It should be written down in the presence of the defendant. The second is stated by: "The reply should be written down by the one who has heard the matter. The third is stated by: "Then the plaintiff should immediately cause [the proof] to be written. And the fourth is stated by: "Upon its establishment, [he obtains] success. In this context, by the word "success" (*siddhi*), there is denoted the deliberation (*parāmarśa*) of the judges—the means for determining victory and defeat regarding the plaintiff and defendant—which consists of the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) such as the *pratyākalita* and so forth, according to which it follows from the scriptures that "this person possesses this [evidence]. It is called this because it has "success" as its fruit. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says:
The prima facie argument, the rejoinder, the determination of each, and the section on legal procedure— therefore, this is declared to have four feet.
For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
"The first quarter is known as the plaint (pūrvapakṣa), and likewise the second is the reply (uttara).
The third quarter to be stated is the stage of legal procedure (kriyāpāda), and the fourth is the decision (nirṇaya)."

And here, by the word "decision" (*nirṇaya*), the reflection on the means of proof (*nyāyaparāmarśa*) which results in that decision is indicated. Therefore, the rule "the plaintiff shall immediately cause [the document] to be written" refers to the case of a plea of denial (*mithyottara*). In other types of pleas, however, the burden of proof lies with the defendant alone. Thus says Hārīta:

"In a plea of prior judgment (*prāṅnyāya*) or when a reason (*kāraṇa*) is stated, the defendant shall point out the evidence (*kriyā*); but in a plea of denial (*mithyā*), the plaintiff shall do so; in a plea of admission (*pratipatti*), there shall be no such burden."
In this context, action (*kriyā*) is the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
"For it has been stated that the object to be accomplished (*kārya*) is what is to be brought about; however, the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is called action (*kriyā*).
Furthermore, that [action] should be known as being of two kinds: divine (*daivikī*) and likewise human (*mānuṣī*).
The wise consider documentary evidence, witnesses, and so forth as human proof, while execution and the like are considered divine proof.

Vyāsa states that in cases concerning prior transactions and subsequent claims, the human being alone is the subject of the document of victory and so forth: "In a case concerning a prior transaction, by means of the document of victory, as well as by the presiding judge and others, the speaker of truth obtains whatever he has declared. [617]
The presiding judge and others have been previously described as the observers of justice. (2.8)

[Thus ends the first chapter, on the General Introduction to Judicial Procedure, in the Aparārka— a commentary on the Yājñavalkya-smṛti composed by the illustrious Parameśvara Ādityadeva, born in the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the glorious Vidyādhara clan.]
[Now, in the Yājñavalkya-smṛti with its commentary, the section on the General Introduction to Judicial Procedure (2):
Judicial procedure is generally fourfold; he now states its sequence.
One should not bring a counter-charge against someone without having first resolved one's own accusation;
nor should one, once accused by another, lead the matter to a different state than what was stated. (2.9)

Without having refuted a charge brought against oneself by another, one should not counter-accuse or cast blame upon that accuser. In that legal proceeding, the meaning is that once the opponent has been dealt with by the plaintiff who initiated the case, one should not subsequently become a plaintiff oneself and commence a separate lawsuit against him. Likewise, one should not bring a charge against someone already accused by another plaintiff until that prior proceeding has been concluded. Furthermore, one should not lead to a contradiction—that is, a conflict—between what was stated as part of the legal proceedings; the meaning is that one should not speak in a manner that contradicts what was said previously. (2.9)
Regarding this, he states an exception:

"And one may bring a counter-charge in cases of quarrels and acts of violence. One who has been charged in a quarrel or similar matter may bring a counter-charge even without having fully resolved the original charge. For example, one who is accused, saying "I have been cursed by him" or "I have been beaten by him," might say—without providing a defense—"I have been cursed by him" or "I have been beaten by him. It is for this very reason that Nārada states the legal decision regarding this matter:
He who first utters abuse will certainly be the one to bear the fault;
he who does so afterwards is likewise an offender, yet for the former, discipline is more severe.
"He would revile" means he would commit an offense. Regarding simultaneous offenses as well, that same author says:
"When two people, obscured by the fault of harshness, engage together at the same time, if no distinction can be found, the punishment shall apply to both equally."
Discipline is punishment; quarreling is verbal abuse; violence is physical assault.
The duties of the plaintiff and the defendant have been stated. Now he describes the duty of the examiners:
"A guarantor capable of deciding the case should be taken from both parties. (2.10)

[618] A surety (*pratibhū*) should be accepted from both the plaintiff and the defendant—one who is capable of determining the case; that is to say, one who has already determined the subject matter of the case. Once the case has been determined, the winner must pay the fine to the opponent and a monetary penalty to the king. The taking of a surety occurs prior to the formal adjudication of the matter by virtue of the circumstances. Regarding the absence of a surety, Kātyāyana says:
"If there is no surety suitable for the case for either of the two litigants..."
Having protected him until the end of the day, he should give the wage to the servant.
That proponent is defeated. 2.10
Regarding the defeated party, he says: "If one denies [the claim] and is proven [guilty], he shall pay the wealth to the plaintiff and an equal amount to the king;
the one who brings a false accusation shall pay double the amount of the claim. (1.11)

Denial is a false reply. One who makes such a denial, when proven by the force of divine or human means of proof (*pramāṇa*) by the plaintiff, shall be compelled to accept the matter asserted; he shall pay a fine equal to that amount to the plaintiff and an equal fine to the king. However, he who brings a charge devoid of proof shall carry—and deliver to the king—a sum of money double the value of the subject of the charge. This rule applies specifically to legal proceedings involving a wager (*sapaṇa-vyavahāra*). There is also legal procedure that is free from a wager. As Nārada says:
It should be understood as having two characteristics: with superior and without superior.
That which is "with superior" is where the previous stake is surpassed by an exceeding amount due to the wagering.
A lawsuit in which a fine greater than the amount of wealth that is the subject of the dispute is stipulated is an *uttara* (higher) lawsuit. (2.11)
Regarding the examination of legal cases, he states the specific times for particular subjects:

"In cases of violence, theft, verbal or physical assault, denial of a debt, and the abduction of women, one should litigate immediately; in other matters, the time is declared to be according to one's wish. (2.12)

*Sāhasa* (violence) is that which is committed suddenly, by force, or by compulsion in the presence of people, such as the injury of others; *steya* (theft) is well known; *pāruṣya* (harshness) is the production of suffering in another through speech or body; the word "cow" (*go*) is intended to indicate any object of livelihood. *Abhiśāpa* (false accusation) is the charging of someone with a sin. Although it is included within *pāruṣya*, its separate mention is for the sake of emphasis. *Atyaya* is destruction. Regarding these matters, as well as those concerning women, one should adjudicate the dispute—that is, examine the legal case—on the very same day. Other than in the cases mentioned, if the defendant does not wish to give an answer immediately but desires a later time, then another period for the answer may be granted according to his wish. On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
Once the prima facie case has been determined and the subject matter of the plaint— distinguished by what is to be accepted and what is not—
has become firm, one should then cause the reply to be written.
Likewise, due to timidity or a lapse of memory, an opponent may seek time;
in such a case, he deserves to obtain this [time].
Kātyāyana states: In matters that have been recently committed, one should litigate immediately;
however, in a case where time has elapsed, the master [the judge] should grant a period of time to the defendant.
The intention is that because memory arises immediately regarding things done recently, the response must be given at once.
For if, after hearing the meaning of what is being written, the defendant requests time for the dispute on account of a valid reason, time should undoubtedly be granted to him.
In the case of a death that has just occurred, the impurity lasts for that very day; if it has passed, one should add a full day.
For a death six years ago, it lasts three nights; for twelve years, seven days.
Beyond twenty days, he shall receive ten days' wages;
beyond half a month, a month's wages; and when thirty months have passed, it shall be three fortnights' wages thereafter.
Within a year from this time, however, he may act according to his desire,
having ascertained the appropriate time, the capacity [of the subjects], and the relative strength and weakness of the tasks to be performed.
The lord may grant [the property] to the defendant for a short or long period of time,
or whatever custom has been handed down through successive tradition.
Having examined that [evidence] according to the rule, the king should cause a reply to be given;
whether it be the original document or witnesses, even when they are situated in a foreign land.
In that case, the time for men to pay [the debt] in their own country shall be one month [from the time of the agreement?].

"Year" (*samā*) means a year; "root" (*mūla*) means the principal amount. The mention of witnesses is intended as an illustration of the means of proof. The meaning is this: for those men who have their wealth or the means of proof—such as witnesses—in another country, the time required for that principal wealth and so forth to be brought back is the time they are entitled to for payment.
It may be a day, a month, half a month, a season, or even a year.
However, the other party must grant a period of time that corresponds to the duration of the action.
Likewise: "In the case of a cow, a bull, a field, women, and offspring; likewise in the case of a deposit, a loan for use, a gift, and in buying and selling."
In cases of defiling a maiden, theft, quarrel, violence, deposits, fraud, and false testimony, one should institute legal proceedings immediately.
Where dignity departs, as well as destruction and abandonment, one should not delay there; for that matter is urgent. (2.12)
He states the characteristics of the wicked:
"He goes from one place to another, and he licks the corners of his mouth;
his forehead perspires, and his face becomes discolored. (2.13)
With parched lips and faltering speech, he speaks much that is contradictory;
he does not honor his words or his eyes, and he even distorts his lips. (2.14)
If one undergoes a change from their natural disposition through actions of mind, speech, or body—whether during a legal proceeding or while giving testimony—they are proclaimed to be corrupt. (2.15)

He licks—that is, touches with his tongue—the *sṛkkiṇī*, which are the inner parts of the cheeks, on all sides. He utters speech with a parched mouth; thus, he is one whose speech is parched and faltering. "Contradictory" means internally inconsistent, such as a discrepancy between speech and the clarity of the eyes. He distorts—that is, makes crooked—[his natural state]. Natural disposition (*svabhāva*) is one's inherent quality. A "distortion" from that nature is its reversal. In this regard, a distortion of mental action consists of ignorance, doubt, and error; of vocal action, stammering and the like; and of bodily action, trembling and the like. One who is of such a character is declared to be corrupt and a speaker of falsehood in legal proceedings, litigation, and as a witness. The rest is easy to understand. Regarding this, Manu says:
One should discern the internal disposition of men by external signs:
through their voice, complexion, gestures, appearance, eyes, and movements.
By means of appearance, gestures, gait, movement, and speech,
as well as by changes in the eyes and face, the mind within is perceived.

If the validity of the characteristics of defects (duṣṭalakṣaṇa) were established in their being defects, then, once the defeat of either the proponent (vādin) or the opponent (prativādin) had been determined by those very characteristics, the legal proceeding would reach its conclusion even without divine means of proof (*daivamānuṣapramāṇa*). Consequently, there would be a pointlessness (*vaiyarthyam*) to the divine and other such proofs. As for the statement that these [characteristics] are meaningful when there is an absence of defective characteristics, in that case, the prescription of written documents and other proofs as being without witnesses would not be logical; for it has been stated: "The third part shall be the section on legal action (*kriyāpāda*). Therefore, these are not proofs regarding defectiveness, but rather they are presented for the purpose of determining, amidst the proponent and the opponent, who is worthy of proof when the question arises: "Who among us shall provide the proof? [Objection: But surely, when a specific reply exists and the presentation of proof is verbally determined toward a specific proponent, there is no occasion for the aforementioned inquiry. [Response: That is true in cases such as the non-payment of debts (*ṛṇādāna*). However, in cases such as an accusation of theft and the like, the inquiry arises when a divine ordeal (*divya*) is applicable. For a divine ordeal is possible even for a proponent who offers a false reply (*mithyottaravādin*), whereas written documents, witnesses, and so forth are not. Therefore, like reasoning (*tarka*), these are auxiliary to the means of proof (*pramāṇānugrāhakatva*), not themselves means of proof. And this is appropriate, because they can arise even in the absence of a defect due to fear and other such motives. (2.13, 14, 15)
He states the grounds for being considered defeated:

"One whose case is based on doubtful evidence, one who attempts to prove it independently, one who absconds, and one who says nothing when summoned—he is declared defeated and liable to punishment. (2.16)

One who, without examining the evidence for or against [a claim], would obstinately establish or force another to accept a matter that is doubtful as to whether it is provable or not—being independent and regardless of examiners and others—and one who, having established a matter even by means of methods prescribed in the scriptures, would depart without delivering it, and one who, when summoned by the king for a legal proceeding, would not state the proof for his own position or the refutation of the opponent's position: he is defeated, he is vanquished, and he is to be punished by the king. Furthermore, what has been established must be given to the claimant. The separate mention of "he is to be punished" is intended to indicate that the punishment for the defeated party applies only where there is a specific statement [to that effect]. —Nārada.
But he who proceeds with regard to a doubtful matter without first informing the king should be forcibly punished, and his purpose shall not be accomplished.

One who speaks otherwise, one who hates the performance of legal acts, one who does not appear, one who is unable to provide an answer, and one who flees when summoned— these five are recorded as those who have lost their case.
The man who, having abandoned his initial position, resorts to another, should be known as a debater who has shifted his ground; indeed, such a person is one whose argument has failed.

He who, having been asked about a matter, does not delight in it even though he has correctly resolved upon its meaning, but instead pursues some other objective after having pointed it out; [he is a speaker of falsehood].
Having stated, "There are those who know," if one who has been asked to point them out does not do so,
the judge, by these grounds, shall declare that person as well to be defeated.

The judge, the court member, or the king [is the authority]. Kātyāyana says: When, after having had the case heard, one should abandon the matter or state something else, that litigant has relied upon the opposing side; therefore, he is defeated.
But when one seeks to prolong the debate through mere pretext,
one should recognize that as a "pretextual" (sāpadeśa) move, which is recorded as causing defeat in the debate.
A pretext is a form of cavil (*chala*).

However, if a litigant, having committed his statement to writing, should subsequently state it as either deficient or excessive, he shall suffer defeat; he does not deserve to maintain his accusation.
The formal charge (*abhiyoga*) constitutes the initial plea (*pūrvavāda*); he is the plaintiff (*pūrvavādī*). Likewise:
"Having brought a charge against another, one should not subsequently speak of a different matter;
one who speaks falsely in this manner should likewise be declared defeated."

This is the meaning: one who, having promised to prove a case that is to be established, speaks in contradiction to what he previously stated by saying "I did not promise this," should be declared defeated. Furthermore: "But the plaintiff who, having pointed out witnesses, does not proceed to litigate by his own will—he is defeated after thirty nights have passed."
Bṛhaspati says: One who flees after being summoned, one who remains silent, one defeated by the witnesses,
and one who admits the claim in his own statement— these are the four kinds of litigants who lose their case.
One who flees is defeated after three fortnights; one who remains silent, after seven days;
one whose testimony is contradicted by witnesses, at that very moment; and one who admits the claim, is likewise defeated.

One who has entered [the court] is one who has agreed with the opponent. Nārada says: When a person, having performed the ritual acts and determined to appear for the ordeal, does not present himself, one should not employ deception in that case.
If at that time there should be a fault caused by fate or the king,
he shall not be considered defeated merely by the abandonment of his defense.
When a dispute has arisen between two parties situated as plaintiff and defendant, and it has been settled through mutual agreement, they shall pay a fine double the amount in question. (2.16)
Furthermore:
When there are witnesses on both sides, the witnesses belong to the plaintiff.
When the prima facie position has been defeated, the proponents of the rejoinder prevail. || 2.17 ||

The general rule is that when witnesses are available for both sides, those witnesses designated by the plaintiff (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) are the authority. However, when the plaintiff’s case has failed, then the witnesses designated by the defendant (*uttaravādin*) become the authority. What kind of legal dispute (*vyavahāra*), then, is the subject of this statement? It cannot be one involving a "denial" (*mithyā-uttara*). For in that case, witnesses for both parties are not possible. To illustrate: suppose a person accused by a plaintiff saying, "You owe me a hundred gold pieces," replies with a denial, "I do not owe you anything. In such a case, witnesses are simply impossible; for witnesses can only exist regarding matters that others are capable of perceiving, and the matter asserted by one who denies does not fall within the range of perception for others, which would otherwise qualify them as witnesses. Furthermore, the validity of possession (*bhukti*) or written documents (*likhita*) need not even be suspected here. Therefore, a dispute involving a denial is not the subject of this rule. Nor is it a dispute involving a "counter-claim" (*pratyavaskanda-uttara*). In that instance, there is no need for the plaintiff to present evidence, because the defendant has already admitted the debt. To illustrate: when the plaintiff says, "You owe a hundred gold pieces," and the defendant makes a counter-claim, saying, "It is true I owed it, but I have already paid it to you," since the debt has been acknowledged by the other party, it is no longer a matter to be proven. This would result in the absurdity of proving what is already established. Rather, it is the defendant alone whose evidence must be presented by the plaintiff. Likewise, a dispute involving a "prior judgment" (*prāṅnyāya-uttara*) is also not the specific subject of this statement. For a prior judgment is not established merely by the witnesses cited by the defendant, nor by the verdict of the judges in that previous case, nor by a document of victory (*jitapatra*) granted therein. In those cases, the defeat of the plaintiff and the victory of the defendant are already settled. Therefore, this statement seems to be without a subject matter. The answer is: the subject of this rule is a legal proceeding where the defendant employs either a "counter-claim" or a "prior judgment. In such cases, witnesses for the plaintiff are indeed possible. To illustrate: when the defendant says, "That which I owed you has been returned by me to you," and the plaintiff replies, "It is true it was returned, but it was given to another person and not to me to discharge my own debt; I believe this based on witnesses"—in such an exchange of reply and counter-reply, witnesses exist for both sides. Similarly, in the case of a "prior judgment," when the plaintiff replies, "It is true that I was once defeated by you in a prior trial, but having had that trial wrongly decided, I have defeated you in this subsequent trial"—then witnesses exist for both sides as well. It is with reference to these cases that the following verse applies: [Verse 624] *If witnesses are produced for both sides, the king should accept those who are most reliable.* *In a case of denial, he should accept the witnesses of the plaintiff; in a case of a counter-claim, those of the defendant.* *In a case of a prior judgment, he should accept the witnesses of both.* *But if the witnesses are equal in number and quality, he should accept those who are more virtuous.* *If they are equal in virtue, he should accept those who are more numerous; if they are equal in number, he should accept those who are more eloquent.* *If they are equal in eloquence, he should accept those who are more consistent; if they are equal in consistency, he should accept those who are more truthful.* *If they are equal in truthfulness, he should accept those who are more compassionate; if they are equal in compassion, he should accept those who are more impartial.* *If they are equal in impartiality, he should accept those who are more learned; if they are equal in learning, he should accept those who are more experienced.* *If they are equal in experience, he should accept those who are more honest; if they are equal in honesty, he should accept those who are more pure.* *If they are equal in purity, he should accept those who are more self-controlled; if they are equal in self-control, he should accept those who are more steadfast.* *If they are equal in steadfastness, he should accept those who are more wise; if they are equal in wisdom, he should accept those who are more righteous.* *If they are equal in righteousness, he should accept those who are more meritorious; if they are equal in merit, he should accept those who are more generous.* *If they are equal in generosity, he should accept those who are more humble; if they are equal in humility, he should accept those who are more patient.* *If they are equal in patience, he should accept those who are more forgiving; if they are equal in forgiveness, he should accept those who are more compassionate.* *If they are equal in compassion, he should accept those who are more benevolent; if they are equal in benevolence, he should accept those who are more noble.* *If they are equal in nobility, he should accept those who are more ancient; if they are equal in antiquity, he should accept those who are more traditional.* *If they are equal in tradition, he should accept those who are more respected; if they are equal in respect, he should accept those who are more venerable.* *If they are equal in venerability, he should accept those who are more beloved; if they are equal in being beloved, he should accept those who are more dear.* *If they are equal in being dear, he should accept those who are more affectionate; if they are equal in affection, he should accept those who are more loyal.* *If they are equal in loyalty, he should accept those who are more devoted; if they are equal in devotion, he should accept those who are more faithful.* *If they are equal in faithfulness, he should accept those who are more constant; if they are equal in constancy, he should accept those who are more enduring.* *If they are equal in endurance, he should accept those who are more stable; if they are equal in stability, he should accept those who are more firm.* *If they are equal in firmness, he should accept those who are more resolute; "When there are witnesses on both sides, the witnesses belong to the plaintiff. This is said when the plaintiff falls into a state of inferiority due to the existence of a rebuttal; for it is stated: "When the initial plea has been defeated, the witnesses belong to the defendant."
For this very reason, Nārada says:
"When two parties are disputing over a matter and there are witnesses for both,
the witnesses shall belong to the one whose case is the first plea."

Kātyāyana says: "For even the plaintiff's case (pūrvapakṣa) attains the status of the defendant's case (uttara) due to specific grounds; therefore, legal proof (kriyā) is always declared to be that which establishes the plaintiff's case."
The action consists of the examination [of the case]. Nārada says:
"In whatever dispute the weakness of the plaintiff's position arises due to the nature of the matter, there the witnesses of the defendant must be questioned. (2.17)
Regarding what must be paid by one defeated in a particular type of legal proceeding, he says:
"If a dispute should involve a wager, the judge shall cause the loser to pay that wager, as well as a fine, his own stake, and the debt itself to the creditor. (2.18)

If a dispute involves a wager (*paṇa*), that is a legal suit (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, in such a case, the judge (*prāḍvivāka*) shall cause the defeated litigant to pay the wager to the king along with the punishment prescribed by the scriptures, and cause the proven wealth to be given to the creditor. In the absence of a judge, the king himself shall take [the fine] and cause the wealth to be given to the creditor. A "wager" (*paṇa*) is the wealth agreed upon by the winner to be paid, thinking, "I must give this much. (2.18)
Regarding the king’s duty to oversee legal proceedings, he states what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted:
"The king should conduct legal cases by setting aside deception and relying on the facts;
for even a fact, if not presented, is lost in a legal proceeding. (2.19)

Having abandoned the sophistry (*chala*) or the negligence (*pramāda*) uttered by either the plaintiff or the defendant, the judge should decide the legal proceedings (*vyavahāra*) based on what is real and factual (*bhūta*). For even a fact, though it exists, is lost—that is, forfeited—by the legal process if it has not been presented or declared by the plaintiff and defendant. Indeed, in legal proceedings, documents and other means of proof (*pramāṇa*) are employed; yet there is no rule that these must necessarily follow the facts, for it sometimes happens that once a debt has been discharged and a document exists, one who is staying in another country might, by the force of that document, initiate a lawsuit again. The same applies to witnesses who are located in another country. Therefore, the judge should, through means such as conciliation (*sāma*), cause both the plaintiff and the defendant to speak the truth. This is the primary method in legal proceedings. In its absence, a procedure based on documents and other evidence should be adopted. —Bṛhaspati.
When the former and latter claims have been written down and the determination of the case has begun,
a reconciliation may occur between the two heated parties, like that of two pieces of iron.
Where there is equality of authority despite a difference between the scriptures and established practice,
a reconciliation of both is recommended by royal decree.
Conduct is behavior. 2.19.
He demonstrates how even a fact that is real may be lost through a fraudulent legal proceeding:

"When a defendant has denied a claim and it is subsequently written down, if he is proved on one part, he must be made by the king to pay the entire amount; however, what was not declared [at the outset] shall not be accepted. (2.20)

Various items, such as jewels, gold, silver, and so forth, may have been recorded by the plaintiff (pūrvavādin) in this manner: "This, that, and this person owes me. When the defendant (uttaravādin) denies it, saying, "I owe nothing at all," if the opponent is made to admit even a single portion of what was recorded by the plaintiff through evidence and other means, then the defendant must be compelled by the king to pay the entire claimed amount. However, whatever matter was not presented by the plaintiff at the time of the plea, even if it is valid, should not be accepted as something for which the defendant can be made liable by the king. This statement should be understood as applying to a defiant rebuttal from a defendant who denies the claim, such as: "If he proves even one of these matters, then I shall pay all of them. Why is this so? Because this sentence is intended as an illustration of a quibble (*chala*). Otherwise—
Even when multiple claims are brought forward, a creditor recovers only that much wealth as he establishes through witnesses;
only that much proven wealth does he obtain.

Thus, there would be a contradiction with the statement of Kātyāyana. In that case, the plaintiff must employ another means of proof to establish the portion of the claim remaining after it has been proven by witnesses. As for what was stated by Nārada: "When one who is accused on multiple counts denies the entire matter, but a part of it is established, he must pay what is claimed."

Thus, that too refers to the subject of a defiant false reply (*sāvaṣṭambha-mithyottara*). As for what Kātyāyana said: "Even when the portion of the matter to be proven has been declared by the witnesses, it shall be considered complete in cases involving sexual intercourse, violence, and theft, regarding whatever was intended as the matter to be proven."

Thus, this is its meaning: when, regarding a matter such as sexual union with a woman, witnesses have stated that the person in question was inseparably connected (*avinābhūta*) with even one part of that very matter to be proven (*sādhya*), then the entirety of that matter to be proven is considered stated. For example, if witnesses state that a young man lay for the entire night in secret, in a place devoid of light, upon the same bed with another woman who is not his wife, sister, or the like, then his sexual union with her is established even without further testimony from the witnesses. (2.20)

A conflict between two *dharmaśāstras* is to be resolved by means of logical reasoning (*nyāya*). However, regarding a conflict between a *dharmaśāstra* and an *arthaśāstra*, he states that the *arthaśāstra* is sublated [by the former].
"But when there is a conflict between two *smṛtis*, logical reasoning is stronger than judicial practice;
however, a *dharmaśāstra* is stronger than an *arthaśāstra*: this is the settled rule. (2.21)

When there is a conflict between two Smṛtis both rooted in the Veda, the principle consisting of inference (*anumāna*) and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)—which establishes a distinction of their respective domains in order to maintain their authority—is more powerful because it must be relied upon; for only when that principle is present does the Smṛti possess authority. However, when there is a conflict between a Dharmaśāstra (treatise on law) and an Arthaśāstra (treatise on worldly affairs), the Dharmaśāstra is stronger and the Arthaśāstra is weaker; therefore, the latter is sublated by the former. One who, by following the Arthaśāstra, sublates the Dharmaśāstra, incurs the expiation for killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*). This was stated by Āpastamba: "In a collision between Dharma and Artha, this [expiation] applies to one who grasps after Artha. Inference is the knowledge of the possessor of a mark (*liṅgin*) derived from a mark (*liṅga*) characterized by five features. The five features are: presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), existence in similar instances (*sapakṣe sattva*), exclusion from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣād vyāvṛtti*), having a non-sublated object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*), and having no counter-balancing argument (*asatpratipakṣatva*). In the absence of these, there are fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*): the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), the mistimed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), and the equal to the point at issue (*prakaraṇasama*). Presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is the postulation of something else to account for what has been seen or heard. An Arthaśāstra is a Smṛti whose subject matter consists of things perceived through other means of knowledge. A Dharmaśāstra, however, has as its subject matter things cognizable solely through the Veda. Thus says the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*: [text follows].
Some traditional law (smṛti) has its purpose visible in this world, while another has its purpose invisible [in the hereafter];
yet another consists of both visible and invisible purposes, and still another is rooted in logic (nyāya).
But another fifth kind of tradition, known as *anuvādasmṛti*, has been observed by the learned;
all of these are rooted in the Veda, with the exception of those whose purpose is merely perceptible.
The examples for these are also found in that very same place: "As follows:

Through the application of the sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya) as appropriate, and due to the gravity of the task, there is the employment of the means (upāyas), such as conciliation (sāman) and the rest, both in detail and in summary."
O elder brother of Garuḍa, this Smṛti proclaimed by the sages concerning the appointment of supervisors and the investigation of thorns [criminals] is said to have perceptible purposes.
The twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsti) must always be performed, and one must not eat the flesh of a dog;
such is the Smṛti proclaimed by the sages who were experts in knowledge, for its purpose is transcendental (adṛṣṭārtha).
The wise know that one should carry a staff made of *pālāśa* wood for both purposes;
however, in case of conflict, there shall be an option, just as in the case of the scriptural injunctions regarding *japa* and *homa*.
If that which is seen in the Śruti as a duty is not similar in the Smṛti,
then the latter merely restates the former, just as the rule for wandering mendicancy follows from the rule for leaving the home.

Regarding the phrase "as in the case of *japa*, *homa*, and *śruti*": the Smṛti concerning the recitation of the Sāvitrī from sunrise until [midday] and the *homa* performed before sunrise is a restatement (*anuvādinī*), that is, it speaks of what has already been stated. For example, the Manusmṛti says, "A Brāhmaṇa should renounce his home and go forth," which restates what was already declared in the Śruti: "Having turned away from the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, they then lead the life of a mendicant. This being so, when there is a conflict with the Śruti, the Smṛti is sublated except in its specific domain.
Therefore, investigators must establish a systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) regarding conflicts in other cases as well.
When there is a conflict with the purpose of the *Smṛti*, the treatise on worldly affairs (*Arthaśāstra*) is set aside;
however, when there is mutual conflict between two [Smṛtis], that which is consistent with logic is authoritative.
But when a conceptual construction regarding an unseen purpose is possible within a fixed rule,
and when a conceptual construction from a traditional scripture fulfills a requirement, [it is accepted].

When two Smṛti texts have unseen purposes (adṛṣṭārtha) and are mutually independent, and there is no reasoning principle to determine their respective domains, there is an option (vikalpa) between their objects. However, if they are dependent, there is a combination (samuccaya). When they are independent but a determining reasoning principle exists, there is a restricted option (vyavasthitavikalpa). In the absence of that [reasoning principle], an unrestricted option (avyavasthitavikalpa) is to be understood. In this regard, the reasoning principle that determines the domain is the principle of the general and the particular (sāmānyaviśeṣanyāya), which is well-known in the usage of elders, such as: "Let curds be given to the Brāhmaṇas, but buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya. By that reasoning principle, the contradiction between Smṛtis is resolved. For example: [Text follows]

"One should never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is situated in all manner of sins"—this is the general prohibition against killing a Brāhmaṇa. There is, however, a specific exception to it in certain cases, as Manu himself has stated:
"Whether it be a teacher, or a child, or an elder, or a Vedic scholar (śrotriya) of great learning..."
"One should indeed kill an assassin who approaches, without hesitation.

[628] Thus, the contradiction between certain Smṛtis should be resolved by the principle of the general and the particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣanyāya*), while for others it should be resolved by another principle, such as the consequence of the futility of postulation (*kalpanānarthakyaprasaṅga*). Between the *Manusmṛti* and other Smṛtis, however, the *Manusmṛti* is more authoritative. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says: "The *Manusmṛti* holds primacy because it is based upon the meaning of the Vedas."
"That Smṛti which is contrary to the meaning of the Manu [law-code] is not praised. (2.21)
He states the means of proof regarding the matter to be established:
"Evidence is declared to be written documents, possession, and witnesses;
in the absence of any one of these, any one of the divine ordeals is prescribed. (2.22)

*Pramāṇa* (proof) is that by which something is measured or determined, such as written documents and the like. If not even one of these is available among them, then the matter must be proven by some of the ordeals (*divya*) such as the water-jar (*ghaṭa*), which will be described hereafter. Bṛhaspati states:
"Legal action (*kriyā*) is said to be of two kinds: human (*mānuṣī*) and divine (*daivikī*).
Each of these has been divided into many varieties by the seers who know the truth."
Witnesses, documentary evidence, and inference constitute the threefold human means of proof.

Inference is enjoyment (*bhukti*). By means of that, the ownership of the enjoyer over the object of enjoyment is inferred. Likewise, Kātyāyana states: "From the jar up to the categories of properties (*dharmajāti*), there are nine kinds of divine action."
In all disputes whatsoever, the lord of men should always reach a definitive conclusion by means of authoritative proofs, through reasoning, or even by divine ordeal.
But in the absence of the former, one must strive diligently; it cannot be otherwise by any means whatsoever.

First, human evidence is the standard of proof; in its absence, divine evidence is used. If one party employs human evidence while the other employs divine evidence, the king should accept the human evidence there, and not the divine procedure.

Just as the first litigant says, "He owes me a thousand gold pieces; I shall prove it by human means of proof," while the defendant replies, "I do not owe a thousand gold pieces; I shall clear myself through divine ordeal"—if there were a human means of proof available even for a single part of the case, that would be the proper course for men speaking, rather than a divine one, even if the latter were complete.

For example, suppose I have given him a hundred gold pieces at an interest rate of two hundred percent, and subsequently agreed to an interest rate of five hundred percent. In that case, while human procedure (*mānuṣī kriyā*) applies to the portion of the principal (the thousand gold pieces), divine procedure (*divyā kriyā*) applies to the portion of the interest; even though the human procedure covers only a single part of the object of proof (*prameya*), it is nevertheless the one to be adopted, and not the divine procedure, which—though covering the entire object of proof—is nonetheless excluded. However, where human procedure is not possible regarding the portion of the object of proof, there the divine procedure alone is to be adopted. Thus says Pitāmaha.
In disputes concerning immovable property, one should avoid ordeals;
rather, one should settle such a case by means of witnesses, a written document, or possession.

Kātyāyana states: In cases of verbal abuse, disputes over land, and regarding what has been given, what has not been given, or what was improperly taken— once a determination has been made by the owner— one should not employ an ordeal.

In matters concerning the non-delivery of what has been sold, when one has purchased wealth but does not pay for it, and likewise in disputes arising from gambling and betting when a legal case has been brought before the court.
For guilds, corporations, assemblies, and the like, witnesses are declared to be the means of proof, neither divine ordeals nor written documents; such is the established rule proclaimed for them.
In such cases, however, the proof must be documentary; neither ordeal nor witnesses are applicable.
This applies likewise to matters concerning doors, paths, usage, enjoyment, water-conduits, and the like.
In a lawsuit concerning an act of violence, verbal abuse, or physical assault, possession alone shall be weighty evidence; neither documentary proof nor witnesses are required.
In matters arising from children, witnesses and even divine proof are required.
Vyāsa says: Legal business is said to be of two kinds—private and public. Public matters are to be determined by witnesses; private matters are to be determined by divine means (ordeals).

Bṛhaspati: In cases of verbal abuse, disputes over land, and even in all four types of violent offenses, divine proof (ordeals) is prohibited; it must be administered with great care [only in other cases].
If doubt arises regarding a written document, oral testimony,
or confused inference, then divine proof (divya) is the means of purification in that case.
In cases of treason against the king and in acts of violence, one should employ divine means of proof.

This refers to the absence of human evidence; yet the statement is not meaningless, because it serves the purpose of establishing the legal procedure for one who offers a false plea. For one who offers a false plea does not obtain a trial by ordeal. Nārada [630]:
"In a forest, in a deserted place, at night, inside a house, in cases of violence, and likewise in the denial of a deposit, a divine trial is permissible."
The Grandfather [Manu] said:
In cases involving a great curse or a false accusation, as well as in the misappropriation of a deposit,
