the king should examine the matter by means of ordeals, even when witnesses are available.

For in that case, he will prescribe the false testimony of witnesses with the words, "In cases where there is the execution of those belonging to the [caste] orders," and so forth. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says:
"Where there is equality among witnesses, one should purify them even by means of ordeals;
[this applies] when witnesses are available in disputes involving the loss of life."
When the litigant relies upon divine proof, he need not question witnesses therein.

When witnesses are equal in terms of their qualities and number, or when there is a conflict between them, an ordeal (*divya*) is to be understood as the means of proof. For example, in cases where the punishment for either the plaintiff or the defendant is one involving the loss of life, an ordeal must be used even if witnesses are available. Vyāsa states:
"If one says, 'I did not write this document;
it was forged by him,' then, setting aside that document, a decision regarding the matter shall be made by means of an ordeal."

The word "should do" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Kātyāyana states: "Where there may be a document involving fraud, if it has been brought to the king's attention, the king, seated upon the seat of justice, shall have that cleared by means of an ordeal."
Nārada says: Once a legal dispute has been decided, the evidence—whether documentary or testimonial—is rendered fruitless, provided it was not previously presented. (2.22)
In all disputes whatsoever, the subsequent legal act is stronger;
however, in the case of a pledge, a gift, or a purchase, the prior act is more powerful. (2.23)

When litigants perform one legal act and subsequently perform another act that contradicts it, in such cases of dispute, the latter act is stronger and subverts the former. For example—Devadatta first gives his own wealth to a debtor on the condition of a five-hundred-fold interest, but later, for some reason, stipulates a two-hundred-fold interest. Or, for instance, a creditor takes a field or other property as collateral (*ādhi*) and gives money; afterwards he says, "I do not accept this collateral; rather, let Your Honor hold that same amount of money even without collateral. In that case, only the second act is authoritative. However, in a dispute concerning the acceptance of collateral or a sale, only the prior act is to be followed, not the latter. For example—if, after taking a field or other property as collateral, selling it, or giving it away, the debtor then performs an act of giving or selling that same field to another person—then the prior act is true and the latter is false. Since ownership has ceased through the two prior acts of giving, the subsequent acts of giving or selling performed by one who no longer owns it are not valid. Even though ownership is not terminated by the act of pledging (*ādhi*), it is nonetheless obstructed; consequently, as long as the status of that field as collateral has not ceased, it is impossible to establish a new pledge in favor of another person. (2.23)

Regarding ownership over property such as land and the like, he will state that possession is authoritative in some cases when it depends upon title and in others when it is independent of it; first, he states its qualification:
"Loss of land occurs after twenty years for one who watches and does not speak, and loss of other property occurs after ten years while it is being enjoyed by another. (2.24)
Except for property placed within boundaries, deposits, and the wealth of the mentally dull or children;
likewise, except for the wealth of sealed deposits, the king’s wives, and those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya). (2.25)

When land other than a pledge (*ādhi*) and the like is enjoyed by an adversary for twenty years, the owner who sees it—perceiving directly that "this person is enjoying this land"—yet remains silent and does not protest, suffers loss; that is, his ownership relation to the property ceases. Likewise, there is loss of property other than land when it has been enjoyed for ten years. Indeed, such possession is inconsistent with the status of an owner who remains silent while watching; rather, possession serves as proof of ownership only when it belongs to the enjoyer himself, and thus it is enjoyed. A pledge (*ādhi*) is wealth deposited with someone for the sake of gaining the creditor’s confidence, with the understanding: "As long as I am giving you this wealth, let this [property] remain held by you. A boundary (*sīmā*) is well known. An open deposit (*upanikṣepa*) is simply a deposit (*nikṣepa*); regarding this, Nārada says: [text follows].
"That wherein one deposits one's own property out of trust, without hesitation, is called 'deposit' (*nikṣepa*); this is declared by the wise to be a title of law.
A "child" (*bāla*) is one who is dull-witted or of slow intellect; one under sixteen years of age is a child. Thus says Nārada:
A child is to be known as being like one still in the womb until the eighth year;
a boy is to be known as such until the sixteenth year, and he is also designated as *paugaṇḍa*.
One who knows legal procedure may act independently on his own behalf, except in the case of his parents.

Gautama states that the property of a minor must be protected by the king in the absence of another protector: "The property of a minor is to be protected until he reaches legal capacity. [632] He will discuss deposits later. The rest is well known. The mention of the "idiot" (jaḍa) is intended to indicate incapacity in general. On this point, Vyāsa says: "If land has been enjoyed here by others for twenty years, even while a capable king is ruling, that possession is not established as his own."
Nārada says:
Through actual enjoyment, however, the property of an owner is lost after twenty years;
even pledges and the like may be forfeited, with the exception of the property of a woman or a king.

Even mortgages and the like would be lost, let alone anything else. Therefore, ownership is established for one distinct from [the mortgagee] by means of possession as previously described. In this way, there is no contradiction with the rule concerning pledges, boundaries, deposits, and so forth. Likewise:
"For him who remains silent and indifferent while time passes, the aforementioned legal proceeding is not established."

The meaning is that for one who remains indifferent, neither the legal transaction, nor the fruit of the transaction, nor ownership is established. Vyāsa says: "Just as a cow neglected by its keeper perishes, so land, while being watched over by others, is lost through time due to possession."
Bṛhaspati: If property is delivered by heirs or others in the presence of someone else who subsequently enjoys it, that person does not deserve to recover it.
He who, seeing another giving away land, does not restrain him,
shall not regain that land even by means of a valid document.

Even by means of a document recording purchase, acceptance, or other such transactions, he would not acquire that land; and this is stated with reference to the established state of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), not the actual course of possession of the land. For this very reason, Manu says: "If [the owner] is neither mentally incapacitated nor a minor, and his property is enjoyed in his presence, the possessor deserves that wealth, as it has been lost through legal process."

And thus, that which is in reality another's property, yet has been acquired through mere worldly transaction, must be restored to its rightful place out of fear of sin. As for what was stated by Nārada:
"The king should punish like a thief that sinner who enjoys property without legal title, even for many hundreds of years. [633]

[Thus, this refers to] property consisting of much wealth belonging to children and others, or to the person who was the previous possessor of the land. For this very reason, he will say: "But the title-deed has been made by whom," and so forth. (2.25)
He states the punishment for one who misappropriates a pledge or other such property:

"The king shall cause the one who destroys a pledge or similar items to pay the value to the owner, and likewise a fine equal to that amount to the king, or else [a fine] according to his capacity. (2.26)

One should cause the thief to restore to the respective owner whatever property, such as a deposit (*ādhi*), was stolen from those mentioned in the preceding verse. Furthermore, he shall pay a fine equal to that amount to the king—either more or less according to his capacity—since the purpose of punishment is to effect restraint. As Gautama says: "They say that punishment is so called because it restrains; therefore, one should restrain those who are unrestrained. And Manu states: "If he is unable to restrain thieves even with wealth, then he should employ all these four [means of coercion]."
There are four types of punishment, beginning with the staff of censure and the staff of speech. Regarding these, he states that the punishment of physical death does not apply to a Brāhmaṇa:
"Manu, the son of Svayaṃbhū, has declared ten places for the application of punishment;
these may be used against the three [lower] castes, but a Brāhmaṇa should depart unhurt."
The generative organ, the belly, the tongue, the hands, and the feet as the fifth;
the eyes, the nose, the ears, wealth, and likewise the body.
Kātyāyana says:
Having ascertained that [the debtor] is unable to pay the debt, one may compel the master to perform labor;
if he is incapable [of labor], he should be cast into prison, except in the case of a Brāhmaṇa.

Gautama states: "For a Brāhmaṇa, there is no corporal punishment; rather, there shall be the assignment of tasks, public proclamation of his crime, banishment, or branding, provided he does not reform. "Provided he does not reform" means when he is incapable of paying a fine. This should be understood to apply to cases where the penalty of the highest amercement would otherwise be incurred. As Nārada says: "Killing, confiscation of all property, banishment from the city, branding, or the amputation of that specific limb—this is declared to be the punishment for the highest amercement."
This rule of punishment is prescribed for all social classes without distinction:
shaving the head is the punishment, followed by banishment from the city.
On the forehead of one accused of a crime, a mark shall be branded, and he must travel on a donkey;
for violating the Guru's bed, the mark of a female organ shall be made, and for drinking liquor, the sign of a liquor flag.
But for theft, his own feet should be made [the head], and he becomes a man whose head is the murder of a Brahmin.
Āpastamba states: "The eyes of a Brāhmaṇa shall be covered. The meaning of this is: at the time of banishing a Brāhmaṇa, his two eyes should be covered with a cloth. 2.26.
Having established that possession (*bhoga*) is a means of proof, [the author] now states another auxiliary factor regarding a specific object:
"Title (*āgama*) is superior to possession, except in the case of possession inherited through prior succession;
even when there is title, it has no strength at all where there is not even the slightest possession. (2.27)

*Āgama* (title-deed) is that which establishes ownership, such as purchase, acceptance of a gift, and so forth; it is "additional" (*adhika*), meaning it is another, second factor compared to *bhoga* (enjoyment). The meaning is that with respect to the object of enjoyment, *āgama* acts as a cooperative cause for determining the owner's right of ownership. For it is not possible to ascertain the ownership of an enjoyer over an object of enjoyment based on enjoyment alone when it is devoid of *āgama*; for we observe enjoyment even by one who is not the owner, such as in the case of fruits and objects of enjoyment. Now, an objection is raised: "But surely, regarding an object enjoyed by three generations—father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—the enjoyment of a fourth person, even without *āgama*, establishes the ownership of that enjoyer. So how can it be said that [the validity of possession] depends upon *āgama*? To this he says: "Except for that which has come down through prior succession. Enjoyment that has come down through the sequence of the ancestors—the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—is "prior succession"; other than that, any enjoyment distinct from it is valid only when dependent upon *āgama*. Now, an objection is raised: "But surely, *āgama*—as determined by evidence such as witnesses—independent of enjoyment, establishes ownership. What need is there here for enjoyment? To this he says: "Even in *āgama*, there is strength," and so forth. Regarding an object where even a small amount of enjoyment is not found, there is no "strength"—that is, the capacity characterized by validity—belonging to the *āgama* relied upon. The intention is this: although it may have been determined by means of documents and the like that a purchase or acceptance of a gift occurred here in this field or property in the past, nevertheless, present-day ownership is not established without enjoyment, because in the interim, the possibility of gifting, selling, or other transfers may have arisen. Therefore, in order to establish present-day ownership, the enjoyment existing at present must be required as a cooperative cause for the *āgama*. On this point, Nārada says: [The text continues with the citation of Nārada.]
Even when a document exists and witnesses are living,
that possession of immovable property is not secure where it has not been enjoyed for a long time.
Likewise:
"Possession that is purified by a clear title attains the status of valid proof;
possession with an unclear title does not attain validity. [635]
The meaning is that possession accompanied by a pure title, determined by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), attains the status of being authoritative. Manu says:
"Where enjoyment is observed but no title is seen anywhere, there the title is the cause [of ownership], not the enjoyment; such is the settled rule."

In this regard, it has been stated that title (*āgama*), accompanied by possession (*saṃbhoga*), is the cause [of ownership], but possession alone is not. Vyāsa says: "Title, long duration, freedom from defects such as interruption, and the presence of the opponent—possession is held to have these five components."

This concerns the objects of enjoyment for the original progenitor. Bṛhaspati states the specific types of acquisition: "Through learning, purchase, bondage, valor, partition, inheritance, and from a sapinda who is childless—the immovable property is thus established as being acquired in seven ways."
Likewise:
"Immovable property acquired through partition, by purchase, inherited from a father, or received from a king, attains legal perfection through possession; otherwise, it is lost through neglect."
Whatever has been obtained and eaten by someone after having accepted it without opposition, that [result] reaches him; likewise, through neglect, there is loss.
If one’s enjoyment of possession has begun with occupation and has continued for thirty years without interruption, one shall not displace him from that possession.
Possession is acquisition.
If, within a single legal title, villages, fields, and groves are recorded, then even if only one part is enjoyed, all of them are considered to have been enjoyed. (2.27)
This possession is one of limited duration; it is not a possession of the entire period, as it depends upon [prior] title.
To this he says: "But he by whom title was established is the one who, being diligent, shall uphold it;
neither his son nor his grandson [need do so]. In that case, possession is more weighty. (2.28)

He who made the acquisition—whether by purchase or other means—and is thus accused, must establish that acquisition through evidence such as written documents. However, the son or grandson of that person who made the acquisition need not establish the acquisition when accused; for in their case, possession alone is more weighty (*garīyasī*). This is because its status as valid proof exists even without the establishment of the acquisition, owing to its superior weight. Now, one might object: since enjoyment is seen to occur without ownership in the case of a pledge (*ādhi*), it is not logical for possession to be authoritative independently of acquisition, as it would be a cause for doubt. This is not so. In the legal treatises (*śāstra*), the authority of possession with respect to ownership is indeed proclaimed as the general rule (*utsarga*); however, the enjoyment of pledges and the like constitutes the exception (*apavāda*). Consequently, the exception applies only where it is established by witnesses, documents, and so forth that "this is the enjoyment of a pledge. In all other cases, the authority of possession lies precisely in the relationship between owner and property according to the general rule. Thus, it is stated here that even for the son of the one who made the acquisition, ownership is established by possession alone. This should be understood to apply when the period of memory (*smārta-kāla*) has elapsed. And the period of memory consists of the time of possession by three generations of persons. Accordingly, another Smṛti states: [The text continues with the citation from the *Smṛtyantara*.]
"In the period of memory (smārta-kāla), possession of land is held to be valid when accompanied by title;
in the period beyond memory (asmārta), due to the absence of such a record, it is valid by succession through three generations.
Regarding the duration of the period of possession for a person, Nārada says:
Possession for twenty years, when declared by the owner, is "possession by one person" (pauruṣī); possession that is double that duration is "possession by two persons" (dvipauruṣī).
And the three-puruṣa [measure] is tripled; no scriptural authority needs to be sought there.
Kātyāyana states: Possession inherited from a grandfather is primary, and that from a father is also esteemed;
when uninterrupted by these three, it is considered stable possession lasting sixty years.

And thus, the period before sixty years is one for which there is memory (*smārta*); after that, it is beyond memory (*asmārta*). Alternatively, "possession by a person is said to last thirty-five years"—according to this traditional rule (*smṛti*), a period of one hundred and five years is *smārta*, and beyond that it is *asmārta*. In these two views, the distinction is based on the presence or absence of persons capable of remembering [the title]. When the *smārta* period has elapsed for the original acquirer (*āhartṛ*) and a formal challenge (*paryanuyoga*) is made, the title-deed (*āgama*) must indeed be produced as proof. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati has stated without qualification:
"The acquirer shall establish possession or title in an assembly.
Furthermore, that which was stated immediately thereafter:
"His son [shall establish] possession alone; among grandsons and so forth, nothing at all."

Thus, this should be understood as applying to the possession of the son of the acquirer during the period covered by the Smṛtis, and to that of the grandson during a period exceeding that; as for the statement of Kātyāyana:
"In the beginning, the cause is the gift; in the middle, possession must be accompanied by title (āgama);
but in the case of continuous possession extending over three generations, possession alone is the cause."

Thus, it implies that the possession of the fourth person must be presented as a means of proof; this is to be understood provided that his possession also falls within the period prescribed by the Smṛti. As for the statement of Vyāsa:
"That which has been possessed for a very long time by three preceding ancestors without a title-deed cannot be taken away, having come down through the succession of three generations."
Thus it is said; and this is the word of Nārada:
"Even that which was enjoyed through improper means by a father and three preceding ancestors cannot be taken away, having been possessed for three generations in succession."

Thus, although in reality there is no legal title (*āgama*) for the original person, nevertheless, land that has been enjoyed by three generations of persons starting from him for more than a hundred years cannot be taken away by anyone other than the fourth generation, because there is no certainty regarding the absence of a title. For the certainty of the absence of a title is what subverts possession; in its absence, [possession] is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is just as the knowledge of hot water possesses validity despite being an error, because it is not subverted in practical usage (*vyavahāra*). However, when the first enjoyment lacks the certainty of having a title even after the lapse of a hundred years while the fourth person’s enjoyment is still ongoing, then the land being enjoyed must indeed be taken away from him. For in that case, the first enjoyment is invalid due to its connection with a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*), and because they originate from an invalid source, the subsequent enjoyments are also invalid. It is precisely regarding such cases that [the following applies]:
But the king should punish that sinner with the punishment due to a thief who enjoys property that has not been transferred to him, even for many hundreds of years.

Such are the statements of Nārada and others. In this matter, the punishment applies only to the first possessor, and not to his son or descendants; however, from them, the land itself must be recovered. Accordingly, another Smṛti states:
"He by whom the acquisition was made shall be punished if he does not relinquish it;
neither his son nor his grandson [is liable], for there is no loss of possession even for those two."
Bṛhaspati:
Possession for three generations is established even against others; there is no doubt in this matter.
However, as long as the sapinda relationship has not ceased, it is not established against kinsmen (sakulyas).
But that house, field, shop, or other property which has been enjoyed by one who is not the owner—
provided it belongs to a friend, a kinsman, or a relative— is not lost through such enjoyment.
That which has been eaten by those related by marriage, by Vedic scholars, and likewise by kings and ministers,
does not succeed for them even after a very long time.

Kātyāyana says: "That which has been enjoyed by uterine kinsmen, other relatives, and likewise by one's own kin—there is no legal proof established by such enjoyment; one must consider that enjoyment as having occurred elsewhere. (2.28)

To provide an exception to the rule "whether he is his son or not his son," he says: "If one who has been accused should have died, one should restore his inheritance to his heir; in that case, possession does not constitute a ground [for ownership] if it was established without a legal title. (2.29)

[638] He who was accused regarding the subject matter of title (āgama), having passed away—that is, died—once the legal proceeding had been decided, then his heir, the receiver of the wealth, such as a son or other relative, shall clear that accusation. The meaning is that he shall conclude the legal proceeding. Because, in that case, possession devoid of the aforementioned subject matter of title is not a cause; it is no proof regarding ownership. Therefore, the clearing of the accusation must be effected by means of proof. 2.29.
He states the relative strength and weakness of those who oversee legal proceedings:
"Groups authorized by the king, guilds, and then families—each preceding one is to be known as more authoritative than each succeeding one in the procedure for legal disputes among men. (2.30)

"Appointed by the king" means those commissioned by the monarch for the administration of justice; "guilds" (*pūga*) refers to associations; "corporations" (*śreṇi*) refers to those who subsist by a single craft; and "families" (*kula*) refers to cultivators. Among these, according to the order of enumeration, each preceding one is more authoritative than the subsequent ones in the administration of justice among men. Therefore, when a legal matter has been examined by a family, if there is a suspicion regarding its examination by that family, it is proper to have it reviewed by a corporation (*śreṇi*); if examined by a corporation, by a guild (*pūga*); and if examined by a guild, by those appointed by the king—but not by the reverse order. On this point, Nārada says: "Families, corporations, guilds, and the king as the authorized official..."
The foundation of worldly transactions is heavy, each succeeding one more so than the last. (2.30)
He states the grounds for the invalidation of legal proceedings:
"One should set aside legal proceedings brought under force or fraud, as well as those conducted by women, at night, inside a house, outside [the jurisdiction], or by enemies. (2.31)

The king should set aside legal proceedings brought about by force (*bala*) and those committed by women and the like; thereafter, he should reinstate those very same proceedings. This is the intended meaning. *Bala* means violence. *Upādhi* refers to motives such as greed, hatred, and so forth. The agency of women may be either as witnesses or as plaintiffs and defendants. "Committed at night" means performed during the night. "Committed inside a house" means performed within a dwelling. "Committed outside" means performed outside the village. "Committed by enemies" means witnessed by enemies. By the mention of "night," "inside a house," and "outside," secret transactions are indicated. — Nārada.
A legal transaction entered into with women, at night, outside the village, or within a house during the nights—even if already completed—must be performed again. (2.31)
Furthermore:
A legal proceeding initiated by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted by illness, beset by calamity, a child, or terrified, as well as one that is incoherent, is not valid. (2.32)

[639] Legal proceedings conducted by those who are intoxicated and so forth do not succeed; the meaning is that they are set aside. "Intoxicated" means one who is drunk with wine and the like. "Insane" means one who is possessed by spirits and the like. "Afflicted" means one suffering from disease and the like. "Addicted" refers to a gambler and the like, or one who has suffered the loss of a son and so forth. "Child" and "fear" are well known terms. One who has not been dispatched by either the plaintiff (*arthin*) or the defendant (*pratyarthin*) to conduct the legal proceeding is "unauthorized" (*asaṃbaddha*). And thus Kātyāyana says: "The right of authority belongs to the one who is formally charged (*abhiyukta*), and not to another, due to the lack of connection."
The other [party] is also considered an official when dispatched by the accused.

Even another person who is unrelated and has not been appointed by the defendant— the one sent as the respondent, authorized as the respondent, made the respondent, or accepted as the respondent by Manu and others;
or one who is supported by the plaintiff and is another distinct person in the judicial office—
should be known as the respondent (*prativādī*), as well as one who has voluntarily admitted the claim.
One who has been accepted as a defendant before a judge presiding over legal matters, having been personally acknowledged by the plaintiff;
or, for those who are not arrogant, nor dull-witted, insane, aged, female, minor, or diseased,
a kinsman or another person appointed may state the plea and the reply.
Kātyāyana states:
In cases of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, violating the teacher’s wife,
and other intolerable accusations, no counter-plaint may be allowed.
The representative of both the plaintiff and the defendant is the respondent (prativādī).
[In cases of] killing a human being, theft, violating another's wife,
eating what is forbidden to eat, and the abduction or defilement of a maiden—
In cases of harsh speech, forgery, and likewise treason against the king, the defendant shall not be made to pay;
rather, the perpetrator himself shall plead the case.
Whether commissioned by the plaintiff or even sent by the defendant,
he who litigates on behalf of either of them shall share in their victory or defeat.
Nārada: He who is neither a brother, nor a father, nor a son, nor an appointed agent,
yet speaks on behalf of another while testifying falsely in legal proceedings, shall be punished.

Kātyāyana states: "Slaves, laborers, disciples, appointed agents, and likewise kinsmen—these litigants shall not be punished; whoever other than these is the offender, he shall bear the penalty. (2.32)
Furthermore:
Property lost and subsequently recovered shall be given by the king to the owner;
if he cannot prove his ownership by signs, he deserves a fine equal to that amount. (2.33)

[640] If, in the kingdom, the wealth of someone has been lost and has been recovered by the king himself, either directly or through another person, and if the owner who lost it identifies it by its characteristics, such as its form and number, and verifies it, then it must be restored to him by the king; if he does not identify it, then, because of his involvement in theft, he shall be punished with a fine equal to the value of the lost property. || 2.33 ||

Now he speaks concerning the discovery of a treasure without an owner: "Having found a treasure, the king shall give half to the twice-born; but a learned twice-born man may take the whole, since he is the master of all. (2.34)

Upon finding a treasure—such as gold and other valuables—buried within the earth whose owner is unknown, the king shall give half of it to the Brāhmaṇas; it follows by implication that he himself shall take the second half. However, if a learned and preeminent twice-born man, who knows the meaning of the Vedas, should find it, then he may take the whole of it, because he is the master of everything found on the earth. Manu says: "Wherever the king sees an ancient treasure buried in the ground, he shall give half of it to the twice-born and deposit the other half in the treasury."
By saying "ancient," he indicates that the owner is unknown.
But a learned Brāhmaṇa, having found a treasure previously deposited,
may take it entirely, for he is the master of all.
Vasiṣṭha: "If a Brāhmaṇa, engaged in the six duties, acquires [wealth], he may take it all. (2.34)
Regarding a treasure found by someone other than a learned man, [Yājñavalkya] says:
"When a treasure is obtained by another, the king shall take a sixth part.
If it is discovered without having been reported, he shall be made to pay that [treasure] as well as a fine. (2.35)

When a treasure-trove is found or obtained by another—a Brāhmaṇa who is ignorant—the king, as the protector of the realm, shall take a sixth part of it. Thus it has been stated by Vasiṣṭha: "Whatever property is found whose owner is unknown, the king shall take that, having given a sixth part to the finder. Gautama says: "The discovery of a treasure-trove is the property of the king. Some say that even a non-Brāhmaṇa, if he is a learned man (*abhirūpa*), shall receive a sixth part when the treasure is reported to him. Furthermore, regarding one who is *aniveditavijñāta*: here, "reporting" (*nivedana*) refers to the announcement of the discovery of a treasure; that which is so reported is "reported" (*nivedita*). One for whom such a report does not exist is "unreported" (*anivedita*); and being both unreported and discovered is "unreported-discovered" (*aniveditavijñāta*). Such a person must be made to pay both the treasure and a fine. This is what is meant: having found a treasure, if one does not report it to the king, then both the treasure and a fine are to be taken by the king. However, with respect to one who recovers his own lost treasure, Manu says: [Manu 8.30–32] "One who finds a treasure-trove in an inhabited place shall give a sixth part to the king, provided he is other than a Brāhmaṇa; a Brāhmaṇa may keep the whole, for he is the ultimate owner of all. But if a king should discover a treasure-trove buried long ago in the earth, he should give half of it to the Brāhmaṇas and keep the other half for himself; this is the settled law. If, however, someone should find a treasure-trove buried in the dwelling of an inhabitant, he shall give a sixth part to that inhabitant and a twelfth part to the king; the rest he shall keep for himself. [641] He who, on the other hand, is *aniveditavijñāta*—where "reporting" means the declaration of finding a treasure, and that very act constitutes "reporting"—one for whom no such report exists is "unreported"; and being both "unreported" and "discovered" makes him *aniveditavijñāta*. He must be made to pay that treasure and a fine. This is what is intended: having obtained a treasure, if one does not inform the king, then both the treasure and a fine are to be seized by the king. But regarding one who recovers his own treasure, Manu speaks to him: [Manu 8.30–32] "One who finds a treasure-trove in an inhabited place shall give a sixth part to the king, provided he is other than a Brāhmaṇa; a Brāhmaṇa may keep the whole, for he is the ultimate owner of all. But if a king should discover a treasure-trove buried long ago in the earth, he should give half of it to the Brāhmaṇas and keep the other half for himself; this is the settled law. If, however, someone should find a treasure-trove buried in the dwelling of an inhabitant, he shall give a sixth part to that inhabitant and a twelfth part to the king; the rest he shall keep for himself."
If a man should truthfully declare, "This treasure belongs to me," the king shall take a sixth or even a twelfth part of it.
But one who speaks falsely shall be fined twelve [paṇas] by the king.
The smallness or greatness of the discourse should be established in relation to its qualities. 2.35.
The king must restore property stolen by thieves to the subject;
for by not restoring it, he incurs the same guilt as the one to whom it belongs.
[Thus ends the section on the matrix of unique legal procedures.

The king, having recovered property stolen by a thief, must restore it to the local inhabitant who is the owner of that wealth; for by failing to restore it, he incurs the sin of the owner of the wealth. Manu says: "The king must restore to people of all castes the property stolen by thieves."
And the king, by consuming that, incurs the guilt of the thief.
Gautama: "Having recovered what was stolen by thieves, one should restore it to its proper place or provide it from the treasury. Vyāsa:
"But if one is unable to recover wealth stolen by thieves, that indeed must be given from his own treasury by the king who is powerless [to retrieve it]. (2.36)

[Thus ends the second chapter, on the General Table of Contents of Judicial Procedure, in the Aparārka— a commentary on the Yājñavalkya-smṛti composed by the illustrious Parādityadeva, born in the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the noble Vidyādhara race.]
Now begins the section on the Recovery of Debts (*ṛṇādāna*) in the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* with its commentary.
(3) There exists, indeed, a title of legal dispute (*vyavahārapada*) called the recovery of debts; regarding its essential nature, Nārada says:
"Debt that is to be paid and that which is not to be paid, by whom, to whom, when, and what—
according to the rules for giving and receiving— that is called the non-payment of debt.
Regarding that, he states the rule for interest: "The interest shall be one-eightieth part every month when there is collateral;
otherwise, according to the order of the castes, it shall be two, three, four, or five percent. (2.37)

In a loan secured by a pledge (*ādhi*), the interest shall be one-eightieth part of the principal amount lent each month. Otherwise, in a loan without a pledge, the debtors belonging to the *brāhmaṇa* and other castes shall pay interest at the rate of two, three, four, or five percent per hundred, respectively, according to the order of their castes. "Two, three, four, and five" means that interest is paid at the rate of two, three, four, or five [units] for every hundred. Vasiṣṭha states:
"Two, three, four, and five percent per hundred is prescribed."
One may take interest for a month, according to the successive order of the social classes.
Bṛhaspati said:
Interest is declared to be fourfold by some, proclaimed as fivefold by others, and described as sixfold by yet others; understand them according to their true nature.
There is bodily interest, periodical interest, and another known as compound interest;
likewise, there is stipulated interest, interest on a pledge, and profit from use.
Interest is of four kinds: that which is connected with bodily labor, that which is to be taken month by month, compound interest, and the interest agreed upon by the debtor.
That interest which is collected daily is known as *śikhāvṛddhi* (top-knot interest);
it increases constantly like a top-knot, but ceases upon the cutting off of the head.

When one gives the principal [loan] in this same manner, that is known as *śikhāvṛddhi* (interest on the principal). Interest received from a herd of cattle is proclaimed as *stoma*, while profit from a field is called *bhogalābha*.
The creditor may collect the interest on the principal, as well as bodily labor and the acquisition of goods,
only so long as the principal has not been repaid.
*Stoma* is that which is caused by dwelling; *śada* is the produce of the field. Listen now to the rate of interest proclaimed by the words of Vasiṣṭha regarding usury:
five *māṣas* on twenty [pieces of silver]; thus the law is not violated.
Kātyāyana says: If one who has been asked for a loan and has already agreed to repay it should depart for another region without having paid the principal,
he shall be liable for interest on that debt after the lapse of three seasons.
But he who, even while residing in his own country, does not pay when asked repeatedly— even if summoned by the creditor— shall incur interest against his will. — Nārada.
There shall be no interest on gifts made out of affection, provided they are not requested;
however, even if unrequested, interest accrues after half a year has passed.
"Unasked" (*anāyācitam*) is neuter because it functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). Likewise:
"Whatever is given out of affection, if unasked, does not increase;
but he who does not give when asked increases [the debt] by five percent."
This [is to be performed] before half a year has passed. 2.37.
He states the specific rates of interest according to the particular nature of the debtor:
"But those traveling through wildernesses shall pay ten percent; those traveling by sea, twenty percent;
or all may pay the interest agreed upon by themselves among all classes. (2.38)

Those who go to the wilderness—that is, those who travel through great forests to trade in clothes and other goods—should pay ten percent per hundred. Those who cross the ocean—the seafarers—should pay twenty percent per hundred. When a hundred *niṣkas* or more have been received as a loan, they should pay twenty *niṣkas* per month; the same applies even when the principal is a hundred *paṇas*. Alternatively, all castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, may pay interest at a rate agreed upon by the creditor according to their own custom among the various castes, provided they belong to the higher castes. This rule should be understood to apply in the absence of a pledge (*bandhaka*) and when the debtors are eager to travel to the wilderness or across the sea. (2.38)
He states the specific rate of interest for particular types of goods:
"But for livestock and women, the maximum interest is eightfold;
for clothes, grain, and gold, it is four, three, and two times the principal respectively. (2.39)

For female animals such as buffaloes and the like that have been lent for the purpose of increase, their offspring alone constitutes the interest. For liquids such as clarified butter, the interest is eightfold; for clothes, fourfold; for grains, threefold; and for gold, twofold. The word "parā" (maximum) is connected to each [category]. "Parā" means supreme; the meaning is that there is no interest higher than this. And this should be understood to apply when the interest has been stipulated by oneself and remains unpaid for a long period. Gautama states: "In the case of a long-term loan, the principal becomes doubled. This means the wealth that was lent. Manu says:
Interest on a loan, once stipulated, shall not exceed double [the principal].

Even if the interest has doubled, it continues to accrue upon being applied toward the principal through the debtor’s agreement; this is established by the use of the term "once" (*sakṛt*). And this rule pertains specifically to gold. Kātyāyana states:
"The wealth lent by creditors shall always be recoverable as double."
If he does not receive it, he shall not calculate further interest beyond the double amount.
Bṛhaspati says:
When the gold has doubled and the debtor is ruined, [the creditor shall not claim more].
Having taken possession of that person's property, one may sell it in the presence of witnesses.
Or he may keep it for ten days in the assembly of people after its price has been paid;
thereafter, having received a deposit corresponding to the debt, he should relinquish it.
Having stabilized his own wealth with men skilled in accounting, he should accept it while it is known to its kinsmen and relatives; thus he would not commit an offense.
Manu says:
In the case of grain, fodder, wool, or a beast of burden, the interest does not exceed five times the principal.

In the case of grain and the like, when not paid, the interest—though unpaid for a long time—does not exceed fivefold the principal. *Śada* refers to the produce of a field, such as flowers, roots, fruits, and so forth. *Lava* refers to wool from sheep, hair from goats, and the like. *Vāhya* refers to draft animals such as horses, oxen, and so on. However, Vasiṣṭha states that liquids have a threefold increase: "Gold is doubled; grain is tripled. By grain alone are liquids explained. Flowers and fruits are [triple]. That which is weighed on a scale is eightfold. These statements regarding the number of maximum increases should be applied according to the debtor's capacity. Bṛhaspati says:
Interest on gold is said to be double; on cloth and base metals, triple;
on grain, fourfold; and likewise on wool, beasts of burden, and salt.
Base metals refer to tin and lead.
It is stated that the fivefold increase applies to vegetables; for seeds, an eightfold increase is prescribed;
and for salt, fats, and liquors, an eightfold increase is traditionally ordained.
It is stated that when molasses and honey have been used for a long time, [the purification is as follows]:
for grass, wood, bricks, thread, leaven, leather, bone, and armor.
Furthermore, the growth of seeds, flowers, and fruits never ceases.

*Kiṇva* is the fermenting agent used as the material for *surā* liquor. *Carman* is a shield; *varman* is armor; *heti* is a weapon. Viṣṇu states: "For yeast, cotton, thread, leather, armor, weapons, bricks, charcoal, and gold, the fine is inexhaustible (*akṣaya*). For items not mentioned here, the fine is double. (2.39)
Furthermore:
One who, having entered [the court], establishes his case, should not be censured by the king;
but one who, while being tried, departs for the king [to appeal elsewhere], shall be punished and made to pay that wealth. (2.40)

[645] When there is a dispute, a creditor seeking to recover a debt that has been admitted or accepted by the debtor is neither to be censured nor obstructed by the king. If that debtor, while being pursued for recovery, should go to the king, then he shall be punished by the king and made to pay that wealth to the creditor. As Manu says:
"By means of moral conduct (*dharma*), legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), artifice (*chala*), and customary practice (*ācāra*)."
One should accomplish one's purpose when joined with the fifth power as well.

*Dharma* is truth. *Vyavahāra* is the collection of means of proof such as written documents and witnesses. *Chala* is deception. *Ācarita* is local custom. *Bala* is oppression by means of withholding food and so forth; however, one who speaks according to justice (*nyāyavādī*) must not be oppressed. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says: "If a creditor should oppress a debtor who speaks according to justice, he shall be deprived of that wealth and shall incur a fine equal to its value."
The king, however, should cause the Brahmin to pay his master by means of conciliation alone;
but others who are wicked, he should cause to pay by afflicting them according to local custom.
One should not cause an heir or even a friend to pay by means of fraud.
Regarding the payment when a debt is due to several creditors simultaneously, he states the order:
"The debtor shall be made to pay according to the sequence in which the debts were received;
however, having paid the Brāhmaṇa first, he must pay the king immediately thereafter. (2.41)

The order of repayment among creditors of the same caste should be understood to follow the order in which they received the loans; however, among those of different castes, it follows the order of the social classes (*varṇa*). The mention of the Brāhmaṇa and the King is intended to illustrate the case of the Vaiśya and the Śūdra as well. Kātyāyana states:
"That debt which was recorded on the same day, one should discharge equally;
otherwise, [the order shall be] according to the sequence of receipt, security, and interest."

On a single day, the king shall make the debt recorded for many creditors equal and uniform with respect to all those creditors. Likewise, he shall make the seizure of the pledge, its preservation, and the recovery of the profit equally available to each creditor. However, if there is a difference in the dates of the written records, he shall settle the debt and so forth according to the order as written.
Whichever debtor can demonstrate that a particular commodity was acquired using his own wealth, that wealth must be returned by that very debtor; it cannot be otherwise.

When a debtor has taken merchandise for the purpose of trade using the goods of a creditor, that very creditor obtains the wealth acquired through the transaction of that merchandise; in this case, the previously mentioned rule need not be applied. (2.41)
The king shall compel the debtor to pay ten percent on the amount proved due;
and the creditor who has recovered his wealth shall be made to pay five percent. (2.42)

With respect to the amount of the claim established by legal proof, the debtor shall be made to pay ten percent; the meaning is that the king shall take from the debtor an amount equal to one-tenth of the proven debt. Likewise, the creditor who has recovered his debt shall be made to pay five percent as interest to the king; the meaning is that the king shall take it. On this point Viṣṇu states: "If the creditor goes to the king, the debtor, having been proven [guilty], shall pay to the king a fine equal to one-tenth of the money [claimed]; and the creditor, having obtained his object, shall pay one-twentieth part. Nārada says:
But a debtor who possesses wealth yet does not pay due to wickedness should be made to pay by the king,
after taking a twentieth part as a fee.
And it should be understood that this applies when [the goal] is achievable with very little effort. || 2.42 ||
Regarding a debtor who is unable to discharge his debt, he states the means for its discharge according to the system of castes:
"One may compel a man of low birth who is impoverished to perform labor for the sake of the debt;
but a Brāhmaṇa who is impoverished should be made to pay gradually, according to his income. (2.43)

A creditor who is a Brāhmaṇa or of a higher caste may, for the sake of recovering a debt from a debtor of a lower caste such as a Kṣatriya who is impoverished and destitute, compel him to perform labor—such as fetching grass, fuel, and water—for the purpose of clearing the debt. The mention of a "lower caste" is illustrative; by this, one of the same caste is also included. If the debtor is a Brāhmaṇa who has become impoverished, then he should be made to pay gradually and without pressure, according to his means—that is, in accordance with the arrival of wealth. The mention of a "Brāhmaṇa" is intended to indicate any person of a superior caste relative to the creditor's caste. Consequently, a Kṣatriya toward a Vaiśya, or a Vaiśya toward a Śūdra, should be made to pay only the money according to his means, and not be compelled to perform labor. And so says Manu:
A debtor should repay the creditor in a manner consistent with his own status;
one of equal or lower birth may pay at once, but one of superior birth should pay it gradually.
Even after performing work required by the creditor, the debtor should make himself free from debt by rendering it equal to or commensurate with the debt. Bṛhaspati states:
"One should bring a debtor who is destitute of wealth to his house and compel him to work;
however, a Brāhmaṇa should be made to pay gradually, starting with tasks such as serving a liquor-seller."

A *śauṇḍika* is a maker of liquor. [647] Kātyāyana says: "If, however, one should first cause an unordained evil act to be performed, he shall incur the first *sāhasa* fine, and the debtor shall be released from his debt."

If a creditor should cause a debtor to perform labor that is unpleasant, such as the removal of filth and the like, even though it was not previously ordered or stipulated, then he shall be punished with the first amercement and the debtor is released from that debt. (2.43)
Regarding one who, out of greed for interest and so forth, does not accept the wealth being offered by the debtor, he says:
"He who does not accept his own lent wealth while it is being given shall have it deposited with a neutral third party; beyond that point, it no longer accrues interest. (2.44)

If the creditor does not accept the wealth being offered by the debtor for the sake of interest and so forth on the loaned capital, then that [debt] must be placed in the hands of a neutral third party by the debtor; from that point forward, it shall no longer increase. (2.44)
Regarding those by whom a debt must be discharged when the debtor has died or gone abroad, he says:
"But that debt which has been contracted for the sake of the family by undivided members, the heirs shall pay it when the head of the household has died or gone abroad. (2.45)

When the householder has gone abroad or is deceased, whatever debt has been contracted by undivided brothers and others for the sake of maintaining that family, all the heirs shall pay it. The plural number in the word "undivided" (*avibhaktaiḥ*) is not intended to be restrictive. Thus says Manu: "If the borrower has perished, having incurred expenses on behalf of the family, then the debt must be paid by the kinsmen from their own shares, even if they have divided their property."
Nārada says: Whatever debt has been contracted by an undivided paternal uncle, or by a brother,
or by a mother for the sake of the family, all of that must be paid by the heirs.
Bṛhaspati: What has been borrowed for the sake of the family by a paternal uncle, a brother’s son, a wife, a slave, a pupil, or a dependent, that the householder ought to repay.
Kātyāyana says: That which was taken by one who is incapable [of repayment] for the sake of his family, or by one who is diseased,
or on account of a calamity— that indeed should be paid when the time of distress has passed.
Whatever was performed for the marriage of a daughter and whatever was performed for funeral rites—
all this must be given by the family to the master.
The meaning is that the master should give to the master. || 2.45 ||
Regarding this, he states an exception together with its counter-exception:
"A father does not incur [the debt] for what was done by his wife, his son, or by his own son."
Likewise, a husband shall not be liable for a debt contracted by his wife, except for what was incurred for the sake of the family.

A woman shall not pay a debt incurred by her husband or son that is other than one contracted for the sake of the family; likewise, a father shall not pay a debt incurred by his son, nor a husband a debt incurred by his wife. Bṛhaspati says:
"A debt incurred by a son must be cleared by the father if it was approved [by him], or he may pay it out of affection for his son; otherwise, he is not obliged to pay."
Kātyāyana states: A debt contracted for the sake of the family by a slave, a wife, a minister, or a pupil—even without the consent of the master—must be paid by the son; so says Bhṛgu.
Nārada says: Whether incurred by the father's own command, for the maintenance of the family, or in times of distress, the father shall pay that debt which was contracted by his son. (2.46)

He will state that "a debt must be paid by sons and grandsons"; he now states an exception to that: "A son shall not pay, as a paternal obligation, a debt contracted for liquor, pleasure, or gambling, nor the remainder of fines and taxes, nor likewise a gift made in vain. (2.47)

A son shall not pay a paternal debt incurred for the purpose of drinking liquor, sexual intercourse with women, or gambling; nor that which remains unpaid of a fine or a tax; nor that which is a gift made in vain. On this point, Kātyāyana says:
"Whether it be a written document or one not in writing, that which is promised to be given, or what men know to have been given out of lust to a woman previously married to another."
The phrase "what remains" is not intended to be emphasized. Thus Uśanas said:
"Neither a fine nor the remainder of a fine, nor toll, nor the remainder of that, nor anything that is not part of a legal transaction should be paid by a son."
The meaning is that it is neither conventional nor proper. It is stated in another Smṛti that such a gift is fruitless:
"A gift given to a rogue, a bard, a wrestler, a quack doctor, a gambler, a cheat, a flatterer, a wandering minstrel, or a thief becomes fruitless."
Nārada says: A father shall not pay a debt incurred by his son, but a son may pay one incurred by his father,
except for that contracted through lust, anger, liquor, gambling, or as a surety.

Kātyāyana says: "In a case where, having caused injury or having destroyed property out of anger, one speaks words intended to cause satisfaction, one should know that it is an act committed through anger. [649]

This is the meaning: having inflicted injury upon another or caused the destruction of their wealth, whatever substance was promised as a compensation for their satisfaction—that is a debt conquered through anger. (2.47)
To refute the aforementioned exception—that "the husband is not liable for what is done by the wife"—he says:
"The husband shall pay the debt of those women who are the wives of cowherds, vintners, fowlers, washermen, and hunters, because their livelihood depends upon him. (2.48)

A debt contracted by the wives of Ābhīras, liquor-vendors, actors, washermen, and hunters shall be discharged by their husbands; for the livelihood and subsistence of these [classes], such as cowherds and others, are dependent upon them and thus dependent upon their women. This statement is intended to show that even if a debt contracted by the wives of cowherds and others is not for the sake of the family, it must nevertheless be cleared by their husbands. Otherwise, this statement would be redundant, since it would already be established by the rule that "the husband is not liable for what is done by his wife if it is for the sake of the family. And so says Nārada:

And a debt incurred by a wife shall in no way become the husband's responsibility, except for that contracted during a time of distress; for the maintenance of a family is indeed difficult to accomplish.
Except for the wives of washermen, hunters, cowherds, and vintners; for them, there is a return [to the path] through that very conviction, and their families depend upon them. (2.48)
He states that a woman shall not pay any debt other than those specific types of debts:
"A debt acknowledged by a woman must be paid, as must one contracted jointly with her husband; likewise, she must pay a debt contracted by herself. She is not liable for any other debt. (2.49)

A debt incurred by a husband or son, even if not for the benefit of the family, which has been acknowledged or accepted [by the woman], as well as that which was contracted together with her husband and that which was contracted by herself—this must be paid by the woman. She shall not pay any other debt. The mention of "contracted by herself" is for the purpose of establishing that a debt incurred by a mother, even if not for the benefit of the family, must be paid by the son; otherwise, the statement would be redundant. For this is already known—even without such a statement—that a debt contracted by oneself must be paid by oneself. Thus says Kātyāyana.
A debt contracted in this manner must be paid by the husband or the son, or by the individual himself; it is not otherwise [binding] upon a woman for what was done by them.

That which was incurred by her husband or her sons is what is meant here. If a woman has been told by her husband, "You must pay this debt," she should be made to pay it even if she has not consented, provided that the wealth was entrusted to her by him.
Wealth refers to the husband’s wealth. || 2.49 ||

[650] Even when the father has gone abroad, is deceased, or is overwhelmed by calamity, the debt must be paid by the sons or grandsons, provided it is established by witnesses in case of denial. 2.50.

If a father has gone abroad, died, or is addicted to vices such as drinking, his debt must be paid by the son or grandson without having been discharged. If the son or others should say, "We do not know whether our father or grandfather owed anything to you," then it must be paid once it has been established by the defendant through any one of the means of proof, such as witnesses. And since the rule for the payment of debt is prescribed here on grounds such as [the father's] being abroad, the debt must be paid by the sons even in the absence of paternal wealth, and in their absence, by the grandsons. On this point, Nārada says:
If the father has gone abroad, the son shall not pay the debt before twenty years have passed;
nor [shall he pay it] to a paternal uncle or to an elder brother.
Kātyāyana says: Even if the father is afflicted by disease, or even if he has gone abroad from his own country,
the debt incurred by the father must be paid by the sons after twenty years.
In such cases, one should cause even sons who are still living to pay the debt of those who are diseased, insane, elderly, or long away on travel.
Even while the father is present, the debt must be paid by the sons if it has been proven;
however, this does not apply to those who are blind from birth, outcastes, insane, or afflicted with consumption, leprosy, and similar diseases.
Bṛhaspati says: A debt to the ancestors must first be paid, and thereafter one's own personal debt;
between those two, the debt to the grandfather must be paid first—this is how a debt should always be settled.
Therefore, once a son is born, he should diligently strive to liberate his father from debt so that he does not go to hell, even at the cost of setting aside his own interests.

And this refers to the case of a son who has attained legal capacity (*prāptavyavahāra*). However, one who has not attained legal capacity has no entitlement even if he is born, because of his incapacity. Thus says Kātyāyana:

"When the father has passed away, [the debt] must never be paid by one who has not attained legal capacity; rather, it should be given at the proper time according to the rule. Otherwise, they shall dwell in hell."
And a grandson must discharge his grandfather’s debt without interest. As Bṛhaspati says:
"A son must pay a proven paternal debt like his own;
a grandfather’s debt is to be paid in equal [principal] by him, but it is not to be paid by that grandson."
"Equal" means devoid of interest (*vṛddhi*). The genitive case in "of his son" (*tatsutasya*) denotes the agent; thus, the meaning is that the debt must not be paid by his son. Kātyāyana says:
"That which was seen [by the father], or the remainder of what was given, or that which belongs to the grandfather—such a debt should be paid.
However, a debt that is defective or was opposed by the father must never be paid by anyone. [651]

That which was seen [as a debt] by the father, and that which remained after what was given by him, must be paid by the grandson as a paternal grandfather’s debt. However, that which was contested or rejected by him, and that which is tainted with fault due to being caused by vices such as liquor, need not be paid as a paternal grandfather’s debt; this is the meaning. Regarding the debt seen by the father which has descended in succession from the grandfather, Bhr̥gu states that if it is faultless and has not been cleared by the sons, it must be paid by the grandsons.
Likewise: "One should compel the son to pay the debt if he is free from affliction, capable of wealth, and fit for the burden; otherwise, one should not compel the son to pay."
*Draviṇārhaḥ* means worthy of his father’s wealth; *dhuryaḥ* means one who bears the burden of his father’s responsibilities. || 2.50 ||

The heir to the estate shall be made to pay the debt, as shall the one who takes the wife; likewise, the son whose property has not been alienated [to others] shall pay for the father who leaves no heirs. (2.51)

In this context, the completion of the sentence occurs at every step; that is, the phrase "he shall be made to pay the debt" is connected to each clause. "The heir (*rikthagrāha*) shall be made to pay the debt. *Riktha* is paternal wealth; therefore, the son is the primary heir. In his absence, a substitute for a son (*putrapratinidhi*), such as the *kṣetraja* son and others, [is the heir]. In their absence, the wife, daughter, and so forth [are the heirs]. And here, the term "heir" (*rikthagrāha*) does not refer exclusively to the son, because the obligation for the son to discharge the father's debt has already been established by the rule: "The debt must be paid by sons and grandsons. Consequently, the meaning is this: if a person who is an heir—such as a *kṣetraja* son or another—takes the inheritance, he must be made by the king to pay the debt belonging to that [deceased] to the creditor. One who takes another's woman—that is, his wife—is a "woman-taker" (*yoṣidgrāha*). He too must be made to pay whatever debt belongs to her husband. And here, the intended order of recitation is followed; thus, in the absence of an heir, the woman-taker is the one who provides the payment of the debt. (Nārada).
The last among women who have been self-willed and the first among those who have remarried—
whosoever enjoys the property of these two shall pay the debt incurred by their husbands.
And he himself defines them:
"Other women who have had previous husbands are said to be seven in number, respectively;
among them, the *punarbhū* is of three kinds, and the *svairiṇī* is of four kinds."
A maiden who, though her virginity remains intact, has been defiled by the taking of the hand in marriage,
is declared the first type of *punarbhū* (a remarried woman) in the rite of re-consecration.
A woman who, having disregarded the laws of the land, is given away by her elders to another man out of impulsive passion,
is proclaimed as the second [type of remarried woman].
[652] That woman who,
in the absence of brothers-in-law, is given by her kinsmen to a man of the same caste who is not a sapinda relative is proclaimed as the third [kind of niyoga].
Whether she has borne children or not, if a woman, while her husband is still alive,
out of lust resorts to another man, she is the first type of unchaste woman (svairiṇī).
She who, having abandoned her husband from childhood, resorts to another man and then returns again to her husband's house, is proclaimed as the second [type].
She who, upon the death of her husband, rejects his brothers-in-law and others who have come to her and approaches another out of desire is proclaimed as the third [type of woman].
She who has come from another country, purchased with wealth, and being afflicted by hunger and thirst,
approaches you saying "I am yours"— she is proclaimed as the fourth type.
Likewise:
"For he who takes the wife of one who has died without wealth and without a son inherits his debt; that [wife] alone is declared to be his property."
That very thing refers to the wife herself; or, the phrase "and likewise the one who seizes a woman" refers to the case of liquor-sellers and others. As Kātyāyana has said:
"But that debt which is contracted by those who are penniless and childless, such as liquor-sellers and the like, the enjoyer of their wives must indeed pay that debt."

It has been stated that a son must discharge his father’s debt; regarding this, he states a specific qualification: "a son whose property is not dependent on others. That son who is *ananyāśritadravya*—meaning one whose wealth is under his own control—is liable for the paternal debt. One whose property (*dravya*) or wealth (*dhana*) is dependent on others (*anyāśrita*) or subject to the authority of others is called *anyāśritadravya*; one who is not such is *ananyāśritadravya*. Consequently, those brothers whose wealth is dependent on a particular brother are not liable; rather, only he among them who acts with independence is liable. Here, the order of the words is not intended to be significant. For in this case, the verbal root-meaning of "giving" (*dāna*) is not being enjoined; rather, it is the son's quality (*dharma*), characterized by having property not dependent on others, that is meant. And that quality is not itself to be performed; rather, the verbal root-meaning is qualified by that quality. Therefore, where the verbal root-meaning is enjoined in a sequence, there the rule of order is intended; but not elsewhere. Thus, the order here is not intended to be significant. As for what was stated by Nārada:
Among those who take away wealth, a wife, or sons, he who takes the wealth shall bear the debt;
if there is neither a son nor a wife possessing wealth, the one who takes the wife shall bear it in the absence of both the wealth-holder and the son.

Thus, that [rule] refers to sons who are unworthy of a share of the paternal estate. From the statement of Gautama, “Even a son of equal caste, if he is of improper conduct, shall not receive [a share]—according to some,” it is understood that even a son may be unworthy of a share. Likewise, the unworthiness of the blind and others will be stated in the section on partition. However, regarding those who are worthy of partition, it has been said that even in the absence of paternal wealth, the father’s debt must be discharged: “The debt is to be paid by sons and grandsons. As for the statement that, having first declared that a son is to be made to pay in the absence of one who takes the wife, it is further stated that “in the absence of a son, the one who takes the wife is to be made to pay”—that refers to a case where someone takes a woman other than the aforementioned *punarbhū* (a remarried woman) or *svairiṇī* (an unchaste woman). The phrase “the heir of one who has no son” refers to the heir in the form of a grandson; for they alone, and not others such as brothers, possess the fitness to take the inheritance of a grandfather who has sons. As Manu says:
Neither brothers nor fathers are the heirs to a son's inheritance;
rather, the father shall take the inheritance of one who dies without a son, or else the brothers themselves.
For he will say:
"But for those whose fathers have died, the allotment of shares is according to the fathers."

Regarding the rule that "the debt must be paid by sons and grandsons," this is stated—"by the heirs of one who has no son"—in order to prevent the over-extension of the principle that even the debt of a grandfather who has a living son must be discharged by his grandsons. Here, the term *rikthin* (heir) refers to one who is connected with the act of taking the inheritance, not exclusively to one who has already taken the inheritance. Consequently, in the case of a grandfather who is destitute and lacks a son, the grandsons are entitled to discharge the debt only in the absence of a son, and not when a son exists. However, those who have taken the inheritance are entitled to do so even when a son exists; they should discharge the grandfather’s debt according to their respective shares. For this very reason, Nārada says:
From this point forward, the sons of the father shall pay the debt according to their respective shares,
whether they are divided or undivided, provided that he who bears that burden [pays it].
Even if he is independent, one who has not attained legal majority remains liable for debt;
for independence is traditionally attributed to the eldest, based on qualities and age.
Likewise:
"The debt which was contracted by the sons and cleared in succession without obstacle, the grandsons shall pay; that [debt] of the grandfather ceases after the fourth generation."

There is another explanation for the phrase "a son whose property is not dependent on another": here, by the word *anya* (other), the father is meant because he is the subject under discussion. By the compound *anyāśritadravya* (property dependent on another), the father’s wealth is denoted. A son who does not possess such [wealth] is one whose property is not dependent on another (*ananyāśritadravya*). Therefore, in the absence of both an heir to the estate (*rikthagrāha*) and an heir to the wife (*yoṣidgrāha*), the son shall be made to pay the debt. But when they exist, those two alone shall be made to pay, respectively. Furthermore, there are certain sons who are unworthy of inheritance. As it is said regarding the twelve kinds of sons, Vasiṣṭha, after mentioning six types of sons, states: "They are kinsmen entitled to inherit. Likewise: "If among his first six [types of sons] there should be no one who takes the inheritance, these [others] shall take that gift. And likewise: "But those who have entered other stages of life (*āśrama*), as well as the impotent, the insane, and the outcastes, are non-partakers of shares (*anaṃśāḥ*). The established meaning of these [texts] is this: the son or others who are heirs to the estate (*rikthagrāha*) are to be made to pay; in their absence, the heir to the wife (*yoṣidgrāha*); and in his absence, the son who is unworthy of inheritance. Thus says Nārada: [654]
Among those who take the wealth, the wife, or the son, he who takes the wealth shall bear the debt;
if neither the wife nor the wealth exists, the son bears it; and if neither the wife nor the son exists, the one who takes the wealth bears it.

In this context, after stating that "in the absence of the wife and the one who takes the property, the son is the one who must pay the debt," it is further stated that "in the absence of both the creditor's property and the son, the one who takes the wife is the one who must pay the debt. Regarding this, the rule of application (*vyavasthā*) is as follows: the previously mentioned "taker of the wife" bears the debt when a son exists; however, the "other taker of the wife" bears it only in the absence of a son. Nārada himself says: "If a woman, having abandoned her son who has a son of her own, resorts to another man, the creditor shall take everything from her; but if she is destitute of wealth, the son alone [shall pay]."
The one who takes a woman [as a wife] is a debtor. And so he himself says:
"For when a man dies without wealth and without a son, whoever takes his wife incurs the debt; that very [debt] is traditionally held to be his wealth."
But if a woman who has brought dowry, along with her children, should resort to another man,
he shall pay her husband's debt or she may leave him in that same manner.
*Pradhana* means excellent wealth; *sapradhanā* means accompanied by that. Kātyāyana states:

"If a woman with young children has incurred a debt for the sake of another purpose and has resorted to another man, the man she has resorted to shall pay that debt; this is the rule regarding women with young children."

The property of the wives of those who are long-traveling abroad, or who are obstinate, dull-witted, insane, afflicted, or disguised as ascetics, must be given by their dependents even while they are still alive. (2.51)
He states the prohibition regarding debt, along with its relevant implications, in respect to specific subjects:

"Indeed, among brothers, between husband and wife, and between father and son, standing as a surety, contracting debt, and acting as a witness are not recorded [as permissible] so long as they remain undivided. (2.52)

It is not prescribed by the *Smṛtis* that brothers and others should act as sureties for one another or perform similar duties while their wealth remains undivided; rather, such acts are expressly prohibited. The term *dampatī* (husband and wife) refers to the couple (*jāyāpatī*). *Prātibhāvya* is the state of being a surety (*pratibhū*). A surety is one who undertakes to provide assurance through his appearance or to pay a debt. *Ṛṇa* (debt) is well known. *Sākṣya* is the state of being a witness (*sākṣin*). Here, the mention of "undivided" applies to the case of brothers or to that of father and son, but not to the case of husband and wife. For there is no division of property between them; indeed, the wife is the mistress of the husband’s wealth simply by virtue of being his wife. Therefore, the common property of a husband and wife cannot be divided. For this very reason, Āpastamba states: [655] "There is no division of property between husband and wife, for from the taking of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*) they become partners in religious rites, as well as in the fruits of merit and in the possession of property. Thus says Nārada.
Brothers who have divided their inheritance may act as witnesses, stand surety for one another, and engage in giving or receiving gifts; those who have not divided may not do so among themselves.
And these transactions regarding their own property proceed among them in the world;
one should recognize those who have been divided even without a written document. (2.52)
He states the specific types of surety and the specific consequences thereof:
"Surety is ordained for appearance, for confidence, and for payment;
but in the event of failure, the first two must pay, while the sons of the latter must also pay. (2.53)

The role of a surety (*pratibhū*) is prescribed in matters of appearance, confidence, and payment. Among these, if the sureties for appearance and confidence prove false—that is, if they are found to be in default—then those two must cause the debt in dispute to be paid to the creditor. However, as for the surety for payment, if he proves false—that is, if he defaults—he himself must pay; and in his absence, his sons must pay. Bṛhaspati says: "In the scriptures, wise men have observed four types of sureties: for appearance, for confidence, for payment, and likewise for the delivery of the debtor's property."
One says, "I shall produce him," and another, who is a witness, says the same;
both must be made to pay the wealth that was previously declared, even if their testimony proves false at first.
But in case of a disagreement, those two [elders] are the authorities; in their absence, it is likewise their sons.

Kātyāyana says: For the purpose of a gift, attendance, trust, dispute, or an oath, one must certainly cause a surety (lagnaka) to be given, according to the circumstances; otherwise, it shall be reversed.

"Attendance" means appearing in person. "Dispute" means legal litigation. "Oath" refers to a divine ordeal. "Delivery" and "confidence" are well known. In these matters, one should compel the guarantor (*lagnaka*) or surety (*pratibhū*) to pay the amount in dispute. Likewise:
"If the surety for appearance does not produce the person at the proper place and time, he shall bear the liability there, except in the case of an act committed by the king."
A security (nibandha) consisting of property must be provided. Likewise:
"But for the purpose of searching for what has been lost, the debtor shall be made to pay after a maximum of three fortnights;
if he produces it there, the surety shall be released."
Likewise:
"But he who, having taken a pledge, remains [in hiding] from the sight [of the creditor],
his son shall be made to pay that debt there, once he has been identified by the plaintiff."

If one who, having taken a pledge from a debtor and having agreed to act as a surety for appearance, dies, his son—having established that "your father acted as a surety preceded by the taking of a pledge"—must be made to pay the disputed sum by the plaintiff; the meaning is that he should be made to act in such a way that he pays. Bṛhaspati states: "The creditor shall grant time for the search of what is lost to the surety, according to the place, the journey, and the form [of the debt], for a fortnight, a month, or even half a month."
They should not be excessively oppressed; rather, they should be made to pay the debt gradually.
They may be employed as witnesses against themselves; such is the rule for sureties.

If, out of a sense of propriety, those of dull intellect should pay a debt even though they have not been formally instructed, they shall by no means recover that for which they were made to pay it. (2.53)

Where a guarantor for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) or a guarantor for confidence (*prātyayika*) has died, their sons shall not pay the debt; however, those who stand as sureties for payment (*dāna*) must pay it. (2.54)

A *prātyayika* is a surety for confidence. This is a restatement intended to exclude the grandson; therefore, the grandsons of a surety for payment (*dānapratibhū*) need not be made to pay. And Vyāsa has said:

"The grandson shall pay the debt of his grandfather, and the son shall pay that which arose from suretyship; however, it is the settled rule that the sons of those two [the grandson and the son] need not be made to pay."

One should pay the paternal debt in its entirety, free from interest. Likewise, the son of a surety must pay what was occasioned by his father's suretyship. The sons of these two—the grandson of the debtor and the grandson of the surety—are not liable to pay the debt or that which arose from suretyship. Kātyāyana states:
"That which arose from suretyship need not be paid by grandsons at any time;
however, a paternal debt must always be paid by the son in its full amount."
A debt incurred through becoming a guarantor must be paid by the son in all cases equally; the meaning is that it need not be paid by grandsons. (2.54)
If there should be many sureties who pay the debt with their own respective shares, then among those who have resorted to a single liability, the creditor may act according to his pleasure. (2.55)
