When many persons stand as sureties for one individual, they shall pay the debt to the creditor according to their respective shares. When they have resorted to a single shadow—that is, when each has individually assumed the obligation to pay the entire amount as an alternative—then it must be paid according to the creditor’s wish; the meaning is that whichever among them the creditor demands, he shall pay. Those who have resorted to a single shadow are called *ekacchāyāśritāḥ*, meaning those who each individually have taken on the likeness (*sādṛśya*) of the debtor. (2.55)
He states what must be done by debtors when there is a surety:
"Where a surety, having been compelled, has paid the money to the creditor publicly, the debtors must pay him twice that amount; it shall become his. (2.56)

In a legal proceeding where a surety publicly, in the presence of people, pays the debt due from the debtor to the creditor, in that case the debt must be paid by the debtors at double the amount. The plural number in "by the debtors" (*adhamarṇaiḥ*) is intended to be significant. Nārada says:
"Whatever sum the surety may pay when pressured by the creditor, the debtor shall cause the surety to be reimbursed for that amount doubled."
Because of the statement "if [the debtor] is oppressed," it should be paid equally even to one who is not oppressed. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
"Whatever was given for whose sake by whom, having been requested according to rule, the surety shall receive that once he has been proven by witnesses."
Likewise:
"But he who, being pressured by those in distress, gives a surety, shall be entitled to receive double the amount of that object after three fortnights have passed. (2.56)

Since a doubling of the amount would otherwise apply in all cases when the time limit has expired, the author states that one should pay to the surety that maximum interest which has been prescribed for each specific kind of property:
"Offspring [is the interest] on women and cattle; grain becomes tripled; clothing is declared to be fourfold; and liquid substances are traditionally held to become eightfold. (2.57)

Those female animals, such as cows, buffaloes, and so forth, which have been given by a guarantor to a creditor, must be returned by the debtor to the guarantor along with their offspring, for as long as they have produced progeny. The rest is clear. 2.57.

Since the surety (*pratibhū*) is a cause for the creditor's confidence, as well as the pledge (*ādhi*), the author begins the section on pledges immediately following the section on sureties, as it is a related topic. Regarding that, Nārada first defines the nature of a pledge:
"That which is employed [as security] is known as a pledge (*ādhi*); it should be understood as being of two kinds:
one to be removed at a fixed time, and likewise one held until the debt is paid."
Furthermore, it is said to be of two kinds: that which is to be concealed (gopya) and likewise that which is to be enjoyed (bhogya).

In this regard, when such a period has elapsed, a pledge (*ādhi*) made for a fixed time to be redeemed—on the understanding that "after this time has passed, he shall be released by me upon payment of the debt; otherwise, he remains yours"—is one that must be redeemed once the time is reached. Likewise, a pledge made for as long as the debt is not paid is one that lasts until the amount due is offered. Each of these is further of two kinds: movable and immovable. Regarding these, the author states both conditions under which the status of a pledge is lost and how ownership reverts to the creditor (*uttamarṇa*):
"If the debt becomes double and the pledge is not released, the pledge is forfeited. (YDh 2.59ab)
That which is produced by time may perish with time, but that which is to be enjoyed as its fruit does not perish.

The pledge (*ādhi*) has been defined above. When the condition of failing to pay the interest arises and the principal has doubled, if the debtor does not redeem it by paying that amount, then it shall be lost; it shall no longer belong to the debtor, but rather shall belong to the creditor alone—this is the meaning. However, as for that pledge made for a fixed period (*kālakṛta*), which is to be released at the expiration of that time, if it is not redeemed by the debtor when the agreed time arrives, it shall be lost as previously stated. But a pledge to be enjoyed for its produce (*phalabhogya*) shall never be lost; rather, the creditor must enjoy only the produce generated until his own principal is recovered. On this point, Vyāsa says:
When gold has doubled and the stipulated time has expired,
the creditor becomes the owner of the pledge after waiting for fourteen days.
Therefore, having paid the interest in the interim, the debtor shall recover the pledge.
Bṛhaspati: A pledge for custody, once it has doubled in value and the stipulated time has expired according to rule,
may immediately thereafter be enjoyed after having notified the debtor's family.
One should also cause a drawing of the site to be made, specifying the time limit for that period.
Kātyāyana states: Where the depositor is not present, the owner shall report the pledge [to the court];
it is the settled rule that it may then be publicly proclaimed by the king as "for sale."
Having taken the amount together with the interest, he should then hand over the remainder to the king.
When a pledge consisting of a cow or other animal has been used for its milk or labor, no interest shall accrue; likewise, no interest is due if it is damaged or lost.
If the animal perishes or is destroyed, except by act of God or the king, the owner must provide another of equal value. 2.59.

In the case of a pledge (*ādhi*) that is to be kept secret—such as cattle, buffaloes, clothing, gold, silver, and so forth—if the creditor (*uttamarṇa*) makes use of it for riding, milking, ornamentation, or other purposes, no interest accrues; the meaning is that the principal sum lent does not increase. Likewise, in the case of a pledge that yields a benefit, such as land whose fruits are enjoyed, if it is neglected and allowed to deteriorate, the rule "no interest accrues" applies. Here, "deterioration" (*hāni*) means its incapacity to perform its intended function. This refers to cases where the debtor (*adhamarṇa*) consents to the use of the pledge or to the payment of interest. If the pledge is lost or destroyed by either party through no act of God or the king, it must be restored to the debtor by the creditor. "Lost" (*naṣṭa*) means transformed or altered; "destroyed" (*vinaṣṭa*) means ruined, stolen, or carried away. Bṛhaspati says: [659] (The text continues with Bṛhaspati’s verse.)
When the enjoyment has been consumed and its essence exhausted, a loss of the principal arises;
in such a case where a great value has been lost, one should satisfy the debtor.

Vyāsa states: If a pledge consisting of gold or other valuables is lost due to the fault of the receiver, the debtor must clear the debt along with the interest; the creditor shall then be made to pay its value.
The creditor is the one who receives [the pledge]. "Bandha," "bandhaka," and "ādhi" have the same meaning. Kātyāyana states:
"If one should cause labor to be performed on a pledge against its will and without permission, that enjoyer shall be made to pay the fruit of the labor, or he shall not receive the interest."
This concerns the subject matter of intention, form, and additional property. Nārada says:
"If [the object] is destroyed, there shall be loss of the principal, except in cases caused by fate or the king.
Manu says:
A prudent man who enjoys a pledge without the owner's permission shall not receive interest on that very pledge, even if it is one that yields profit.
He must enjoy half the interest as compensation for that enjoyment.

This refers to the case of limited enjoyment. However, regarding the enjoyment of a pledge for great luxury, it has been stated that there is no interest. Therefore, the reduction of interest must be carried out in accordance with the degree of enjoyment. || 2.59 ||
He states the means of recovering the pledge:

"The success [of the pledge] comes from its formal acceptance; even if it is being preserved, if it has become worthless, another pledge should be provided, or the creditor shall receive his share of the wealth. (2.60)

The establishment of a pledge (*ādhi*) results from its acceptance and formal possession. Acceptance, in the case of a pledge for use (*bhogyādhi*) and the like, extends up to the point of actual enjoyment; however, in the case of a pledge for custody (*gopyādhi*), it extends up to its entry into the storehouse. Thus says Nārada: "A pledge is declared to be of two kinds: movable and immovable. The validity of both is established through enjoyment, and not otherwise."
Bṛhaspati: When a single field has been given as a pledge to two parties at the same time,
whoever should have enjoyed it first shall obtain its legal title.
For both [of them], when they arise at the same time, it would be equal.

Viṣṇu: "He who gives to another land that has been mortgaged to someone else—provided it exceeds the measure of a *gocarma* and has not been released from that person—is to be executed. If it is less than that, he shall be made to pay sixteen *suvarṇas*.
That amount of land which yields a fruit sufficient for one man to eat for a year, whether it be small or large, is what constitutes the measure of a *gocarma*."
When two men dispute over a pledge that has been deposited with them,
the victory belongs to the one whose possession has been established without force.

If that pledge, even while being guarded by the creditor, undergoes deterioration, then the principal sum together with one year’s interest must be discharged. If he is unable to do so, then another pledge must be offered by the debtor; otherwise, the creditor may take his own capital and apply it to his use. (2.60)
He states an exception to the rule that "the pledge shall be forfeited when [the debt] has doubled":

"One should cause a debt contracted by means of a personal bond (*caritrabandhaka*) to be paid with interest; one should cause a substance contracted by way of a formal agreement (*satyaṅkāra*) to be returned when it has doubled. (1.61)

That very same *caritradharma* (the law of customary conduct) applies here: whatever debt has been contracted by means of a pledge (*bandhaka*) or a mortgage (*ādhi*), the debtor shall be made to pay that, along with interest, to the creditor. The intention is that in such a case, there is no loss of the pledge. Consequently, for the debtor who does not repay the money, there is no portion of freedom from debt. Having made an agreement that "this [item] must be set aside," whatever property is first delivered is termed a *satyaṃkāra* (token of truth). If the sale fails due to the seller's own fault, he shall give double that amount to the purchaser. This has been mentioned incidentally. (2.61)
When the debtor has arrived, the pledge must be released; otherwise, he would become a thief. If the creditor is absent, he should deposit the money with a local family and recover his pledge. (2.62)

When a debtor, having first paid the money, is intent on redeeming the pledge, the creditor must take back his money and return the pledge; otherwise, the creditor shall be liable for the punishment due to a thief. The creditor is the one who employs the loan. In his absence—whether he be dead or gone abroad—the debtor, having deposited that man’s wealth with the creditor's family, may recover his own pledge. (2.62)
He states another alternative:
"Or, having its value determined at that time, it may remain there without interest.

At the time for the repayment of the debt, the pledge—its value having been fixed and determined—shall remain in the family of the lender exactly as it was, free from interest, until the arrival of the lender. Upon his arrival, the debtor shall return the pledge or its value to him. This rule applies to the case of a lender who has gone abroad.

It will be stated immediately hereafter that when the principal debt has become double the original amount, the creditor must restore that pledge to the debtor, provided the pledge is one to be enjoyed for its yield. In that regard, he now says: "Or even without the debtor, he may sell the pledge in the presence of witnesses. (2.63) This means: if the debtor or some relative of his is absent, the creditor may sell that pledge in the presence of witnesses. Thus he speaks now. "Or even without the debtor, he may sell it in the presence of witnesses. (2.63)
"From the debtor who holds the obligation," meaning in his absence; the word "or" (vā) is intended to include the absence of his kinsmen as well. [2.63]
But when the debt has doubled, then indeed the pledge must be released once the money produced from it has entered [the creditor's possession] and become double [the original loan]. (2.64)
Thus ends the section on the non-payment of debts. 3.

When indeed the principal debt has doubled and a pledge is made as a counter-security (*pratyādhi*), then you must subsist on the wealth produced from that pledge which is to be enjoyed for its fruit, until the principal debt has been subsisted upon [paid off] twice over; after that, the pledge must be returned to me. That is to say, when the amount has reached double the value of that pledge, the creditor must restore the pledge to the debtor. And thus it is said: "The pledge shall be forfeited when the debt has doubled, if it is not released."

Regarding this statement, one should not suspect any contradiction with the rule "when [the debt] has doubled," because they refer to different subjects. To explain: the rule "when the principal has doubled, the pledge is to be released" concerns the mutual agreement between the creditor and the debtor; whereas the statement beginning with "when [the debt] has doubled" concerns the pledge made as a limit for the repayment of the lent money—namely, that "the pledge shall be forfeited when [the debt] has doubled. The pledge established by the words beginning with "when [the debt] has doubled" is called a *kṣayādhi* (a pledge for loss). And such a pledge for loss is indeed established either at the commencement of the loan transaction or in its course; it serves as the limit for the loss [of the pledge]. Thus ends the section on the Recovery of Loans (*ṛṇādāna*). 2.64.

[Thus ends the third chapter, on the Non-payment of Debts, in the Aparārka, a commentary on the Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra, composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, born in the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the glorious Vidyādhara race.]
Now begins the section on deposits (*upanidhi*) in the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* with its commentary.
Since it is based solely upon mutual agreement, the legal title known as "deposit" (*nikṣepa*) is introduced.
When an object is placed in another's hand without being described and is handed over as a deposit, that is an *aupanidhika* deposit; it must be returned in exactly the same condition.

That vessel into which gold and other items are deposited is called a "container" (*vāsana*). When gold or other property situated therein is handed over to another person’s hand or similar location without specifying the nature, number, or dimensions of the substance, it should be understood as *aupanidhika* (sealed deposit). *Aupanidhika* is simply a sealed deposit (*upanidhi*). One should restore that very same thing to the depositor exactly as it was, with the seal unbroken. Regarding this, Nārada says: "That property which is deposited in another's house, separated from other goods and left unmarked, is known as *aupanidhika*."
Likewise: that which is deposited in the unfathomable and unknown ocean, one should know that as an *upanidhi*; the wise know a *nikṣepa* to be what is counted.
Bṛhaspati says: When property is deposited in another's house out of fear of kings, thieves, or enemies, or due to deception by heirs, that is proclaimed as a *nyāsa* (deposit).
That which is given unspoken, delivered at a distance, not numbered, or not pointed out,
as well as that which is marked with a seal and that which is given as a deposit (upanidhi), is so declared in the Smṛti.

Kātyāyana states: "Purchase, an object deposited while one is away, a pledge, an object sent for delivery, that which is borrowed, and that which is entrusted as part of a Vaiśya’s trade— such property is known as *upanidhi*."

*Kraya* (purchase) and *krayana* (the act of buying); in the phrase "deposited by one who has gone abroad," the mention of "having gone abroad" is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). That which is entrusted to another for the purpose of giving to someone else is *anvāhita*. That which is brought forth for the sake of ornaments and the like is *yācita* (borrowed). *Kusīda* (lending at interest) and the like constitute the livelihood of a Vaiśya; that wealth which is entrusted to another for that purpose is also *upanidhi* (a sealed deposit). Nārada says: "Furthermore, that [deposit] is said to be of two kinds: with witnesses and otherwise.
Likewise, in the event of a dispute, the means of proof for its restitution shall be the same."
The divine authority is Bṛhaspati:
"Whatever merit may accrue from giving gold, base metals, garments, and so forth,
that same merit belongs to one who protects a deposit and likewise one who has come for refuge."
Just as there is guilt for a woman in betraying her husband, or for a man in killing his son or friend, so too is there guilt for men in consuming or neglecting a deposit. (2.65)
In the same way, he states an exception for the other [the depositary]:
"He shall not be made to pay that which has been taken away by the king, by fate, or by thieves.

That deposited property (aupanidhika), if it has been seized or destroyed by the king and others, need not be paid back by the other to the depositor. "By fate" refers to events such as fire and so forth. — Nārada.

That which is lost together with the object by the receiver is lost to the giver, provided it was caused by fate or the king; this is not so, however, if it was brought about by fraud. [663] "Fraud" (jihma) means dishonesty. — Kātyāyana.
If a deposit is lost where it was placed, even though neither the king nor fate was the cause of its loss,
that loss is said to belong to the depositor together with the goods, provided they were not taken by the recipient.
Manu says:
"If [the property] has been stolen by thieves, carried away by water, or burnt by fire,
one need not pay for it, provided that he does not take anything from that [remaining estate]."

Therefore, "if he does not withhold"—meaning he does not take even a small or trifling amount from that wealth—[he is liable]. Kātyāyana states: "Whatever is lost or stolen through one's fault, that person shall be made to pay for that property with interest, except in cases caused by fate or the king."
This includes both the principal and the interest. Bṛhaspati states:

"If the depositary, through negligence or by treating it with indifference, should cause the deposit to be lost, or if he does not return it when requested, he shall be made to pay it along with interest."
If it is lost while being searched for and not returned, he shall be compelled to pay [the value] and a fine equal to that amount. || 2.66 ||

If, when the depositor has sought out and requested his deposit, the other person retains it and—despite the loss or destruction occurring through the power of fate or other causes—the depositary must nevertheless pay an amount of money equal to that to the owner, and the king must likewise cause him to pay a fine equal to that same amount. (2.66)
One who uses a deposit for his own livelihood at will should be punished by the king and made to pay that [deposit] along with interest.

That is to say, a guardian who uses a deposit (upanidhi) at will—without the permission of the depositor—and makes it his means of livelihood, shall be punished by the king and compelled to restore that property to the depositor together with interest. Kātyāyana states:
"A deposit may be reclaimed at the proper time; however, one should avoid reclaiming it when the time has passed."
One who imposes a fine out of season shall be made to pay double that fine.
If a deposit was placed out of fear of someone, it should be reclaimed once that person has passed away; however, if that person is still living, giving it back would be untimely.
This same rule applies to articles that have been borrowed, pledged, deposited, or placed in trust, and so forth. (2.67)

[Thus ends the section on deposits (upanidhi) || 4 ||] This previously mentioned rule is to be understood as applying to borrowed items and the like. The nature of borrowed items and so forth has been explained. Manu says: "He who does not return a deposit, and he who demands what he did not deposit;"
Both of them should be punished like thieves and made to pay a fine equal to that amount.
Bṛhaspati says: "He who, having taken [an object], denies it, whether by means of witnesses or by an oath..."
Having meditated upon it, one should cause the nyāsa to be performed, as well as the corresponding humility.
Manu:
Whatever deposit was made by whomsoever, and of whatever amount, in the presence of witnesses, it must be understood to be exactly that much; one who speaks falsely regarding it deserves punishment.
Speaking falsely means speaking untruthfully.
He who, when asked for it, does not return a deposit to the depositor,
shall be questioned by the judge in the absence of that depositor.
If he should practice it exactly as it was laid down and in the proper sequence,
there would be nothing therein by which he could be challenged by others.
If, however, he does not pay that gold to them according to the rule, he shall be seized himself and compelled to pay; such is the settled principle of Dharma.

Having seized that gold and its value—two pieces of gold, doubled as a fine—he should be compelled to pay it after being punished. Bṛhaspati says: "In cases where a dispute arises regarding a deposit made in secret, an ordeal is ordained as the means of proof for both parties."

The meaning is "of one out of the two. This same rule is declared to apply in the case of what has been deposited, what has been borrowed, the relinquishment of a craft, a pledge, and likewise for one who has come for refuge.

Kātyāyana says: He who, having taken a borrowed article, does not return it when asked for, shall be seized by force and compelled to give it back; and he who gives it only under threat of punishment shall likewise be made to pay.

Having restrained him by force and compelled him to perform acts such as fasting, the mediator (sthāpaka) shall cause the debtor to pay or take [the debt]. Even so, he who does not pay shall be punished by the king. Thus it is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"He who, having taken what was requested, does not give it back while speaking falsely, shall be restrained and likewise compelled to pay, or else be fined the first amercement (*pūrvasāhasa*)."

The word "vā" (or) is used for conjunction. The authority of experience (*bhukti*) has been stated, and by way of that context, [the authority] of perception (*pratibhū*) and so forth has also been stated. Thus ends the section on non-prohibition (*niṣedha*). 2.67.

Thus ends the section on deposits (*upanidhi-prakaraṇa*) in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, who was born in the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the glorious Vidyādhara race. Section Four.
[665] Now begins the section on witnesses in the Yājñavalkya-smṛti with its commentary. (Chapter 5)
Now he describes the witnesses:
"Ascetics, those of a charitable disposition, those of noble birth, speakers of truth, those for whom dharma is paramount, the upright, those with sons, and those endowed with wealth. (2.68)

Witnesses should be known as at least three in number, devoted to the performance of rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti; they are traditionally held to be either of the same caste and class as the parties, or all may serve for all classes.

"Asceticism" (*tapas*) refers to practices such as the *kṛcchra* penance or adherence to one's own duty (*svadharma*); those who possess these are [ascetics]. "Generous by nature" (*dānaśīla*) means those who give by their very disposition. "Noble-born" (*kulīna*) means those born of a virtuous lineage. "Truthful" (*satyavādin*) means those whose character is to speak of things exactly as they have been perceived. "Preeminent in dharma" (*dharmapradhāna*) means those who renounce wealth and pleasure when they conflict with dharma. Likewise, they should be untiring in the performance of rites prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*. "At least three" (*tryavara*) means having a minimum number of three; if the number is fewer, then there must be three and not less than that—this is the meaning. Witnesses of this kind are to be understood as those who are to be appointed; this is the intended sense. Furthermore, they should be appointed according to caste (*yathājāti*), without overstepping the caste of the plaintiff and the defendant; the meaning is that they should be of that same caste. This should be understood to apply when the plaintiff and defendant are of the same caste. However, if they are of different castes, it means according to the class (*varṇa*), in the order of the *brāhmaṇa* class and so forth. Or rather, all classes, beginning with the *brāhmaṇas*, may be accepted as witnesses among litigants of all various classes. On this point, Nārada says:
A witness is to be understood as one who has seen with both ears and eyes;
for the ear, it is that which another says, and for the eye, it is the performance of an action.

The "direct perception" (*samakṣadarśana*) refers to that which pertains to the subject matter of the statement a person makes when presenting a legal case; it means that which is related to the hearing of the ear. Likewise, the "direct perception" of the eye has as its object the bodily activity in the form of a legal proceeding. Manu says: "Women shall give testimony for women; twice-born men of similar status for twice-born men; virtuous Śūdras for Śūdras; and those of low birth for those of the lowest castes."
Likewise:

"Householders, those with sons, indigenous inhabitants, those born of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes, and those who understand the matter—these are fit to give testimony, but not just anyone, except in times of emergency. [666]
Nārada says: In guilds, the members of the guild shall be witnesses; in all classes, those belonging to the same class; among outsiders, outsiders; and among women, women shall be the witnesses.
Kātyāyana says: The Guru spoke concerning those who bear sectarian marks, guilds and corporations, merchant associations, and others, as well as whatever other groups exist within assemblies.
For each of the groups— slaves, wandering performers, wrestlers, and those who live by elephants, horses, and weapons—
there were leaders and troop commanders.
Their dispute is among their own groups; those belonging to those groups are the witnesses.
Prajāpati says:
Witness is to be known as being of two kinds—one formal (kṛta) and the other informal (akṛta).
That which is recorded in writing is to be known as formal; that which is not so recorded is called informal.
Nārada: Eleven kinds of witnesses are seen in the scriptures by the wise;
among them, five are said to be appointed and six are unappointed.
The written witness, the reminded witness, the incidental witness,
the secret witness, and the corroborating witness— thus the witness is declared to be of five kinds.
Six kinds of witnesses have been proclaimed by the learned;
furthermore, three types of witnesses are declared to be those who are not specifically designated.

The village headman, the presiding judge, and the king shall be involved in the affairs of litigants; so too shall anyone who is present within the precincts of the case or has been dispatched by the plaintiff.
In disputes concerning water-channels and their boundaries, they too shall be witnesses.
Bṛhaspati says: The written, the recorded, the secret, the reminded, the hereditary, the messenger, the incidental,
the respondent, and another who is present within the matter itself.
The king, the official, and likewise the village headman are recorded as twelve kinds of witnesses;
I shall explain their distinctions correctly and in due order.
He by whom one's own [name], that of one's father, and the place of residence have been recorded, including [one's] caste and name, should be known as a witness designated as "written."
Having performed an act of cognition through various types of action— such as lending money and so forth—
that which is recorded in writing while it is still present before one's eyes is called "documentary evidence" (lekhita).
But he who is made to hear the statement regarding a debt while separated by a wall,
and who denies it as it actually occurred, is called a hidden witness.
He who is summoned and made a witness in matters such as debts, deposits, and transactions,
and who is repeatedly reminded, is declared to be a "reminded" (smārita) witness.
One who is employed in the distribution of shares, in trade, or as a kinsman,
and who is impartial toward both parties, is proclaimed as a *kulya* by those who know the Dharma.
He who, having been sent, listens to the statements of both the plaintiff and the defendant,
being approved by both and being virtuous— he is declared to be a messenger (*dūtaka*).
But when a duty is being performed, whoever comes of his own accord and says,
"You are our witness in this matter," he is called an incidental witness (yādṛcchika).
Where a witness departs for another direction, or where one who is about to die does so in due order,
and causes another to hear [the testimony], one should know that person to be a subsequent witness (uttara-sākṣin).
He whose confidence is placed by both parties and to whom their business is also disclosed,
should be known as a secret agent stationed within the midst of the undertaking.
Whatever statement has been heard by the king himself from the plaintiff and the defendant,
that alone shall be the witness in case of a disagreement between the two.
But when a legal case has been decided and a new trial should take place, the presiding judge, together with the members of the court, shall act as witnesses therein; it cannot be otherwise.
Where something has been stolen or destroyed on all sides of a boundary,
the village itself shall undoubtedly be the witness to the matter.
Kātyāyana says: Where the arrival of the opposing litigants from a foreign land is impossible,
one should cause documentary evidence or witnesses sent by those learned in the three Vedas to be presented there.

When litigants traveling abroad arrive in a hostile country where entry is forbidden, they should present as witnesses the document sent by the members of the court (*sabhyas*) who are learned in the three Vedas (*traividya*). The meaning is that, having ascertained the contents of the document, the witnesses should speak in the presence of a person dispatched by the court members. Thus ends the section on witnesses. (2.68, 69)

Then he speaks regarding those who are incompetent witnesses: "Women, children, the elderly, gamblers, those intoxicated, the insane, those accused of crimes, performers, heretics, forgers, and those with impaired faculties. (2.70)

An outcast, a relative, one interested in the matter, an associate, an enemy, a thief, one who commits violence, one whose fault has been observed, and one who has been expelled—these are not competent witnesses. (2.71)

Women, children, and others are non-witnesses. Since they are not included among those prescribed [as witnesses], their status as non-witnesses is already established; however, this specific statement is intended to indicate that when a prescribed witness is unavailable, those other than the prohibited persons may serve as witnesses. An "accused" (*abhiśasta*) is one who has been charged with being an evildoer. A "stage-player" (*raṅgāvatārī*) is an actor and the like. A "heretic" (*pāṣaṇḍī*) is one who follows a tradition based on a *smṛti* that does not have the Veda as its source. A "forger" (*kūṭakṛt*) is one who produces false weights and the like. An "intimate" (*āpta*) is one related by ties of Brahmanical or matrimonial kinship. A "violent person" (*sāhasī*) is one who acts with force or arbitrariness. One "of proven vice" (*dṛṣṭadoṣa*) is a thief and the like. A "despised" (*nirdhūta*) person is one censured by the learned. The rest is well known. — Nārada.
For even one who is not a witness is seen by the wise in the treatises to be of five kinds:
[the witness] by word, by fault, by division, by self-accusation, and by dying in the interval.

Since a conflict of testimony among witnesses in a legal dispute may arise from their being learned Vedic scholars (on one side) or from their perceiving guilt in a thief (on the other), there may be a disagreement due to such a division.
A "self-accuser," however, is one who, not being designated as a witness, comes of his own accord and speaks;
he is considered equivalent to one who dies after the claimant has departed, or one who is on the verge of death, unless he had been previously informed of the suit.
Vedic scholars, ascetics, the elderly, and those men who have renounced the world are not witnesses; no reason for this has been stated here.
Thieves, violent men, the fierce, gamblers, and likewise kinsmen.
They are not witnesses because they have been seen; truth does not exist in them.
Ascetics, forest-dwellers, slaves,
deceitful persons, the impure, the elderly, women, children, and those who subsist by driving carts;
the intoxicated, the insane, the heedless, the afflicted, gamblers, and village priests.
The deceitful, the fraudulent, the wheelwright, the potter,
long-distance travelers, sea-faring merchants, renunciants,
and the sick; couples, a single Vedic scholar, those devoid of proper conduct, eunuchs, and actors.

Atheists, those who have abandoned the Vedic way of life, those who have forsaken their wives and sacred fires, those who officiate at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, those who live together as companions, and those who are unrelated kinsmen; [these are excluded].

Those who have previously been seen to be defective, snake-charmers, those who live by poison, snake-catchers, those afflicted by disease, fire-worshippers, debtors, Śūdras, outcasts, and those who commit heinous crimes;
Those exhausted by reckless acts, those weary, those driven out, and those who have reached the lowest state—

these "lowest-state" persons are those born of inverse unions (pratiloma). Furthermore, there are those of broken conduct, those who have returned [to the fold], the dull-witted, oil-pressers, and Pāuṣikas.
A seller of cooked food;
one possessed by spirits; those who incite kings, cause droughts, or predict the positions of the stars;
one who proclaims misfortune; one who sells himself; one with deficient limbs; and one who lives by the profession of a *baka* (or *bhaga*).
One with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one with white leprosy, a betrayer of friends, a rogue, a vintner, a magician, a hunter, a fierce person, and those who oppose guilds or corporations.
A murderer, a painter, a naked ascetic, one who has fallen from his caste, a forger, a cheat, one who has been defeated in a lawsuit, a thief, and a royal officer.
A Brahmin who sells human beings, poison, meat, bones, honey, milk, water, or clarified butter, as well as a twice-born man who is a usurer;
One who has fallen from his own duty, a member of a guild, an informer, a servant of the low, one disputing with his father, and a creator of dissension— these are non-witnesses.
But if someone within groups such as guilds should become an object of hatred, he may be called as a witness by them; yet all of them would be his enemies.

A sea-merchant is one who travels by sea. One who is afflicted is one on the verge of death. A pair consists of two; one is well-known. A *klība* is a eunuch or one lacking vigor. An actor (*kuśīlava*) is a dancer. A *śailūṣa* is a mime. One who lives by poison is a seller of poison. A snake-catcher is an *ahituṇḍaka*. A poisoner is one who administers poison. A *kīnāśa* is a plowman. One who is exhausted is one who is weary. One who is cast out is one who has been expelled. An *antyāvasāyin* is one born of a reverse-order union. One of broken conduct is one of evil behavior. A *paupika* is a seller of soups and the like. A slanderer is one who utters curses. One who lives by his wife is one who makes his wife a prostitute for his own livelihood. A *śauṇḍika* is a seller of liquor. [Thus says] Kātyāyana.
Furthermore, those who live by their profession, those who perform services for them,
their kinsmen, friends, servants, and trusted associates are not to be witnesses.
The daughter of a maternal aunt, the husband of a sister,
the father, a kinsman, a paternal uncle, a uterine brother’s son, and a maternal uncle— these are indeed to be honored as those with whom one may intermarry.
These are declared to be "sapindas" (blood relations); one should not employ them as witnesses. Nor should kinsmen, relatives by marriage, nor the husband of a sister.
The father, a kinsman, a paternal uncle, a father-in-law, and likewise teachers,
as well as those appointed to positions within cities, villages, and districts.
And those royal officers, being devoted to you, would not ask about your beloved ones.
Likewise: "Among witnesses who have been written down or specified by the plaintiff,
if even one of them speaks otherwise, all are not valid witnesses because of their disagreement."
Likewise:
"One person should not cause another who has been made a witness by someone else to testify;
in his absence, however, either a commissioned official or a relative may cause him to testify."
Thus end the non-witnesses. 2.70, 71.
Even a single person who knows the law may be a witness if he is approved by both parties.

That is to say, if one who knows the law is approved—that is, authorized—by both the plaintiff and the defendant, he may serve as a witness even if he is alone. In the absence of anyone approved by both, however, there must be at least three witnesses possessing the characteristics previously described.
In cases of adultery, theft, verbal or physical assault, and acts of violence, everyone is a witness.

Adultery (*saṃgrahaṇa*) means illicit intercourse with another's wife. Theft (*caurya*) is well known. Assault (*pāruṣya*) consists of both verbal and physical violence. Regarding acts of violence (*sāhasa*), Manu says:
"Killing a human being, theft, violating another's wife," and so forth.
Harshness and both [of these] constitute the fourfold category of violence (sāhasa).

In the context of the phrase "theft, verbal abuse, and *sāhasa*," the term *sāhasa* is intended to refer specifically to the killing of a human being, and not to theft and the like, because those have already been mentioned by their own specific names. Furthermore, the word *sāhasa* does not denote theft and so forth in general, but rather a particular instance thereof. As Nārada states:
"Whatever act is performed impulsively by those arrogant of their strength, that is declared to be *sāhasa*; here, *saha* is said to mean strength (*bala*)."

Therefore, even in cases of *sāhasa* (violent crimes) such as theft and the like, the separate mention of *sāhasa*, theft, and so forth is for the purpose of prescribing that everyone may serve as a witness. The meaning is that everyone is a witness, not only those who possess virtuous qualities (*guṇavān*). However, even in those cases, one who possesses defects (*doṣavān*) must certainly be excluded, because the defects of the speaker are a cause for the invalidity of the testimony. Kātyāyana states:
"In cases of conflict with the king's command, in matters of seizure, in violent crimes (*sāhasa*), and in theft and verbal assault, one should not examine the witnesses. [671]
"In cases of violations or breaches of the king's command"— this is the meaning.
"Whatever occurs within the inner apartments, at night, or outside the village—
if the legal action concerns these very matters, one should not examine the witnesses."
Manu says:
"Whoever, being an eyewitness, should give testimony for litigants within a house, in a forest, or even in a matter involving the loss of life;"
In the absence of women, the task may be performed by an elder,
or by a disciple, a kinsman, a slave, or even a hired laborer.

An *anubhāvī* is one who has personally witnessed [the event]. It should be understood that in this context, only those such as women who are free from defects such as corrupt intent are eligible to serve as witnesses. Uśanas states:

"A slave, a blind man, a deaf man, a leper, women, children, the elderly, and so forth—even these are considered witnesses in cases of violence (*sāhasa*), provided they are not otherwise disqualified."
"Unconnected" means being devoid of the relationship of friend or enemy.
Those who have been designated as non-witnesses— such as slaves, rogues, and so forth—
may also become witnesses if the gravity of the case requires it.
Among them, neither a child, nor one who is alone, nor a woman, nor a forger,
nor a kinsman, nor an enemy shall give false testimony.
A fool may testify falsely through ignorance; a woman, through lack of truthfulness; a forger, through the habit of sin;
kinsmen, out of affection; and an enemy, for the sake of revenge.

This being the case, it is precisely those defects that cause a statement to lack authority which must be avoided. However, when their absence is ascertained, even children and the like are to be accepted; thus, there is no contradiction with the statement prescribing children and others as witnesses. For it has been declared: "One should challenge witnesses only when defects exist;
a litigant who challenges those who are faultless deserves a penalty equal to the claim."
"Equal to that" means equal to the punishment for false witnesses. Kātyāyana states:
"One should not invalidate a means of proof with a groundless defect;
in the case of a false accusation, there shall be punishment, and one is deprived of the matter to be proven."

Indeed, those defects of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) which are hidden must be stated by the disputant, whereas those that are manifest must be pointed out by the members of the assembly (*sabhyas*) at the proper time through the citation of authoritative treatises (*śāstra*). [672] The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: when a means of knowledge is employed with the intention that it be a valid means of knowledge, its hidden defects must be stated by the disputant, while its manifest defects must be stated by the members of the assembly. Bṛhaspati states the time for pointing out the defects of the means of knowledge:
Whatever defects of a written document there may be, as well as those attributed to witnesses, must be stated at the time of the trial; one should not raise them after they have already been spoken.
Vyāsa: Whether it be well-known among the members of the assembly or even established in common worldly usage,
the disqualification of witnesses is to be accepted, for it cannot be remedied by the absence of fault.

The refutation of the "unprovable" is itself unprovable, because it is free from defects; that is to say, because that which is established by court members and that which is established by common worldly consensus are devoid of defects. Others, however, argue: "If the proof were to be refuted by other witnesses, there would be the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), since for those [later] witnesses, others could also exist."
Bṛhaspati: In a legal dispute, if either the documents or the witnesses are found to be tainted,
the case of that party shall not be adjudicated until they have been cleared of suspicion.
When there is corruption among witnesses, the purification of the witnesses must first be carried out;
once the witnesses have been purified, one should thereafter purify the case itself.
Vyāsa:
The defendant must set forth all the defects of the witnesses in court;
having recorded them all in writing, they must then be stated as rebuttals.
They can never serve as witnesses regarding the performance [of an act];
therefore, they must be treated otherwise by the defendant through the legal procedure.
If he fails to prove his case, the defendant must clearly be compelled to pay the witnesses;
those witnesses who have been proven [to be false] are to be excluded, having been disqualified from the duties of witnesses.

If the plaintiff is free from further desire and remains established in the truth of the witnesses, the defeated party should be made to pay with humility by means of the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.

"One who fails to establish [the truth] regarding the witnesses shall be made to pay a fine"—this means that the defendant, for failing to prove the witnesses or for failing to admit their fault, shall be made to pay a penalty. Witnesses who have been "vindicated" (*bhāvitāḥ*), meaning their fault has been admitted, are to be excluded. This being the case, when the respondent has no further expectation regarding other means of proof, he is then defeated and liable to punishment. Kātyāyana states: "He by whose greed false witnesses were appointed—having seized all his property, one should thereafter banish him from the realm."
But he who, after the matter has been stated, should impeach witnesses who were previously unimpeachable, and cannot state the reason for doing so, shall incur the first amercement. (2.72)
He states the rule for hearing the witnesses:
"He should cause the witnesses to hear [the charges] while they stand in the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant.
The judge should cause the witnesses to hear [the case] in the vicinity of both the claimant and the respondent. (Manu).
In the presence of the gods and Brahmins, the twice-born witness, being himself pure, should question the pure witnesses in the forenoon, while they face either north or east.
Anticipating the question "What should he cause to be heard?", he says:
"And those worlds of the sinners, as well as those of the great sinners. (2.73)
Whatever worlds belong to those who set fire to dwellings and to those who kill women and children—all those he attains who gives false testimony. (2.74)
Whatever merit you have performed throughout hundreds of previous births,
know that all of it belongs to him whom you defeat through falsehood.

This has been explained by the preceding words. Here, although it may appear at first glance that the merit accumulated over hundreds of births by false witnesses goes to the defeated litigant, nevertheless, that should not be accepted as such. For Vedic injunctions such as "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra" teach that dharma bestows its fruit upon the agent. To avoid contradiction with those [injunctions], it is said—"Whatever merit you have"—and so forth, merely for the purpose of intimidating the witnesses. Therefore, Nārada says:
One should also greatly terrify him by means of ancient declarations of dharma, by proclaiming the greatness of the assembly, and by censures against falsehood.

Thus he spoke. Furthermore, those Smṛti statements which are not in contradiction with the Śrutis are indeed authoritative. To this effect, Nārada himself said: "False witnesses shall dwell in the Avīci hell for a kalpa. Bṛhaspati [said]:
One who speaks falsehoods for personal gain, a false witness, and a killer of a Brahmin are considered equal.

And so forth. For this very reason, in the section on penances (*prāyaścitta-prakaraṇa*), Manu prescribes the penance for killing a Brahmin for those who give false testimony, stating: "Having spoken a falsehood in witness-deposition, and having committed the murder of a woman or a friend... (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.229). This censure is directed specifically against Śūdra witnesses, not against the twice-born (*dvija*). Therefore, Manu says:
One should say "Speak" to a Brāhmaṇa; "Speak the truth" to a king; to a Vaiśya, [one should say] "With cattle, seed, and gold"; but to a Śūdra, with these very sins.
Whatever worlds are ordained for those who slay Brahmins, for those who kill women and children,
for the betrayer of friends, and for the ungrateful— those same worlds shall be yours if you speak falsely.
Whatever merit and auspiciousness you have performed since birth, O gentle one,
all of that would go to a dog if you were to speak otherwise.
If you consider yourself, O Kalyāṇa, thinking "I am alone," this self that dwells eternally within the heart is, moreover, the observer of merit and demerit.
Yama Vaivasvata, the god, resides within your heart;
if you have no dispute with him, then go neither to the Gaṅgā nor to the Kurus.
Naked, shaven-headed, carrying a skull-bowl, hungry and thirsty, and blind— such shall he be who gives false testimony in court, as he goes to the house of his enemy.
With his head turned downward into blinding darkness, the sinner shall go to hell—
he who, when questioned during a legal determination of dharma, speaks a falsehood in response.
Indeed, for that man speaking whom the wise Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) does not distrust,
the gods know no other person in this world to be superior to him.
Listen, O gentle one, to the sequence of kinsmen whom a witness slays by speaking falsehood in testimony, according to their number.
One kills five by lying about cattle, one kills ten by lying about cows;
one kills a hundred by lying about horses, and one kills a thousand by lying about men.
One who speaks falsehood for the sake of gold destroys both those born and those unborn;
one destroys everything by speaking falsehood regarding land. Therefore, one should never speak a falsehood concerning land.
Having considered all these faults of speaking untruth,
speak the truth directly, exactly as it was heard and exactly as it was seen.
One should treat cowherds, merchants, artisans, actors, servants,
and usurers as Śūdras, even if they are Brāhmaṇas.

Nārada says: Having summoned the witnesses, he should question them individually after restraining them with solemn oaths—those who are all of known conduct and who have knowledge of the matter. [675]
Likewise: When the witnesses have arrived within the assembly hall in the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant,
the judge shall examine them while consoling them according to this rule.
Whatever you know of the mutual conduct of these two parties regarding this matter, tell it all in truth; for your role here is that of witnesses.
A witness who speaks the truth in testimony attains abundant worlds;
he also gains unsurpassed fame in this world—this word is honored by Brahmā.
A witness who speaks falsely while giving testimony shall be bound with terrible fetters, rendered helpless for a hundred births; therefore, one should speak the truth in testimony.
For the self alone is the witness of the self, and the self alone is the refuge of the self;
do not despise your own self, the supreme witness of men.
People indeed think, "No one sees us," yet the gods see them, as does the inner person within oneself.
Heaven, earth, water, the heart, the moon, sun, fire, Yama, wind, night,
the two twilights, and Dharma are the witnesses of the conduct of all embodied beings.
Bṛhaspati says: A fraudulent court member, a false witness, and a slayer of a Brahmin are declared to be equal;
a destroyer of an embryo and a betrayer of a friend are said to be no greater than these.
Nārada said: Your ancestors hang suspended, having come to you as their witness;
will he deliver us, or will he cause us to fall?
Kātyāyana states: Witnesses must give their testimony while standing within the court, and not elsewhere;
this rule applies to all types of testimony, except in cases concerning immovable property.
Bṛhaspati says: Having removed his sandals and turban, he should raise his right hand;
taking gold, cow-dung, and darbha grass, he should speak the truth.
Kātyāyana states: "But that which is seen by those assembled together must be declared exactly as it was;
however, that which pertains to separate individual matters must be declared separately."
But when a matter is learned by witnesses at different times, one should have each individual examined therein;
for Bhṛgu has declared that such a case involves separate timings.
The testimony of those witnesses, when stated spontaneously and free from defects, is to be accepted;
once the witnesses have spoken, they must not be questioned again by the king.
Then, having examined the witnesses who have appeared, the king himself,
together with the members of the court, shall examine the statement uttered by those witnesses.
When pure action is established through reasoning, then there is the purification of that statement;
and he who is purified by a pure statement is the truly pure object, but not otherwise.
Action refers to documentary evidence and the like. Purity means the absence of any perceived defects. Nārada says:
"There are men who, out of greed, would give false testimony;
there are also other wicked men who forge false documents."
Therefore, both of these must be examined especially by the king:
the written document according to the rules for writing, and the witnesses according to the rules for witnesses.
The discernment between the fraudulent and the honest is the duty of conduct; thus says Bṛhaspati.
When they have appeared, they should be examined by means of their voice, complexion, gestures, and so forth;
thus says Nārada.
But he who, because of being corrupted by his own faults, appears as if unwell,
moves from place to place and pursues each one in turn.
He coughs violently and repeatedly for no apparent reason,
sighs deeply, scratches the earth with his feet, and frequently shakes his garments.
The color of his face changes, his forehead perspires, and his lips become parched; he gazes upward and sideways.
One who speaks excessively without being asked, as if in great haste, should be known as a false witness; one should severely punish that sinner.

Regarding one who does not speak even when summoned according to the prescribed rule, he says: "For a man who fails to give testimony regarding a debt, the king shall cause him to pay the entire debt along with a ten-percent fine on the forty-sixth day. (2.76)

He who, having accepted the role of a witness, does not state what must be said by a witness when questioned according to the prescribed rule, shall be compelled by the king to pay the entire debt along with interest, together with a fine of one-tenth (daśabandha). In this case, the one-tenth is to be taken by the king because it is a penalty; however, the debt itself is to be paid by the creditor because it is simply a debt. In this statement, only this much is enjoined: that the witness who fails to speak must pay what is due from the debtor. There is no fault for one who speaks before the forty-sixth day, because of the rule stating "on the forty-sixth day. — Bṛhaspati.
If a witness who is free from disease does not come when summoned,
he shall be made to pay both the debt and a fine after three fortnights have passed.

The inclusion of the term "free from disease" is intended as an indicator of general competence. This refers to legal proceedings concerning debts and the like. Thus says Manu: "If a man who is free from disease fails to give testimony regarding a debt or similar matters within three fortnights, he shall be liable for that entire debt and a fine of one-tenth in every case. (MDh 8.108) [677] 2.76.
Furthermore, regarding matters other than debts and the like, he states the penalty differently:
"For that lowest of men who, though knowing [the facts], does not give testimony, is indeed equal to false witnesses in his sin and also in his punishment. (2.77)

Even though he knows the truth and falsehood regarding legal transactions, that lowest of men who transgresses injunctions and prohibitions neither gives nor employs truthful testimony—which settles a dispute and consists of true speech. Since the employment of truthful speech benefits both oneself and others, it is equal to a gift; therefore, it is designated by the verb *dadāti* ("he gives"). Such a person should be understood as equal to false witnesses in terms of the sins characterized by the slaughter of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) and so forth, as well as the punishment to be described hereafter. On this point, Kātyāyana says: "If a witness does not state his testimony, he shall bear the debt and the same penalty."
Therefore, in other disputes, he deserves a fine of three hundred.
Three hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*. Viṣṇu:
"Those who, though capable of testifying, remain silent while the case is being heard, are indeed equal to false witnesses in their sin and in their punishment."

Kātyāyana states: "The time for witnesses to be summoned is when there is a full understanding of the proper procedure; however, where the testimony may be doubtful, one should have the defendant questioned in court. (2.77)
Regarding what must be done when there is a conflict among witnesses, he says:
"In case of a division, the testimony of the majority prevails; likewise, when the numbers are equal, that of those possessing superior qualities.
But when there is a division even among those of superior qualities, the testimony of those who are most excellent in virtue is to be accepted. (2.78)

When there is a conflict or disagreement among witnesses, the testimony of the majority is to be accepted as authoritative. Here, it is stated that the plurality of speakers alone is the cause for the authority of the testimony. However, when the number is equal, the testimony of those who possess qualities such as asceticism (*tapas*) and so forth is to be accepted as authoritative. When there is a disagreement even among those possessing such qualities, the testimony of those who possess them to the highest degree is to be accepted. The "highest degree" of qualities refers either to their abundance or their proficiency. On this point, Manu and Viṣṇu state: "In the event of a conflict among witnesses, the king should accept the majority."
Among equals, choose those distinguished by their virtues; where there is a conflict between virtuous men, choose the best among the twice-born.
Nārada: In the event of a conflict among witnesses, many are considered authoritative;
when they are equal in number, those who are pure should be accepted; when even they are equal, those who are more pure should be accepted. [678]
As for that which was stated by Nārada:
"When witnesses have been accepted by the king for the determination of a single matter,
if their statements should differ, they shall be non-witnesses because of that discrepancy."
Thus, it should be understood that this applies when there is equality in both number and content; for in that case, there is no removal of doubt among the listeners. (2.78)
He whose claim is supported by the witnesses shall be the victor;
for him who asserts otherwise, defeat is certain. (2.79)

The statement of the matter to be proven is the *pratijñā* (proposition). In this context, it first belongs to the plaintiff; however, because the *pratyavaskandana* (rebuttal), *prāṅnyāya* (adjudication on prior judgment), and *uttara* (reply) also have that as their primary object, they are included under the term *pratijñā*. Therefore, whichever party—whether the plaintiff or the defendant—the witnesses declare their *pratijñā* to be true, that person is the victor; but for whomsoever they declare it to be false, that person is certainly defeated. The defeat of the second party upon the victory of the one is not directly perceived from the testimony of the witnesses, but is understood only by implication (*arthāt*). On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
He whose entire claim has been corroborated by witnesses shall be the victor; otherwise, he shall not obtain the object of his suit.
One should reflect upon the entirety of what was proposed in the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa);
however, that which is stated there as deficient or excessive would not be considered properly articulated.
The mention of the "prior claim" (pūrvapakṣa) is for the sake of illustration. It has been declared and determined:
"Where one contradicts the place, time, day, number, appearance, caste, form, or age in testimony, the wise know that to be unspoken [or inadmissible]."
In disputes concerning debts and the like, which are generally of a stable nature, once a decision has been reached,
the claim is not established even if the amount stated is either deficient or excessive.
Wherever there may be a deficiency or an excess in testimony, one should reject that testimony;
in such a case, the witness should not be punished, for he deserves punishment for failing to speak.
Even when only a portion of the matter to be proved has been stated by the witnesses, the entire case shall be established;
this applies in matters of sexual intercourse, violence, and theft, as well as in whatever else has been specifically defined as the matter to be proved.
He states the reason for the difference in the authority of witnesses' testimony:
"Even when the testimony has been given by witnesses, if others who are more virtuous, or twice as numerous, should declare it otherwise, the former witnesses shall be considered perjured. (2.80)

[679] Even when a statement has been made by witnesses designated by either the plaintiff or the defendant, if those designated as opposing witnesses—who are more authoritative than the former witnesses due to being twice as many or more—should state that very matter otherwise, then the former witnesses are defeated and shall be considered false speakers. And so says Kātyāyana:
"In whatever case the matter to be proven should belong to the plaintiff according to the witnesses..."
In that case, the opponent should then perform the rite otherwise.
Or, there may be many previous witnesses who are of the same family as [the defendant].

The mention of "noble birth" (*kulīna*) is intended to indicate an excellence of qualities. Now, one might ask: how can there be witnesses in a single legal proceeding for both the plaintiff and the defendant? For it has been said:

"In a single dispute, however, there should be only one means of proof (*kriyā*) for the two parties; there is no establishment of the claim for both simultaneously, nor can there be two means of proof in one case."

True; indeed, for both parties alike, there is no attainment of the legal proceeding. What is meant by this is that when a person’s case has been decided according to the scriptures, one should recognize that decision as being false and, in order to demonstrate its falsity, present another witness. And in this regard, there is a specific rule stated in another Smṛti: "If one should consider a case as having been decided or adjudicated contrary to the law, he should impose double the fine and have that matter retried."

*Adharma* is indeed *vidharma*; therefore, from that *vidharma*, this has been adjudicated and recorded. As for the instruction regarding witness testimony: if one should think [the witnesses are false], he must impose a double fine and have that case—that legal proceeding—re-examined by other witnesses; this is the meaning. However, as stated by Vyāsa:
"But when the discrediting of previous witnesses is to be proven by other witnesses, there would be the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because others could likewise be produced."

Thus, that [rule] regarding the disqualification of witnesses is intended to mean that other witnesses should not be called; for an infinite regress would result only when there is equality among the witnesses, and not when there is a disparity in number and so forth. As for what was stated by Nārada:
"Once a legal dispute has been decided, further evidence is fruitless—whether it be a document or witnesses—if it was not previously presented."

[Thus,] when the determination of victory or defeat for the proponent or the opponent has occurred through the purification of the formal debate, he declares that the presentation of another previously mentioned means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is fruitless; however, this is not the case prior to that determination. 2.80.

He states the punishment for false witnesses: "The forger and the witnesses are each to be punished separately; the fine shall be double the amount in dispute, and it is ordained that a Brāhmaṇa shall be banished. (2.81)

[680] He who makes witnesses false by means of bribes and the like, or he who forges a document, is a "forger" (*kūṭakṛt*). Both he and the false witnesses shall each be punished individually with a fine double the amount of the property that was the subject of the dispute. However, a Brāhmaṇa is not to be fined, but rather banished from the country. This rule of punishment is to be understood as applying to cases of minor offenses and when there has been no habitual practice on the part of the forgers and others. Manu says: "Out of greed, one should be fined a thousand; out of delusion, however, the first *sāhasa*."
In cases such as fear and so forth, the middle fine is prescribed; for acts out of friendship, it is four times the previous amount.
From desire, the former [retribution] is tenfold; from anger, the latter is threefold;
from ignorance, it is two full hundreds; and from childishness, it is exactly one hundred.

These [fines] are reckoned in *kārṣāpaṇas*. Some believe that false testimony (*kūṭasākṣitva*) is of two kinds: that caused by greed and so forth, and its opposite. In that regard, they hold that the rule of punishment for false testimony caused by greed and so forth is that of Manu, whereas for the other case, it is that of Yājñavalkya. That is incorrect; false testimony is indeed caused only by greed and so forth. To this effect, Manu says: "Testimony is declared to be false because of greed, delusion, fear, friendship, desire, anger, as well as ignorance and childishness. (MDh 8.120)

Therefore, the established rule as stated is indeed logical. Greed (*lobha*) is the pursuit of material gain; delusion (*moha*) is error. Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is a lack of knowledge or partiality; childishness (*bālabhāva*) is immaturity. Likewise, having observed that the gravity or lightness of a fault depends on the specific substance involved, one should infer the same principle regarding the punishment. As it was said by Manu: "He kills five [members of his family] for lying about cattle," and so forth. Similarly:
"The king, as protector, having punished them, shall banish members of the three [lower] castes who give false testimony, but he shall exile a Brāhmaṇa."

Having punished the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriya, one should banish them from the country; however, a Brāhmaṇa should not be punished, but rather merely banished. Yet, in the case of repeated offense or when the matter is of great gravity, even a Brāhmaṇa may be punished. Viṣṇu states: "For false witnesses, confiscation of all property shall be carried out. This refers specifically to the subject of false testimony regarding land. Nārada says:
"If, within seven days of the witness giving his testimony, disease, fire, or the death of a relative should occur for him, he shall be made to pay the debt and a fine."
Having confiscated all the property of one by whose greed for a particular matter false witnesses were appointed, the king should thereafter banish him from the realm. (2.81)
He who, having been made to hear the testimony from others, conceals it, being shrouded in darkness, shall be made to pay a fine eightfold; but a Brāhmaṇa, however, one should banish. [2.82]

He who, being shrouded in darkness and characterized by *tamas*, having been duly made to hear the formal statement of questioning from the court members at the time of the trial, conceals his own testimony and witness-status from the other witnesses—denying it by saying, "I am not a witness here"—he shall be made to pay eightfold the fine for a witness. The meaning of the word "from others" (*anyebhyaḥ*) in the instrumental case is that he informs the other witnesses of his own concealment of witness-status. Since he himself first conceals his witness-status and then desires to cause others to do so as well, he is extremely wicked and must therefore be made to pay an eightfold fine. If such a person is a Brāhmaṇa, the king should banish him from his country—that is, expel him—but he should not inflict a monetary fine upon him. From the use of the word "having been made to hear," it is understood that this man had previously accepted the role of a witness. (Nārada).
He who, having caused others to hear [the testimony], then denies his status as a witness, must be punished even more severely; for he is worse than a false witness.
He states an exception to the rule that "the truth must be spoken by witnesses" in a certain case:
"In a matter where the death of those belonging to the [four] classes would result, a witness may speak untruth.
To purify himself from that, the twice-born should offer a *caru* oblation to Sarasvatī. (2.83)
Thus ends the section on witnesses. 5.

When speaking the truth would entail the execution or killing of a Brāhmaṇa or others, the witness should speak an untruth. To purify that act and remove its fault, the twice-born (but not a Śūdra) should perform four oblations dedicated to Sarasvatī. Although the killing of a Brāhmaṇa is forbidden—even for one who stands guilty of all possible crimes—one must never kill a Brāhmaṇa;
rather, one should banish him from the kingdom, leaving him with his entire wealth and unhurt.
Nowhere does a sin more base than the killing of a brahmin exist;
therefore, a king should not even contemplate his execution in his mind.
Thus, by such statements of Manu and others, the punishment is nevertheless equal to killing; as Manu has said:
"Shaving the head is prescribed as the death penalty for a Brāhmaṇa, but for the other castes, the punishment may indeed be one that ends in death."
Therefore, even punishments such as expulsion from the city are equal to execution. Thus it is stated in another Smṛti:
"For a Brāhmaṇa, there shall be execution, shaving the head, expulsion from the city, branding on the forehead, and being sent forth on a donkey."
Alternatively,
one should treat Brahmins who are cattle-herders, merchants, artisans, actors, servants, or usurers just as one would Śūdras. [682]

According to this statement of Manu, even for a specific type of Brahmin, capital punishment may be incurred in the case of a grave offense. Nor should it be argued that in the phrase "for the killing of those belonging to the [social] classes" (*varṇinām hi vadhaḥ*), the mention of *varṇa* (class) refers specifically to the Brāhmaṇa; for Manu says:
"Where the death penalty has been prescribed for Śūdras, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, or Brāhmaṇas, there one must speak untruth, for that is superior to truth."

Alternatively, this applies where a Brahmin-slaughter is committed in violation of prohibitions. Gautama states: "There is no fault in speaking a falsehood if life depends upon it, but not for the sake of the life of a wicked person. Viṣṇu says: "To purify himself from that, a twice-born man should offer oblations into the fire with the *Kūṣmāṇḍī* verses; a Śūdra should give a mouthful of food to ten cows for one day. Manu says:
"And they should worship Sarasvatī with sacrificial porridges (*caru*) dedicated to the deities of speech, effecting the supreme expiation for the sin of that untruth."

The statement "with *caru* offerings" intends to refer to a plurality of performers. Alternatively, one should offer clarified butter into the fire according to the prescribed rule with the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras,
or with the verse beginning with "ud," which is addressed to Varuṇa, or with the three-verse hymn addressed to the Waters (*ab-daivata*).

The word *ud* is the opening of the verse beginning with "Lift up the highest bond of Varuṇa from us. In the Baudhāyana Smṛti: "If the primary rite is performed otherwise than prescribed, the performer, drinking milk for twelve nights, should offer oblations with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras. (2.83)
Thus ends the section on witnesses, the fifth.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, on Witnesses, in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra*, composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, born of the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the noble Vidyādhara race.
Now begins the section on documentary evidence (*lekhyaprakaraṇa*) in the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* with its commentary. (6) Possession and witnesses have been explained; now he sets forth written evidence.
Whatever matter has been settled by mutual agreement through their own consent, a document with witnesses must be executed; in that case, the creditor's name should be mentioned first. (2.84)

Whatever matter, such as a debt or the like, has been mutually agreed upon by a creditor and a debtor according to their own will—whether in terms of its nature, amount, or rate of interest—in that regard, a document should be executed preceded by the name of the creditor and joined by the names of the witnesses. [683] Bṛhaspati states: "A royal document, one executed at a specific place, and likewise one written in one's own hand—that document is said to be of three kinds; furthermore, it is divided into many types."
A document concerning shares, gifts, purchases, agreements, slaves, debts, and so forth is sevenfold and is secular; royal edicts are of three kinds.
When brothers who have divided their inheritance among themselves by mutual consent execute a deed of partition,
that is called a *bhāgalekhya* (document of division).
But that which one makes into a document after giving land, valid for as long as the moon and sun endure—
indestructible and irremovable— that they know to be a deed of gift.
Having purchased a house, field, or the like, that document which one causes to be made, accompanied by the letters [specifying] the equal price,
is called a *krayalekhya* (purchase deed).
When one executes a document after providing movable or immovable property as a pledge,
that document, involving the acts of custody or enjoyment, is known as a mortgage-deed (ādhi-lekhya).
Whatever mutual agreement a village or a district may make for the sake of dharma or worldly affairs, provided it does not conflict with the king, they call that a "contract document" (saṃvit-patra).
If one who is destitute of clothing and food performs written work for a mendicant in the wilderness,
saying, "I shall perform this task for you," that is considered a "slave-deed" (dāsapatra).
Having received money at interest, whether one performs the transaction oneself or causes it to be done by another,
that is declared by the wise to be an *uddhāra-patra*, a document of debt.
Vasiṣṭha says: One should know that documentary evidence is of two kinds—royal and secular. Royal documents are of four types, while secular documents are of eight types.

The royal edict is to be known as the first; likewise, the next is the decree of victory (jayapatra). The document for the proclamation of a command is the fourth; thus, the royal writ is of four kinds.
The *cīraka*, the *svahasta*, the one known as the *upagata*,
the *ādhipatra* as the fourth, and the fifth is the *krayapatra*.

The sixth is called the document of recollection (smṛtipatra), the seventh is the six-fold document (ṣaṭipatraka), and likewise the document of purification (viśuddhipatraka); thus, the worldly [legal procedure] is said to be eightfold.
Having bestowed enjoyments and various kinds of jewels upon the twice-born,
the king should grant them land and provide for its protection.
It is connected with the action and its factors (kāraka), endowed with the meaning of the compound and the action;
it is characterized by the names of the month, the fortnight, the half-month, the day, and the king.

One should personally write with one's own hand the caste and other details of the recipient, their lineage, their status as a fellow student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī), as well as the location and the dimensions.
And whoever shall be the scribe there, appointed for peace and war,
being personally commanded by the king, he shall write the royal edict.
Thereafter, one should write one's own name, sealed with the royal seal;
such is the royal edict for villages, fields, houses, and so forth.
Kātyāyana states: A royal edict attains purity when it is pure in its seal, pure in its execution, pure in its enjoyment, marked with the [king's] insignia,
and authenticated by the king’s own hand.
Nārada says:
That should be known as a decree of victory which contains the entire first part, along with the subsequent portion, as well as the action taken, and the definitive conclusion.
The written document authorized by the king, having had the matter proclaimed to both parties, shall be determined by the members of the court;
thereafter, the king shall punish him according to the scriptures.
But having fined one who has received a double penalty,
he should then issue a formal document of victory (jayapatra) to the victor, exactly as it occurred.
Whatever property— whether movable or immovable— has been deposited in the middle [of the transaction],
that shall later be returned with interest to the victor, along with the document of victory.

Kātyāyana says: Once the matter has been established, the king should first honor the plaintiff and then give him a written document, signed with his own hand, which connects him with the proven fact.
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
A document of victory is held to be that which is joined with the matter to be proven as it was presented, which includes the subsequent proceedings, and which contains a definitive conclusion.
Once the matter has been settled, the judge shall give the winning litigant a certificate of victory (*jayapatra*), marked with the hand of the presiding judge and sealed with the royal seal.
Furthermore:

[A document is valid] when it is marked with the year, month, its specific purpose, the day, the name [of the parties], the caste, the lineage (gotra), the fellow-student status (sabrahmacārin), the word "one's own" (ātmīya), and the names of the fathers, and so forth. (2.85)

One should prepare that document marked with the year, month, and so forth. "Year" (*samā*) means a *saṃvatsara*. "Month" (*māsa*) refers to Caitra and the others. "Half of that" (*tadardha*) refers to the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) and the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). "Day" (*ahaḥ*) refers to the lunar date (*tithi*) beginning with the first day (*pratipad*). "Name" (*nāma*) means a designation. "Caste" (*jāti*) refers to being a Brāhmaṇa and so forth. "Gotra" is that which is common to Kaśyapa and others; that itself is "sagotra. One who practices or has studied a branch of the Veda (*brahma*) that is common to or not different from the Kaṭhas and others is a "fellow-student" (*sabrahmacārī*); the state of being such is "sabrahmacārikam.
