[685] "One's own father’s name and so forth" refers to the father’s names and so forth of the creditor, the debtor, and the witnesses. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the wealth’s caste, number, quantity, and other such details. Here, the name, caste, gotra, fellow-student status, and so forth, belong specifically to the creditor and the others. Vyāsa says:
Birth, name, residence, purpose, number, and the year;
the month, fortnight, and day—these must be recorded clearly as the evidentiary details. (2.85)
Moreover:
When the matter is concluded, the debtor shall sign it with his own hand:
"What is written above is approved by me, the son of so-and-so. (2.86)

When the matter agreed upon between the creditor and the debtor has been completed in the document, the debtor shall, with his own hand, enter—that is, write—the following: "This is the opinion of me, the son of so-and-so, that what is written here at the beginning of the upper line of this document [is correct]. (2.86)
Furthermore:
"And the witnesses, with their own hands, preceded by the name of the father, should write: 'I, so-and-so, am a witness here'"; thus they are unequal [in number]. (2.87)

Not only the debtor, but the witnesses as well, in this matter, should each write their own name with their own hand, preceded by the name of their father, stating: "I, the son of so-and-so, named so-and-so, am a witness. The meaning is that they should not be unequal, i.e., they should not be an odd number. The word "equal" (*samāḥ*) means that they are equal in number for both the plaintiff and the defendant before the king. If the debtor or a witness is illiterate, then another literate person should cause their opinion to be written down in the presence of all the witnesses. Regarding this, Nārada says:
One who is illiterate or a debtor should have his own statement recorded by another witness in the presence of all the witnesses.
The phrase "by another witness" is intended merely to indicate one who is literate; otherwise, it would serve no visible purpose. (2.87)
Furthermore:
"And at the end, the scribe shall write: 'This has been written by me, the son of so-and-so, requested by both parties; it was written by so-and-so. (2.88)
At the end of the document, the scribe shall record: "This document was written by me, [Name], the son of [Father's Name], at the request of both the creditor and the debtor. (2.88)
[686] It has been stated that a document must be executed with witnesses; he now states an exception to this rule in certain cases:
"But a document written in one's own hand is valid even without witnesses."
All that is traditionally recognized as authoritative is valid, except for that which is produced through force or fraud.

That which a debtor writes with his own hand is valid evidence even without witnesses, provided it was not made by force (*bala*) or through fraud (*upādhi*). "Force" means compulsion; "fraud" means deception. By the use of the word "even," it is implied that a document written by one's own hand is valid even if it possesses witnesses. Furthermore, that which is not written by one's own hand is valid evidence only when it possesses witnesses. One should know that documents are of two kinds: those written by one's own hand and those written by another. Among these two, validity is established by those who reside in the relevant locality.
Likewise:
"But that which is executed by force against a woman, a child, or one who is intoxicated,
as well as a document executed under fear or fraud, is invalid."

In this context, the cause of invalidity is solely the fact that [the document] was produced under fear and so forth; it is not the fact that it was produced by women and others as well. For if that were the case, even a written document prepared in accordance with the facts by women, children, and the like would be invalid. And it is not possible for something that accords with the facts to be invalid. As for the separate mention of women and others, that is for the purpose of indicating that they are frequently subject to fear and other such influences. Kātyāyana states: "A document may indeed be rendered defective due to the fault of the witnesses or the scribe; likewise, it may be so due to the fault of the creditor's fraud or the debtor's."
Bṛhaspati [states that] solely due to defects of intention:

"A document executed at night, by fraud, by force, or by one who is about to die, an infant, one who is terrified, one who is afflicted, a woman, one intoxicated, or one overcome by calamity, is not valid."
Kātyāyana states: A document written by the creditor’s own hand, even if devoid of witnesses,
shall be considered forged unless it can be demonstrated that "it was indeed executed by the maker."
If the creditor does not cause the defendant to acknowledge— meaning to believe— that "this has been written by me with your consent," then [the document is invalid].
That which is contrary to local custom, that which is ambiguous, that which lacks proper sequence,
that which was executed by one who is not the owner, and that which is devoid of a matter to be proved, is defective.
Bṛhaspati says: Where a single witness is placed who is tainted or censured, that is a forged document;
such is what the scribe also declares.

A document that is brilliant [in appearance], though written long ago; or one that is stained, though written recently; or one that is broken or contains indistinct syllables—such a document shall be considered forged.

But when letters are displaced from their positions, lack beauty, are indistinct, or have fallen away from their proper characteristics—if they remain thus, Bhṛgu declares that the writing is defective. (2.89)
Moreover:
A debt contracted by means of a written document must be paid by three generations of persons; however, the pledge is released only when that debt is not paid. (2.90)

A debt recorded in a document (*lekhya*) is to be paid by three persons: the borrower, his son, and his grandson; for it has been stated that "a debt is to be paid by the son and grandson. Therefore, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*). However, the rule beginning with "the pledge (*ādhi*), meanwhile, is enjoyed" is intended as an injunction (*vidhi*). For a debt secured by a pledge does not fall within the scope of the restriction regarding the number of persons liable. And thus, as Hārīta says: "In whose hand the document may be, to him one should assign the enjoyment [of the pledge]."

Thus it has been stated without limitation; that [statement] should be understood as referring to the subject of a pledge (*ādhi*). For, were this statement not present, the sentence "it does not perish so long as the fruit is being enjoyed" would apply only to the case of three persons; therefore, this commencement of the sentence is purposeful for the sake of excluding that [limited application]. (2.90)
Furthermore:
"If a document is located in another country, is illegible, lost, erased, stolen, torn, burnt, or likewise cut, one should have another document prepared. (2.91)

If a document is located in a difficult place, its letters are illegible, it is destroyed, its letters have been rubbed out, it has been stolen, torn, burnt, or split in two, one should cause another document to be made. Nārada says:
"When a document is deposited in another country, decayed, poorly written, or lost, there is the making of a fresh copy for that which exists;
for that which does not exist, there is the examination of witnesses."

The meaning is this: when a document exists but is located in another place, a time-limit is established for the purpose of bringing it, such as "you must produce that within this much time"; this constitutes the fixing of a time-limit. However, when the original document does not exist, a new document must be prepared after making a copy of the previous one and showing it [to the other party], so that the person who saw the former document may refute any claim of alteration regarding the second writing. Kātyāyana says:
"If a document is marred by stains, burnt, torn, or even faded, or likewise rubbed away by sweat, one should have another document executed."
Vīta means departed or gone away. || 2.91 ||
Moreover:

In the case of a disputed document, its validity may be established by means of handwriting samples such as those written in one's own hand, as well as through reasoning, acquisition, performance, signs, connection, and evidence of provenance. (2.92)

When a document is doubted regarding its validity, its purification—the removal of doubt characterized by the ascertainment of its authenticity—should occur through signs of validity such as being written in one's own hand, and through reasons such as *yukti* (presumption) and so forth. This refers specifically to a document executed in the debtor’s own hand that is devoid of witnesses; for in such a case, it is possible for the debtor to contest it, saying, "This was not written by me. In that situation, a decision is reached by means of another document written in his own hand. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the father’s name, lineage (*gotra*), and status as a fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*) is intended. Among these, *yukti* and the others serve as determinants either as direct evidence or as corroborators of other evidence within that very document. *Yukti* is presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*). *Prāpti* is the presence of the plaintiff and defendant at a particular place and time. This is a cause for purification by way of corroborating other evidence, not independently. For if they were not present together at a certain place and so on, then once it is determined that the document is invalid, the judges would have no desire even to investigate the signs of validity such as writing in one's own hand. *Kriyā* is social transaction (*saṃvyavahāra*). Where there is no mutual transaction between two people—as, for example, between an Ārya and a Draviḍa—there the possibility of validity regarding a document is ruled out by impossibility. A *cihna* is a seal. *Saṃbandha* is the prior relationship between the plaintiff and defendant based on mutual trust, involving transactions such as receipt and delivery. *Āgama* is the means of establishing the relationship between owner and property regarding the subject of dispute, such as purchase and so forth; it is the thought: "This much wealth belongs to this claimant, as it is possible for him to have acquired it through means such as purchase. *Hetu* is inference. Writing in one's own hand and the like cannot be the sole cause for the validity of a document without depending on *yukti* and the rest, because of the lack of certainty (*anaikāntikatva*). Indeed, there are clever men who can produce a document identical to one written by another person, or the identity of the father’s name and so forth may be coincidental. Vyāsa says:
Some skillful men write a written document as if it were a painting;
therefore, success based on the power of that writing is not considered absolute.
Skilled forgers, knowing the proper time and place for their work, produce a document that appears authentic; therefore, one should examine such a document with great care.

One's own kinsmen deceive women and children who are illiterate by preparing a document marked with their own names; that [deception] is to be recognized through logical reasoning and traditional authorities.
Nārada says: A document that bears another's name or has been produced for some other purpose must, in case of dispute, be examined by means of connections, provenance, and reasons. [689]

*Vipratyaya* means doubt or uncertainty. Thus, when there is doubt regarding the validity of a document written by one's own hand that lacks witnesses, the methods for purifying its validity—such as [verification by] one's own handwriting and so forth—have been stated. Kātyāyana states the means of determination even when there is doubt regarding a document that *does* have witnesses: "If it is stated by the defendant that it was not written by the scribe and likewise was not seen by the witnesses, then the document is declared to be forged."
In this way, when a case involving a wicked person is being adjudicated in the king's court,
he should deliberate together with the Brahmins and examine the defects of the written petition.
In the investigation of what has been done and what has not been done, the determination based on written documents is made by witnesses;
direct perception is never sublated by inference.
Therefore, when a document is defective, the determination regarding one's own property must be made by means of the testimony of witnesses;
for a person defiles the document themselves.

The defendant himself may invalidate a document written by himself; however, it cannot be invalidated when there are witnesses, because all defects are removed by the testimony of those witnesses. Likewise:
"One should set aside a written document by another writing, and one with witnesses by witnesses;
a document written by the defendant that lacks witnesses should be set aside by another document executed by him, but one with witnesses should be set aside by witnesses. Likewise:
In the case of false testimony, the document shall be cleared by the statements of the witnesses and the scribe;
he who does not purify it as being forged shall be made to pay the highest fine.

The meaning of this is as follows: In the case of a fraudulent statement made against a scribe, if a litigant does not establish the document's purity through the testimony of witnesses, he shall be punished with the highest amercement. However, if the scribe has met his death along with the witnesses, then [the authenticity] of that [document] shall be verified by their own handwriting and so forth; of this there is no doubt.

Likewise, even in the case of the ocean, all those who dwell therein are recorded as deceased upon such a written record; for indeed, once that document is established as authoritative, they remain so even though they have died.
"In a document accompanied by the royal seal" means in a royal edict (*śāsana*). Nārada says:
"Whatever has been shown at the proper time, whatever has been recited, and whatever has been reminded—that document is established as valid everywhere, even when the witnesses have died."

And this [statement] merely establishes the possibility of proof by means of a document; it does not, however, preclude formal investigation. As it has been said: "When there is doubt regarding a debtor’s own handwriting—whether he is living or deceased—the determination of that document is made by other documents written in his own hand."
Likewise:

A written document should be verified by another written document, and a document should be corroborated by witnesses; a document is superior to witnesses, but witnesses are not inferior to documents.
This refers to cases concerning witnesses who have been recorded but not entered [into the formal record]. Kātyāyana states:
"When witnesses are available, no divine ordeal (*daivikī kriyā*) should be administered;
likewise, when there is a written document (*lekhye*), in legal disputes there should be neither divine ordeal nor witnesses."

But when a debtor declares that a document lacking witnesses was not executed by him, and there is no means of clearing his name—such as a writing in his own hand—Hārīta states that it must be cleared by means of an ordeal: "If a debtor says, 'This document was not executed by me;
it is a forgery made by this person,' then, having set aside that document, the decision regarding the matter shall be reached through an ordeal."
Prajāpati says: When the names and lineages [of the litigants] are identical, and the form and number [of the objects] are likewise the same,
a decision in such a case where wealth has been seized must be made by means of an ordeal.

This applies when there is no document written in the witnesses' own hands and so forth. Nārada states: "If the debtor does not point out a manifest defect in a document that is suspected of being fraudulent, then after twenty years, that document shall be established as valid."

If a document is defective, how can there be possession by the holder for a period of twenty years? Thus, the meaning is that a written record whose authenticity is doubtful becomes stabilized for the purpose of countering [the need for] divine ordeals (*divya*). Vyāsa states:
"When a document executed by one person is seen in the hand of another, he must necessarily explain the provenance of that document."

The meaning is that whoever is seen to hold this document stating, "This is the writing of so-and-so; it was brought to me by him through such-and-such a means," must speak and establish its validity. Kātyāyana says:
"If a person who is capable [of asserting his rights] enjoys a property by means of a document for twenty years, that document is free from defect."

The meaning is "without divine proof. In the previous statement, however, it was said that for a defective document whose defects have not been pointed out, its validity is to be established by means of divine proof after twenty years of possession. Here, however, the establishment of the validity of a non-defective document—such as one lacking witnesses or one not written in the debtor's own hand—is stated to be achieved by possession alone over the aforementioned period; thus, there is no contradiction. Likewise: "A mortgage that has been enjoyed for twenty years is well-ascertained; the document by which that is established is valid and free from defects."
This has the same scope as the preceding [rule].
Once a boundary dispute has been settled, a boundary-deed (sīmāpatra) is prescribed;
its defects must be challenged for up to twenty years.
Where a debt instrument is recorded together with the pledge,
they know that it is valid evidence even when the enjoyment [of the pledge] has been slight, provided the witnesses are deceased.

*Ādhāna* means a pledge (*ādhi*). *Mṛtasākṣi* means that which has deceased witnesses. Nārada says: "If something has been received or if a formal agreement has been made, the document is indeed authoritative even if the witnesses are deceased."

If the creditor has received something from the debtor by virtue of the written document, or if a declaration has been made to the debtor stating, "This document exists in my possession regarding this matter," then even in the absence of witnesses recorded in the document, the document is authoritative; such is the meaning. Regarding the conflict between documents, Vyāsa states what other means of proof is required: "A document executed in one's own hand is more authoritative than a public document, and a royal edict is indeed considered even more authoritative when it comes before a court of law."
Regarding this, he states the justification:
"One who knows two or three scripts, by means of his own handiwork, drawings, and logical reasoning, can indeed produce a similar document; therefore, a local document is auspicious."

It must be supplied that a document executed by one who is skilled in drawing, proficient in writing, and knowledgeable in various scripts does not attain validity [if it is forged]. For such a person is capable of producing even an exact replica. Therefore, the meaning is that a local document is preferable.

A document that is not public, which is attested by witnesses, stamped with the scribe's signature, and well-known to the world is better than one made by another, even if the latter is auspiciously composed.
Where a document concerning the local population has been executed by a provincial governor or similar official,
whether at the same time as or after the king’s own document, the royal document therein is the authoritative one.

Between those performed at the same time and those performed later, that which is performed by the king alone is distinguished as superior. Saṃvarta says: "In a written document, the legal act is declared to be written; in a verbal matter, it is considered verbal.
But in a verbal matter, that action which is based upon a written document shall not be established."
Testimony that is contrary to what is written in a document is called fraudulent;
for it is a gateway to unrighteousness, and therefore the king should avoid it.
If the efficacy of syllables is obstructed by verbal [impediments],
there would be the total destruction of ritual actions and an infinite regress would arise.
The meaning is that testimony which contradicts a written document must be rejected. Regarding "actions," this refers to documentary actions. Kātyāyana states:
"A written document is never invalidated by ordeals or even by witnesses;
the rule of documentary evidence is always superior, for it cannot be subverted by anything else."

The execution of a written document should always be set aside by means of a counter-document containing the same reasoning or one that is superior to it; it should never be overturned by witnesses or oaths.

Bṛhaspati: When a person who is capable does not request a debt from one who is wealthy and nearby, that document— due to the suspicion that it may be a mere claim for a pure debt— shall become weak in legal force.
A document that is pure, given,
and more than thirty years old, which has neither been seen nor heard by [the parties],
does not attain validity, even though witnesses may still exist.
But when a peaceful settlement has been reached, he who does not produce the written document nor demand it from the debtor shall incur doubt regarding that matter.

The meaning is that when money has been lent at a fixed rate of interest, and the interest has ceased upon the repayment of the principal, if one neither presents the document nor demands payment from the debtor, that document shall incur doubt regarding its validity. Nārada says:
"Where the witnesses, the creditor, the debtor, and the scribe have died, that document is also invalid, unless there is a mortgage as a stable basis."
The basis [of validity] is enjoyment, because it does not depend on being subject to measurement. Vyāsa states:
A document that has not been seen or heard, one where the creditor or debtor is deceased, and one that lacks a pledge or a guarantor, does not remain valid for a long period of time.
"Of long duration" means lasting for a long time. Bṛhaspati says:
"The written document of those who are insane, dull-witted, or children; of those fleeing from fear of the king; and of those who are timid or afflicted by fear, shall not suffer invalidation. (2.93)
Regarding what must be done when the matter has been brought to a conclusion, he says:
[693] Having paid the money, the debtor, or the creditor upon the arrival of the debt, should write on the back of the document, marked with his own hand. M. 8.173; Y. 2.93.

When the debtor returns the debt little by little according to his capacity, then as much as has been paid should be recorded on the back of the document. Alternatively, the creditor may give a receipt marked with his own hand to the debtor; after writing "this much has been returned by him," it is called an *upagata*. Nārada says: "Having received the *upagata*, the creditor shall give the debtor a receipt (*udaya*);
but if, when requested, he does not give it, he shall incur the loss of the remainder."
That which was ordained by the rule, "The debtor shall be made to pay gradually according to his income" (2.93).

One should tear up a document that has a false appearance, or cause another to be made for the sake of purification; or whatever [document] possesses witnesses, that should be given back along with witnesses. (2.94)

Having paid the debt along with interest to the creditor, the debtor should tear or break the written document. If, however, it is lost or too far away and cannot be torn, then for the sake of purification—that is, to establish his freedom from debt—he should obtain a document from the creditor in the presence of witnesses. In this way, he should discharge the debt before many witnesses who are more numerous than those previously involved. On this point, Nārada says: "When the debt is cleared, he should give back the document; in its absence, a receipt.
In this manner, there shall be mutual purification between the creditor and the debtor."
By the word *pratiśrava*, the hearing of the witness is intended. || 2.94 ||
Thus ends the definition of a written document.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, on Documents, in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra*, composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, born of the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the noble Vidyādhara race.
Now begins the section on Ordeals (*divyaprakaraṇa*) in the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* with its commentary.
The three types of evidence, beginning with written documents (*likhita*), have been described; and when those are unavailable, ordeals have been prescribed. Their nature is now stated.
The balance, fire, water, poison, and the sacred libation (kośa) are the ordeals for the purpose of purification here.

Those ordeals prescribed for the sake of purification when a formal accusation is made—such as the balance and the others—are to be understood [as the standard ones]. It should not be said that only the sacred libation and so forth are to be understood [as such], for Pitāmaha says:
"The balance, fire, water, poison, and the sacred libation as the fifth."
The sixth is declared to be *taṇḍula*, and the seventh is *taptamāṣaka*.
The eighth fruit has been described; the ninth is that born of the Dharma. All these divine [powers] have been pointed out by the Self-Existent One.
Nārada says: When no witness is found in a dispute between litigating men,
then one should examine them by means of ordeals and various oaths individually.
Truthful speech, vehicles, weapons, cattle, seeds, gold, the gods, the ancestors, and meritorious deeds— all these have been bestowed.
These are designated by the term "divine" (divya), because the word "divine" is applied to them. Likewise, they are also designated by the term "oath" (śapatha). And so says Nārada himself:

"Even when other means of proof are inadequate, one should pursue the matter through oaths—namely fire, water, good deeds, and so forth—having regard for the nature of the case, the time, and the strength [of the parties]."
The water-pot, fire, water, poison, and the fifth, the sacred libation—
these ordeals have been declared by the great-souled ones for the purpose of establishing purity.

Śaṅkha says: "One may cause [the defendant] to undergo what is called a divine ordeal—ascending the scale, consuming poison, entering water, the blade of steel, or the gift of *iṣṭāpūrta*—as well as other forms of oath. Manu says:
"In matters where there are no witnesses, between two parties disputing with one another, one should cause the truth to be established through an oath, even while they are still in dispute."
One should cause him to carry fire, or immerse him in water;
or else, one should firmly make him touch the head of his wife and children.
Because they were employed by the wise gods for a difficult task in order to purify one another, they are therefore known by the name "divine" (divya).
(Regarding the phrase "in cases lacking witnesses," the meaning is "in cases devoid of human means of proof. As for that which was stated by Pitāmaha:
"For those accused on the basis of a formal charge, one should prescribe ordeals such as the balance and so forth;
and rice and the oath should be used in cases of suspicion alone—of this there is no doubt."
Likewise: "The jar, fire, poison, and water—these are indeed the fourfold means of proof;
this fifth variety belongs to the divine, occurring in cases of doubt regarding treasure. [695]

Thus, this [trial by] *kośa* (the ordeal of the sacred water) is prescribed for cases involving minor charges or where there is suspicion. However, in the case of major charges or charges based on personal insult (*avaṣṭambha*), the *kośa* must be administered only when the accuser is prepared to stake his own head (*śīrṣaka*). There is no contradiction here. Likewise:
"The ordeal of the heated *māṣa* coin is ordained for those accused of theft on suspicion;
likewise for those involved in establishing trust amidst suspicion, and in the partitioning of inheritance among heirs."
In matters concerning the performance of various ritual activities, one should cause the treasury itself to be presented;
likewise in cases of trust, in all instances of suspicion, and in the business of making peace.
This treasury must always be offered for the sake of the purity of mind.
Now he speaks in order to specify the particular scope of the aforementioned ordeals, such as the balance and others, and to prescribe the specific procedure for the plaintiff:
"But in a case of grave accusation, these [ordeals] [are used] when the plaintiff has placed his head [as a stake]. (2.95)

Regarding these divine ordeals, beginning with the balance (*tulā*) and ending with the treasury (*kośa*), which have been declared for the purpose of purification: one statement is that they apply in cases of great accusation (*mahābhiyoga*), and not otherwise. Likewise, there is a second statement: "when the accuser has placed his head [at stake] (*śīrṣakasthe 'bhiyoktari*). In these two statements, the word "these" (*etāni*) is the common remainder (*sādhāraṇaḥ śeṣaḥ*). A "great accusation" (*mahābhiyoga*) is an accusation concerning property of a value of a thousand *paṇas* or more, or concerning a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*). "Head" (*śīrṣa*) refers to the admission by the accused that, in the absence of fault when undergoing the ordeal, he is indeed guilty and shall pay a fine proportionate to the offense. Thus, when the accuser is made to place his head at stake, it follows by implication that the performance of the ordeal is restricted to the accused; this is what Pitāmaha says.
In ordeals, the plaintiff is assigned the position of the head;
however, according to the instruction of the sacred scriptures, it may also be given to the defendant.

But surely it is logical that the plaintiff alone—the one who states the matter to be proven (*sādhya*) and the one who indicates what is to be established—is the proponent of the proof (*sādhanavādī*), and therefore he alone should undergo the ordeal (*divya*). To this, the reply is: "Because of the specific mention in the sacred text (*śruti*). This is the meaning: just as human evidence (*mānuṣa-pramāṇa*) must be presented by the plaintiff when there is a plea of denial (*mithyottara*), so too the application of the ordeal is established by logic; however, it is set aside by the explicit statement of the text. Kātyāyana also says:
"One should not appoint anyone who is a plaintiff to undergo ordeals."
"The divine [ordeals] should be administered by those expert in the divine tests to one who is accused. (2.95)

Now, he states an exception to the rule regarding the placement of the head by the plaintiff as the performer of the ordeal, based on a certain cause: "Or, by mutual consent, one may perform [the ordeal] and the other shall bear the head. By "consent" (rucyā), either the plaintiff or the defendant may perform the ordeal; the other, distinct from the performer of the ordeal, shall bear the head. By this, the status of the plaintiff as the performer of the ordeal is effectively enjoined. Furthermore, in ordeals such as the balance-scale (dhata) and others, one must necessarily bear the head. As Pitāmaha says:

"One should avoid divine ordeals that are devoid of the 'head' (śiras), beginning with the balance (dhaṭa) and ending with poison; the ordeal of the holy water (kośa) alone is remembered as being without a head. This refers to the case of the ordeal of the holy water when used for a charge based on suspicion. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states a specific rule:
The ordeal should not be administered to those guilty of mortal sins (mahāpātaka), especially to atheists,
nor to those who are habitually engaged in sinful acts.

Bhṛgu says: In those cases where ordeals have been proven clear through diligent effort, even if they involve sins, one should cause them to be performed by virtuous men; Manu says that one should not abandon a person accused of such.

The meaning is this: one who has previously committed a great sin (mahāpātaka) and subsequently incurs the charge of another great sin in a different matter shall not perform the ordeal himself; rather, he should have it performed by virtuous persons acting in the capacity of officiating priests (ṛtvij). Manu maintains that there is no liberation for one who is accused but does not undergo the ordeal.
He states that even a *ghaṭa* (water-pot) and so forth may, in certain cases, serve as a divine head (*divyaśīrṣaka*) even without [the formal] head-piece:
"One may perform [the ordeal] even without the head-piece in the case of treason against the king or a mortal sin. (2.96)

In a charge of treason against the king or in a charge of a heinous crime (*pātaka*), even if the accuser is not present in person, the accused shall nevertheless undergo the ordeal (*divya*). Treason (*droha*) means the intent to kill, the seizure of wealth or a wife, taking the side of an enemy, or the divulging of secret counsel. This refers specifically to cases involving charges of treason against the sovereign or heinous crimes. Viṣṇu states: "In cases of treason against the king and acts of violence, [the ordeal may be administered] even without the presence of the head-accuser. The meaning is that one should undergo the ordeal. Pitāmaha says: "Now, if a man proceeds to undergo an ordeal for the sake of his own purification..."
"Its head must be given [as an offering]; such is the determination of the scriptures."
For those suspected by kings, for those pointed out by bandits,
and for those intent on proving their own purity, the ordeal should be administered with the exception of the śiras ordeal.
"Let these men, who act in concert, be robbed by us"—when they have been thus pointed out by bandits, the ordeal is divine and not the *śira* (the water ordeal). Kātyāyana says:

For those corrupted by public scandal and those suspected by bandits, the ordeals beginning with the balance and ending with poison are prescribed; in that case, indeed, Bhṛgu has declared that the *śira* ordeal is not used.
One should never fashion a head-enclosure within the sanctuaries.
[697] He describes the divine rite: having summoned [the initiate], one who has fasted should perform a bath with his clothes on at sunrise.
One should cause all the divine ordeals to be performed in the presence of the king and Brāhmaṇas.

The judge shall cause all ordeals to be performed in the presence of the king and the brahmins, having summoned the performer of the ordeal—who has fasted on the previous day and bathed with his clothes on at the time of sunrise. Nārada says:
"The trial by fire should take place in the forenoon, and one should bring up the balance in the forenoon;
water should be administered at midday, and the poison after midday."
The purification of the ordeal by the sacred jar is prescribed for the forenoon of the day;
however, poison should be administered at night during the last watch, when it is very cool.
Likewise:
"For a man who has fasted for a day and night, bathed, and is wearing wet clothes,
the administration of all ordeals is prescribed in the forenoon."
Divine gifts should always be given to one who is pure and wearing wet clothes.

For the water-pot, the balance, and fire, the forenoon is prescribed; for others, it is optional. Pitāmaha says: "Divine ordeals must always be administered to one who has fasted for three nights or one night, provided he is pure and dressed in wet garments."
In all divine matters, the judge shall proceed with his duties,
remaining fasting by the king's command, just as the Adhvaryu priest does during the sacrifices.
Kātyāyana says:
If there is a contradiction in the means of proof, one must establish that which is to be proven once again;
for even though the divine ordeals have been described as they should be given, the king should avoid them.
Indeed, those [objects] must be given back again by fools, the greedy, and the wicked.

For when there is a contradiction in a divine ordeal (*divya*)—that is, when it lacks the power to determine the truth—one should establish the matter to be proven once again by means of a divine ordeal. Furthermore, the meaning is that even if divine ordeals have been administered contrary to the scriptures, the king may set them aside and administer those that are prescribed according to the rules. The mention of "fools" and so forth is intended to illustrate administration contrary to the scriptures. Likewise: "Ordeals administered at an improper place or time, or those performed outside the designated hall, undoubtedly cause a miscarriage of justice regarding the matters at hand."
"Vāsa," "nivāsa," and "grāma" have one and the same meaning. Therefore, the ordeal must be administered by experts according to the prescribed rule;
however, when applied contrary to the rule, it is not capable of establishing the truth for him. [698]
The Grandfather said:
Caitra, Mārgaśīrṣa, and likewise Vaiśākha—
these months are common and not opposed to the celestial [reckoning].
The iron vessel (dhaṭa) is declared suitable for all seasons; however, one should avoid it when the wind blows.
One may employ fire in the cool season, the winter, and even during the rains.
It is said that water is [pure] in summer, yet it is poison during the time of snowfall;
there can be no purification by water in the cold season, nor is there purification by fire in the heat of summer.
A king should not administer poison during the rainy season, nor should he employ the balance scale when there is a strong wind.
He states the restriction regarding the performers for the divine ordeals:
"The balance [is for] women, children, the elderly, the blind, the lame, Brāhmaṇas, and the sick;
fire or water for a Śūdra; or seven barley-grains for poison. (2.98)

This has been explained by the very words [of the text]. Here, women, children, and others are prescribed as being connected with the balance (*tulā*). Therefore, the restriction that "the balance belongs only to those headed by women" is logically established. For in every case, that which is to be enjoined is restricted by the injunction. And in this context, the balance is not what is being enjoined; rather, it is being referred to (*anūdya*) because of its priority. As it has been said: "Connection with the word *yat*, priority, and so forth, are the characteristics of the subject (*uddeśya*). Consequently, when the balance is impossible for women and others due to factors such as illness or wind, another divine ordeal (*divya*) may also be administered. But if it is possible, the balance alone is used. Thus says Kātyāyana:
One should administer the fire ordeal to a Kṣatriya, the balance to a Brāhmaṇa, and water to a Vaiśya;
or one may employ any of all these ordeals for anyone, except for the poison ordeal, in the case of the best of the twice-born.
Cowherds, merchants, artisans, actors,
servants, and usurers— one should cause these twice-born men to be treated like Śūdras.
Nārada says: The balance should be administered to a Brāhmaṇa, fire to a Kṣatriya,
water is prescribed for a Vaiśya, and one should cause poison to be given to a Śūdra.
The Grandfather (Brahmā) said:
"The treasury has been declared by the wise to be common to all;
however, for a Brāhmaṇa, all these [ordeals] except poison apply to these three [castes]."
Water, fire, and even poison should be administered to powerful men;
however, children, the elderly, and women should always be tested by means of the balance.
But as for that which was stated by him:
"The ordeal should not be administered to Brahmins, to those with emaciated limbs, to children, the elderly,
and ascetics, nor to women, if justice is to be observed."
Thus, this refers to ordeals other than the balance. Regarding the prohibition of specific ordeals for specific diseases, that same author says:
[699] One should avoid fire for those suffering from leprosy; water for those afflicted with asthma and cough;
and one should always strictly avoid poison for those with an excess of bile and phlegm.
Nārada said: Those learned in the treatises on Dharma must not allow women, children,
the sick, the elderly, or men who are weak to enter the water.
Kātyāyana states: "The fire ordeal is not prescribed for metalworkers, nor the water ordeal for those who subsist on water,
nor indeed is the fire ordeal ordained for those who know the application of mantras."
One should not administer rice to one who has an ulcer or a disease of the mouth.
The Grandfather said:
The wise should not administer an ordeal to those who drink liquor, to those addicted to women, to gamblers, nor likewise to those who follow the ways of nihilists.
Nārada says:

One should avoid administering the ordeal by sacred libation (kośa) to one who has committed a great offense, to one devoid of righteousness, to an ungrateful person, to a coward, to one who is contemptible, to an atheist, and to one whose guilt has already been proven. 2.98.
It has been stated that "these [ordeals] are for great charges"; regarding that, he explains at what amount of wealth a charge becomes "great" in cases such as the non-payment of debt:
One should not administer the *pāla* ordeal, nor poison, nor the balance, for less than one thousand [paṇas].
For matters concerning the king and in cases of grave accusation, however, pure men should always undergo them. (2.99)

In a dispute involving a value of one thousand copper *paṇas* or more, ordeals (*divya*) should be administered; however, not in a dispute concerning a number of *paṇas* less than a thousand. Regarding this, there is an exception beginning with "in matters for the king," and so forth. This means that those accused in royal affairs—that is, in matters of state—and likewise in cases of false accusation or the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, being pure and essentially innocent, should undergo [the ordeal]; they may bear the ordeals even without a subject matter involving a thousand *paṇas*. The *kośa* (ordeal by sacred libation) is not mentioned here in order to indicate that it applies even in cases of small value. For this very reason, Nārada says: "One should cause the *kośa* to be administered even in a small case. Bṛhaspati [says]:
The number of rays has been declared by Manu to be rooted in the goat;
that [scale] ending at a kārṣāpaṇa should be employed in the ordeal, and one should likewise cause it to be weighed.
When a thousand *paṇas* have been stolen, poison is administered;

when three-quarters [of a thousand] have been stolen, fire; when two-quarters [of a thousand] have been stolen, water; and when half [of a thousand] has been stolen, the balance is always to be employed.
In a lawsuit involving four hundred [paṇas], the heated gold bean (taptamāṣaka) must be administered;
for three hundred, rice grains (taṇḍula) should be given, and the ordeal by sacred libation (kośa) for half of that amount.
When a hundred [paṇas] have been taken and denied, a purification by ordeal must be administered according to the law;
the members of the court must diligently apply the plough-ordeal to one accused of stealing cattle.
One unit is prescribed for those of low status, twice that for those of middle status, and four times that for those of superior status; this is how it should be calculated by the examiners.

When there is no fixed rule for all the social classes (*varṇas*), this determination of the number [of repetitions] should be understood as having been stated by resorting to the position that all divine ordeals may be employed, according to the relative degree of their qualities. But when the ordeals, such as the balance (*dhaṭa*) and others, are used according to the specific class, and the performers are virtuous, Pitāmaha says:
"One should employ the balance for a thousand [paṇas], likewise iron for half a thousand;
for half of that, water; and for half of that, poison is prescribed."
Regarding a person of exceedingly superior character, however, Kātyāyana states:
"In a case where there is a denial of what has been given, one should establish proof;
even in a matter of small value, one should cause an ordeal to be administered for theft or acts of violence."
Having ascertained the measure of all the materials, one should fashion the gold;
then, endowed with the proper measure of gold, one should employ that divine [image].
Having determined the number of gold pieces, poison is prescribed for the loss of one hundred;
indeed, for the loss of eighty, one should offer oneself to the fire.
If sixty coins are lost, water should be administered; if forty, the ordeal by balance;
but if twenty or ten are lost, one should touch the heads of one's sons and others.
Then, upon the destruction of the Vārddha, worldly rites are prescribed.

A *suvarṇa* consists of sixteen *māṣas*. Viṣṇu states: "In all matters concerning wealth, one should calculate the value in gold. In that regard, for a Śūdra, an ordeal by *kośa* (water) should be administered when the amount is half a *suvarṇa*; beyond that, any one of the ordeals of the balance, fire, water, or poison should be used according to the merit of the case. When the amount is double [that], the prescribed procedure for the ordeal applies. For a Vaiśya, when the amount is triple; for a Kṣatriya, the same except for the *kośa*; and for a Brāhmaṇa, when the amount is fourfold, one should administer the *kośa*. One who has been previously seen to be guilty should be made to undergo any one of the ordeals even for very small amounts. But one whose good character is well-known among the people should not be subjected to them, even in a great matter. (2.99)
He states the procedure for the application of the balance:

"The accused, having relied upon the balance, is weighed by experts skilled in the maintenance of the balance; once he has been made equal to the counterweight, lines are drawn and he is lowered. (2.100)
[701] O Tula, you were created of old by the gods as the abode of truth;
therefore, speak the truth, O auspicious one, and release me from my doubt.
"If I am a doer of evil, O Mother, then lead me downward;
if I am pure, lead me upward"—with these words he should consecrate the balance. (2.102)

The accused, having performed the divine ordeal (*divya*), having resorted to the balance (*tulā*), having ascended the balance, and having been equalized by means of a counterweight (*pratimāna*)—such as clay—by goldsmiths and others skilled in the measurement of balances, shall have lines marked upon those parts of the balance-beams and strings which were joined at the time of equalizing with the counterweight; then, having descended from the balance, he should consecrate the balance with the mantra beginning with "O Balance" (*tule*) and ending with "lead me upward" (*gamaya ūrdhvam mām*). The meaning is that, facing the balance, he should recite this mantra. Thus says Pitāmaha.

Having cut down a tree suitable for sacrifice, like a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), according to the prescribed mantras, and having bowed to the guardians of the world (*lokapālas*), the wise should construct the balance scale.
A gentle mantra dedicated to the Vanaspati must indeed be recited when cutting [the tree].
Nārada says:
One should have a sacrificial post made there from khadira wood, free from wounds and devoid of white [patches];
or, if that is unavailable, from śamī or sāla wood, provided it is without hollows.
One should prepare such pieces of wood for the purpose of the balance.
The beam of the balance should be straight, made of *khadira* or *tinduka* wood.
It is square, with three points consisting of the pivot, the hook, and so forth.
The *dhaṭa* (balance) has two middle hooks (*karkaṭaka*) and two hook-turns (*karkaṭakāvarta*). It is the Grandfather (*pitāmaha*).
The balance should always be placed facing east, motionless, in a pure location—either in the place of Indra, in an assembly hall, in a court of law, or at a crossroads.
It is also pointed toward the north; regarding this, Nārada says:
"One should place the man on the northern side and the stone on the southern side;
by virtue of propriety, it is pointed northward from the north."
At the gate of the royal palace together with its retinue, and at the courtyard of the temple of the gods.
It is to be determined as immovable and worthy of worship with perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
Accompanied by the auspicious sounds of recitation and the fragrance of curds, parched grain,
and oblations, Dharma was summoned for the sake of protection and presided over by the world-protectors; thus spoke the Grandfather.
In that very place, one should install the world-protectors (lokapālas) in all directions;
one should worship them at the three junctions of the day with incense, garlands, and ointments.
The world-protectors, as well as the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus—
who are worthy of worship and endowed with great power— manifest their presence there.
One should cause a spacious, elevated, and bright weighing-hall to be constructed,
situated where [the person being weighed] cannot be harmed by dogs, Caṇḍālas, or crows.
The king should cause it to be made non-empty, provided with door-bolts, protected by attendants, and supplied with water and fire.
One should always cause a sacrificial pillar (dhaṭa) to be made, adorned with banners and flags,
accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments and drums, and provided with incense, garlands, and ointments.
Likewise:
"The balance should be made square and straight;
furthermore, rings should be carefully attached at three places."
The balance-beam should be made four cubits long, and its two supports above it should be equal to that; the distance between them should be two cubits, or indeed one and a half.

*Kaṭakas* are iron rings. *Adhyardha* means one and a half. *Vyāsa* [refers to the width]. Two cubits should be buried for both feet as well; likewise, two arches (*toraṇas*) should be constructed on both sides.
Ten finger-breadths higher than the threshold, two downward-facing pendants should always be made from the two arches.
Having suspended two clay scales, connected by a cord and touching the top of the beam,
on both sides [of the balance].
One should arrange the ends of both suspension cords facing east;
one should weigh the performers on the western cord and auspicious earth on the other.
One should have a pit constructed for it with bricks and clods of earth;
examiners who are experts in the measurement of weights should be appointed.
Merchants, goldsmiths, and likewise workers in bell-metal must always have the balance-beam of their scales tested by examiners so that it remains perfectly level.
[703] And water should be poured by the wise upon the balance;
that one upon which the water does not float is to be known as a balanced scale.
Having first weighed the man, he should subsequently cause him to descend;
one should always have the balance constructed, adorned with flags and white banners.
Then, the knower of mantras should invoke the deities according to this rite,
accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments and drums, and with perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
Facing east and with palms joined in reverence, the judge shall then say:
"Come, come, O Lord Dharma; enter into this ordeal."
Accompanied by the guardians of the world, the Vasus, Ādityas, and the hosts of Maruts,
he wrote down on a leaf the purpose for which he had approached him.
Accompanied by this mantra, one should place it upon his head:
"The sun, the moon, the wind, and the fire; heaven, earth, the waters, and the heart;
Yama, day and night, both twilights, and Dharma—these know the conduct of a man."
One should apply this entire ritual procedure for the Dharma to all divine beings; then, one should perform the invocation of the deities and arrange it accordingly.
O Dhaṭa, you were created by Brahmā for the purpose of examining the wicked-minded;
because of the letter *dha*, you are the embodiment of Dharma, and because of the letter *ṭa*, you are the crookedness of men.
Because you uphold the Dharma, you are therefore called Dhaṭa.
Viṣṇu:
O Dhaṭa, you alone know those things which even the gods do not know;
this man, accused in a legal dispute, is being weighed against you.
Therefore, you ought to save him from this doubt in accordance with dharma;
for those worlds that are ordained for the slayers of Brahmins are the same worlds as those for false witnesses.
"O Tulādhāra, worlds await you who hold the scales with such honesty."
Śrī Nārada said: Having secured him with the ritual observances (samaya), he should then cause the man to mount [the seat] again;
having placed a leaf upon his head in a windless place free from rain.
If, when weighed, he increases, then by the nature of things he is pure;
but if he remains equal or decreases, that man would not be purified.

If, when weighed against a weight, it rises upward according to the law and not through trickery, then it is pure and its pledge is true. If it remains equal or sinks downward, then it is impure and its pledge is false. As for what was said by the father:
"One who has committed little sin should be known as equal; one who has committed much sin sinks. But through the majesty of the reverence for the Dharma, the superior one is purified."

Thus, that [statement] refers to the minimum degree of punishment and penance. In legal proceedings (*vyavahāra*), however, even for one who is equal [to the opponent], there is only defeat. Indeed, it is not possible to establish a specific reduction in the number of coins to be paid as a fine based merely on the smallness of the fault, such that the smallness of the fault would also result in a specific course of action in the legal proceeding. Bṛhaspati says:
"If one who has been accused in the balance is weighed and found deficient, he shall suffer loss;
if he is equal, he is equal again; if he is heavier, he becomes the victor."

This being the case, if after weighing together in the first instance, the scales remain balanced when weighed again, then impurity must be determined; it is not determined by the first weighing alone. Victory [in the case of fraud] is to be determined by the breaking of the pans and so forth, even in the absence of any visible cause for such failure. As Nārada says: "In the case of the breaking of the side-pans, the breaking of the beam, or likewise of the pivot-joints (*karkaṭaka*), as well as the breaking of the strings or the breaking of the axle, one who has fainted shall obtain purification."

*Kakṣā* refers to the sling. The *karkaṭau* (crabs) are two iron hooks that support the sling. *Tulā* is well known [as the balance beam]. *Akṣaḥ* is the wooden beam situated above the two pillars that serves as the support for the balance. The assembly of the balance and its components is called a *dhaṭa*. However, when the breaking of the sling or similar incidents occur due to a visible cause, then the procedure must be repeated. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says: "In the event of the breaking of the sling, the snapping of the balance beam, or likewise of the cord;
and in cases of doubt regarding purity, one should examine the man again."
Nārada said: When, impelled by the wind, the breath wanders from the two heads of the scale, becoming unstable and losing its characteristic mark, it moves either upwards or downwards.
If the balance is suddenly released, he shall not proceed with either side;
in the event of a break in the scale-pan or a fracture of the beam, the king shall order a fresh trial for purification.

The meaning is this: when the two ends of the scale swing or move; when the water or other substance placed there for the purpose of knowing the balance’s equilibrium wavers; when the balance, impelled by the wind, trembles upward or downward; and when the balance is suddenly released by the keeper—on these occasions, one should not declare victory or defeat. Rather, one should weigh it again. The same applies in cases such as the breaking of the strings. This is the procedure for the balance. (2.100, 101, 102)

Now, following the sequence, he describes the application of the fire-ordeal (*agnidivya*): Having rubbed the two hands with rice grains, one should then place seven *aśvattha* leaves upon them and wrap them with thread for that same duration. (2.103)

Having performed the rites beginning with the fast (upavāsa) and ending with the concentration (dhāraṇā) as prescribed for the purpose to be accomplished, one should then mark both hands by crushing grains of rice (*vrīhi*) between them—those two hands being called *vimṛditavrīhī* because the rice has been crushed (*vimardita*) by them. One should observe and mark whatever injuries or signs are found upon them, so that it may be known: "This [mark] existed prior to the application of fire. Then, one should place seven leaves of the holy fig tree (*aśvattha*) into those two hands joined in the gesture of reverence (*añjali*). Thereafter, one should wrap them with exactly seven threads. Thus says Hārīta.
Then, facing the east, he should stand with his fingers and limbs extended,
wearing wet clothes, remaining pure, and having placed a leaf upon his head.
The Grandfather [said]: "He should stand in the western circle, facing east, pure and with palms joined in reverence;
the judges should observe any wounds or other marks on the hands of that performer."
At the very beginning, one should observe his hands as being marked by the impressions of crushed rice grains.
Nārada said: One should observe the marks on both his hands—
those that are ordinary and those that are hidden, as well as those with scars and those without.
Having thus performed the first ritual of hand-marking for the one under attack,
one should offer clarified butter into the fire according to the prescribed rite for the sake of pacification.
Likewise, in all hand-wounds, one should apply drops of ink;
then one should look again at those very hands, now variegated with drops.
Having placed seven *aśvattha* leaves in the hands of the accused, they should be carefully bound with threads provided by his own wife.
The Grandfather said:
One should place seven pippala leaves, śamī leaves, and unbroken grains (akṣata) there,
as well as seven threads of the cord upon the two hands.
The Elder says: "But red-hot iron, covered by seven *arka* leaves, he shall carry in his two hands;
if he is not burned at the seventh step, he is pure. (2.103)
Moreover:
O Agni, Purifier, you move within all beings;
like a witness, O Sage, declare the truth to me regarding my merits and sins. 2.104
When he has spoken thus, one should place upon both his hands a ball of iron weighing fifty palas, heated to the color of fire.

After the litigant has recited the mantra beginning with "tvam agne" and ending with "mama," the judge shall place in his hands an iron ball weighing fifty palas, heated to the color of fire and devoid of sharp edges; it must be even, neither depressed nor raised. Pitāmaha says:
"Having heated it, the pure [judge] should thereafter invoke Agni with [the mantra]:
'O Agni, you are the four Vedas; you are offered in sacrifices.'"
You are the mouth of all the gods; you are the mouth of those who discourse on Brahman. You abide within the bellies of all beings; therefore, you know the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Since you indeed purify evil, you are therefore called Pāvaka;
manifest yourself among the wicked and become radiant, O Pāvaka!
Alternatively, O one of great power, become cool toward those of pure disposition;
even toward one who licks iron with his tongue, one should offer instruction.
Likewise:
having made it symmetrical and devoid of sharp edges, one should heat a uniform iron ball weighing fifty palas in the fire for eight finger-breadths.

The meaning is that one should heat [the iron] equally on all sides. Nārada says: "One who is a blacksmith by birth, skilled in the work of fire, and experienced in other practical applications—he should heat the iron in the fire."
Having further caused a lump of iron, fifty palas in weight, to be made red-hot like fire with sparks and well-restrained [in its movement], the pure twice-born man [should proceed].
When he has been heated in the third ordeal, the judge, placing truth before him, should say:
"Listen to this law of Manu, presided over by the guardians of the world."
O Agni, you dwell within the hearts of all beings and know their every action;
both truth and falsehood are perceived by you through the tongue.
"This was proclaimed by the Vedas and other authorities; you ought not to act otherwise. This was proclaimed by him in the beginning; if he were to say this is false, then he would be a liar."
In every way, just as it is false, so do I hold this fire;
by this truth, may this man rend you asunder.
May the word of the speaker of truth be effective; O Consumer of Oblations, become cool! But burn the hands of this sinner who utters false speech.
Having caused the accused to hear this very matter as it stands in the document according to the facts,
and having assigned it to the powerful [judge], the judgment should be delivered according to the prescribed procedure.
"You are the tongue of the gods"—this is the grammatical connection. The meaning is that the oath must be sworn, that the oath must be administered. || 2.104, 105 ||
Taking that [staff], he should walk slowly for exactly seven circles;
each circle should be known to be sixteen finger-breadths in width, with an interval of the same measure.

Thus enjoined, he should take that iron ball, red-hot as fire, with both hands and walk slowly, without hurrying, taking seven steps across seven circles. Each circle shall measure sixteen finger-breadths, and the intervals between the circles shall likewise each be sixteen finger-breadths. Pitāmaha says:
"I shall declare the procedure for the fire exactly as ordained by the scriptures;
one should cause eight circles to be made in front, and likewise a ninth."
The first mandala belongs to Agni, the second likewise to Varuṇa;
the third has Vāyu as its deity, and the fourth has Yama as its deity.
The fifth, however, has Indra as its deity; the sixth is said to belong to Kubera;
the seventh has Soma as its deity, and the eighth has Śarva as its deity.
That which is the ninth [altar] in front, they know to be the great earthly one;
it should be made with cow dung and saturated with water.
They say that the distance between one mandala and the next is thirty-two finger-breadths.

Now, a row of mandalas should be made facing east and aligned straight. Among them, the westernmost mandala is for the divine performer to stand upon; for standing there, he consecrates and takes up the fire. As that very [text] says:
"He should stand in the western mandala, facing east, with palms joined in reverence, and purified.
The ninth mandala, however, is for the purpose of depositing the fire, because that same [text] says:
One should not walk in haste, but should proceed slowly and steadily when composed;
one should not overstep the prescribed circle, nor place the foot in between.
Having reached the eighth mandala, the wise one should deposit the ninth.

As for the statement that the second [mandala] is thirty-two finger-breadths from the first, this should be understood as the measurement of the intervening space inclusive of the mandalas; it does not refer to the intervening space alone, nor to the mandala alone. Thus, there is no contradiction with such statements as "sixteen finger-breadths. In that regard, if the mandala is sixteen finger-breadths, its intervening space must also be exactly sixteen finger-breadths. However, when the mandala is measured by the foot of the practitioner, then its intervening space should be made seventeen finger-breadths; otherwise, the mandala together with its intervening space would not amount to thirty-two finger-breadths. — Nārada.
Henceforth, I shall explain the subsequent procedure for the fire;
they say that the distance from one mandala to the next mandala is thirty-two finger-breadths.
With seven circles in this manner, the measurement of the ground is calculated as two hundred and twenty-four finger-breadths.
One should make the measurement of the mandala equal to that [specific] measure.
The Grandfather said:
"In every circle, kusha grass should be laid down as enjoined by the scriptures;
the performer must always place his foot upon them—this is the established rule."
Nārada said: Having stood at one [point], he should then proceed straight forward to seven others;
remaining unperturbed and free from anger, he should go toward the fire with those [steps].
One would not reach that stage which has been conceptually designated as "the stage not yet reached. (2.106)
Having released the fire and having rubbed his hands on rice grains, he who is unburned shall attain purification;
if the ball falls between [the two fires] or if there is doubt, he shall take it up again. (2.107)

Having walked seven circles and released the fire, if his hands are not burned after rubbing the rice grains with both hands, he is pure; otherwise, he is impure. Furthermore, if the iron ball falls midway, or if doubt arises due to some other cause, one should have him carry it again. Pitāmaha says:
"Then, in the same manner, one should have them throw either rice or barley;
when they have rubbed those [grains] with their hands without hesitation," [the judge should examine them].
One should declare its purification at the end of the day, when it is free from change.
Nārada says:
One should perform the examination of the hand for that very person whose funeral rice-ball has been offered;
one should observe it according to the previously mentioned marks, and also look elsewhere.
A mandala that appears red, or one where fire is produced,
should be known as impure, being established upon untruthful phenomena.
But when the two hands are no longer perceived as being burnt,
then one should rub rice grains with great care seven times.

If he has been rubbed by the court members themselves and found not burnt, and is thus determined to be pure, he shall be released after being purified; but if he is burnt, he shall be punished according to the sequence of the rules.
Nārada says:
But if someone causes it to fall in between and it is not perceived as burnt, one should have that fire brought back; this rule has been firmly established.
Kātyāyana says: If the accused stumbles and is burned elsewhere than the designated spot, the gods consider him not burned; one should make him undergo the ordeal again.

The place for the burning is the hands; the meaning is that if the person has been burned elsewhere on a limb, one should cause the ordeal to be performed again. Thus ends the procedure for the fire ordeal (agnidivya). 2.107.
Now he states the procedure for the ordeal by water:
"O Varuṇa, protect me by the truth," having thus addressed the water;
standing in water reaching up to his navel, he should grasp his thighs and enter the water. (2.108)

If a swift man could bring back the discharged arrow at the same moment [it was shot], and if he should see the defendant with his limbs submerged when that man has departed, he shall obtain purification. (2.109)

One should consecrate the water with the mantra: "O Varuṇa, protect me by means of truth. At this very moment, a strong man should be stationed at the spot where the arrow released from that point of water falls. Then, taking hold of the thighs of the man standing in water reaching up to his navel, the one seeking purification should submerge himself. At this same time, a very swift man should run with great speed to the place where the arrow released by a highly skilled archer has fallen. Then, having taken that arrow from that place and returning with the speed of its fall, if the submerged person sees the entire body purified, then the submerged one attains purification; otherwise, he is not purified. Thus says Pitāmaha.
Therefore, I shall proclaim the righteous and eternal ritual for the water-offering;
a wise person should cause a mandala to be prepared with flowers and incense.
One should worship the arrows and the bamboo bow with devotion;
one should adorn them with flowers and incense, and thereafter perform the ritual act.
Kātyāyana states: For the sake of purity, one should have the arrows made with iron tips;
they may also be made of bamboo stalks, and the shooter should discharge them with great firmness.
The Grandfather said: A Kṣatriya who is skilled at casting [arrows] should be appointed, or even a Brāhmaṇa who follows that profession;
being of gentle heart and tranquil, he should cast the arrows while fasting.
A wise man should discharge arrows even when the wind blows violently,
or on uneven ground crowded with trees and stumps.
Nārada said:
A cruel bow is known to be seven hundred [inches], a medium one six hundred, and a mild one should be known as five hundred; this is to be understood as the rule for bows.

One hundred and seven is *saptaśatam*. Likewise, six hundred, five hundred. This is the measurement in finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). The Grandfather [Brahmā] said: "The wise man, having set his target at one hundred and fifty cubits (*hasta*), should shoot three arrows with a bow of medium size."
And among those arrows discharged according to the injunctions of the treatises,
a man of great strength should seize the middle one.
One should observe the falling of arrows and avoid their gliding path;
for as they glide and glide, they always go from afar to even further away.
Nārada said:
Having discharged three arrows with a bow that is not excessively cruel,
one should perform the immersion in water at a place where no apprehension arises.
Uśanas states that there should be the complete immersion of the limbs of arrows that have been discharged. Kātyāyana [states as follows].
When [the first man] has been thrown in, he must perform the immersion; his departure and [the second man's] arrival must be simultaneous.
Upon the departure, however, another man must enter the water.
The Grandfather said: One should immerse oneself in water that is still, not flowing, nor too shallow;
it should be free from grass and aquatic moss, and devoid of leeches and fish.
One should perform purification using water found in natural reservoirs;
one should always avoid water that has been drawn up for transport, as well as water from rivers with rapid currents.
Men should perform their immersion in rivers that are not too swift, as well as in tanks, lakes,
and ponds with still waters.
The Grandfather [Manu] says:
One should first place a man firmly in the water like a pillar; desiring purification, those seeking purity should take hold of him and submerge themselves.
Nārada said:
A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya, free from passion and hatred,
should be made to stand like a pillar in water reaching up to the navel, remaining as firm as a strong post.
Seizing his thighs, one who is under a curse should submerge himself;
a youth endowed with speed [should do so] from the spot where the arrow was discharged.
[711] Another man of similar capacity should go with his utmost strength to where that middle arrow has fallen, and having taken up that middle arrow, he likewise proceeds.
He should return with speed to where that man had gone;
but when the arrow-retriever has arrived and does not see him in the water, [he should act accordingly].
Then, one should correctly declare it to be pure when it has entered into the water.
Bṛhaspati says:
When the middle arrow has been drawn back, one whose body is immersed [in water] shall attain purity.
Nārada says: Otherwise, there would be no purification even upon seeing a single limb [of the corpse],
whether from its original place or from another location where it was previously deposited.
Kātyāyana says: "If only the head should be seen, and neither the ears nor the nose,
one should declare that person pure even if he has entered the water."
If a man who has been seen by a living being dives and then surfaces,
he shall dive there once more, identified by the local landmarks.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the water offering. 2.108, 109.

Now he describes the application of the poison ordeal: "O Poison, you are the son of Brahmā, established in truth and righteousness; protect me from this curse; by truth, become nectar for me. (2.110)
Having spoken thus, one should consume the Śārṅga poison produced from the Himālaya mountains;
for him by whose bodily humors it is digested without violent symptoms, one should declare that he is purified.

When the matter to be proven is one common to all divine ordeals (*divya*), and the procedure consisting of the taking of a written document has been completed, and the formula of the judge (*prāḍvivāka*) about to be mentioned has been employed—or when the formula to be used for the accused has been applied and the poison consecrated with the mantra: "O Poison, you are the son of Brahmā"—the accused shall consume seven barley-grains of *śārṅga* poison produced on the Himavat mountains. He whose consumed poison is digested and reaches its transformation without violent symptoms is pure; the opposite is impure. The bodily constituents (*dhātu*) are skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen. For the poison residing in any one of these constituents, there is a rapid transition to the next constituent. Therein, poison residing in the skin produces horripilation; reaching the blood, that same poison causes perspiration and dryness of the mouth; reaching the flesh, it causes discoloration; reaching the fat, it causes trembling; having reached the bones, it causes loss of control over the eyes; but having reached the marrow, it causes despondency and delusion; and that same poison, having reached the semen, produces death. —Nārada.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme procedure for poison:
at what time it is to be administered, when, and of what kind it is said to be.
This [gift], measured by a barleycorn, has been prescribed by those who know the true meaning of the Dharma;
it should be given at the proper time when one desires [to give], specifically during the onset of winter.
One who knows the Dharma should not [study] in the afternoon, nor at midday, nor during the twilight;
one should avoid [studying] in autumn, summer, spring, and the rainy season.
One should carefully avoid *kālakūṭa* and *alābu* poisons, whether they are broken, held, fumigated, or mixed with other substances.
In the rainy season, the measure is six barley grains; in summer, it is recorded as five barley grains;
in winter, seven barley grains; and in autumn, it is even less than that.
The Grandfather said:
One should avoid all poisons that are water-born, those that are extremely decayed, those that are artificial, and likewise those that are earth-born.
One should examine medicinal herbs, mantra-applications, and gems that neutralize poison, as well as other secret substances residing within the body of the practitioner.
Kātyāyana says: The poison of horned animals is known to be dark like the horn of a goat, very thick, originating from the horn,
and resembling ginger when it breaks.
That [substance] which is red should be made black and hard at that very moment;
by this procedure, poison is to be recognized by those expert in the divine [sciences].
Yellow and resembling the *vatsanābha* poison, its identification is certain through the knowledge of its color;
one should know that the *sanābhaka* is likewise shell-shaped and breaks like a conch.
Combined with honey and milk, it becomes clear in that very instant;
thus has the external characteristic been described by those who accomplish the Dharma.

The meaning is that blood which, when mixed with it, instantly becomes black and solid, should be known as *śṛṅgi* poison. Pitāmaha says: "Seven barley grains should undoubtedly be administered for the sake of purification, [using] either *vatsanābha* or *himaja* poison from a horned creature."
Kātyāyana states: One should administer poison to living beings in the cool of the forenoon,
having ground it finely and mixed with thirty times its weight of clarified butter.

The grammatical connection is with the phrase "with ghee thirty times [the amount]. Nārada says: One should give [the gift] to one who has observed a fast, in the presence of the gods and Brahmins, after having worshipped Maheśvara with incense, offerings, and mantras.
In the presence of the twice-born, standing facing south,
the Brahmin, composed in mind, should give while facing north or east.
Kātyāyana says: Of the poison, that portion which is one-twentieth of a sixth part of a *pala*—
that, reduced by one-eighth and saturated with clarified butter, should be administered to the person to be cleared of suspicion.
The Grandfather said: Having taken the poison in his hand while it is being given, he should administer the oath:
"O Poison, you were created by Brahmā for the purpose of testing the wicked."
Reveal yourself among the wicked; for those who are pure, become nectar.
Viṣṇu said: "O Poison, because of your poisonous nature and your treacherous nature, you are cruel toward all embodied beings;
you alone know those things which human beings do not know."
This man, accused in a legal dispute, desires success;
therefore, you ought to rescue him from this doubt in accordance with dharma.

And this mantra should be recited by the judge (*prāḍvivāka*) by virtue of his authority. Pitāmaha says: "If, at the end of the day, he remains healthy, free from fainting or vomiting, and shows no physical change, one should declare him to be pure."
Nārada says: He should be kept under guard for the remainder of the day, placed in the shade, and deprived of food;
once he is freed from the exhaustion caused by the force of the poison, Manu declared him to be purified.
Bṛhaspati:
He who has digested poison administered by the rule, without the use of mantras or medicine, shall be considered pure; otherwise, however, he is to be punished and made to pay that wealth.
The Grandfather said:
The king may cause the ordeal by balance to be administered by his own men, supervised for three or five nights,
out of apprehension regarding a fraudulent substitution.
Thus ends the procedure for the ordeal by poison. 2.110, 111.
Now he describes the procedure for the ordeal by sacred libation: Having worshipped fierce deities, one should take water used for their ablutions;
having made [the accused] hear [the oath], one should have him drink three handfuls of that water. (2.112)

When the common rite for all divine ordeals has been performed, having properly worshipped the fierce deities such as Āditya and others with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and having brought the water used for their bathing, the judge (*prāḍvivāka*)—this is the understood subject—should cause the performer of the ordeal to drink three handfuls from that water which has been consecrated with the mantra: "By truth, O Varuṇa, protect me.
