Pitāmaha says: "One should cause that man to drink the water belonging to whichever deity he is devoted to; but if there is no specific preference among the deities, one should cause him to drink from that of Āditya."
Bṛhaspati says:
Whichever deity the accused person is devoted to, that very circle of weapons should be washed and he should be made to drink three handfuls of that water.

Nārada says: The drinking of the ordeal-substance (kośapāna) is prescribed for one who has fasted in the forenoon, who has bathed, whose clothes are still wet, who possesses a beard, and who is free from vices.
For one who desires [to perform a rite] and has faith, in the presence of the gods and Brahmins,
whatever deity that person is devoted to, one should cause an offering to be made for that deity.
One who possesses a sense of shame is an *āstika*. According to Kātyāyana:
"If a minor offense has been committed against the gods, one should bathe them and drink water from their weapons;
if there is a transformation [of the offense] and he remains impure, he must be restrained, but otherwise he is pure."

*Pāyyaḥ* means "to be made to drink"; the word *kośam* (the ordeal) is to be understood as the object. *Vikāraḥ* means "an undesirable change. *Niyantryaḥ* means "to be punished. Regarding the Grandfather [Yama]:
"One should make the thieves and those who live by weapons drink from the Durgā [ordeal];
however, that which is the water of the Sun, one should have the Brāhmaṇa drink."
One should bathe the trident of Durgā and the mandala of Āditya;
for the other deities, one should likewise bathe their weapons.
The treasury should not be given by the wise to those addicted to liquor and women, nor to gamblers, nor likewise to those who follow the conduct of atheists.

Nārada says: One should avoid the ordeal of drinking from the vessel (kośapāna) in cases involving a great offense, one devoid of dharma, a gambler, a contemptible eunuch, an atheist, a vrātya, or a slave.
Having summoned that accused person and placed him within the mandala,
one should have him face the sun and drink three handfuls [of the ordeal substance].
He states the criterion for determining victory or defeat:
"If, within fourteen days, no terrible calamity caused by the king or by fate befalls anyone, he shall be considered pure; of this there is no doubt. (2.113)

From the day of the *kośapāna* (drinking from the vessel) onwards, for fourteen days, he in whom no terrible, intense misfortune or cause of suffering—whether caused by the king or by fate—arises, should be known as truly pure. However, after that period, even if a misfortune should arise, impurity is not to be suspected. Nārada says: "If a great calamity should occur more than two weeks (fourteen days) later, he must not be accused by a wise man, because the appointed time has elapsed."
Viṣṇu: Within fourteen days, or even within twenty-one days,
one may encounter illness, fire, the death of a kinsman, or even punishment from the king.
One should know that to be impure, and likewise pure in the opposite case.
The Grandfather said:
"If, after three nights, seven nights, or even fourteen days,
a deformity is observed in [the corpse], that man is indeed a doer of evil."
If that [misfortune] were to befall only one person and not all people— such as disease, fire, or the death of a kinsman— that indeed would be a cause for reflection.
Kātyāyana says: Now, in the case of a disagreement with the gods (divine ordeal), one should cause the accused to pay [the debt], as well as the fine, after three weeks,
having exerted effort toward that matter.

In this matter, the shortness or length of the number of days is to be understood according to the smallness or greatness of the subject of the accusation. Therein, in the case of an extremely great accusation, a period of twenty-one days [should be granted], while in the case of a merely great accusation, fourteen days, and so forth, should be determined.
Thus ends the procedure for the *kośa* ordeal. Pitāmaha says:
I shall explain the rule regarding rice, both in its consumption and avoidance;
it should be understood that "rice" refers specifically to stolen rice, and not to any other kind—this is the certainty.
One who is pure should have white rice grains of *śāli*— and not of any other kind—
prepared in an earthen vessel before the Sun.
One should let them remain mixed with bathing water in that very place during the night;
at dawn, they should be given to the performer while he faces the sun.
The one who administers the ordeal should face the sun— that is, he should face the east—
after having eaten rice grains, he should spit them out into a leaf;
it must be a leaf of *bhūrja* and not of anything else, though in its absence, that of the *pippala* tree may be used.
Where blood is seen, and the jaw and palate waste away,
and whose body trembles— one should designate him as impure.
One whose rice grains are stained with blood, or where they have not been well-chewed,
and who exhibits distorted spitting— such a person one should designate as impure.

To those with an upajihvā (frenulum linguae), those who have fallen from their palate, and likewise those suffering from diseases of the mouth, rice should not be given, due to the suspicion that they may bleed.
In this case as well, the entire collection of rules common to all ordeals must be performed. Furthermore:
I shall describe the auspicious procedure for extracting the heated ball of gold (taptamāṣa). One should have a vessel made of iron, copper, or even gold.
One should fill with ghee and oil a circular vessel made of clay, four fingers in height and weighing twenty palas.
Then, one should cast a gold māṣaka coin into that well-heated [liquid] and subsequently extract the heated māṣaka using the thumb and finger together.
He whose fingertips do not tremble, nor does a blister arise,
becomes pure according to the Dharma, his fingers and limbs free from distortion.
Now follows the procedure for the *pāla* ordeal. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states:
"An iron plowshare weighing twelve *palas* is called a *phāla*.
If the person is not burnt, he attains purification; otherwise, he is defeated."
Now follows the ritual for the Dharma:
on two leaves, Dharma and Adharma are to be written in white and black respectively,
[accompanied] by mantras such as those for the gift of life and by Sāman chants beginning with the Gāyatrī.
Having addressed [the deity], one should worship with perfumes and white and black flowers;
then, having sprinkled [the area] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), [the two images] should be enclosed within lumps of clay.
Having made those two equal, they should be placed in a vessel so that they are not distinguished;
then, one should take a single morsel from the vessel without delay.
When the Dharma has been correctly grasped, one becomes pure and worthy of worship by those who investigate.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, on Ordeals (*divya-prakaraṇa*), in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, who was born in the lineage of the illustrious King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the lineage of the glorious Vidyādharas.
Now begins the section on the partition of inheritance in the Yājñavalkya-smṛti with its commentary. (8) [717]

The legal topics known as "Recovery of Debts" and "Deposits," along with the human and divine means of proof which are ancillary to them, have been explained. Now, the legal topic known as "Partition" is commenced.
"If the father should make a partition, he may divide the sons according to his will; either by giving the eldest a superior share, or all may be equal sharers. (2.114)

*Vibhāga* (partition) is the act of distributing the wealth of a father and others by setting aside specific portions for the sons and others. In this regard, the general rule (*utsarga*) is that "the father shall divide the paternal estate. However, due to a particular cause, even the sons may perform the partition; this will be explained later. In that context, if the father performs the partition, he may distribute the wealth among his sons according to his own will regarding the scope of smaller or larger shares. That is to say, he should establish the arrangement: "This is your share of my wealth; this is your share. Śaṅkha states: "If he has only one son, then he should take two shares for himself. Now, it might be argued that the word "according to his will" (*icchayā*) need not be stated, since that [will] is already obtained simply from the fact of being the agent of partition. For no conscious being becomes independent in actions without desiring them; indeed, one who is independent is called the agent. True. From the very fact of being the agent of partition, the desire regarding the subject of partition is already obtained. Therefore, what is not enjoined by the phrase "he should divide according to his will" is something else entirely. And the subject of that [desire] is an unequal division, such as one son receiving a smaller portion of wealth and another a larger. Consequently, the meaning is: "He should divide the sons with smaller or larger shares according to his will. Although only "partition" (*vibhāga*) is understood from the verb "he should divide" (*vibhajet*), and not specifically one characterized by inequality, nevertheless—
The eldest shall receive a twentieth part as his preferential share, and whatever is the best among all the goods;
from that, half shall belong to the middle son, but a fourth to the youngest.

By means of such rules for allotment (*uddhāra-śāstra*), all the various methods of allotment that have been prescribed are here indicated. Consequently, by the principle of remainder (*pāriśeṣya*), it is established that the inequality of division according to the will of the divider is what is enjoined in the rule, "One should divide the sons according to one's wish. On this point, Nārada says:

"But those who have been divided by the father himself with unequal shares of wealth—whether greater, less, or equal—for them that very [division] shall be the law, since the father is the master of everything."

Nor should it be said that this [rule] concerns the subject matter of the *uddhāra* (preferential share), because of the statement "the father is the master. For the father's mastery does not reside in the *uddhāra*, but rather in the scripture. Bṛhaspati states:
"Those shares—equal, deficient, or excessive—which have been assigned by the father, must be maintained exactly as they are; otherwise, they would be acts of misconduct."

Now, regarding the statement "if he should divide [the estate] according to his own wish" (*atha cecchayā vibhajet*), since this implies that the father’s wish is the cause of partition precisely by virtue of his being the agent of partition, there arises the contingency of the sentence becoming redundant. To avoid this, it must be accepted as a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*) stating that the sons’ wish does not effect partition. Accordingly, Manu says:

"After the death of both the father and the mother, the brothers, having assembled, shall divide the paternal inheritance equally; for they have no power over it while the parents are living. (MDh 9.104)
Devala says: When the father has passed away, the sons shall divide the father’s wealth;
for as long as the father remains free from defect, they would have no ownership over it.

Lack of ownership means lack of independence. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "From this point forward is the division of inheritance. Sons shall not divide the inheritance while the father is alive, even if it should be acquired by them later; for sons are indeed unworthy [of independence] regarding wealth and religious duty due to their lack of autonomy. Nārada says:
"Where the division of the paternal estate is arranged by the sons, that is declared by the wise to be the legal title of dispute known as *dāyabhāga* (partition of inheritance)."

And here, the phrases "of the paternal [property]" and "by the sons" are for the sake of illustration. The rule "if the father should make a partition" refers to property acquired by the father himself. However, regarding property acquired by the father or others, the agency to effect the partition belongs equally to both the father and the sons. For this very reason, Viṣṇu says: "If the father should divide his sons, he may act according to his own will regarding wealth acquired by himself; but even regarding wealth acquired by the father, the sons themselves sometimes become the agents of the partition. For this same reason, Nārada says: "After this, the sons shall divide the father's wealth equally."
Having established that sons have the right to divide the estate equally after the death of both parents,
[the text continues]: "When the mother's menses have ceased, when the sisters have been given away in marriage,
and when the father’s sexual desire has ceased and his longing for worldly things has ended."

Thus he spoke. The phrase "sons shall divide the wealth equally" is understood to follow here. Śaṅkha says: "The partition of the inheritance takes place against the father's will when he is aged, mentally deranged, or afflicted by a chronic illness. Nārada says: "A father who is diseased, angry, whose mind is attached to sensual objects, or who acts contrary to the scriptures, has no authority regarding the partition."

One who acts otherwise is a transgressor of the scriptures and a violator of injunctions and prohibitions. Even regarding wealth acquired by the father, the sons possess independence in partitioning it when there is a cause such as the father’s lack of desire [to divide]. However, while the mother is not deceased, the sons remain entirely dependent. As Śaṅkha says: "The eldest alone shall protect the assets like a father; for the others, the family is rooted solely in inheritance. They are dependent, being under the care of their father, provided the mother remains thus situated. [719] This applies when the mother has the capacity to maintain the family. As for the statement that the eldest shares undivided wealth with his younger brothers, this should be understood to apply when the Veda is to be studied by some among them. When the Vedas have been studied, the meaning of the Vedas understood, and they are capable of performing the *agnihotra* and other rites, then partition itself is better. As Manu says:
Thus they may dwell together or separately out of a desire for the Dharma;
the Dharma increases through separation, therefore separate activities are in accordance with the Dharma.
Vyāsa says:
While the parents are alive, the co-residence of brothers is prescribed;
in their absence, for those who have divided [the estate], their dharma increases.

However, when younger brothers have divided their wealth with the eldest due to a lack of confidence [in remaining together], even the Vaiśvadeva and other such rites, which are mandatory for them, are not divided. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"For those living under a single cooking fire, the worship of the ancestors, the gods, and the twice-born shall be one;
for those who are divided, that same worship should be performed in each individual house."
Having stated that when a partition is made by the father, a partition of the property also occurs for the sons, Manu states an exception regarding its specific details:
"If there should be a joint effort among brothers who have already been divided, the father must under no circumstances give them unequal shares. (2.114)
Furthermore:
"If he should divide the shares equally, the wives must be made equal sharers, provided that no separate property (strīdhana) has been given to them by the husband or by the father-in-law. (2.115)

If a father should make an equal division of wealth for the sake of his sons, then those wives to whom no separate property (*strīdhana*) has been given by the husband, the father-in-law, or the father, shall be made sharers equal to their sons. The meaning is that each wife shall receive a share equal to the share of one son. (2.115)
He states another reason for the inequality of the division:
"The act of separating [the property] by giving something to one who is capable but not exerting himself."

If a son, being capable of acquiring wealth, does not desire his father’s property, or if he, though capable of acquiring wealth, out of deceitfulness does not engage in efforts conducive to its acquisition and preservation, the father should separate him by giving him some small amount of worthless wealth; otherwise, there would be a dispute with him or his descendants. This rule applies to wealth acquired by the sons collectively. However, in the case of ancestral property, he certainly receives an equal share. Manu says:
"But among brothers, he who, though capable through his own labor, does not desire the wealth..."
He shall be divided from his own share by giving him something for his subsistence.
The meaning is: "from his own share" refers to that which has been acquired by the brothers themselves. In this connection, something else is stated. On this point, Nārada says:
"If one who is engaged in the affairs of the family performs those duties, he should be supported by his brothers with food, clothing, and transport."

Āpastamba states: "For all those who are united in dharma are entitled to shares; however, even if he is the eldest, one should exclude from his share him who acquires wealth through unrighteous means. By "unrighteous means," such as gambling and the like, he means that he squanders or misappropriates wealth—gold, cattle, clothing, and so forth—or diverts it elsewhere. Gautama says: "According to some, even the son of a wife of equal caste does not receive [an inheritance] if he is of improper conduct. Manu says: "All brothers who persist in forbidden occupations (vikarma) are unworthy of the wealth."

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "For one who has been excluded [from the community], inheritance, the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa), and water offerings cease. One who has been excluded is one who has been cast out by his kinsmen due to having fallen [from his status]. "Inheritance" refers to paternal wealth; it also includes the wealth of kinsmen for one who stands in the place of a son.
Having stated that an unequal division is not to be transgressed because it is a matter of dharma, he says:
"The law regarding those who have divided their inheritance unequally is declared to be that established by the father. (2.116)

When a man’s wealth has been exhausted by his sons, the same law that applies to the distribution of property made by a father applies to the distribution of the divided shares among the sons; therefore, it must not be transgressed. Bṛhaspati says:
"Those portions—equal, deficient, or excessive—which have been assigned to them by the father, must be maintained exactly as they were; otherwise, they should be disciplined. (2.116)
Now he states another division distinguished by the agent, the object, time, and manner:
"After the death of both parents, the sons shall divide the estate and the debt equally;
the daughters [shall take] the remainder of the mother's [estate], and in their absence, the heirs. (2.117)

After the death of the mother and father, their very inheritance and debt, the sons—however many brothers there may be—should divide them equally, making as many shares for each as there are brothers, neither less nor more, both for the debt and for the wealth. Consequently, whatever portion of the wealth one receives, that same portion of the debt he must also bear. This being so, regarding the rules for unequal division—such as "those who would have four, three, two, or one share," or "by whomsoever among them [the property] was produced by himself," and so forth—it should be understood that the rule for dividing the debt follows the distribution of the wealth. As for the mother's wealth, once the discharge of the debt has been made, the daughters shall divide what remains; in the absence of daughters, her lineage (the daughter's lineage) shall take it. In the absence of daughters or their lineage, the sons themselves shall divide the mother's wealth. Thus says Kātyāyana:
In the absence of daughters, however, that inheritance shall go to the sons;
but property given by kinsmen goes to the kinsmen, and in their absence, it goes to the husband.
"Sisters, together with their kinsmen, shall share [the property] along with their husbands;
this is the law regarding women's property, and thus the division has been ordained," so says Manu.
"But when the mother has passed away, all the uterine brothers and the uterine sisters shall divide the maternal inheritance equally.

Here, the word "ca" (and) signifies an option (*vikalpa*) and not a conjunction (*samuccaya*). And in the case of an option, unmarried daughters are entitled to the inheritance first. As Manu himself has said:
"But that which may be the mother's separate property (*yautaka*) shall indeed be the share of the unmarried daughter.

Gautama, however, states that even for daughters who are unmarried and unsettled, there is a right to inherit their mother’s wealth: "The woman’s property belongs to the daughters, both those who are unmarried and those who are unsettled. "Unsettled" means those who are childless, destitute, or unfortunate. Bṛhaspati says:
"The woman’s property shall belong to the offspring, and the daughter is entitled to a share thereof."
But if she has not been given away and is married, she receives only the mere title.

*Yautaka* means separate property; *mānamātraka* means a very small amount. Vasiṣṭha states: "Women shall divide the mother’s *parīṇāhya*"; *parīṇāhya* refers to ornaments and the like. Regarding the wealth of a childless woman, Manu says:
"Whatever property may belong to a woman, having been given by her father in any manner, a Brāhmaṇī daughter shall take that, or it shall belong to her offspring."

The term "father" (*pitṛ*) is used figuratively; it refers to the father's co-wife (*sāpatnī*), specifically a Brāhmaṇa woman, as restricted by the qualifying term "Brāhmaṇa. This being the case, when daughters have been given in marriage and are established in their own households, the sons also acquire a right to their maternal wealth. Regarding this very matter, Manu states another distinction:
[722] "Of those [daughters], whatever daughters there may be, to them also something should be given from the maternal grandmother’s wealth, according to their merit and with affection."

The meaning of the statement "the sons shall divide [the estate] after the parents" is this: if they should divide after the death of the parents, then they should divide the inheritance and so forth equally. This refers specifically to a division performed by the brothers; therefore, even while the father is alive, the brothers may divide equally. However, it follows by implication that this rule does not apply to a father who is himself dividing [the estate]. Nor should it be interpreted to mean that they *must* divide after the parents' deaths. As Manu says: "In this manner, they may live together or separately, out of a desire for dharma."
The dharma increases separately; therefore, the ritual action pertaining to the dharma is performed separately.
As for that which was stated by him [Manu]:
"The eldest alone shall take the paternal wealth in its entirety;
the rest shall live dependent upon him, just as they lived upon their father."

Thus, this should be understood to apply to those younger brothers who have not completed their study of the Vedas, who are incapacitated due to insanity or similar conditions, or who have not yet attained legal capacity. On this point, Kātyāyana says: "The division [of property] is ordained for those who have attained legal capacity; and for men, such capacity arises at the sixteenth year."

And the state of being one who has not attained legal capacity (*aprāptavyavahāratva*) is mentioned for the sake of illustration; for even the fact of not having mastered the Vedas is a cause for non-division. As Hārīta says: "If they are younger brothers who have not completed their Vedic studies, then they should live together. Nārada says:
"The eldest brother should support all [the others] if they so desire, just as a father;
or a capable younger brother may do so. The stability of the family depends upon capability."
Nārada, however, has stated that the inheritance should be divided only after the father’s debt has been discharged:
"Whatever remains after the father’s debts have been paid from the paternal estate, that is to be divided by the brothers; otherwise, the father would remain a debtor."
The paternal inheritance includes the *navaśrāddhas*. Thus says Gautama: "They should perform the *navaśrāddha* together. Kātyāyana states:
"A debt contracted for the sake of the family by a brother, a paternal uncle, or a maternal uncle must be paid in its entirety by the heirs at the time of partition."
That debt must be paid to the creditor; one should not cause it to be paid otherwise.
If, however, after [the initial trial], it is subsequently proven by evidence to be contradictory, [then the decision may be reversed].
After the dispute due to opposition has been settled, [723] likewise: "In this manner,
debts of the paternal kind cleared by the father's estate, as well as those belonging to oneself incurred by oneself—
such debts are to be cleared by the kinsmen together during the partition."

A debt contracted for the sake of religious duty (*dharma*), or given out of affection (*prīti*), or one for which one has personally provided security—such a debt, when it becomes apparent, shall be divided; however, a gift from the paternal estate shall not be divided.

The meaning of this is as follows: whatever was intended for the sake of religious duty (*dharma*), whatever was given by word of mouth out of affection, and whatever debt was incurred—just as it was directed by the father that "this debt must be discharged by you through your own son"—that [debt] which is currently visible or being realized should be divided; however, the division of wealth is not to be performed after first clearing that debt from the paternal estate.
As for what is visible and to be divided, [it consists of] houses, fields, and quadrupeds;
in cases where there is suspicion of hidden property, the means of proof (*pratyaya*) therein has been declared.
Household utensils, vehicles, milch cattle, ornaments, and tools for craftwork—
Bhṛgu declared that visible property is to be divided, while hidden treasure belongs to the finder.

The ordeal is divine. The mention of the "taking of the sacred water" (kośa) is intended as an illustration for all divine ordeals. Manu says: "One should never divide goats, sheep, or single-hoofed animals unequally;
however, goats and sheep may be assigned unequally, and this is prescribed for the eldest alone."
"Uneven" means having a different number [of syllables] than that of its brother. (2.117)

He states what is not subject to partition: "Whatever else has been acquired by oneself without detriment to the paternal estate, as well as what is obtained through friendship or received at marriage, shall not belong to the heirs. (2.118)

Among those whose property has not been divided, whatever additional wealth has been acquired by one person alone—without conflict with, without injury to, and without depending upon the paternal estate—as well as what is obtained from a friend (*maitra*) and what is received at a wedding (*audvāhika*) from the father-in-law and others, that shall not belong to the co-heirs. It is not to be divided; rather, the meaning is that it belongs to the acquirer alone. Manu says:
"That which one acquires through one's own labor without injuring the paternal estate, and that which is obtained through one's own effort, one need not give away against one's will."

*Śrama* refers to labor such as warfare, agriculture, and so forth; *īhā* here denotes activity free from such labor. Kātyāyana states: "Whatever is obtained at the time of acquisition together with a maiden of the same caste—that wealth acquired through a maiden is declared to be pure and a source of livelihood."
One should know that wealth brought by a wife at the time of marriage is matrimonial; all such property should be understood as being for the fulfillment of dharma. [2.118]
Likewise:
"But he who recovers property that was lost and subsequently found, as well as what has been obtained through learning, need not give that to his heirs. (2.119)

If property such as fields, gardens, and so forth, which has come down through the succession of ancestors, should somehow be seized by another, he who recovers it with the consent of the heirs shall not have to give it to those heirs. However, that which is recovered without the consent of the heirs, the recoverer shall take a fourth part of it; the remainder, along with the recoverer, all shall divide among themselves. As Ṛṣyaśṛṅga says: "But he who alone recovers land that was previously lost, others shall receive their shares after giving him a fourth part."

Furthermore, that which is obtained through learning (*vidyā*) acting as the instrumental cause, that too he shall not give to his co-heirs. Manu says: "But whatever is the property of learning, that shall belong to him alone;
as also that which is received from a friend, that which is received at marriage (*audvāhika*), and that which is received during the honey-mixture offering (*mādhuparkika*)."
Kātyāyana says:
"But that wealth which is acquired through knowledge obtained from another by means of subsisting on another's food— that is called 'wealth acquired through learning'."

"Bhakta" means food. "From another" means from someone other than the father. That which is obtained by one who has been initiated [as a student] through learning, on the basis of a wager, should be known as "wealth acquired by learning" (vidyādhana); it is not excluded from partition.

That which is obtained from a disciple, from officiating as a priest, from answering questions, from resolving doubtful inquiries, from proclaiming one's own knowledge, from debate, and from study; |||

They say that the wealth acquired through learning is not to be divided at the time of partition; for this same rule applies even to arts, as does whatever may be in excess of the value [of the craft].

That which is obtained through the sale of knowledge, or likewise from officiating at sacrifices or from being a pupil—this they call "wealth of knowledge"; whatever is otherwise than this is common property.

Bṛhaspati states that what is obtained through learning after having expelled a co-heir by means of gambling and the like should be known as "gains from learning" (vidyādhanam), and it is not to be divided.

That which is obtained through a promise of instruction, that which is received from a pupil, and that which is obtained according to the rule of the officiating priest— Bhṛgu declares this to be "wealth acquired through learning."
When they boldly undertake an action after having entered into uncertainty, if their master is pleased with that action, he bestows his favor upon them.
Whatever wealth may be obtained therein, or whatever may be gained through valor;
Vyāsa:
Whatever wealth acquired through learning, whatever consists of valor, and whatever is a gift from a wife's family (saudāyika),
that shall not be sought back by the heirs at the time of partition.
Kātyāyana states: That which is acquired by means of a banner (i.e., booty) shall not be partitioned at all—
that which is brought back from battle after having routed the enemy force.
Having sacrificed one's life for the sake of the master, that is called "seized by the banner."

There is no division of the riches of benevolence (*maitrī*) and so forth, which are acquired without utilizing paternal property. However, regarding that which is acquired by utilizing such property, Vyāsa says:
"Whatever vehicle or weapon one acquires through valor and other means by relying upon common property, the brothers are sharers in that wealth."
Two shares of that [property] should be given to him, while the remaining [heirs] share equally.
Kātyāyana says:
A learned man shall never give his wealth of learning to those who are ignorant;
however, that wealth may be given by the learned man to those who are equal or superior in learning.
Nārada says: A physician should not, unless he so desires, give a share from his own wealth to another physician,
unless that [other] has acquired it by relying upon the paternal estate.
He who maintains the family of a brother who is acquiring knowledge shall receive a share from that wealth acquired through learning, even if he himself has not studied.
Whatever property the eldest son acquires after his father has died,
a share therein belongs to the younger brothers, provided they are devoted to learning.
Those who preserve their learning and are devoted to the practice of sacred knowledge are the younger [brothers]. Manu has stated another thing that cannot be divided:
"Clothing, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, water, women, security of possession (*yogakṣema*), and pasture grounds—these they declare indivisible."

The interpretation offered by some that the word *patra* here refers to a vehicle (*yāna*) contradicts the statement of Kātyāyana. For it is said: "Wealth recorded in a document, property designated for religious purposes, water-rights, wives, and an inheritance acquired through succession."
Ghee, clothing, and ornaments— whatever may not be appropriate—
should be employed by kinsmen in such a way that they are suitable for the occasion.
Pasture land for cattle, protection, clothing, and whatever has been applied to the body—these should not be divided when being used; so says Bṛhaspati for the sake of dharma.

That which is disproportionate, or inconsistent with the division, or unequal in number relative to the sharers, must be divided at the appropriate time in accordance with the number of sharers and according to the requirements of the occasion. As for the statement that clothes and such items are indivisible, that refers to their physical form; however, they must certainly be divided in terms of their value. As Bṛhaspati says: "Those who stated that clothes and so forth are indivisible did not consider the case where wealth belonging to the affluent consists of clothes and ornaments."
That which stands in the middle and cannot sustain life cannot be given to a single person;
it must be distributed with skill, otherwise it would become useless.
Having sold clothing and ornaments, having collected wealth by means of a written document,
and having exchanged cooked food for uncooked food, the property is then divided.
Just as water from a well or a pond is drawn out and taken according to its depth,
so too is a field divided by a boundary according to the proportion of shares.
One should have a single woman perform work in each house according to her share; many women should be assigned work in equal shares. This same rule applies even to male slaves.
The acquisition of property that ensures security and well-being shall be divided equally;
the heirs must always manage its use according to their respective shares.

The phrase "one woman" refers to a female slave who has not yet been enjoyed [by her master]. Regarding one who has been enjoyed, Gautama says: "There is no division of water, of what is acquired for security, of prepared food, and of women who are united [in marriage]. The meaning is as follows: regarding the "gain of one who possesses security and acquisition" (*yogakṣemavato lābham*), the "possessor of security and acquisition" is a lord such as a king or the like, who has acquired [property] by his ancestors for the sake of maintaining their own family; whatever gain—that is, whatever wealth—has been obtained from that, it is to be divided equally. "Traffic" (*pracāra*) refers to the ground for ingress and egress. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "And there is no division of food, water-vessels, ornaments, and the clothing of women who are joined together; so says Prajāpati, provided they are for the purpose of daily use. (2.119)

When the property arises as a common whole, the division is traditionally held to be equal; however, for those who have more than one father, the allotment of shares is determined according to the fathers. (2.120)

[727] "The acquisition of wealth" means the earning of property. When all [co-heirs], who are mutually dependent, acquire wealth, an equal division must be made. In this matter, even the father shall divide it equally. Regarding this, Manu says:
"If there should be a joint effort among brothers who are undivided..."
In that case, the father must not, under any circumstances, grant an unequal share.

And this being the case, it is understood that in other instances, a division made by the father may even be unequal. Likewise: "But if all those who are unlearned should acquire wealth through their own efforts, the division therein shall be equal; such is the settled rule regarding what is not ancestral."

If brothers who have not divided their inheritance should die, some of them may have one son, some two, and some many; in that case, the allotment of shares is according to their fathers. Whether there be two or many sons, they shall each take the same share as their father’s own share; the meaning is that there is no equal division among those [sons] themselves. Bṛhaspati says: "Whatever is acquired by those who are united, all are equal sharers therein;
their sons, whether unequal or equal [in number], are declared to be heirs to their father's share."
Kātyāyana says:
When a father has died without partition, one should provide for his son as an heir to the estate with that by which the father himself did not receive a share from the grandfather.
For he indeed receives his paternal share either from his paternal uncle or from that uncle’s son;
by right, that very same share belongs to all the brothers.
His son also obtains it, or else there shall be cessation thereafter.

When a brother has died while the wealth was undivided, his son who has not yet received a share from the grandfather may take his own paternal share from the uncle or from that uncle’s son. The meaning is that, in this manner, the grandson (the son of that son) would not receive it. Regarding this, there is a specific rule stated by Devala: "Among kinsmen who live together, whether they are undivided or have already divided, a further partition of inheritance shall take place up to the fourth generation; such is the settled law."
To that extent, they shall be kinsmen (kulya) and sapinda; beyond that, there is a division of the funeral cakes (piṇḍabheda).
They desire an equal distribution of the funeral cakes as well as of the inheritance.
The rule for many siblings of the same caste has been declared:

there shall be only one [representative] of the same caste, and in this case, the inheritance is not divided. Viṣṇu states: "Now, regarding the division of inheritance among brothers, those women who may be childless—until they obtain a son, a division [of their shares] belongs to the brothers; these women are the wives of the brothers. For those whose offspring have not yet been born, who are pregnant, or whose husbands are deceased, their inheritance must also be given until a son is obtained. However, in the absence of the birth of a son, the share ceases; this is because of the statement, "until the obtaining of a son" (2.120).
Regarding what was stated—"If the father makes a partition, he may divide [the property] among his sons according to his will"—he states an exception to that:
"In the case of land acquired by the grandfather, or a pledge, or even other wealth, the ownership therein shall be equal for both the father and the son. (2.121)

The grandson’s ownership over the grandfather’s property is equal to that of his own father; therefore, even if he is unwilling to divide it, the father may divide the grandfather’s wealth at the desire of his son for partition. Furthermore, in the division, it must be equal and not made unequal as if it were the father’s self-acquired wealth. *Nibandha* (a fixed assignment) means: "In this share, so much wealth from each field and each house shall be given to such-and-such a person. Kātyāyana says: "The grandfather’s property shall be common to both the father and the son;
however, regarding what was acquired by the father himself, the son does not deserve equality."

This should be understood to apply when [the property] has been acquired by the father without subsisting upon the grandfather's wealth. Vyāsa states: "In the case of a house or field inherited through succession, the father and sons have equal shares;
sons are entitled to a partition of the paternal estate even against the father's will."
Bṛhaspati:
Regarding property acquired by a grandfather, whether immovable or movable,
equal ownership has indeed been declared for both the father and the son.
Regarding property inherited from the grandfather that was acquired by the father through his own power,
or obtained by means of learning, valor, and so forth, the father's ownership over it is declared in the Smṛti.

Regarding wealth inherited from one’s grandfather that was seized by others and subsequently recovered by the father through his own power, or whatever was acquired by him alone through learning and other such means—in these cases, the ownership belongs to the father alone, not to the sons. For this very reason, it is said:
"He may, according to his own will, make gifts and provide enjoyment from that wealth;
but in his absence, the sons are declared to have equal shares."
Kātyāyana:

That which was lost after being taken away by one's own power, as well as that which may have been acquired by oneself—none of this is to be made good by the sons at the time of partition; the father alone is responsible.

The meaning is that whatever has been stolen or lost, and which the father recovers by his own effort, need not be given by the sons at the time of partition. Thus, the *Smṛtis* declare that in ancestral wealth, the grandson possesses ownership equal to that of his own father. Nor does this contradict such Vedic injunctions as "one should establish the sacred fires," which would otherwise require interpretation in a figurative sense—namely, that while the father has a son, he should not give away or enjoy his paternal wealth in its entirety, but should rather reserve some for the sake of his son; for the ownership of one who has a son over the wealth does not depart, such that the Vedic texts concerning matters to be accomplished with one's own wealth would be contradicted. Even though that wealth is common to both himself and his son, he does not thereby cease to be the owner simply because of the son’s consent, the formal separation of the son through partition, or the acquisition of other property. For partition merely establishes the ownership of each individual co-owner over their respective share of the common property; it does not create a new ownership where none existed before. This is just as in the world among those who work together for a common goal (*saṃbhūya-samutthāyin*), or in the Veda among those performing a sacrificial session (*satrin*), ownership arises upon the completion of the undertaking. Furthermore, if partition were the cause of ownership, then even a partition performed by force or other improper means would generate ownership. As for what was stated by Gautama—"One is an owner in cases of inheritance, purchase, partition, seizure, and finding"—that refers to the fact that a settled partition generates the status of ownership. (2.121)
A son born after the partition of the estate from a wife of equal caste is entitled to a share.
Or rather, its distinction [from the seen] would arise from that which has been purified by income and expenditure. (2.122)

Among sons whose wealth has been divided, a son born of a wife of the same caste becomes a sharer in the father’s portion. However, in the absence of a paternal portion, if land or other property is discovered after the division has already been made, a division must be carried out by deducting from that discovery the income and expenses accrued since its production. Manu says: "But a son born after partition shall take the paternal wealth alone;
or he shall share it with those who were reunited with him."

One born after the partition shall take only the father’s wealth, not the brothers’ wealth; however, in the absence of the father and the brothers, he shall divide the paternal share together with those who were reunited with the father. The singular number in the word “born” (*jāta*) is not intended to be restrictive. As Bṛhaspati says:
“Those who were divided from the father—whether stepbrothers or uterine brothers—and even those who are junior to them, they are the ones who inherit the paternal share.”

In that regard, even if the share of those previously divided is large while the share of the younger brothers who take only their paternal portion after partition is small, nevertheless, the shares of the brothers previously divided must not be taken by them; thus he himself says:

"The elder brother born before partition has no authority over the paternal estate; the son born after partition has no authority over the share of his brothers. That which was acquired by the father himself after he had been divided from his sons..."
All that belongs to one born after partition, his predecessors are declared to have no authority over.

But when he does not obtain even a small portion from anyone through partition—by the manner previously described—then the meaning is that he should take [his share] from the shares of his brothers. Viṣṇu states: "They should give a share to one born after the partition of the paternal estate has been made. (2.122)
He states another type of indivisible property:
"Whatever has been given by both parents to a son shall be his own wealth.
This means that whatever gratuity has been given by the mother or the father to a son, whether before or after the partition, belongs to him alone; it is not to be divided with other sons. — Nārada.
Both the property acquired by valor and that acquired by a wife, as well as whatever may be the property acquired through learning— these three are indivisible, as is any gift from a father.
And for one to whom his own property has been given by his mother out of affection, this same rule is seen to apply; for a mother is as beloved as a father.
Vyāsa:
That which was given by the grandfather or by the father out of affection,
as well as that which may have been given by the mother, must not be taken away from him.
Regarding immovable property, Nārada states an exception:
"The father is indeed the master of all gems, pearls, and corals;
but of all immovable property, neither the father nor the grandfather is the master."
By the favor of the father, garments and ornaments may be enjoyed;
however, immovable property should not be enjoyed while the paternal favor remains.
But rather:
"When dividing after the father's death, the mother also shall take an equal share. (2.123)

When sons divide the inheritance after the death of their father, the mother shall also receive an equal share in the partition. The plural number [of "sons"] is not intended to be restrictive; therefore, the meaning is that the mother receives a share exactly equal to whatever share is allotted to a single son. The mention of the "mother" is intended to include her co-wives and others. Vyāsa states:

"The childless wives of the father are declared to be entitled to equal shares; and all those [wives] who are the grandmothers are declared to be equal to mothers. This refers to cases where the woman has not received separate property (strīdhana). 2.123.

Regarding other matters for those sons who are dividing [the estate], he says: "And those brothers who have not been consecrated should be consecrated by their brothers who have already been consecrated; and the sisters, having received a fourth part from their own share, [should be so consecrated]. (2.124)

Those younger brothers who have not been consecrated by their father through the *jātakarman* and other rites are to be consecrated by their elder brothers. Sisters for whom the rite of marriage has not been performed are to be consecrated—that is, married—by giving each of them a fourth part of whatever share belongs to a single son. Nārada states: "For those whose rites of consecration were not performed in due order by the father, they must be performed by the brothers from the paternal wealth itself."
If no paternal share exists, the sacramental rites for brothers must nevertheless be performed by those already consecrated, either by taking [funds] from their own shares or otherwise.

Vyāsa says: But those who there have not been consecrated [with sacraments] are to be consecrated by their elder brothers from the paternal estate alone, as well as the unmarried girls, according to the prescribed rule.
Manu: "The brothers shall give to their unmarried sisters portions from their own respective shares individually;
they shall give a fourth part from each of their own shares. Those who are unwilling to give shall become outcasts."

Here too, the two words “from their own shares” (*svebhyaḥ aṃśebhyaḥ*) are intended to mean only the share of a son. The plural number is intended to indicate a plurality of daughters. The repetition “from each one’s own” (*svāt svāt*) is intended to include daughters of various castes. This is what is meant: when a Brāhmaṇa has wives from all the [four] castes and each of them has a daughter, then whichever daughter belongs to the Brāhmaṇa wife receives a fourth part of whatever share would belong to a son of that Brāhmaṇa father. In this way, the daughters of Kṣatriya and other wives of a Brāhmaṇa father likewise receive a fourth part of the share belonging to a son of a Kṣatriya or other caste. And this is not an inheritance (*dāya*). Therefore, there is no contradiction with the statement by Baudhāyana, which follows the rule “a woman deserves [a share],” namely: “There is no inheritance for those who are powerless; for women are considered non-inheritors—so says the Śruti. Thus ends the rule for the distribution of inheritance among those of the same caste (2.124).
He now states the division of inheritance for those of different castes:
"The sons of a Brāhmaṇa, according to their respective castes, shall have four, three, two, and one shares;
the sons born of a Kṣatriya shall have three, two, and one shares; but the two born of a Vaiśya shall have two and one shares. (2.125)

Among the sons born to a Brāhmaṇa from his four wives, beginning with the Brāhmaṇī and ending with the Śūdrā, they shall take four shares of the father’s wealth divided into ten parts: three for the son of the Brāhmaṇī, two for the son of the Kṣatriyā, one for the son of the Vaiśyā, and one for the son of the Śūdrā. Similarly, of the wealth of a Kṣatriya father divided into six parts, the sons of the Kṣatriyā wife shall take three shares, those of the Vaiśyā two, and those of the Śūdrā one. The estate of a Vaiśya father is to be divided into three parts; of these, two shares belong to the sons of the Vaiśyā wife and one to the son of the Śūdrā wife. However, for a Śūdra, there is no wife of a different (higher) caste. Regarding this specific point, Bṛhaspati says:
Land received as a gift must not be given to the son of a Kṣatriya or others;
even if their father should give it, once he is dead, the son of the Brāhmaṇa shall take it.
However, even that which is obtained through other means by accepting a gift must not be given to the son of a Śūdra. Likewise, another Smṛti states:
"A Śūdra born of twice-born men does not deserve a share of land.
As for what they [the authorities] remember:
The son of a Śūdra woman by a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya father does not share in the inheritance;
whatever his father may give to him, that alone shall be his wealth.
Thus, this [text] prohibits partition when wealth has been obtained through the favor of the father; otherwise, the rule regarding partition for the son of a Śūdra wife would be meaningless. (2.125)
Regarding what must be done when property stolen by a brother is discovered among the assets to be divided, he says:
"If property stolen from one another is found after the partition has been made, they shall divide it again into equal shares; such is the settled rule. (2.126)

If property that was to be divided has been taken away by one brother and is subsequently recovered after the partition, then it must be divided by all [the brothers] with equal shares; it is not to be divided unequally by taking into account the *uddhāra* (preferential share). This statement is appropriate when this much meaning is established; it does not serve as proof for the absence of fault on the part of the taker. Now, if it is argued: "The partitioners are Brāhmaṇas and the property to be divided is gold; therefore, if the taker incurs loss of caste (*pātitya*) due to the theft of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold, the rule that 'they should divide it again with equal shares' would be inappropriate, because one who has lost his caste is entitled to no share. That is not so, because the statement remains valid even if it refers to other types of property. Furthermore, there is no contradiction in restricting a general statement to a specific case. Or, let this sentence refer specifically to the gold of a Brāhmaṇa; even so, it does not imply the absence of fault for the taker, since the prescription of an equal share is appropriate for one who, having performed penance, is fit to engage in legal transactions. Alternatively, let the statement "they should divide it again with equal shares" refer to cases other than those involving the taker. Nor should it be said that before the partition it belonged to no one at all, for it has been stated: "It is simply one's own common property that is being divided; existence [of ownership] does not arise from the act of partition. — Kātyāyana.
But whatever property was concealed, upon being discovered again, they shall divide it equally with their brothers; indeed, in the absence of the father, the sons [shall do so].
Likewise:
Property that has been taken from one another, or that which was improperly divided, as well as what was stolen, lost, or recovered, and what was previously mentioned, shall be divided again.
It was stated previously that [the property] was either poorly partitioned or stolen. (2.126)
The division of wealth concerning the legitimate son has been stated; now he speaks regarding the specific case of the field-born son:

"A son procreated by means of *niyoga* upon the field of another by one who is sonless is, according to the law, the heir to the estate and the giver of the funeral oblation (*piṇḍa*) for both. (2.127)

It has been established in the first chapter that a son produced through *niyoga* is one authorized by his father; however, regarding the specific rule of *niyoga* mentioned here—where a son is begotten by a brother-in-law or similar relative upon the wife of another man who is childless, for the sake of both himself and the other—that son known as a *vyāmuṣyāyaṇa* must be understood from the *Dharmaśāstras* as the heir to the estate and the giver of the funeral oblation (*piṇḍa*) to both fathers, the progenitor and the owner of the field. As for what was stated by Nārada:
"A *dvaimātura* (son of two fathers) should offer the *piṇḍa* and water separately to both."
Between the owner of the seed and the owner of the field, the latter shall also receive a half-share of the inheritance.
Thus, this should be understood to apply when a *kṣetraja* son has been born and subsequently a *aurasa* (legitimate) son is produced. Kātyāyana states:
"When a legitimate son is born, the other sons who are of the same caste (*savarṇa*) shall receive a fourth share;
however, those who are of a different caste (*asavarṇa*) are entitled only to food and clothing."

Therefore, when a legitimate son (*aurasa*) has not been born, the *kṣetraja* son takes the entire inheritance from both fathers; but when one has been born, his share of the paternal estate is a fourth part—this is the settled rule. As for that which was stated by Manu: "When dividing the paternal inheritance, the legitimate son should give a sixth part of the father's wealth to the *kṣetraja*, or even a fifth."

In that regard, the granting of a sixth or fifth share pertains to the case of a son born of the wife (kṣetraja) who possesses few qualities. Likewise: "The legitimate son (aurasa) and the son born of the wife (kṣetraja) are both sharers of the father's inheritance; but the other ten [types of sons] are, in order, sharers of the family name and a portion of the inheritance."

This should be understood to apply when the legitimate son (*aurasa*) is devoid of qualities and the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*) possesses good qualities, because an equal division is prescribed. Among the ten types of sons other than the legitimate son, the son born of the wife, and the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*), if a legitimate son should be born after they have been produced, then the entire inheritance belongs to the legitimate son alone; the others merely receive a share of that portion. However, their lineage (*gotra*) remains the same as that of the legitimate son. Nārada says: "The offspring of whichever man's seed succeeds in the field with the consent of the owner of the field belongs equally to both—the owner of the field and the owner of the seed. [734]

Hārīta says: "They say that while [the biological father] lives, the son born of the field (kṣetraja) belongs to two lineages (dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa), because of the lack of independence [of the biological father], provided he has not sown his own seed. For a field does not bear fruit without seed, nor does seed sprout without a field; since both are observed [to be necessary], the offspring belongs to both. The phrase "because of the lack of having sown seed" means because the owner of the field did not sow his own seed. (2.127)
Having described the division of inheritance among the primary sons, [the author], intending to describe those who are secondary, states their characteristics preceded by those of the primary ones:

"The legitimate son (aurasa) is born of the lawful wife; equal to him is the son of an appointed daughter (putrikāsuta); the son of the field (kṣetraja) is one begotten on the wife by a kinsman of the same lineage (sagotra) or by another. (2.128)
One born secretly in the house is therefore known as *gūḍhaja* (secret-born).
A son born of an unmarried girl is considered a *kānīna*, the son of his maternal grandfather. (2.129)
One born of a woman who has been previously married, whether she was still a virgin or not, is known as a *paunarbhava*.
One whom the mother or the father gives away is known as a *dattaka* son. (2.130)

One who is purchased, one who is sold by his parents, one who is made so (kṛtrima), one who makes himself so, one who gives himself, one who is given by himself, one discovered in the womb, and one born of a pregnant bride (sahoḍhaja). || 2.131 ||
But he who is taken after having been abandoned becomes an apaviddha son.

He who is born of the lawful wife (*dharmapatnī*) is to be known as the legitimate son (*aurasa*). She with whom one practices the religious duty (*dharma*) is the lawful wife. Although the term *patnī* alone denotes a co-practitioner of religious duty, nevertheless, because of the inclusion of the word *dharma*, the term *patnī* here refers specifically to a wife [of equal status]. By the term *dharmapatnī*, the Śūdra woman is excluded, since she lacks the capacity for co-practice in religious duty. As Vasiṣṭha says: "Women of dark complexion are indeed for pleasure only, not for religious duty. And thus, his son is not a legitimate son. For this very reason, Manu mentions him among the substitutes for a son.
Svāyambhuva Manu has declared twelve kinds of sons for men;
among them, six are kinsmen and heirs, while six are kinsmen but not heirs.
The legitimate son of the body, the son begotten on the wife, the adopted son, the made son, the son secretly born, and the cast-off son— these six are both heirs and kinsmen.

The son born of an unmarried girl, the son received with a bride, the purchased son, the son of a remarried woman, the self-given son, and the Śūdra-born son— these six are kinsmen who do not inherit.
The wise declare that these eleven sons, beginning with the *kṣetraja* as previously described, are substitutes for a son, intended to prevent the omission of religious rites.

The meaning is that the wise, fearing the loss of the performance of those duties [performed by a son] in the absence of a legitimate son (*aurasa*), have declared the eleven substitutes for a son, beginning with the *kṣetraja*. Although the son of a Śūdra woman is a substitute, it has already been stated previously that he possesses a share of the inheritance even when legitimate sons exist; for this very reason, the Lord of Yoga (Yājñavalkya) did not mention him among the substitutes. Nor should it be asked: "How then is it said that the son of a Śūdra woman is not an heir? For Manu himself has stated that he is excluded from the division of the inheritance only when there is wealth given to him as a favor by his father.
"The son of a Śūdra woman by a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya does not inherit property.
Alternatively, the statement regarding his lack of inheritance may be intended to mean that he does not receive a share of the paternal wealth exceeding one-tenth. As Manu himself has stated:
"Whether there be a legitimate son or even if there be no son at all..."
"According to the law, one should not give more than a tenth part to the son of a Śūdra woman.
"More than a tenth part" means [more than] that share. Bṛhaspati states that the wealth of one who has no offspring belongs only to the *sapiṇḍas*:
"The son born of a Śūdra womb who serves his father and possesses good qualities [is entitled to a share]."
He shall receive the remainder of his life's earnings, and the sapindas shall obtain [the rest].

The subject at hand is now stated: the *aurasa* (legitimate) son is one born of a twice-born woman who has been wedded according to the scriptures. This is a term based on its etymological meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*); thus, he is called *aurasa* because he exists in her lap (*uraḥ*). Therefore, being produced by oneself is the defining characteristic of the *aurasa* son. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha says: "The first [son] is he whom one has procreated oneself in one’s own consecrated field. "First" means primary. Thus, that alone is the primary meaning of the word "son"; in the case of the *kṣetraja* (field-born) and others, it is secondary. Consequently, this is the complete definition of the *aurasa*: he is described by the two phrases "the *aurasa* born of the lawful wife" (*dharmapatnīja*). Equal to him—that is, equal to the *aurasa*—is the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāsuta*). A daughter herself is the "daughter-son" (*putrikāputra*). For she, possessing the characteristics of an *aurasa* son apart from [the physical presence of] masculinity, is equal to an *aurasa*. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
Thirteen sons have been declared by Manu in former times;
among them, the son of the body (aurasa) and the appointed daughter (putrikā) are the causes for the continuity of the lineage.
Just as oil is remembered by the wise as a substitute for clarified butter when the latter is unavailable,
so too are the eleven types of sons considered substitutes in the absence of the appointed daughter (putrikā) and the legitimate son of the body (aurasa).
Even the son of an appointed daughter (putrikā) is here referred to by the term "son of an appointed daughter" (putrikāputra). For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha says:
"I shall give you an unbrothered maiden, adorned;
whatever son is born of her, he shall be my son. [736]

Gautama says: "A childless father may designate a daughter as an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) after performing a sacrifice to Agni and Prajāpati, having made a formal agreement that 'this offspring is for my sake. According to some, she becomes an appointed daughter by the mere act of such an intention; therefore, one should not marry her while harboring doubts about this status, nor should one marry a girl who has no brother. Jābāli says: "In the case of giving away an appointed daughter, the knower of dharma, having performed a sacrifice to Agni and Prajāpati with a *sthālīpāka* offering, should do the same when giving away a son."

The son known as *kṣetraja* (born of the wife) belongs to the owner of the field; he is one begotten upon the wife of another by a relative of the same lineage or by someone else. He who is born in the house of a man upon his wife, secretly and without the specific identity of the progenitor being known, is the son known as *gūḍhotpanna* (secretly born); he belongs to the owner of the mother. This [son] is mentioned immediately after the *kṣetraja*, because, being produced by another upon one's own wife, he is similar to the *kṣetraja*. Furthermore, he who is born of an unmarried maiden is designated as *kānīna* (maiden-born); according to Manu and others, he is the son of the maternal grandfather. He too is mentioned immediately after the *gūḍhotpanna* due to a similarity with it, insofar as he is somehow born in a "field" in the form of a daughter belonging to a relative of his own. Vasiṣṭha says:
If the unmarried daughter of one should obtain a son through a husband of equal status,
that son shall offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his maternal grandfather and inherit his wealth.

That girl who has not been given in speech is here termed "not given" (*aprattā*). Because of this specific qualification, a son born after the formal gift (*pradāna*) but before the marriage belongs to the husband alone; with this intention, Manu says: "But the son whom a maiden secretly bears in her father’s house, one should call him by the name *kānīna* (the maiden-born), as he originates from the maiden and belongs to the husband."

A son born of a woman who has been married again—whether she was previously unwidowed or widowed, whether she was "unbroken" (akṣatā) or "broken" (kṣatā), that is, enjoyed by others, and having been taken back and consecrated with rites—is designated as *paunarbhava*. The term *punarbhū* was explained in the first chapter. These [sons] are mentioned first because they are closely related, being born from the field (*kṣetra*) belonging to their own kin. Those for whom there is no such connection even through the field are considered inferior and are therefore mentioned later. Among them, he who is given away by both parents, or by the father alone, or by the mother with the husband's consent, is his *dattaka* (given) son. Manu says:

If the mother or the father, being both filled with affection, should give a son away during a time of distress by means of a water-libation to one who is similar [in status], he is to be known as a "given" (dattrima) son.

The phrase "with water" (*adbhiḥ*) is intended as an illustration for all the duties of giving (*dānadharmopala-kṣaṇārtham*). "In times of distress" (*āpadi*) refers to famine and the like; or alternatively, to the distress of the recipient. "In the absence of a son" means one who is similar, that is, of the same caste (*savarṇa*) for both the giver and the recipient. "Endowed with affection" (*prītisaṃyuktau*) means they are not motivated by fear or other such factors. Likewise:

"A son given in adoption (*dattrima*) shall not inherit the lineage (*gotra*) or the estate (*riktha*) of his biological father. The funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) follows the estate; the ancestral offering (*svadhā*) ceases for the one who gave him away."

Consequently, the *dattaka* (adopted son) shall not take the lineage (*gotra*) or the inheritance (*riktha*) of his biological father, nor shall he offer the funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) to him. Rather, he shall be the one who takes the lineage and so forth, and offers the *piṇḍa* to his second [adoptive] father. Here, the word *piṇḍa* is intended as an indicator for all post-mortem rites (*aurdhvadaihika*). Having thus defined the thirteen types of sons by analogy with the principles governing the *kṛtrima*, *dattātmā*, and *apaviddha*, the *Brahmapurāṇa* describes their legal status according to the order of castes:
"The *dattaka*, the *svayaṃdatta*, the *kṛtrima*, and the *krīta*..."
And those sons who have been cast away must indeed always be supported.
Those who belong to different lineages (*gotra*), have separate funeral offerings (*piṇḍa*), and likewise maintain distinct family lines,
share in the three-day period of impurity (*āśauca*) both at birth and at death.
Furthermore, in some cases, a Śūdra who is a Pāraśava slave may exist among Brāhmaṇas who provide clothing and food, as well as those who possess seeds and fields.
But for kings who have been consumed by a curse, who are constantly subject to decline,
or who are habitually engaged in battle, these [omens] never appear—
whether it be a legitimate son or the son of an appointed daughter.
Indeed, for them, the Kṣetrajas and others are not to be recognized;
those eleven, belonging to separate lineages, merely perpetuate their own families.
All of them constantly perform the ancestral rites (śrāddha) and other duties for them like servants;
this applies to the son born in secret, the maiden-born son, the son received with a pregnant bride, and likewise the son born of the wife.
Furthermore, for Vaiśyas, there is rebirth even out of fear of royal punishment;
the five who are powerful are excluded, while all the rest indeed remain.
For Śūdras who live by servitude, subsist on the food of others,
and whose bodies are dependent on others, a son is not desired anywhere.
Therefore, from a male slave and a female slave, only a slave is indeed born.

Vasiṣṭha: "A person is produced from blood and semen, having the mother and father as his cause; therefore, the mother and father have authority over his giving, selling, or abandoning. However, one should not give away an only son, for he is for the continuation of the ancestors. A woman, moreover, may neither give nor receive a son except with the permission of her husband. One intending to adopt a son should summon his kinsmen, announce it to the king, perform oblations in the middle of the house with the *vyāhṛti* mantras, and then adopt a boy who is not a close relative (*adūrebāndhava*). When a doubt arises, one should establish a distant relative (*dūrebāndhava*) as a *śūdra* until certainty is reached; for it is known that by means of one [son], many are saved. The phrase "one should not give away an only son" uses the verb "to give" (*dadāti*) merely as an illustration; thus, this prohibition applies to selling and other such acts as well. Likewise, because the expression "one intending to adopt a son" is also illustrative, the entire set of rules beginning with "having summoned his kinsmen" must be performed even in cases of purchase and so forth, since the underlying principle is the same. The term *adūrebāndhava* means "one whose relatives are not distant. Because the relatives are not far away in space, his noble birth can be ascertained. Therefore, the meaning is that one should adopt a son whose lineage is known—that is, one who is not a close relative. It does not mean that one should adopt him in the presence of his kinsmen, for that is already established by the rule "having summoned his kinsmen. One should adopt someone who is not a close relative (*asaṃnikṛṣṭa*), meaning not a blood relative. When a doubt regarding caste arises, one should treat a distant relative—meaning one residing in a remote region—as a *śūdra* until certainty is reached. The essential point is that one should reach a decision through great effort. He cites a Vedic text as the reason for this: "For it is known that by means of one, many are saved," meaning that by means of one son, many ancestors are saved. Therefore, the essential point is that one should adopt only one whose lineage is known, and no other. A son who is obtained after being sold by his parents is called a *krīta* (bought) son. A son who is made one's own by saying "You yourself become my son" is designated as *kṛtrima* (artificial). He who gives himself, saying "I shall be your son," without being asked, is called a *svayaṃdatta* (self-given) son. A son conceived in the womb of a woman while she is being married is called *sahoḍhaja* (born of a pregnant bride). —Manu.
If one should purchase from someone else a son for the sake of his own parents, that son is a "bought" (krītaka) son; he may be either similar or dissimilar [to the purchaser].
The statement "similar" or "dissimilar" refers to an assessment of qualities, not to caste.
However, he who would make one similar— endowed with the qualities of a son and discerning of virtues and faults— that son is to be known as the *kṛtrima* (artificial).
In this context, the mention of "similar" refers to similarity of caste.
One who is deprived of his mother and father, or has been abandoned without cause,
and who offers himself to someone— that person is known as a *svayamdatta* (self-given) son.
The cause for forfeiture is falling from one's status (pātitya); "should touch" means he should give her.
When a woman who is pregnant—whether her condition be known or unknown—is consecrated [in marriage], the child belongs to the man who marries her; such a child is called *sahoḍha*.
One who is adopted by someone after having been abandoned by his parents—without cause such as loss of caste (*pātitya*) or the like—is his son known as the *apaviddha* (cast-off). Manu says:
"Whomever one may adopt as a son when he has been abandoned by both his mother and father, or by either of them, he is called an *apaviddha*. (2.128–131)
The one who offers the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) and the one who takes the inheritance among these are such that, in the absence of each preceding one, each subsequent one succeeds. (2.132)

Among these aforementioned sons—the legitimate son (*aurasa*) and the others, both primary and secondary—each subsequent one is entitled to offer the *śrāddha* and receive the inheritance in the absence of each preceding one. Among the substitutes for a son (*putrapratinidhi*), only the adopted son (*dattaka*) is to be accepted in the Kali age. For this very reason, Śaunaka has stated in the continuation [of his work]: "In the Kali age, however, the acceptance of others as sons, with the exception of the *datta* and *aurasa*, is prohibited. When a legitimate son is born after a daughter has been appointed as an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), Manu says:
But if a son is born after a daughter has been appointed as an heir, the division of the estate shall be equal; for there is no right of primogeniture for a woman.
Manu himself states a specific rule regarding the son born of the wife (kṣetraja):
"If the legitimate son of the body (aurasa) and the son born of the wife (kṣetraja) should both be heirs to the same estate,
whatever paternal property belongs to one, he alone shall take it, and not the other."

This [verse] establishes the entitlement of the *kṣetraja* son and the *dvaimātura* (*dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*) son to the seed-owner’s property. However, Vasiṣṭha states a specific rule regarding the case where a legitimate (*aurasa*) son is born after a son has been adopted: “If a legitimate son is born after that adopted son has been received, the latter shall be entitled to a fourth share. All these variations in shares—whether less or more—are to be determined with regard to whether the sons possess merit or lack it. As for what is stated by Manu and others—that among all the substitutes for a son, even though the later ones inherit the estate in the absence of the preceding ones, some are heirs and some are not—the intention there is this: those substitutes for a son who are designated as heirs become the inheritors of the estate of a father who has no biological son; others do not. (2.132)
He states the specific rule for all those previously mentioned substitutes for a son:
"This procedure has been declared by me regarding sons who are of the same caste."

The essential meaning is that those born in secret (*gūḍhotpanna*) and the others must be accepted as sons only if they are of the same caste (*savarṇa*) and of the same class (*sajātīya*) as the father, and not otherwise. A son born of a *śūdra* woman, if procreated by oneself in one's own wife (*svakṣetra*), is not a substitute (*pratinidhi*) but is rather a legitimate son (*aurasa*); nevertheless, he is listed among the substitutes by Manu. The intention therein is this: while there are other legitimate sons born of women of higher castes (*anuloma*), there is no substitute; however, even when a legitimate son exists, a son born of a *śūdra* woman must indeed be treated as a substitute for a son. — Manu.
Whether there be a virtuous son or even no son at all,
one should not, according to the law, give more than a tenth part to the son of a Śūdra wife.

It follows by implication that the wife and others take more than a tenth share from the estate of one who dies without a son; furthermore, even a son born to a Śūdra from a female slave shall, if born of desire, be an inheritor of a share. (2.133)
When the father has died, the brothers shall make him (the son of an appointed daughter) a recipient of half a share;
one who has no brothers shall take the whole, except for the son of a daughter. (2.134)

A son born to a Śūdra by a female slave shall be an inheritor of a share according to the father’s wish; the meaning is that he receives whatever share his father desires to give him. When the father has died, the sons who were married by him—his brothers—should give him half of whatever share would fall to one of them. However, one who has no brothers—that is, one born to a father by a wife other than those previously married, and who lacks brothers—and who has no daughters’ sons (dauhitras), shall take the entire paternal estate. But if such daughters’ sons exist, he takes only half a share. From the mention of the Śūdra here, it is understood that a son of a twice-born man born by a female slave has no right to inherit a share of the father’s wealth. (2.133, 134)
He states the order of those entitled to inherit the wealth of one who has died without a son or his substitute:
"The wife, the daughters, and likewise the parents, the brothers, as well as their sons, a kinsman of the same lineage (gotraja), a relative, a pupil, and fellow students. (2.135)
In the absence of these, each subsequent one among them is the heir to the wealth of the deceased who left no son; for this is the rule for all castes. (2.136)

For one who has died without a son—that is, one lacking both primary and secondary sons—the heirs to the wealth and takers of the property are to be understood as the wife and the others mentioned in succession, each succeeding one taking the estate in the absence of the preceding one.
