This rule is common to all social classes (*varṇa*). Bṛhaspati says:
"In the Veda, in the Smṛti scriptures, and in worldly custom, the wise have declared that the wife is half of the body, sharing equally in the fruits of merit and demerit."
For one whose wife has not passed away, half of his body remains alive;
while half of the body still lives, how could another take possession of the wealth?
But when sapindas— namely paternal uncles and other blood relations— are present,
the wife of one who has died without a son shall take his share.
If she dies first, her husband having already passed away, a woman devoted to her husband shall inherit that wealth; this is indeed the eternal law.
Having taken moving property, immovable property, gold, silver, grain, liquids, and clothing, one should cause the śrāddha for the monthly, six-monthly, and other periods to be performed.

One should honor paternal uncles, preceptors, daughters' sons, sisters, brothers-in-law, maternal uncles, elders, the protectorless, guests, and women with offerings to the ancestors (kavya) and charitable works (pūrta).
Her sapindas and kinsmen who act as her adversaries and would seize her property— the king shall punish them with the punishment prescribed for thieves.

Viṣṇu states: "The wealth of one who dies without a son goes to his wife; in her absence, it goes to his daughter; in her absence, to his father; in his absence, to his mother; in her absence, to his brother; in his absence, to his brother’s son; in his absence, to his kinsman (bandhu); in his absence, to his sapinda; in his absence, to his fellow-student; in his absence, with the exception of the property of a Brāhmaṇa, it goes to the King. Bṛhaspati states:
"If a man has died childless, without a wife, and without brothers, father, or mother, all his sapindas shall divide that inheritance according to their respective shares."

Śaṅkha, however, states the sequence differently: "Now, when one who has died without a son departs for heaven, the property goes to his brothers; in their absence, both the mother and father shall receive it, or else the eldest wife. Devala says:
"Then the uterine brothers shall divide the inheritance of one who has no son;
or likewise the daughters of equal status, or even the father, if he is still living."
"Respectively, [the heirs are] brothers of the same caste, the mother, and the wife. Nārada also says:
"If among brothers one should die without offspring, or if he should renounce the world..."
The remaining [sons] shall divide his property, excluding the woman's separate property (strīdhana).
They should provide for his maintenance until the end of their lives;
if they preserve the bed of their husband, they shall receive that [inheritance] when they have passed away.
Likewise: "O Brāhmaṇa, however, the king who is devoted to righteousness should provide a livelihood for those women; this is remembered as the rule regarding inheritance."

Thus, in order to establish the authority of these statements whose contradictions appear at first glance by resolving those contradictions, one must state that they have different scopes (*bhinnaviṣayatā*). On this point, some say: "The statement beginning with *patnī duhitaraḥ* [Yājñavalkya 2.138] refers to a woman who desires a son through a deity, another person, or even a *sapiṇḍa* relative, such as her teacher or father-in-law. That is incorrect; for in this view, there would be a contradiction with many other Smṛti texts that is difficult to resolve. For instance, Vasiṣṭha states: "There is no *niyoga* out of greed for inheritance. By this, the lack of entitlement to *niyoga* is declared for a woman who inherits property. [Objection: Let there be no *niyoga* from him; however, let the status of being an heir to the wealth of one previously authorized (*niyuktā*) be ordained later by the rule "*patnī duhitaraḥ*" [Yājñavalkya 2.138]. [Response: That is not so. If that were the case, the deceased owner of the wealth would possess a son through that very *kṣetraja* son yet to be born. The rule "*patnī duhitaraḥ*" ordains that the wife inherits the wealth of one who has no son. Manu says exactly this.
"He who shall maintain the wealth of a deceased brother, or even his widow,
having procreated offspring for that brother, shall give that very wealth to him alone.
The meaning is that this belongs to him alone, and not to the mother.
For one who has passed away childless, one should continue the lineage through his family name;
whatever share of the inheritance he would have had, that one should bestow upon him.

"For her offspring"—this means for the sake of progeny. Furthermore, how could that desire for appointment (*niyoga*) serve as a reason for inheriting the estate, given that it is contradictory? Gautama clarifies this very contradiction: "Those connected by the offering of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), the lineage (*gotra*), or the purpose [of the estate] shall divide the inheritance; or the wife of one who has no offspring may seek [another's] seed. For by this, an option is established between the wife’s status as the inheritor of her childless husband’s wealth and her desire for appointment, which is indicated by her seeking [another's] seed. Thus, the contradiction is evident. Vṛddha-Manu also says:
A wife who is childless, guarding her husband’s bed and remaining steadfast in her vows,
shall indeed offer that funeral cake (piṇḍa) and receive the entire share.

By saying this, he clarifies that one who seeks appointment (*niyoga*) has no right to inherit the estate. For if that were the case, it would not have been stated that she "protects the bed of her husband. Therefore, this interpretation is not tenable. How, then, is the contradiction to be resolved? It is said: a wife possessing the qualities mentioned in the verse of Manu beginning with "the sonless [wife] [protects] the bed of her husband," even when father and brothers are present, takes the husband's entire wealth herself and performs the *śrāddha* and other rites for the husband. It was with this very intention that Bṛhaspati also spoke.
"The father's funeral rites, consisting of the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa) and the pouring of water, must be performed by the son.
In the absence of a son, however, the wife shall perform them; and in her absence, a uterine brother. Thus it is said.

Likewise, she who has properly performed service to her husband—who earned the wealth himself without depleting his paternal inheritance—and who has restrained her senses, shall take the husband’s entire estate even when brothers-in-law (*devaras*) are present. However, in the case of a wife who is suspected of infidelity due to youth and so forth, the wealth of the deceased husband goes to his brothers and not to the wife, even if she is present. In this regard, the following distinction applies: if the wealth was acquired through joint effort by his brothers without depleting their own paternal inheritance, then the brothers alone are the heirs, even if the parents are alive. But if the wealth was acquired by the father, grandfather, or others, then the brothers have no share; rather, it belongs to the parents. In this way, there is no contradiction among all the scriptural statements regarding the determination of the subject matter. Nor should it be argued: "How can a woman, being ineligible for sacrifice (*yajña*) when alone, take that which was produced for the purpose of sacrifice? For there is no evidence that every production of wealth is for the sake of sacrifice. Only that production of wealth which is prescribed by such injunctions as "one consecrated for twelve nights should hire [priests]" is for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*); otherwise, it is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). As for the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "Therefore women are powerless and non-heirs," that too must be explained according to what is established, since it is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*); thus, it should be interpreted as referring to cases where a son exists. Furthermore, women—even those living alone—possess the right to perform *pūrta* (charitable) religious duties; therefore, they shall utilize the wealth for that purpose. As for what Nārada stated after saying, "If one of the brothers dies without offspring," namely, "Therefore women are powerless and non-heirs"—that too must be explained according to what is established, since it is merely a restatement; thus, it should be interpreted as referring to cases where a son exists. And indeed, women—even those living alone—possess the right to perform *pūrta* religious duties; therefore, they shall utilize the wealth for that purpose. As for what Nārada stated after saying, "If one of the brothers dies without offspring... [the same logic applies].

"And they should provide for her maintenance until the end of her life," and so forth; this, however, should be understood as referring to the case of a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman) or a *svairiṇī* (an unchaste woman), because of the mere use of the word "woman" (*strī*). The word "wife" (*patnī*), however, applies only to one who is joined through marriage and sacrifice, according to the traditional rule of grammar: "The term *patnī* [is used] in connection with the husband's sacrifices. Thus, in the absence of a wife, daughters of the same caste as the father are the owners of the property of one who dies without a son. Nārada says: "In the absence of a son, however, the daughter [inherits], because she is seen to continue the lineage equally."
Both the son and the daughter are the continuers of the father's lineage.
Likewise: "As one is to oneself, so is a son; a daughter is equal to a son.
While she remains as one's very self, how could another take the wealth?"
Bṛhaspati: From limb after limb of men, a daughter is produced just like a son. How then could another man take her father’s property?
A wife who is equal [to her husband], wedded to one who is her equal, virtuous, and devoted to service—
whether she has borne sons or not, she shall indeed inherit the father's wealth.

“Of equal status” means of the same caste (*savarṇā*). Therefore, there is no entitlement for a daughter of a different caste to inherit the estate. [744] The meaning is that she is a “putrikā,” whether formally appointed or not. In this context, the phrase “whether appointed or not” introduces the *putrikā* as an illustrative example; it does not, however, enjoin her right to take the wealth of a father who has no other son. For one cannot say that the father of a *putrikā* is “without a son,” since the *putrikā* herself is also a son. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: “The third [type of son] is recognized as the *putrikā*. By this, the claim made by some—that in the verse beginning with “the wife, the daughters,” the word “daughter” refers specifically to the *putrikā*—should be understood as refuted. Both the mother and the father are the heirs to the wealth of a son who is deprived of his wife and daughters. —Bṛhaspati.
In the case of a deceased son who is without a wife or children,
the mother should be known as the heir to the inheritance, or his brother with her consent.
Manu: The mother shall obtain the inheritance of a son who dies without offspring;
and when the mother has also passed away, the father’s mother shall take the wealth.

In the absence of the parents, the brothers—specifically uterine (sodara) brothers—are entitled [to the inheritance] because they are the most proximate. For, compared to a deceased brother, they perform the *śrāddha* for only one mother’s lineage, and not for a rival mother’s lineage. As for the statement of Śaṅkha, Likhita, and Paiṭīnasi: "The wealth of one who has died without a son goes to his brothers; in their absence, the parents shall receive it, or the eldest wife," and so forth—that should be understood to apply to brothers who have acquired divided property through the inheritance of paternal wealth. In the absence of such brothers, the parents or the eldest wife [receive it]. However, brothers who differ from the characteristics of the aforementioned brothers should be considered heirs to the estate by bypassing the order stated by Yājñavalkya; thus, everything is consistent. Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Devala:
Then, the uterine brothers, or equally qualified daughters, or even the father if he dies, shall divide the inheritance of one who leaves no son.
Sons of the same caste, brothers, mother, and wife, respectively.

Thus, even in that case, it should be understood that among uterine brothers, the right to inherit the estate first follows the method established by the words of Śaṅkha: "In the absence of a brother, his sons; in their absence, the *gotraja*s; there, the one who is most proximate shall first take the wealth. As Manu says: "Whoever is the nearest *sapiṇḍa* to him, his shall be the wealth. And the state of being "nearest" has been stated by that very same [author]:
Water should be offered to three; the funeral cake proceeds for three.
The fourth is the one who bestows them; a fifth is not possible.

Among those who have become the recipients (*saṃpradāna*)—namely the three beginning with the father—the giver of the water libation (*udaka*) and other rites, as well as any other person born in their lineage who likewise gives them the water libation and so forth, is their *sapiṇḍa* and thus closely related. In this regard, however, the uterine brother is most closely related because he shares the same status as a recipient of the water libation and other rites. His son, moreover, is slightly more remote because his status as a recipient is limited to the paternal *piṇḍa*. His grandson is even more remote than him, because the *piṇḍas* of the father and grandfather have different recipients. His great-grandson, however, is extremely remote, because there is a difference in the recipients for all three *piṇḍas*. Thus, in the paternal line, the three beginning with the brother, his son, and his grandson are the closely related *sapiṇḍas*. The same applies to the lineages of the grandfather and the great-grandfather. In the absence of these, the triad of sons and so forth belonging to the great-grandsons of the triad beginning with the father shall take the inheritance due to *sāpiṇḍya*. In the absence of *gotraja*s, the kinsman (*bandhu*)—such as the father’s sister, the mother’s sister, the son of the maternal uncle, and others—takes it. In his absence, the pupil (*śiṣya*), one who has been initiated and taught the Veda, becomes the heir. In his absence, the fellow-student (*sabrahmacārī*), one who has the same teacher, [is the heir]. As for that which was stated by Kātyāyana:
When [the property] has been divided and settled, in the absence of sons, the father shall take the wealth;
or the brother, or the mother, or the father of that [mother], in that order.

Thus, the phrase "absence of sons" is intended to illustrate that context; by extension, it should be understood as the absence of wives and daughters. In the absence of the father, it is the mother, or else the brother with the mother's permission, for there is this scriptural statement: "The mother should be known as the heir to the estate, or the brother with her consent.
In the absence of these, the paternal grandmother inherits after the daughter and the daughter’s son (*dauhitra*). Thus says Bṛhaspati.
In their absence, however, the brothers, the sons of the brothers, the uterine kinsmen (sanābhi),
the lineal descendants (sakulya), the relatives (bāndhava), the pupils, and those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya) are entitled to the wealth.
Nārada says:
In the absence of daughters, the kinsmen on the mother’s side (sakulyas) and likewise other relatives; after them, those of the same caste; and in the absence of all these, it goes to the king.
Except for a Brāhmaṇa, however, a king devoted to righteousness shall provide a livelihood for his wives; this is recorded as the rule for inheritance.

In this context, by the phrase "in the absence of daughters," the absence of both parents is also indicated; as well as the absence of their women—whether they be unmarried, unchaste, or remarried. But in the absence of all these, Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the three Vedas, pure, and self-controlled shall be the heirs to the estate; thus the Dharma is not violated.
"The property of a Brāhmaṇa is always inviolable by the king; this is the settled rule.
But in the case of the other castes, the king may take [the property] when all [other heirs] are absent.
[746] Bṛhaspati says: "The king is the protector of the realm."
Those sons who are Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, and who are deprived of wives and brothers—
the king shall be the taker of their wealth, for he is indeed the sovereign lord of all.

Paiṭhīnasi: "The property of a *śrotriya* belongs to the assembly (*pariṣad*), not to the king; nor may it be seized by the king, provided it is held for a group of deities, or has come down through the succession of deposits, trusts, or legal transactions, or consists of the wealth of minors and women. For thus he says: 'The wealth of a woman and the wealth of minors must not be seized by the king; the property of women is that which comes to them from six sources, and the wealth of minors is their paternal inheritance.'"

The *Smṛti* states: "Whoever receives [property] from someone should perform a *śrāddha* for him and offer the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) for three generations. The phrase "for three generations" refers to the *śrāddha* performed on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). Viṣṇu says: "Therefore, even when the paternal wealth is not available, one should still offer the rice-ball."

Regarding the statement "the wife, the daughters," some raise the following objection: Only a woman who has a husband is entitled to perform *iṣṭāpūrta* (sacrificial and charitable works), not one who is alone, because she lacks a husband; for that reason, she should not indulge in pleasure, but rather in intense austerity. Furthermore, wealth that is of no use for *dharma* or *kāma* cannot constitute a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Therefore, while the father and others exist as vessels for wealth useful for *dharma* and *kāma*, the wife has no right to the inheritance. Consequently, the wife of a deceased man who leaves no son may take only enough wealth for her own maintenance and nothing more; this is the scope of the rule regarding the wife's share of the estate. As for a man who dies without a wife, the rule stating that the daughters inherit the property refers only to cases where the wealth is sufficient merely for their marriage expenses. Thus, it should be understood that in the case of surplus wealth from a deceased person, even when the wife and daughters are present, the *sapindas*—namely the father and others—are the rightful heirs, in accordance with the force of the statements of Śaṅkha and others.

That is incorrect. When the owner of the wealth has died, regarding the arising of ownership in another over that wealth which is to be enjoined, the Blessed One has said thus: the ownership of the wife and daughters is already established by birth and is not something to be produced. By the statement of Āpastamba beginning with “For from the taking of the hand there is joint status,” the ownership of women in the husband’s wealth is established as being accomplished by the very act of marriage (*pāṇigrahaṇa*). It should be understood that for daughters, the attainment of ownership over the father’s wealth is established by birth alone, just like sons. Consequently, while the wife and daughter exist, this sentence should not effect an injunction of ownership for the father and others by setting aside the ownership of those two. However, in their absence, this sentence would have an injunctive force independent of any such setting aside; thus a discrepancy (*vairūpya*) arises. Therefore, to avoid that, the point to be proven here is that the father and others inherit the wealth only in the absence of the wife and daughter. As for what is stated by Śaṅkha and others—that the wife takes the wealth in the absence of the father and others—that should be understood to apply to a case where the wife’s ownership, which is the basis for her entitlement to the husband’s wealth, has been lost due to some other cause. And that other cause has been stated in the verse “one who has been deprived of her authority and is impure,” regarding the loss of the wife’s ownership in the husband’s wealth. Therefore, the settled rule is exactly as stated. For it has been said that for women who are without husbands, there is eligibility for religious acts such as giving, provided they are other than those duties to be accomplished through mantras and fire. Thus, their use of the property is for purposes to which they themselves are independently entitled. (2.135, 136)
Now, he states the sequence for those who take the property of deceased persons belonging to the other stages of life (āśrama), excluding the householder:
"The heirs of forest-dwellers, ascetics, and students are, in order: the teacher, a virtuous pupil, a spiritual brother, and one who shares the same sacred site. (2.137)

Upon the death of any one among those such as forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*), the preceptor (*ācārya*) and others shall take their inheritance in order; the meaning is that in the absence of each preceding person, each subsequent one shall take it. A "good disciple" (*sacchiṣya*) is one who possesses excellent qualities. A "dharma-brother" (*dharmabhrātṛ*) is one who has the same preceptor. An "associate of the same sacred site" (*ekatīrthī*) is one who follows the same philosophical system, or one who dwells at the same holy place (*tīrtha*) such as Vārāṇasī. Because of the statement that a forest-dweller possesses wealth, [it is said]: "In the month of Āśvayuja, he should abandon what has arisen and what was previously accumulated."
From this it is understood that even for ascetics and students, there exists some [food] such as that from a throat-bag (kanthā) and so forth. 2.137.
It has been stated that in the absence of a son, the wife, daughters, and parents [inherit], and in their absence, the inheritance goes to the brothers; regarding this, he states a specific rule:

"But a reunited coparcener shall give to, and take from, another reunited coparcener; and a uterine brother shall do so for a uterine brother; [each] shall give and take the share of one who was born or one who has died. (2.138)
But a uterine brother who is a co-resident shall not take the wealth of one born of another womb;
even if he is not a co-resident, a uterine brother shall take it, and not one born of a different mother. (2.139)

*Saṃsṛṣṭa* means the mixing of divided property with other property by one who has already divided; one who possesses such [property] is a *saṃsṛṣṭin*. Upon the death of such a person, his brother who is a *saṃsṛṣṭin* shall take the wealth. Here, "brother" refers specifically to a uterine brother (*sodara*), and not a half-brother (*anyodarya*), even if the latter is also a *saṃsṛṣṭin*. Furthermore, the living *saṃsṛṣṭin* should give the share of that deceased person to the son born after his death. This has been mentioned here incidentally. On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
Furthermore, one who, having been partitioned by his father or brother,
or even by his paternal uncle, lives together again out of affection, is called "reunited" (saṃsṛṣṭa).

By this, it is restated that there are three types of reunited coparceners (*saṃsṛṣṭin*). Among them, regarding the statement that "the share of a reunited coparcener who dies without a son shall be taken by his reunited uterine brother," a question arises as to whether this applies when the deceased has a wife and other heirs, or in the opposite case. To address this inquiry, [the author] says: "When someone dies or somehow renounces the world (*pravrajati*), his share is not lost; it is ordained for his uterine brother."
"His sister, however, deserves to receive a share from that [inheritance];
this is the law for one who is childless and lacks both wife and father. Thus it is said.

Therefore, even in the case of one who has reunited (saṃsṛṣṭin), if there are wives and others, then this very sequence—"the wife, the daughters," and so forth—applies. Where the inheritance of brothers would otherwise be obtained, it is restricted that only a brother who is both reunited and uterine shall take the wealth, provided such a one exists. The eligibility of a sister should be understood to apply only in the absence of a uterine brother; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the Vedic text: "Therefore, women are devoid of sensory power and are non-inheritors. This has been stated: "The uterine brother who is reunited shall take the share of the deceased reunited brother. To clarify this very point through its contrapositive, he says:
But a uterine brother who is a *saṃsṛṣṭin* shall not take the wealth from one who is not uterine;

this has been explained by the very statement [of the rule]. However, when a uterine brother is a *saṃsṛṣṭin* but the other is not uterine, then, in anticipation of the question "who shall take the share?", he says:
"Even if not a *saṃsṛṣṭin*, the uterine brother shall take it, and not one born of another mother."

Even if a uterine brother is not a reunited coparcener (*asaṃsṛṣṭī*), he alone shall take [the share], and not a non-uterine brother even if he is a reunited coparcener. The fact that being a reunited coparcener is a qualification for the non-uterine brother is understood from the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even though not reunited. By this, the following meaning is established: when both uterine status and the state of being a reunited coparcener exist, then only such a person takes the share. But when the non-uterine brother is the one who is a reunited coparcener, then uterine status alone is the cause for taking the share, and not the other. Manu: "If those who were divided live together again, they should divide [the property] once more..."
In that case, the division shall be equal; there, seniority does not exist.

By this, inequality in partition caused by seniority is prohibited, but not that caused by other reasons; therefore, whatever wealth was commingled at the time of union, one receives a share at the time of partition strictly in accordance with that. On this very point, Bṛhaspati states another distinction:
"But among those who have reunited, whoever acquires wealth through learning, valor, or other means, two shares shall be given to him, and the rest shall be equal sharers."
If among them the eldest or the youngest should be deprived of his share at the time of distribution,
or if either of them should die, his portion is not lost.
The uterine brothers, having come together and assembled, shall divide it equally;
as shall the brothers who are reunited and the uterine sisters.

The "bestowal of a share" refers to partition; from that follows loss [of property] through renunciation (*pārivrājya*), loss of caste (*pātitya*), and so forth, resulting in disqualification. The meaning is that his share is not lost and must be provided for. If there are uterine brothers who are reunited (*saṃsṛṣṭin*), then they alone shall take that share, and not those who are not reunited even if they are uterine. In the absence of reunited uterine brothers, all uterine brothers, having come together, assembled, and joined together, shall divide it equally—that is, without inequality—provided there is no primary claimant. In the absence of uterine brothers, the sisters who are "of the same womb" (uterine) shall divide it; this is the remainder [of the sense]. In their absence as well, the sisters born of other mothers and the brothers [shall divide it]. (2.138, 139)
Regarding those who are not entitled to a share in any circumstance, he says:

"The impotent, the outcast, his offspring, the lame, the insane, the idiotic, the blind, and those afflicted with incurable diseases and so forth, must be maintained, but they shall receive no share. (2.140)

The impotent and others are "without shares. A "share" (aṃśa) means a portion; they are to be deprived of that. Nevertheless, they must be maintained. "Impotent" (klība) means a eunuch. "Outcast" (patita) will be explained later. "Born of him" (tajja) means born of an outcast. Although his inclusion is already established by the mention of the "outcast" itself—as Vasiṣṭha has stated, "They say that one born of an outcast becomes an outcast"—nevertheless, he must be mentioned separately. Otherwise, by the force of the statement, "Of these, the legitimate son (aurasa) and the son of the wife (kṣetraja) [inherit]," he might become entitled to a share. "Lame" (paṅgu) means one devoid of feet. "Insane" (unmattaka) means one who suffers from madness. Madness is a specific type of disease. "Idiot" (jaḍa) means a fool. "Blind" (andha) means sightless. "Incurable disease" (acikitsyaroga) means an irremediable ailment. The word "and others" (ādi) is for the purpose of including those declared in other legal treatises to be unworthy of a share. Regarding this, Nārada says:

One who hates his father, an outcast, a eunuch, and one who is born of adultery—even these, though they be legitimate sons (aurasa), shall not receive a share; how much less, then, those born of the wife (kṣetraja)?
*Pitṛdviṭ* means one who hates his father. *Upapātaka* means a minor offense; one who is possessed of such is called *aupapātika*. Manu says:
"All brothers who persist in improper occupations do not deserve the inheritance, as do those seized by chronic or severe illness, the mentally dull, the insane, the blind, and the lame."
[750] Those who have no share are the impotent, the outcaste, those blind from birth, the deaf, the insane, the mentally dull, the mute, and whoever else is devoid of sense organs.

Vasiṣṭha states: "Those who have entered another stage of life (āśrama) are not entitled to a share. This refers to the status of being in a different stage of life than the householder’s stage (gṛhasthāśrama). Kātyāyana says: "The son of a woman married out of order, one born from a woman of the same lineage (sagotra), and one who has returned from renunciation—none of these are entitled to inherit property."

One who marries out of order—that is, by transgressing the sequence of castes and the sequence of birth—is an *akramoḍhāsuta* (the son of a woman married out of order). One born from a woman of the same *gotra* as the father—meaning she belongs to the same lineage (*samānagotra*) relative to the woman [of the bridegroom]—is one born of a *sagotra* marriage. Regarding these [categories of sons], their lack of entitlement to a share is based on explicit scriptural injunction (*vācanika*), and not because they are disqualified from religious duties (*dharma*); for there is no reason for such a disqualification. Even though one who has fallen from his caste (*patita*) is disqualified from religious duties, this does not apply to those who are blind, lame, and so forth. For them, there is a lack of entitlement only with respect to specific religious acts that require certain ritual components, such as the inspection of the clarified butter (*ājyāvekṣaṇa*), but not with respect to religion in general. Indeed, they do possess the right to perform the desired religion as prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras* and other texts; for they have already taken a wife. Thus says Manu:
If, however, there should somehow be a desire for wives on the part of eunuchs and others,
their offspring— who have produced a lineage— is entitled to the inheritance.

Therefore, since there is a statement regarding eunuchs and others having wives, it is understood that they do undergo initiation (*upanayana*). Nor should it be argued that the statement "if [the father] is requested" refers to a case where blindness or other defects arise after the taking of a wife; for if that were so, the mention of those "blind from birth" (*jātyandha*) would not have been made in the preceding verse. Or, let it be that eunuchs and others lack qualification for the *iṣṭa* (sacrificial) dharma due to their lack of initiation and marriage; however, with respect to the *pūrta* (charitable) dharma, they certainly have the right, just like Śūdras and others. Consequently, their exclusion from inheritance is not caused by a lack of qualification for dharma, but is purely based on scriptural injunction (*vācanika*). As for what Baudhāyana says: "They shall maintain those who have passed beyond legal capacity—such as the blind, the idiotic, eunuchs, the addicted, and the diseased—who are incapable of performing rites, excepting the outcast and his offspring," the term "incapable of rites" means those for whom the means of livelihood such as agriculture and the like do not exist; and "excepting the outcast and his offspring" means that one should maintain others, excluding the outcast and those born of an outcast. (2.140)

Since it follows that the sons of those such as the impotent are themselves excluded from inheritance because their fathers lack a share, the author states this exception: "But the legitimate (aurasa) and the soil-born (kṣetraja) sons of these, being free from defects, are entitled to a share;
and their daughters must be maintained until they are provided with husbands. (2.141)
The childless wives among them who are of virtuous conduct must be maintained;
however, those who are unfaithful or likewise hostile shall be banished.

The legitimate (*aurasa*) and *kṣetraja* sons of these [categories of men], such as the impotent and others, provided they are free from defects such as loss of caste (*pātitya*), receive a share of the inheritance. The offspring of an impotent man may be born through medical treatment and other means; furthermore, their daughters must be maintained until marriage. Moreover, the wives of these very same men, if they are married and virtuous, must be maintained even if they are childless. However, those who are unchaste or hostile toward their brother-in-law (*devara*) and others shall be expelled—that is, cast out from the house. But daughters, even if born of a degraded man, must be nourished and given in marriage. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha says: "They say that one born of a degraded man becomes degraded, except for a woman; for she goes to another [man]. (2.141, 142)
Since a woman does not inherit a share [of the estate], the author, intending first to discuss those who take the woman’s property, states the nature of that property:
"What has been given by her father, mother, son, or brother; what she receives at the nuptial fire; and the gift upon supersession—this is declared to be a woman’s property. (2.143)

That which is given by the father and others is *adhyagni*—that which is obtained with reference to the fire (*agni*) at the time of marriage. *Ādhivedanika* is that which is caused by supersession (*adhivedana*). Supersession is the marrying of another wife while a wife already exists. The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "etcetera"; by it, the inclusion of other types of women's property is intended. For example: "Wives shall be made sharers of equal portions; the mother also shall take an equal share. "From her own share, women who have been superseded shall divide a fourth part among themselves. Furthermore, whatever else is owned by a woman is proclaimed as "women's property" (*strīdhana*) by Manu and others. Kātyāyana says:
Whatever is given to women at the time of marriage in the presence of the fire is proclaimed by the virtuous as *adhyagnikṛta*, the woman's property.
Furthermore, whatever a woman receives when being led away from her father’s house is proclaimed as the woman’s property known as *adhyāvahanika*.
Whatever is given out of affection by a mother-in-law or a father-in-law,
that is called "pādavandanika" (offered at the feet), acquired through personal charm.
That which is obtained from a brother, from parents, or even while in the father’s house after marriage, by a maiden or a married woman, is declared to be *saudāyika* (a nuptial gift).
Vṛddhavyāsa states:
That which is obtained by a maiden at her marriage,
as well as that which is obtained from the house of her father or brother after the marriage, is known as *saudāyika*.
Likewise: Whatever is given to the bridegroom at the time of marriage, having been intended for the bride—that entire property is not to be divided by her kinsmen. [752]
Kātyāyana states: Upon receiving dowry property, independence is granted to women,
because that was given by them for the sake of compassion as a means of subsistence.
Women's independence regarding their dowry is always proclaimed;
they have full authority over its sale and gift, even in the case of immovable property.
Furthermore, as Nārada says:
"Whatever has been given by a husband pleased with his wife, even after he has died,
she may enjoy it at her will or give it away, with the exception of immovable property."
Thus, that refers to immovable property given out of affection. Kātyāyana says:
"Whatever is obtained by a woman after marriage from her husband’s family, or from her husband or her parents, that is called *anvādheya* according to Bhṛgu."
Whatever is obtained as a price for household utensils, vehicles, milch animals, ornaments, or laborers—
that is proclaimed to be *śulka*.
Vyāsa: A woman shall be given no more than two thousand [paṇas] as a share of wealth;
however, whatever property has been given by her husband, she may enjoy according to her desire.

Every year, a portion of wealth amounting to two thousand *kārṣāpaṇas* shall be given to the woman as her maximum inheritance (*para-dāya*). "Maximum" (*para*) means the highest limit; it is called *dāya* because it is given (*dīyate*). She may obtain this inheritance—whether given by her husband or not—according to her desire and through unprohibited means, even without the consent of her brother-in-law (*devara*) or others. From this, it follows by implication that for an amount exceeding this, the consent of the brother-in-law and others must be sought. Manu says: "The ornaments which have been worn by women while their husbands were alive, the heirs shall not divide; those who divide them fall."
This refers to the domain of ornaments worn constantly.
Neither the husband, nor the father, nor the son, nor the brothers have authority over the woman's property,
whether in its acquisition or its disposal.
For if even one among them should forcibly consume the woman's property,
he shall be made to restore it along with interest and shall also incur a fine.

Kātyāyana states: "While she is alive, the husband, sons, paternal kinsmen, and maternal relatives are declared to have no authority over a woman's property; those who misappropriate it, however, are liable to punishment."
Manu:
"But those kinsmen who should take away the property of those women while they are still living, a righteous lord of the earth should punish them with the punishment prescribed for thieves. [753]

With the intention that even the kinsmen have a right to the property of deceased women under the condition of a specific form of marriage, it was stated: "of those who are living" (jīvantīnām). || 2.143 ||

He now states the purpose for which the characteristics of a woman's property were described: "The property given by relatives, as well as the nuptial fee (śulka) and the subsequent gift (anvādheya), the kinsmen shall obtain when she has died childless. (2.144)

Whatever has been given by kinsmen—such as paternal uncles, maternal uncles, and others—and whatever is the nuptial fee (*śulka*), and whatever is the subsequent gift (*anvādheyaka*); by this [verse], all forms of a woman’s property (*strīdhana*) are indicated. When she has passed away childless, her kinsmen shall obtain that; the meaning is that it becomes the property of her relatives. (2.144)
It has been stated in general that kinsmen shall obtain [the property]; now he specifies the case in which particular kinsmen are entitled to it:
"The woman's property goes to the husband even in the four [marriages] beginning with the Brāhma;
if she has borne children, it belongs to the daughters; in the remaining [marriages], it goes to the father. (2.145)

The wealth of a childless woman who was married according to the Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, or Prājāpatya rites belongs to her husband; however, the wealth of one who obtained marriage through the Āsura, Gāndharva, Rākṣasa, or Paiśāca rites goes to her father. But if she has given birth and possesses offspring, it belongs to her daughters alone. And this applies to all forms of marriage. This [rule] is intended to establish that even when a son exists, the mother’s property goes to the daughter; therefore, it is not redundant with the rule "the daughters [inherit] from the mother," for in that [latter] case, the order of succession was not specified. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says:
In the absence of daughters, that inheritance shall go to the sons;
but what was given by kinsmen goes to the kinsmen, and in their absence, it goes to the husband.
The second half [of the verse] concerns women married through the four types of marriage beginning with the Āsura. Manu says:
"Whatever may have been given to a woman by her father, or given in any way whatsoever, that a Brāhmaṇī wife shall take; or it shall belong to her offspring."
And as he himself has stated:
"In the cases of the Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, Gāndharva, and Prājāpatya marriages,
if [the woman] dies without offspring, that [property] is held to belong to the husband alone."

Thus, in that regard, it should be understood that for a woman married by the Gāndharva rite, there is an option (vikalpa) because her property goes to her husband. Likewise, he himself says: "Whatever wealth may have been given to her in marriages such as the Āsura and others, that is held to belong to her mother and father when she has passed away childless. [754]

In an *āsura* marriage, the brothers of the same womb (*sodara-bhrātṛ*) are entitled to receive the bride-price (*kanyā-śulka*); in their absence, it belongs to the mother. As Gautama says: "The bride-price of a sister belongs to the uterine brothers; in their absence, to the mother. Baudhāyana states:
"The uterine brothers themselves shall take the inheritance of a deceased maiden;
in their absence, it shall belong to the mother; in her absence, it shall belong to the father."
Manu says: "But if an appointed daughter (putrikā) dies without offspring,
her husband shall take that wealth without hesitation."

This refers to the case where a daughter has been designated as such with the agreement: "The son who is born of her shall be my son. Regarding the case, however, where she is treated as "my son," Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "The husband does not take the wealth of a deceased daughter who is a *putrikā* if she is childless. Paiṭhīnasi says: "When the *putrikā* has died, the husband does not take the wealth; it should be taken by the mother or the mother-in-law, since she was childless. Bṛhaspati states:
[The inheritance goes to] the mother’s sister, the maternal uncle’s wife, the paternal uncle’s wife, and the father’s sister.
A mother-in-law and the wife of one's elder brother are proclaimed to be equal to a mother.
If these women have no son born of their own body, nor a daughter’s son, nor the son of such a daughter, then their property shall be inherited by those who would receive it from their sister’s son.
The wife of the elder brother, who is the first-born, is called *pūrvajapatnī*. || 2.145 ||
In connection with the division of a woman’s property, he says something regarding the case of a betrothed girl:
"Having given away a maiden, one who takes her back shall be fined and shall pay the expenses along with the interest;
if she has died, he shall take everything after deducting both sets of expenses. (2.146)

Having verbally promised a maiden to a suitor who is free from defects such as impotence, if he fails to give her to that man upon obtaining another, more excellent suitor, he shall be punished by the king. He must also pay to the suitor the amount of wealth spent by him, along with interest. This is the meaning of "he shall be made to pay by the king. Likewise, if the maiden dies before the marriage, the suitor shall take the remainder of the wealth given by him for the sake of the marriage, after first reimbursing the father of the maiden for the expenses incurred for the wedding of both the maiden and himself. (2.146)

It has been stated that, in certain specific circumstances regarding property, the husband may take [the estate] of a deceased woman; now, it is said that in times of famine and so forth, the husband shall not return to the woman the wife’s property (strīdhana) that he has taken.

[2.147] In a time of famine, for the sake of religious duty, in illness, or when there is an obstruction [to livelihood], the husband is not required to give back to the woman the wife’s property that he has taken.

Famine means the absence of food. Religious duty refers to what is necessary, not what is merely desired. Illness means that which is both severe and chronic; for its remedy, she may take her husband's property. Imprisonment means confinement with fetters and the like. In these circumstances, if he lacks his own wealth, she may take the woman’s property to overcome these calamities. Furthermore, if he lacks the means to repay it, he shall not give it back to her. This rule applies specifically to the situation of a calamity such as the inability to recover a debt. For this very reason, Devala says: "Livelihood, ornaments, the nuptial fee (*śulka*), and profits constitute a woman’s property."
The master himself ought not to consume this [property] at his own will except in times of distress.
She may spend it on unnecessary gifts or luxuries, or she may give it to her husband along with interest;
or, in order to remove distress for her son, she is entitled to enjoy the woman's property.

The squandering of wealth for the purpose of gambling, singing, and so forth, is "useless expenditure. "Enjoyment," however, refers to the utilization of women, food, drink, and the like. The meaning is that, in order to relieve the distress of a son, the woman's property may be taken and used. Kātyāyana states: "Neither the husband, nor the son, nor the father, nor the brothers have authority over the woman's property, whether in its acquisition or its disposal."
For if even one among them should consume the woman's property by force,
he shall be made to repay it with interest and shall also incur a fine equal to its value.
If one should eat that very same thing after having obtained permission and with a sense of affection,
he should be made to pay the root fine if he is wealthy.
Having learned that [the debtor] is diseased, beset by calamity, or oppressed by creditors,
he may, out of affection, give what has been relinquished by him according to his own will.
If a woman has given or bestowed wealth with her own consent to free her husband from calamities such as disease,
he shall return it to her at her request; even if she gave it out of affection, if he is married to two wives and does not treat her well, he must be compelled by force to restore it.
Where a woman’s food, clothing, and shelter are withheld, there she may establish her own security; likewise, she shall receive a share from the heirs.
This is the law regarding one who has been written [in a document]: she shall reside in the family of her husband when the time arrives.

This is the law according to the opinion of the great seer Likhita; or rather, this is the law concerning property given by a husband or woman’s wealth that has been invested with her sons. When she has obtained such wealth, a woman should live in her husband’s family and not elsewhere.
[756] If she is ill, she may go to the family of her relatives for funeral rites;
however, one who is intent on doing harm, shameless, or a squanderer of wealth [should not].
A woman who is devoted to adultery does not deserve her woman's property;
therefore, one should employ for sacrificial purposes the wealth that has been produced for that purpose.

In matters concerning those devoted to dharma, but not regarding women, fools, or unrighteous acts, the sons must repay their father’s promised gifts just like a debt; so too must they repay a woman’s property.
She who remains in her husband's family may likewise dwell in her father's family.
He states the subject of supersession:
"An equal amount as *ādhivedanika* (a gift for supersession) should be given to the woman who has been superseded;
however, if no separate property (*strīdhana*) was previously given to her, half of that [equal amount] is prescribed. (2.148)

When another wife is married while one wife already exists, that first wife is called *adhivinnā*. She is a woman who has been superseded (*adhivinna-strī*); for her, *ādhivedanika* means that which is given on account of supersession, the meaning being "because she has been superseded. And that [gift] is equal. When the question arises as to by whom, it is understood from the context to be by the same person who gave [the gift] to the wife recently married. Furthermore, this should be given to her to whom no woman’s property (*strīdhana*) was previously given. But when that [woman’s property] has been given, only half should be given, not an equal amount. This word "half" does not function here to denote an equal division. And the meaning is that when woman’s property has been given, one should give just enough so that it becomes equal to the *ādhivedanika* gift. (2.148)
Regarding the dispute over the existence or non-existence of a partition, he states the means for determining its existence:

"In the case of a denial of partition, the proof of partition is to be known through kinsmen, relatives, witnesses, and documents, as well as by means of separate houses, fields, and personal property. (2.149)
Thus ends the section on the partition of inheritance. 8.

When there is a denial or concealment of partition, such as saying, "There is no division of wealth between us," the proof of partition must be known through kinsmen and others. Likewise, the proof of partition is to be known through separate personal property (*yautaka*), such as houses and fields. Kinsmen and others refer to witnesses and so forth, because kinsmen may serve as witnesses in matters of partition. The mention of houses and fields is intended to illustrate the means of proof for partition as stated in other legal treatises. Nārada says:

"The taking of wives, the possession of cattle, food, houses, and fields, as well as cooking, religious duties, income, and expenditure—these are to be known as distinct among those who have divided."

Brothers who have divided their property may act as witnesses, stand surety for one another, and engage in giving or receiving gifts; those who have not divided their property may not do so with respect to one another.
"These transactions proceed among these [sons] regarding their own inheritance;
one should recognize those who have been divided even without a written document," so says Bṛhaspati.
Those who maintain separate income, expenditure, and assets, and engage with one another in lending,
trade, and commerce, have undoubtedly divided their property.

The merchant's path is trade. Nārada says: If many born of one [father] have separate duties, separate activities, and are endowed with separate qualities of action, they are not to be consulted in affairs unless they are in agreement.
Whether they should give away their own shares or even sell them, they may do all that as they wish; for they are indeed masters of their own property.

The meaning of this is as follows: if brothers, without mutual consent, perform religious acts that require wealth separately, and likewise engage in activities such as agriculture involving separate expenditure of funds—and if they are possessed of the results of those actions, whether merit, profit, or loss—and similarly act with opposition toward other matters concerning assemblies, villages, and so forth, it should be understood that they are divided. Therefore, they may perform the sale of their own shares and so forth as they wish. Bṛhaspati says: "Whatever share has been enjoyed by whom, one should not displace him from that. Likewise:
Furthermore, he who makes a division according to his own whim and then acts in contradiction to it, shall be made to pay a portion of his own share to the king and punished for his misconduct.
"Anubandha" means persistence. Kātyāyana says:
"Those brothers who have lived for ten years with separate religious duties and separate activities shall be known as divided with respect to the paternal wealth."
Whether divided or undivided, heirs have equal rights to immovable property;
for no single person is empowered in any matter of giving, mortgaging, or selling it.

Whether their property has been divided or undivided, the heirs are equal with respect to immovable property; the meaning is that among them, not even a single individual is empowered to give it away or perform other such acts. (2.149)

Thus ends the eighth chapter, on the Partition of Inheritance, in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, born of the lineage of the illustrious King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the family of the glorious Vidyādharas.
[758] Now begins the section on disputes concerning boundaries in the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* with its commentary. (9)
Now, he states the grounds for decision in a dispute over boundaries:
"In a dispute concerning the boundary of a field, the neighbors, elders and others, the herdsmen, those who cultivate the borderlands, and whoever else frequents the forest [shall decide]. (2.150)
They should establish the boundary, marked by landmarks such as mounds of earth, charcoal, husks, trees, embankments, anthills, depressions, bones, and shrines. (2.151)

In a dispute concerning the boundary—the limits—of immovable property such as villages, gardens, and the like, the neighbors (*sāmantas*) are those who dwell in the villages and other places immediately surrounding it on all sides; the elders (*sthaviras*) are the aged. By the word "and the like" (*ādi*), others mentioned in other treatises who determine boundaries are also included. The cowherds (*gopas*) are the keepers of cattle. The field-tilers (*sīmākṛṣāṇās*) are the cultivators of the land bordering the boundary (the word *sīmā* also exists ending in the vowel *ā*). The forest-dwellers (*vanagocarās*) are those who subsist upon the forest. All these, having identified and determined the boundary by means of marks such as mounds and the like, shall settle—that is, decide—it in that dispute. A mound (*sthalam*) is elevated ground; a depression (*nimnaḥ*) is a ditch; a shrine (*caityaḥ*) is a particular mark established by the owners of two adjacent fields that have come to an agreement. The rest is well known. Nārada states the various types of boundaries:
The boundary is recorded as being of five kinds: that marked by a banner, that marked by fish, that established by fire-altars, that free from fear, and that determined by royal decree.

The *dvajinī* (flag-marked) boundary is characterized by trees and the like; the *matsyinī* (fish-marked) is characterized by water containing fish; the *naidhānī* (hidden-treasure-marked) is indicated by jars containing husks, charcoal, and so forth, buried in the middle of the ground. It is to be understood through signs established by the king himself in the absence of all [other marks], or by the petitioners and adversaries when free from fear. Or it may be established by the king himself when no [other] means exist. It is "brought about by royal decree" (*rājaśāsananītā*), meaning it is made by the king's command. Manu says:
"When a dispute arises regarding a boundary between two villages, one should mark it out in the month of Jyeṣṭha, when the landmarks are clearly visible."

The word "village" (*grāma*) is used for illustrative purposes; by it, the inclusion of boundaries and disputes regarding districts (*janapada*), fields, and houses is intended. Thus, the dispute over boundaries is of exactly four kinds. The mention of the month of Jyeṣṭha is not for the sake of a restrictive rule, but rather because it is convenient, for at that time the display of boundary markers is easily accomplished. "Dikes" (*setu*) refers to dikes and the like, which are the causes of boundaries.
At the time of settlement, the determination of the boundary must be made, marked with both public and secret signs, so as to remove all doubt.

*Niveśa* is the commencement of entering into a village or similar settlement. *Sīmābandha* is the fixing or delimitation of the boundary. [This may be done] both secretly and openly. Bṛhaspati says: "Wells, pits, tanks, shrines, groves, and temples—one should always cause these to be made as visible marks at the boundary."
Likewise, other things deposited [as pledges] which the earth shall not consume.
Nārada says: A village is declared to be the neighbor of a village; a field is the neighbor of a field;
and a house is specified as the neighbor of a house; one should consider them as such on all sides.

By the words "village" and so forth, the inhabitants of the village and other such places are indicated. One should examine those neighbors who are perceived all around—that is, situated on every side—of the village that is the subject of the dispute; not merely in a single direction. He [Yājñavalkya] himself also speaks of the elders (*sthavira*), meaning the aged (*vṛddha*): "Those by whom that matter was seen while it was being accomplished, and who are endowed with human virtues—whether they be old or even not old—they are proclaimed to be 'elders' (*vṛddha*)."
By the word "and others" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the elders and others," other [authorities] mentioned in other treatises are also included.
Excess, deficiency, partiality, non-existence,
enjoyment without title, and boundary— these six are the grounds for a legal dispute.
Thus ends the sixfold classification of immovable property. Kātyāyana states:
"In their absence, the neighbors, the original owners, those who have increased the value, those who have cleared it, and so forth [shall decide];
even though immovable property is of six kinds, there should be no hesitation in this matter."
The phrase "of them" is a reference to the witnesses. For this very reason, Manu states:
"If there remains doubt even upon seeing these marks, the decision regarding the boundary in a legal dispute must depend solely on the testimony of witnesses."
Kātyāyana says: In that case, evidence should be employed; it rests upon all witnesses—both those recorded in writing and other witnesses who follow the two paths.
Manu says: "The witnesses to the boundary marks of the village and family groups must be questioned in the presence of both litigants regarding the boundary signs."
[760] But as those neighbors, when questioned, declare the determination of the boundary, so shall he record it in its entirety, along with all those witnesses.
In the absence of witnesses, however, four villages situated on the boundary shall,
being purified, determine the boundary in the presence of the king.
Kātyāyana says regarding the *maula* witnesses:
"Those who were formerly neighbors there but later went to another country are proclaimed by the sages as *maula* because they are rooted in that very place."

He himself has also stated regarding those who have been "extracted": "Because they extract [the truth] from that [source], being characterized by eavesdropping, communal enjoyment, performance of duties, and narration,
they are therefore known as 'extracted' (uddhṛta)."

*Upaśravaṇa* is mutual agreement. *Kārya* is the taking of their hands [in marriage]. *Ākhyāna* is news. Regarding the phrase "those beginning with *uddhṛta*," he himself provides the specification of those who are included by the word "etcetera":
"Next, the *saṃsaktas*, then the *śāmantas*, and then the *tatsaṃsaktas*;
these, ending with the *saṃsaktasaktasaktas*, are proclaimed to be shaped like a lotus."

Regarding a field or other property whose boundaries are disputed: those who enjoy the lands immediately adjacent in all directions are the *saṃsaktas* (direct neighbors). Those who are next beyond them are the *sāmantas* (neighboring lords). Those who are next beyond them are the *saṃsaktasaṃsaktas* (neighbors of the direct neighbors). And those who are next beyond even them are the *saṃsaktasaktasaktas* (neighbors of the neighbors of the direct neighbors). In this manner, they form sixteen groups arranged like a lotus. Likewise:
"In the absence of *sāmantas*, one should determine the field and so forth by means of non-neighboring [witnesses]. The same applies to village boundaries, as well as to cities and districts."
When neighboring vassals have become corrupt in the pursuit of their own interests due to the weight of wealth, one must effect their removal from those with whom they are allied;
of this there is no doubt.
Those who are attached to those who are themselves attached to the wicked are declared to be "associated with them";
however, a king who understands the dharma should not employ such corrupt persons.
Having excluded wicked neighboring lords, one should cause the boundary to be marked by those who are hereditary and others; thus do those who know the Dharma understand it.
The meaning is that he should cause other persons, such as the *maula* (hereditary) witnesses and others, who are mixed [with the former], to determine the boundary. Likewise:
"The neighbors (*sāmanta*) endowed with good qualities are the primary means of proof when there is no objection;
those further removed are to be known as twice as many, and others beyond them are considered three times as many."

The meaning is that when the opponent states something undesirable regarding the neighbors (*sāmantas*), one points out the fault. The subsequent terms, such as *saṃsakta* and so forth, refer to these neighbors. Even though neighbors and the like may not be [formal] witnesses, they certainly qualify as determiners of the boundary when they point out boundary markers such as trees, husks, and so on; for they alone are familiar with them. Although others might also know the nature of the trees and such, they lack the discernment to distinguish, "This tree is a boundary marker, this one is not. Likewise, in this particular location, husks, charcoal, and other items buried there can only be known by the neighbors and the like. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
Dried cow dung, bones, husks, charcoal, gravel, stones, potsherds,
sand, bricks, cow hair, cotton seeds, bones, and ashes.
Having cast these into jars, one should have them deposited at the boundaries;
thereafter, one should carefully show them to children of tender age.
And in their old age, they should likewise show [the boundaries] to the children;
in this way, when knowledge is handed down through succession, no confusion regarding the boundary arises.

Precisely because they possess the power of determination by virtue of indicating the signs [of boundaries], even those such as hunters, fowlers, snake-catchers, and the like—who are otherwise unworthy of serving as witnesses due to their devotion to sinful acts—are included here. Some read the text as "the neighbors, the elders, and the *gaṇas*. In that view, by the word *gaṇa*, those who head a *gaṇa* (members of a group) are indicated, referring to the collective bodies of Brāhmaṇas and others; and they indeed possess authority regarding the boundary. As Nārada says:
"In disputes concerning field-boundaries, the decision is based on the neighbors, and on those who head the groups (*gaṇins*) of cities and villages, and on the men who are most advanced in age."
And those who live by agriculture outside the boundaries of the village.
Nārada, in the context of the rule "they should lead [the boundary]," states:
"In cases where the earth has been swept away or its marks effaced by the waters of a river,
[the boundary] shall be determined by inference from those locations, by means of measurements, and by the observation of possession."
Bṛhaspati says: When land has been brought from another village and given to someone else,
any subsequent acquisition by men shall be considered due to the king or providence.
The decline, rise, and very life of men depend upon the power of fate and the king;
therefore, at all times, one should not subvert what has been ordained by them.
Wherever a river has been established as the boundary between two villages,
if it becomes diminished or increased by the rise [of water], he who causes it to shift deserves punishment.
By the power of fortune or misfortune, it effects the taking away or the bestowing of wealth upon men;
just as on one side there is the collapse of the earth's bank, while on the other there is its firm stability.
One should not alter the boundary that has been established along the riverbank;
when the land becomes divided, having overstepped the field containing standing crops.
The owner of the field shall recover it by means of the flow of the river's current.

The former owner, who sowed the crop, shall receive it— meaning, as much of the crop as was there. But that which was seized by the king through anger or greed, or by force or unjustly, yet later given away by him out of favor to another, shall not attain legal validity.
If land that was taken from someone is being enjoyed by another who lacks legal title,
or if it has been given to one who possesses superior merit, one must not disturb that person's possession of it.
Bṛhaspati says: Bound by their respective oaths, they shall declare the determination regarding the boundary;
they shall point out hidden deposits, for that is the authoritative standard—such is the settled rule.
"Treasures deposited" means husks, charcoal, and so forth, which serve as boundary markers. || 2.150, 151 ||
To address the question of what should be done where there are no witnesses capable of determining the boundary, and where even the neighbors are unable to point out the marks, he says:
"Or else, four, eight, or even ten neighboring villages of equal status—carriers of earth, wearing red garlands and garments—shall lead the way to the boundary. (2.152)

The *sāmantas* are the villages and other settlements situated all around—that is, on every side—of the village or other place that has become the subject of dispute, as well as the men residing in those villages and other places; and they must be equal, meaning equal in number. He shows that very equality by stating: "four, eight, or even ten. By this, two or six are excluded. They, wearing garlands of red flowers and red garments, carrying earth and clods of soil upon their heads, should walk about and determine the boundary. Manu says: "Wearing garlands and red garments, they should carry the earth upon their heads."
Bound by oaths sworn on their own deeds, they should each lead [the case] to its proper conclusion.
Nārada says: A man, even if he is highly trustworthy, should not determine a boundary alone;
because of the gravity of this matter, this procedure is established upon many witnesses.
If one person alone should mark the boundary, he should do so while fasting; thus says Kātyāyana:
"In some cases, if one person, desired by both parties, should determine the boundary..."
Having placed the earth upon his head, wearing red garments, and being composed in mind.
Bṛhaspati says:
Even a single virtuous person, approved by both parties, may act as a witness even without the identifying marks of a witness,
provided he wears red garlands and garments and carries earth upon his head.

A man, committed to truth and observing a fast, shall point out the boundary; this means that there are no identifying marks for those who know it, nor is there any mark for the one who knows it himself. (2.152)
He states the punishment for those who act falsely:
"But those who speak untruth shall be punished separately by the king with the middle amercement.

If the neighbors and others should make a false or erroneous determination of the boundary, then they are to be fined the middle amercement—five hundred and forty *kārṣāpaṇas*. As for that which was stated by Kātyāyana:
But if, among many who have been summoned as witnesses, they do not reach a unanimous decision due to fear or greed, they shall be made to pay the highest fine.
And so forth; this is to be understood as applying when there is gravity in the fault of the judge's intention (*āśaya-doṣa*). Furthermore, he stated another point:
"Neighboring lords are not released from liability regarding the final decision merely by [claiming] ignorance.
Having punished them for stating ignorance, one should investigate the boundary again."
If a dispute should arise regarding what has been proclaimed, the punishment shall be the highest amercement.
Thus it has been stated; that too refers to the subject matter already mentioned. Nārada says:
"If the remaining [witnesses], though appointed for the legal proceedings, should speak falsely, even those of the lowest rank shall each be punished with the first amercement."

The "remaining" ones are those other than the neighboring [village] officials. The "inferior" ones are the village headmen (*maulasaṃsaktaka*) and others. The "first fine" (*pūrvasāhasa*) is the first amercement. Likewise:
"But others, such as the leaders of guilds (*gaṇavṛddha*) and so forth, are to be punished individually;
they are to be disciplined with the very first amercement in cases of falsehood."

The term "gaṇavṛddhādayaḥ" (elders of the community and others) refers to the elders of the community (*gaṇa*) and so forth; by the word "and others" (*ādi*), the members of the *maula*, *uddhṛta*, *nagara*, and *grāma* [communities] are included. These individuals, if they transgress the duty of witnesses, are to be punished with the first amercement (*prathamasāhasa*). Their falsehood (*anṛtatva*) and untruthfulness (*mithyātva*) should be understood to occur when those planted boundary markers are not shown, or when landmarks such as trees on the ground are perceived otherwise. Furthermore, their untruthfulness regarding the traversing of the boundary (*sīmācaṅkramaṇa*) should be understood as arising from some calamity or misfortune. Kātyāyana states: "In the case of traversing the boundary, in the ordeal by sacred libation (*kośa*), and likewise in the touching of the foot..."
A period of three fortnights, one fortnight, or seven days is prescribed for [the duration of] divine or royal calamities.
He states what should be done in the absence of boundary marks and those who know them:
"In the absence of the marks and the knowers, the king is the establisher of the boundary. (2.153)
In the absence of witnesses—such as neighbors and others—as well as landmarks—such as ground features, trees, and so forth—the king himself shall determine the boundary independently. Nārada says:
"And when there are no witnesses to the boundary, nor any marks..."
Then the king himself may, as he desires, establish the boundary between the two.

"Desirable" means by virtue of desire. Furthermore, when a boundary land that is the subject of dispute is extremely beneficial to one village, field, or the like—such that without it, that village and so forth would simply not exist, whereas for the other party it is not so—regarding that case, Manu says:
"When the boundary is impossible to determine, the king himself, knowing the dharma, shall assign the land to those to whom it is beneficial; such is the settled rule."

"Unbearable" means empty of both a knower and an object of knowledge. "One should enter" or "one should cause [another] to enter"—this is the meaning. [This occurs] due to assistance or the causes of assistance. (2.153)

The causes for determining the boundary of a field have been stated; now he declares that these very same [causes] apply to the determination of the boundaries of other things as well, such as groves and the like:
"In the case of groves, temples, villages, water-reservoirs, pleasure-gardens, and dwellings, as well as in the case of rainwater channels and the like, this same rule is to be understood. (2.154)

In matters concerning disputes over boundaries such as groves and the like, this very procedure involving witnesses, neighbors, and others should be understood as the rule for reaching a decision. This same rule applies to disputes regarding the boundaries of water-courses arising from rainwater. A *ārāma* is a grove of mango trees and the like; an *āyatana* is a temple; a *nipāna* is a reservoir; an *udyāna* is a pleasure garden; and the rest are well known. The word "and the like" (*ādi*) is intended to include all disputes concerning the boundaries of land. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says: "This rule has been proclaimed for every dispute concerning immovable property."
Likewise:
From the time of its construction, whatever house, enclosure, shop,
or other property has been enjoyed by someone to whatever extent and in whatever manner, that person shall not be deprived of it.
One should not disturb the windows, water-channels, as well as the turrets and altars, nor the chariot-paths established in the four-winged palace.

A *vātāyana* is a window. A *praṇālī* is a conduit made of wood or other materials for the exit of water. A *niryūha* is a wooden projection at the entrance of a door; it is what is known as a "house-nose" (*gṛhaghoṇī*). A *vedikā* is the ground of a courtyard or similar area. A *catuḥśāla* is a house with four wings and four doors. A *syandanikā* is the edge of the roof-covering. Kātyāyana states:
"One should not support [the roof] by means of a girdle-beam (*mekhalā*), a hollow beam (*bhrāmi*), a spout (*niṣkāsa*), or a window (*gavākṣa*).
One who damages a water-conduit (*praṇālī*) or the structural site of a house (*gṛhavāstu*) shall be liable to a fine."
[765] After the time of settling [the boundary], these [rites] should never be performed;
nor should one construct a water-channel into the houses of others upon casting a glance [at them].

The *mekhalā* is the foundation of the wall-base. The *bhrama* is the water-outlet. The *niṣkāma* is a place for sitting made of wood or other materials, emerging from the walls of a palace or similar structure, not touching the ground. One should not obstruct it nor block it. The *gṛhavāstu* is the dwelling-place. The *dṛṣṭipāta* is a window. Regarding the *bṛhaspati*: the *varcasthāna* is a fire-pit for pouring away food-leavings and wash-water;
it must never be made too close to another's wall.

*Varcas* means excrement; *garta* means a pit or hole. *Atyārāt* means very near. Kātyāyana says: "One should construct a receptacle for feces, urine, and water, as well as a fire-pit and a pit, leaving a space of two *aratnis* from the neighboring wall."
Bṛhaspati said:
That path by which people and even animals go and come without restraint is called *saṃsaraṇa*; it must not be obstructed by anyone.
Whoever there should out of desire create a mixture [of castes], dig a pit, plant trees,
or void excrement, his fine shall be one *māṣaka*.

*Saṃkara* is the state of being mixed with another substance. A *māṣaka* is one-twentieth part of a *kārṣāpaṇa*. Manu says: "He who, when not in distress, should discharge impurity upon the royal highway, shall pay two *kārṣāpaṇas* and must immediately cleanse the impurity."
One who has fallen into calamity, as well as an elderly person, a pregnant woman, or even a child, deserve only a reprimand and not purification; such is the settled rule.

Reproach is the punishment of "fie" (dhig-daṇḍa). Kātyāyana states: "He who defiles tanks, gardens, or sacred bathing places with impurity shall, after having the impurity cleared away, be fined the first amercement."
He who defiles all sacred fords established by great souls—
meritorious and purifying sites— shall be punished with the first amercement.
But for the breaking of a boundary, likewise for the transgression of a limit, and for the seizure of a field, the punishments are low, high, and middling respectively. (2.155)

A boundary is a demarcation such as a watercourse or the like that indicates the limits of a field and so forth. In case of its breach, its destruction, the transgression of the boundary, or the seizure of the field, the first, highest, and middle fines shall apply respectively. This is stated for the sake of illustration; therefore, depending on the gravity of the offense, other punishments—such as death, confiscation of all property, banishment from the city, or branding—must also be applied after considering other legal treatises. (Manu 8.263–264) [766] Manu:
One who seizes a house, a pond, a garden, or a field through intimidation shall be fined five hundred [paṇas]; if it was done through ignorance, the fine shall be two hundred.
Vṛddha-Manu:
Those wicked persons who transgress a boundary established between two villages shall be fined two hundred [paṇas].
Kātyāyana states:
"In the case of trees grown within the boundary between two fields,
one should declare that the fruits and flowers belong in common to the owners of both fields."
One should recognize that person as the owner in whose fields the branches of trees grown in other fields are situated.
They are established and arisen. 2.155.
Furthermore:

A boundary embankment that causes little harm should not be prohibited, for it brings about prosperity; likewise, a well that takes water from another's land is not forbidden if it belongs to one with a small field and provides abundant water. (2.156)

A watercourse being constructed by another on one's own field—which serves as the cause for a small disadvantage and a great benefit—must not be stopped. Likewise, if someone with a small field and little access to water were to divert a well that has abundant water, he too must not be prohibited by the owner. However, a watercourse or a well that have the opposite effect [of causing more harm than good] are certainly to be prohibited. (2.156)
Furthermore:
One may construct a water-channel on a field even without informing the owner;
if produce arises, it belongs to the owner, but in his absence, it belongs to the king. (2.157)

But he who constructs a water-channel or the like in that field without having obtained the permission of the owner of the field does not obtain its enjoyment of the fruit, whether seen or unseen; rather, the owner of the field alone obtains it, or in his absence, the king. Nārada says: "A water-channel should be known to be of two kinds: one to be dug out and likewise one to be built. It is 'dug' by the flowing of water, and it is 'built' by the stopping [of water]."

A *kheya* (ditch) is a dam constructed to divert or discharge water from a field; whereas a *badhya* (bund) is one built to retain water within the field itself. Without water there is no crop, yet when there is excessive water, there is destruction. Whatever fault exists in the absence of water, that same fault occurs when there is excessive water.
But whoever should construct a dam without first asking the owner whether it was previously begun or already completed, shall not partake in its fruit.
