But when the master has died, and furthermore when there is no human descendant of his lineage,
one should then, having addressed the king, proceed with the construction of the embankment.
Otherwise, one would incur affliction by imitating the deer-hunter;
for the arrows of him who shoots again at what has already been pierced are lost.
"Anudarśanam" means "nidarśanam" (an illustration). This refers to that hunter, Kātyāyana [says]:
"But he who performs a consecration without the consent of the owner—such a person who consecrates a house, a garden, or a pond does not obtain [the property]."
If the master has arrived and the gift has not been announced to the king, it must still be given;
however, if it was employed after having been announced, one obtains the fruit pertaining to that [master]. (2.157)
In this context, he says something regarding the subject of fields:

"If one neither cultivates nor causes to be cultivated even a field that has been ploughed, the king shall make him pay the value of the crop that could have been harvested and cause the field to be cultivated by another. (2.157)

[Thus ends the section on disputes regarding boundaries, || 9 ||] If a person, having taken a field that has been ploughed and prepared for sowing, does not sow seeds or perform other such tasks therein, nor cause them to be done, the king shall compel that farmer to pay the "unploughed-share" (*akṛṣṭa-śada*) and have the field cultivated by another farmer. "Share" (*śada*) refers to the fruit of the field; the share of an unploughed field is the "unploughed-share. The meaning is that even if the field remains unploughed, the king shall make him pay that amount and hand over the field to someone else. Vyāsa says: "Whoever, having taken a field, neither cultivates it nor causes it to be cultivated..."
He shall be made to pay the owner the value of the animal, and a fine equal to that amount by the king.
The meaning is that "equal to that" (tatsama) signifies being commensurate with that field-share (*kṣetraśada*). He demonstrates that very similarity [of yield]:
"When [the field] has been neglected for a long time, the tenth [part] is harvested; likewise the eighth;
even when well-prepared, the sixth should be assigned according to the condition [of the soil]."

If the aforementioned cause exists, one who cultivates a field that has long been neglected—that is, not ploughed for a long time—is liable to a fine of one-tenth of the field's produce. However, if the field is currently being ploughed, the fine is one-eighth; but if it is well-prepared, it is one-sixth. Nārada says:
"If the owner of the field is unable, deceased, or lost, and someone else, having been permitted, should cultivate the field, he shall enjoy its fruit."
If a field is being drawn for cultivation, the owner may return;
having received back all the improvements made to the fallow land (*khila*), he shall regain possession of the field.
[768] "Fallow" (*khila*) refers to a field that is difficult to cultivate.
Then, by a reduction of one-eighth each year until eight years have passed,
at the completion of the eighth year, he shall obtain possession of the field.
Kātyāyana states the meaning of this:
"If [the debtor] does not pay due to inability, or if expenses were incurred for the sake of neglected land,
then he shall receive the fruit from the cultivator reduced by one-eighth."
He shall enjoy it for eight years; thereafter, however, it belongs to the owner.

If the owner of the field, considering himself destitute, does not pay the expenses for reclaiming fallow land to the cultivator, then the cultivator shall give one-eighth of the field’s produce to the owner for eight years. After that period, the owner alone recovers the field; this is the meaning. Nārada says:
"A field becomes half-fallow after one year, and fallow after three years;
a field neglected for five years becomes like a wilderness."

Without cultivation, a field becomes half-waste within a year; the meaning is that it becomes difficult to bring back into production through effort. Likewise, after three years, it becomes completely waste, meaning it can only be brought back into production with great effort. A field neglected for five years would become like a wilderness. Therefore, if a cultivator acts in this manner, he must pay a fine to the king and the owner proportionate to his offense. One should not transfer the enjoyment of a field or house held by three generations, or inherited in succession, to another, except by the favor of the king.

Enjoyment derived from royal favor, which has continued for three generations, excludes others from the enjoyment of houses and other property. Thus ends the section on disputes concerning boundaries. 2.158.

Thus ends the eighth section, on Disputes regarding Boundaries, in the Aparārka— a commentary on the Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra— composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, born in the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the noble Vidyādhara race.
Now begins the section on disputes between owners and herdsmen in the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* with its commentary.
(10) Following the context of punishments for offenses against fields, [the author] states the punishment for offenses against crops:
A buffalo that destroys a crop shall be fined eight māṣas; a cow, half of that; and a goat or sheep, half of that again. (2.159)

[2.769] A female buffalo or a male buffalo that damages another's crops by eating or trampling them shall be fined eight *māṣas*. A cow shall be fined four *māṣas*. A goat or a sheep shall each be fined two *māṣas*. Since animals, being destitute of wealth, are unfit for a monetary fine, this rule regarding punishment is applied figuratively to their owners. One *māṣa* is the twentieth part of a *kārṣāpaṇa*. || 2.159 ||

For those who sit down after having eaten [the fodder], the fine is double that which has been stated. This same rule applies even in the case of a pasture; for donkeys and camels, the fine is equal to that for a buffalo. 2.160.

If animals, having grazed upon the crops, sit down there, they shall be subject to a fine double the individual penalty for each animal. Whatever fine has been prescribed for buffaloes and other such animals for damage to standing crops should be understood to apply equally to damage to enclosed pasture lands (*vivīta*). An area of land enclosed for the purpose of grass and fodder is called *vivīta*. A donkey and a camel are to be fined the same as a buffalo. Manu says: "But in other fields, an animal deserves a fine of one and a quarter [paṇas]. However, in all cases, a portion of the crop must be given to the owner of the field; this is the settled rule."

The meaning of this is as follows: Manu has stated that cattle which have committed an offense in certain fields are not to be punished; however, a beast that commits an offense in fields other than those is liable to a fine of one and a quarter *kārṣāpaṇas*. This should be understood to apply to cases of extreme or great offenses. In all offenses by cattle, the owner of the field must be given the value of the crop (*śada*) as prescribed. Regarding the phrase "he shall incur a fine," Śaṅkha and Likhita state in their continuation [of the text]: "A cow grazing at night [is fined] five *māṣas*, three during the day, and one *māṣa* for every *muhūrta*; there is no fine for grazing while eating grass. For all [animals], the calf [is fined] one *māṣa*; a buffalo ten; a donkey and a camel sixteen; and goats and sheep four. Nārada says:
Cows should be made to pay one-quarter [of a paṇa]; buffaloes, twice that amount;
for goats and sheep with their young, a fine of one māṣa is prescribed as the maximum.
For those who have surrendered, the fine is double; for those caught in the act, it is fourfold.
But for those who act as direct spies, the wise have declared the punishment to be that of a thief.

Viṣṇu: "If a buffalo should cause the destruction of crops, its keeper shall be fined eight māṣas; if it is unattended, the owner [shall be fined]. For a horse, a camel, a donkey, or a cow, the fine is half of that; for goats and sheep, the fine is said to be half of that. (2.160)
That [loss] should be given to the owner of the field; now he states what must be done regarding the herdsman:
as long as the crop is being destroyed, the owner of the field shall receive the compensation for the fruit.
The keeper shall be beaten, but the owner of the cow deserves the previously mentioned fine. || 2.161 ||

Until the wise and impartial neighbors have assessed the extent of the crop destroyed, the owner of the cattle shall pay to the owner of the field; he shall also pay the aforementioned fine to the king. The term "owner of the cattle" (*gomī*) refers to the master of the cow; the word "cow" (*go*) is intended to indicate livestock in general. Furthermore, the cattle-herder should be beaten by the king with a whip or similar instrument. Nārada says:
"If a man demands compensation for grain eaten by cattle, the amount of grain that was sown there should be given, with the consent of the neighbors."
A cowherd must provide fodder for the cattle that have grazed there; likewise, a farmer must pay a grain tribute.
Thus has the discipline regarding the trampling of crops by cattle been declared.
As for that which was stated by Uśanas:
"The ancestors do not eat the food of that man who demands back grain destroyed by cattle, nor do the inhabitants of heaven eat it."
Thus, that refers to the case of female cattle. 2.161.
He states an exception regarding the specific details of the aforementioned punishment:

"No offense is found in the case of a field located on a path, at the edge of a village, or at the boundary of a pasture; however, if it is done intentionally, one deserves the same punishment as a thief. (2.162)

If crops are unintentionally damaged by cattle at a field located at the edge or in the vicinity of a village or pasture (*vivīta*), no fault attaches to either the owner of the cattle or the herdsman. Consequently, there is no obligation for the payment of grain or fines, nor is there any corporal punishment for the herdsman. However, if the damage is intentional, the herdsman shall be punished like a thief. Furthermore, this absence of fault applies only when the field is not enclosed. Nārada states: "But if a field is situated near a village, at the edge of a pasture, or on a great road, and it is unenclosed, there is no transgression on the part of the herdsman in the event of destruction."
One should construct a fence there such that a camel cannot look over it,
and one should block any opening therein through which the snout of a dog or a pig might pass.
Nārada says:
A fence should be constructed along the path and the field such that a camel cannot look over it,
nor can a beast, a horse, or pigs break through it.
Kātyāyana said:
One should construct a great enclosure even before the crops have grown;
for deer, having once tasted the delicious flavor, are kept away by one who suffers [from their depredations]. [771]
Manu says:

"If cattle enter an enclosed field on a path, or one at the edge of a village, the owner of the herd, if accompanied by a keeper, deserves a fine of one hundred [paṇas]; however, he should drive away the animal if it is unattended."

If an animal, accompanied by its keeper, should destroy a field of cultivated crops or the like that is enclosed by a fence, then the animal deserves a fine of one hundred [paṇas]. The meaning is that if it is without a keeper, it must be restrained. Nārada says: "But if crops are destroyed by cattle and other animals after they have leaped over the enclosure, the keeper shall be punished there, provided he does not drive them away despite his ability. (2.162)

He states an exception regarding specific types of animals: "A large bull, animals set at liberty, those that have recently calved, newcomers, and others; those for which there is a herdsman, and those seized by the king or a deity—these are to be released. (2.163)

Large bulls and others are not to be punished even for damage to crops. A "large bull" (*mahokṣa*) is one who has been set aside for the purpose of impregnating all the cows. "Dedicated animals" (*utsṛṣṭa*) are cattle such as cows that have been formally released by their owner for the sake of the gods and other purposes according to the prescribed rites. A "cow that has recently calved" (*sūtikā*) is one that has given birth within the last ten nights. An "outsider" (*āgantuka*) is one who is free from enemies and has arrived from another village. Those cattle which have been overwhelmed or afflicted by the king when he is seizing a foreign kingdom, or by fate such as disease and the like, must be released even if they are accompanied by their keepers. The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is intended to include what is stated in other recensions of the scriptures. Thus says Uśanas:
Elephants and horses are not to be punished, for they are considered protectors of the people;
likewise, those that are one-eyed, maimed, or marked with special signs are exempt from punishment.
A cow that has recently calved, one in heat, and one that is carrying a calf are exempt from punishment;
likewise, cows are not to be punished during a festival or at the time of a śrāddha ceremony.

Because of the statement "for they are protectors of the subjects," there is no punishment for elephants and other animals belonging specifically to the king. Regarding a cow that has strayed from the herd and gone toward another: Manu says, "A cow that has recently calved, bulls, sacrificial animals, those without owners, or those without keepers—Manu declared these to be exempt from punishment within ten days [of their birth]."
Nārada says: Within ten days of giving birth, a cow, a bull, a horse, or an elephant must be diligently kept away [from the field]; their owner shall not be subject to punishment.
Likewise:
whether seized by a king's grasp, or struck by a thunderbolt,
or bitten by a serpent, or fallen from a tree;
"Even if [the animal] is killed by tigers and the like, or afflicted by diseases,
there is no fault on the part of the keeper, nor is there any punishment for the owners," says Kātyāyana. [772]
In cases where an owner disputes the beating of animals— whether they be of low, high, or middle quality—
the king shall determine the punishment accordingly.
Regarding the dispute between the owner and the herdsman over cattle, he says:

"The herdsman shall return the cattle in the evening exactly as they were entrusted; likewise, one who has received wages must be made to pay for those that have died or been lost through negligence. (2.164)

Just as at the time of dawn the cattle are counted by the owner and handed over to the herdsman, in that same manner they must be returned by him in the evening. In this regard, if, due to the negligence of the cowherd, as many animals as die or go missing, then the herdsman who has received wages or a salary must restore that many cattle, such as cows and the like, to the owner; he is to be made to pay them by the king. Regarding his wages, Manu says: "A herdsman who is paid with milk may, with the consent of the owner of the cattle, milk the best cow out of ten; that shall be the wage for a herdsman who receives no other wage."

He who is the protector (*gopa*) of cattle, maintained by milk and paid for his milk, may—having been authorized by the owner of the herd—milk for himself one excellent cow from among ten milch cows, such as cows and the like, on the grounds that he is a servant. That very cow shall be the wages or price for the herdsman when he is not remunerated by any other means. Nārada says:
"From a hundred cows, a heifer shall be the wage; from two hundred, a milch cow;
and for the herdsman, there shall be a share of the milk every year on the eighth day."
The *saṃdoha* is the milking of all [the cows]. Bṛhaspati says:
"Likewise, one who maintains the cows receives the entire milk in the tenth month. Manu says:
If cattle have been stolen by thieves after being publicly proclaimed, the herdsman is not at fault,
provided he informs his own master of it at the proper place and time.
Likewise:
during the day, the responsibility for loss falls on the keeper; at night, it falls on the owner, provided the animal remains in his house.
Otherwise, however, the keeper shall incur the responsibility.
"Kilbiṣa" means offense; "vaktavyatā" (blameworthiness) is likewise an offense. Vyāsa states:
"In the case of seizing [cattle], in the destruction of a village, or likewise in the upheaval of a kingdom, whatever may be lost or stolen, the herdsman is not at fault therein. (2.164)
But when damage occurs through the fault of the keeper, a fine is prescribed for the keeper:
twelve and a half paṇas, and the value of the property itself must be paid to the owner. (2.165)

[773] If the herdsman neglects an animal even though it is possible for him to protect it, and the animal is consequently destroyed through that fault, a fine of twelve and a half *paṇas* shall be imposed upon the herdsman. He must also be made to pay the value of the lost animal to the owner of the property. "Twelve and a half" (*ardhatrayodaśa*) refers to those [numbers] of which the thirteenth is a half; a fine consisting of such *paṇas* is a "twelve-and-a-half-*paṇa*" fine—that is to say, thirteen and a half *paṇas*. Nārada says:
"If a calamity should befall the cattle, the herdsman shall strive to remedy it to the best of his ability."
Being unable [to do so himself], he should come quickly and report that matter to his master.
Without exerting himself, without raising a cry, and without informing his master,
the cowherd must bear that penalty and pay a fine to the king.
He should strive—that is, he should exert effort—to remove the loss. But if he is unable to remove the loss, he should report it to the owner, or he may even scold [the animal]. Manu says:
"What is lost, destroyed by worms, killed by dogs, or died in a dangerous place, [and] what is deficient in human effort—the keeper alone must restore that."

The phrase "by way of value" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. "Destruction" means disappearance. Likewise: "But when goats and sheep are hemmed in by wolves and the keeper does not come to their aid, if a wolf should kill them by force, that guilt shall fall upon the keeper."
If, among those cows being kept and grazing together in the forest,
a wolf should attack and kill one, the herdsman is not at fault in that matter.
Nārada says: By this, the dispute regarding all guardians has been fully set forth;
and in the case of those who have died, purification may be established by the discovery of hair, horns, and so forth. (2.165)
The grazing of cattle may take place according to the will of the village or by the authority of the king;
furthermore, a twice-born man may gather grass, firewood, and flowers from anywhere.

Land for the grazing of cattle and other livestock should be set aside according to the will of the village inhabitants, or by virtue of the smallness or greatness of the land, or by royal decree. Grazing (*pracāra*) refers to the consumption of grass and other fodder. Likewise, a twice-born man may take grass and other such things, as well as wealth and flowers, from any portion of land even if it is enclosed. Gautama states: "One seeking pasture for cows or firewood may take grass, fuel, and the flowers of shrubs and trees as if they were his own; and likewise fruits from those that are unenclosed. Because of the expression "as if his own," one taking these things should not be forbidden by the owner. This applies in times of distress. As for another Smṛti text:
Whether it be grass, or wood, or a flower, or a fruit—
one who takes these without asking permission deserves the amputation of the hand.
Thus, this refers to the case of a Śūdra or others who have not fallen into distress. 2.166.
He establishes what was stated—that there shall be a pasture for cattle according to the course of the land—by saying:
"A hundred bows' length shall be the exclusion zone between a village and its fields;
two hundred for a hamlet, and four hundred for a city. (2.167)
Thus ends the section on disputes between owners and herdsmen. 10.

A village (*grāma*) is that which does not include its forest lands; the intervening space between its associated fields is the *parihāra*, meaning a distance of one hundred *dhanus* (bow-lengths) which is exempted from cultivation and other such uses. The *parihāra* for a market town (*kharvaṭa*) is two hundred *dhanus*, while for a city (*nagara*) it is four hundred *dhanus*. A *kharvaṭa* is a cluster of houses that is larger than a village but smaller than a city. As Manu says:
"The *parihāra* of a village shall be one hundred *dhanus* on all sides, or else three throws of a wooden pin (*śamyā*); for a city, however, it is triple that amount."

The *śamyā* is the wooden pin used by the driver of a bullock-yoke in the present age; the distance over which it falls after being thrown is called a *śamyāpāta*. Thus ends the section on the Master and the Protector. 2.167.

Thus ends the tenth section, on Disputes between Master and Herdsman, in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, born of the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the family of the glorious Vidyādharas.
Now begins the section on Sale by One Who Is Not the Owner in the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* with its commentary.
(11) Next, he speaks regarding the legal dispute concerning sale by one who is not the owner:
One may reclaim property sold by another; the fault lies with the buyer if it was not publicly announced.
If it was purchased from a low person in secret, for a low price, or at an improper time, he is a thief. (2.168)

If cattle, land, or other property has been purchased from one who is not the owner, the true owner shall recover it from the purchaser. Furthermore, if the purchaser fails to disclose the seller, he incurs the fault of theft; consequently, he is subject to punishment like a thief. Likewise, if a purchaser buys goods in secret—that is, in a private place—when they are of inferior quality, when the price is low or excessively small, or when the sale occurs at an improper time, he is a thief regarding that very merchandise; the meaning is that he shall be liable for the punishment of a thief. For he knows even before the purchase: "Having stolen this, he is now selling it. Thus says Nārada.
When property belonging to another— whether deposited, lost, found, or stolen—
is sold in the absence of the owner, that is to be known as "sale by one who is not the owner" (asvāmivikraya).
Vyāsa states: When another person's wealth— whether requested as a loan, deposited as a pledge, or placed in trust—
is sold in the absence of the owner, that is to be known as "sale by one who is not the owner."
One who sells what has been deposited, what was entrusted, a pledge,
what was taken on loan, or what was borrowed, or what was sold in secret, is declared to be a non-owner.
But when the former owner arrives and claims that property, the seller must produce the original title; only then will the buyer be cleared of liability.
Nārada says: One who purchases a slave from a non-owner, from one not authorized by him, from an invalid person, in secret,
for an inadequate price, or at an improper time, shall be liable for those faults.
Bṛhaspati: When an article has been purchased from one whose source is unknown, or where the seller is dead,
the owner may take back his own property after paying half the price.
In that case, according to legal procedure, half of the fault shall be assigned to each of the two;
for the fault lies both in the purchase made without due inquiry and likewise in the failure to guard the property.
These two have been declared by the wise to be causes of the loss of one's wealth.

If something is purchased from a seller whose identity is unknown or whose location is unknown, or if the seller’s location is known but he has died, then the owner may recover his property by paying half the value to the purchaser; in this case, the purchaser suffers a loss of half [the price] because both parties are at fault. Regarding this matter, Marīci states: "That which is situated in a merchant's row, is well-known, and is seized during the day by royal officers—the purchaser of such an item is pure and recovers his wealth."
Because it was deposited without being recognized, where no price can be recovered, an equal loss shall be assigned to both the buyer and the non-existent owner. (2.168)
Having recovered property that was lost or stolen, one should cause the thief to be apprehended;
and if there is a lapse of time or place, one should seize the person oneself and hand him over.

[776] Having discovered that his own property has been lost or stolen, he should cause the king to apprehend and restrain its thief. If, while the king is in the process of making the arrest, the thief escapes beyond the boundaries of the country or the stolen property disappears due to the lapse of time, then the owner himself must seize the thief and hand him over to the king. (2.169)

He states what must be done with the seized property: "Purification [of the purchaser] comes from the appearance of the seller; the owner recovers the property, the king receives a fine, and the purchaser recovers the price from him who sold it. (2.170)

But if the seller is produced, there shall be purification—that is, innocence. In that case, the owner shall recover the property sold by one who is not its owner; likewise, the king shall impose a fine upon the seller, and the purchaser shall recover the price from him. Kātyāyana states:
"He may make the purchase public, or he may produce the value;
and the time for producing the source [of the goods] must be granted according to the number of *yojanas* [from which it was brought]."

The meaning is "with regard to distance from the place. Likewise: "When the plaintiff, having presented the original source, should speak of a purchase, he should simply produce that original source; there is no need for the purchase [itself]."

"One should state the purchase; one should state a public purchase"—this is the meaning. Manu says: "Now, if the root source [of the goods] cannot be produced, but they have been cleared by a public purchase, he is released by the king without punishment; the atheist (nāstika) recovers his wealth."

The seller is the root [of the matter], and because his location is unknown, he cannot be brought back. Vyāsa states: "Once the root has been recovered, the purchaser is not to be prosecuted in any way;
rather, at that time, the dispute shall be with the one who denies [the ownership]."
An atheist is one who has lost his right to property. || 2.170 ||

In that regard, concerning a dispute between an owner and a seller, he states what must be done by the owner to recover his own property: "The lost [property] must be proven [recovered] through title and possession; otherwise, if it is not proven by him, there shall be a fine of one-fifth for the king. (2.171)

An atheist (nāstika) must establish his ownership of the property that is the subject of dispute either through a title of acquisition such as purchase or through possession; he must maintain that "I have not made this the property of another by means of gift, sale, or the like, but rather it has simply been lost. Therefore, if the atheist does not prove his case in the manner described above, he must pay to the king a fine known as *pañcabandha*. A *pañcabandha* is a monetary portion equal to one-fifth of the property in dispute, where the term refers to that which is bound (paid). Proof of the title, possession, and loss must be established by those who know the facts. As Kātyāyana says: [The text continues with the verse: "Proof of title, proof of possession, and proof of loss—these three must be established by the claimant. Thus, the burden of proof rests upon the one who asserts his ownership. If he fails to demonstrate these, he is liable for the penalty. The king shall take the fifth part of the disputed wealth as the fine. The term *pañcabandha* signifies that which is fixed at a rate of one-fifth. The recovery of the title, the enjoyment, and the fact of loss are to be proven by the cognizors of the matter. As Kātyāyana states: [The full verse: "Title, possession, and loss—these three must be proven by the claimant. If he cannot prove them, he shall be punished with a fine of five times the value. This concludes the section on the determination of ownership in cases of denial by an atheist.
But a nihilist (nāstika) may take that wealth as his own through his kinsmen;
having made it ungiven, abandoned, or sold, he easily acquires the wealth.
If an atheist does not himself restore the wealth to his kinsmen,
he deserves punishment like a thief in order to prevent the recurrence of such conduct.
The term *prasaṅga* means intention. Likewise:
"The seller should first establish his own ownership of the property with witnesses;
afterwards, for the sake of his own purification, the buyer should effect the purchase in the presence of his own relatives."

The plaintiff is an atheist (or one who denies the validity of the transaction). By him, the kin must prove that the property is his own. If he is unable to do so, then the purchaser, in order to clear himself of fault, must prove the purchase with his own relatives acting as witnesses. Likewise: "But if the price cannot be recovered, the purchaser shall clear the matter by means of the sale itself."
Once the purchase has been cleared by the king, he should not say anything at all.
Likewise:
"One should perform the purchase openly with trustworthy kinsmen and one's own people;
no other procedure is prescribed there, whether divine or human."

The meaning is that one should "make manifest" (bhāvayet)—that is, establish—the purchase as something public, well-known in the world, and previously heard. If the plaintiff does not establish the sought-after property by means of witnesses, he shall be made to pay double the amount by the king; the buyer deserves that property.
This concerns the case of a major offense. Bṛhaspati states:
"If a person has purchased [an item] for its price and previously reported it to the official, no fault attaches to him; however, he would be a thief if the purchase were made through fraud."

"Purchasing from a relative" (*upadhikraya*) means purchasing through fraud (*chadmakraya*). However, when there is no evidence for the ownership of the one who denies it, and the purchaser likewise lacks proof of the purity of his purchase, then he himself says:
"But in a dispute lacking evidence, the king himself shall make the decision based on the character of the individuals, according to whether they are equal, inferior, or superior."
And that [property] should be surrounded by a marketplace for the sake of trade;
otherwise, there would be the fault of an unknown purchase as well as a failure of protection.
[778] These two have been declared by the wise to be causes of loss of substance,
because, since their specific qualities are unknown, no price can be obtained for them.
In that case, the loss should be considered equal for both the buyer and the non-existent owner.

This is the meaning: or rather, if an item purchased in a merchant's row or at a shop cannot be recovered from its seller, then an equal loss shall be assigned to both the purchaser and the non-believer (the owner), since the cause for the loss of the property exists for both. For the purchaser, the cause is his failure to ascertain whether the item was stolen by a thief; for the non-believer, it is his failure to provide adequate protection. (2.171)
Regarding this very subject, he states the specific punishment for the purchaser:
"He who recovers from the hand of another property that has been stolen or lost, without having reported it to the king, shall be fined ninety-six paṇas. (2.172)
He who, without having reported his own stolen or lost property to the king, should take it from the hand of another, shall be fined ninety-six paṇas by the king. (2.172)
In this connection, he says something else as well:
"If property that has been lost or stolen is recovered by customs officials or guards of the station, the owner may reclaim it within one year; after that, the king shall take it. (2.173)

Property that has been lost or stolen, which is brought before the king by those authorized to collect tolls or by the guardians of villages and other localities, shall be recovered by the owner within one year; but after a year, it belongs to the king. Gautama states: "Having found property that was lost and without an owner, they should announce it to the king; having made it public, it must be guarded by the king for one year. Manu says:
"The king shall cause property whose owner has disappeared to be kept for three years.
Within three years, the owner may take it; after that, the king may take it."

This applies to a master who is a Brāhmaṇa of superior qualities. Herein is another distinction: "Then, remembering the duty of the virtuous, the king may take a sixth part, or even a tenth or a twelfth part, of property that has been lost and recovered."
The smallness or greatness of the respective shares should be determined according to the relative weightiness or lightness of the effort involved in protection. || 2.173 ||
Regarding the specific nature of the property, he states what must be paid for its recovery:
"One should pay four *paṇas* for a single-hoofed animal, five for a human;
two each for buffaloes, camels, and cows; and one-quarter each for goats and sheep. (2.174)

[779] When a single-hoofed animal, such as a horse, has been recovered, the owner, having given four *kārṣāpaṇas* to the finder, shall take possession of it. Likewise, in the case of a human being, five [are to be given]. For buffaloes, camels, and cows, two each; for goats and sheep, one-quarter of a *kārṣāpaṇa* for each. And this must be paid per individual, not per species. Thus ends the section on sale by one who is not the owner (2.174).

Thus ends the section on Sale by One Who Is Not the Owner in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, born of the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the noble Vidyādhara clan. Section Eleven.

Now begins the section on the non-delivery of what has been given (*dattāpradānika*) in the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* with its commentary. (12) For the sake of discernment— namely, to distinguish between that which, once given, is not to be reclaimed and that which is to be reclaimed— he states what may be given and what may not be given.

One's own property may be given away without detriment to one's family, except for one's wife and sons; however, when there is a lineage remaining, one's entire estate must not be given, nor that which has been promised to another. (2.175)

One's own property—that is, property distinct from one's sons and wife—should be given where there is no conflict consisting of the ruin of the family’s food and clothing; that is to say, such [property] as does not possess these characteristics should not be given. Likewise, while a lineage (anvaya) or one's own descendants exists, one's entire estate (*sarvasva*) is not to be given. And this applies prior to the partition of inheritance; however, among sons who have already divided their inheritance, the giving away of the entire estate is not prohibited. Furthermore, whatever wealth has been promised or accepted as a gift to another must not be given to anyone else. This being the case, what is rightfully given should not be taken back once bestowed, whereas what is not rightfully given may be recovered. By the word "one's own" (*svam*), property that is not one's own—such as borrowed items—is excluded. Kātyāyana says:
Neither the sale nor the gift [of these] should be carried out against their will;
however, one may employ one's wife, sons, and all property at one's own discretion.
In times of distress, however, giving away or even selling [the sacred objects] must be performed;
otherwise, they should not be used at all—such is the settled conclusion of the scriptures.

Bṛhaspati says: This entire expiation for collective embezzlement has been declared; now the rules regarding what should not be given, what should be given, what has been given, and what has not been given shall be stated.

Common property, such as sons, wives, and the like; everything belonging to all; that which was deposited or requested; and likewise that which has been promised to another—these eight kinds of property are traditionally held to be not to be given away.
Common property belongs to many owners. Likewise:
"That which remains after providing for the family's food and clothing should be given away;
otherwise, it is like the taste of honey followed by poison, and the merit of the donor would be lost."

Food means a meal; clothing means a garment. Whatever field is acquired from among the seven types of gardens, houses, or fields—whether inherited from a father or obtained by oneself—that which is intended for giving must be bestowed.

The meaning is that whatever is accumulated or exceeds [the requirements] from among the seven types of property, such as gardens and so forth, that is intended to be given. Furthermore, regarding the reading "whatever field is given from the sevenfold acquisition of houses and fields," the meaning is that one should give after setting aside [a portion] from houses and fields acquired through the seven modes of acquisition, such as valor; however, that which lacks a legal title to acquisition (*anāgama*) must not be given.
Regarding what may be given at will: "What is self-acquired, a pledge according to custom, and what was obtained in marriage—there is no restriction on giving these away."

A pledge (*bandhaka*) or deposit (*ādhi*) must be returned according to the customary practice regarding pledges. If that [pledge] was obtained as part of a marriage settlement, it must not be given away at all while that wife is still living. Likewise, property inherited through the line of a grandfather or others must not be given away while a son exists.

Whatever has been obtained through a marriage settlement, inherited through the line of a wife’s family, acquired by valor, or given with the consent of the woman, her kinsmen, and the owner, shall remain valid once given.

That which is *saudāyika*—obtained as a wedding gift—should be given by her with the consent of that wife. And that which has come down by inheritance [should be given] with the consent of the kinsmen who have not divided the property. The meaning is that what is obtained in battle by one who is a servant should be given with the consent of his master.
Whether they are divided or undivided, heirs are equal regarding immovable property;
for a single person is not empowered in any case of giving, mortgaging, or selling.

This refers to immovable property that has come down by succession and remains undivided. It should be explained as follows: "If even those who are divided are equal, how much more so those who are undivided? Otherwise, the act of division would be purposeless. This being the case, the mention of equality among those who are divided leads to this understanding: when there are heirs who have been divided and are fit for such acts as giving, the immovable property must be handed over to them alone; but if they are unfit or indifferent, it may be given to others. However, in times of distress and the like, even one heir who has not been granted authority over the immovable property may perform acts such as giving with the consent of the other heirs, even if their wealth is undivided. And so it is stated in another Smṛti:
"Even a single person may perform giving, receiving,
or selling regarding immovable property during a time of distress for the sake of the family, and especially for the sake of dharma," so says Nārada.
When one who has given property improperly desires to take it back,
the learned know that legal dispute to be called *dattāpradānika* (non-delivery of what was given).

[781] Now, that which is to be given and that which is not to be given, as well as what has been given and what has not been given— this fourfold path of giving is to be understood in legal proceedings.
In this regard, eight things are traditionally held to be non-givable, and the givable is said to be of one kind;
one should know that what is given is of seven kinds, and what is not given consists of sixteen types.

That which has been deposited with another, that which has been borrowed, a pledge, that which is held in common, a trust, one's wife and children, and one's entire property when there is offspring; [these should not be divided].
The teachers have declared that even when a person is beset by the most dire calamities, there are things that must not be given away, namely those which have already been promised to another.
Whatever wealth remains in excess after supporting one's family must be given away; by giving anything else, one incurs fault.

Those who know the law of giving understand that what is given as the price for goods, as wages, out of satisfaction, out of affection, as a return for a favor, or for the sake of a bride-price and for the purpose of showing favor, constitutes a gift.

The wise know that gift to be [true] giving which is given as the price for merchandise such as cattle and other items intended for purchase; that which is given to laborers as their livelihood; that which is given on the condition of satisfaction and so forth to those who hear news of the birth of a son and the like; that which is given out of affection to friends and others; that which is given in return for a favor for the sake of protection from fear and so forth; that which is given to royal officials and others for the purpose of customs duties and the like; that which is given to women such as wives and others; and that which is given for the sake of favor to the poor, the helpless, and others. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says: "Where a gift is prescribed for the purpose of obtaining what was previously unknown..."
That which is obtained through the act of perception is proclaimed to be its "remuneration" (bhṛti).
One should recognize that which is obtained through this method for the purpose of protection from fear, for the sake of defense, and for the accomplishment of one's task as a reciprocal service.
Nārada says: But what is given by those overcome by fear, anger, grief, or the force of pain,
as well as through bribery, jesting, exchange, or fraud, is considered *adatta* (not properly given).
It is performed by those who are childish, deluded, lacking independence, afflicted, intoxicated, or insane; and it is done with the desire for gain, thinking, "This person is my benefactor."
Kātyāyana says: Even if one were to say, "I shall give you my entire property if you rescue me from this life-threatening danger," it would not be so [if the promise was made under duress].
That which is given by one who is under the sway of lust or anger, or who is distressed, intoxicated, insane, or deluded,
as well as what is given through error or in jest, may be taken back.
But as for a bribe that has been promised for the sake of accomplishing a desired object—
even for the purpose of accomplishing that object— it must not be given under any circumstances.
If she had already been given away previously, he must be compelled to give her back by force;
Gārgya and the followers of Mānava declare that he shall also pay a fine eleven times the value.
Bṛhaspati says:
[One should not accept gifts] from those who are angry, overjoyed, intoxicated, afflicted, childish, insane, or overcome by fear;
nor from those who are drunk, very old, abandoned, deluded, or overwhelmed by the force of grief.
That which is given by these dull-witted ones is likewise proclaimed as "not given" (adatta),
when it is given with the desire for personal gain to an unworthy recipient while suspecting them to be worthy.
Or, if the work is connected with dharma, the master shall receive that reward again.
Manu says:
Whatever has been given to someone who asks for it may later prove to be contrary to dharma; therefore, such a thing should not have been given to him.

The meaning is that if one gives to someone who requests [the gift] for the purpose of performing a religious duty (*dharma*), but that person does not perform the duty, then it should not have been given to him. However, if he should accomplish it out of pride or for the sake of profit, he must be made to pay a fine of one *suvarṇa* by the king; this shall be the atonement for his theft.

The meaning of this is as follows: if, when that [debt] is being recovered, he does not pay it out of pride or greed, but instead seeks to establish its non-forfeiture by means of legal proceedings in the presence of the king, desiring to prove that the wealth cannot be taken away from him, then he must be made to pay that wealth by the king. Kātyāyana states:
"Whether in health or in distress, what has been promised for a religious purpose must be paid;
if he dies without having paid it, his son must be made to pay it—of this there is no doubt."

Whether one is healthy or afflicted by disease, if a gift or donation has been promised to a Brāhmaṇa after declaring, "I shall give this much to you," and the donor dies without having actually given it, then his heirs must give that gift. If they do not pay it, they should be compelled by the king to pay it. This is to be understood as applying when the promise was made for the sake of dharma; however, [the same applies] due to the reporting of a thief, a perpetrator of violence, a rogue, or a slanderer, or from the discovery of stolen or lost property, or likewise from the practice of falsehood.
Whatever has been obtained by these [mediators] is called a bribe;
in that case, the giver shall not be punished, but the mediator alone shall bear the guilt.

If you do not give it to me on account of [your] informing or declaring [me] as a thief and so forth—that is to say, by stating "you are a thief" and so on—or likewise on account of the sight of one who has been held or lost (i.e., one who was taken and then protected), meaning "I shall show you to the keeper"; or on account of the cause of proceeding with what is untrue as if it were true, or by the reverse thereof; then the wealth obtained under the name of a bribe must be made to be paid back to the giver by the king. The meaning is that both the procurer and the receiver of the bribe are to be punished. (2.175)
The acceptance of a gift should be public, especially in the case of immovable property;
and what has been promised as a gift must be given, and once given, it should not be taken back again.
Thus ends the section on the non-delivery of what has been given. 12.

The acceptance of every kind of property must be done openly, publicly, and in the presence of witnesses; this is especially true for immovable property, which requires great effort [to verify]. Likewise, that which has been promised and accepted—such as "I shall give this to you"—must be given, and once given, it must not be taken back. Kātyāyana states:
He who, having voluntarily promised a gift to a Brāhmaṇa, does not give it, should be made to pay it like a debt and incur the first amercement.
Gautama states: "Even after having given his word, one should not give to one who is engaged in unrighteousness. Kātyāyana says:

"That which is mortgaged or sold under a fraudulent agreement, as well as a gift or a receipt of a gift made under such a fraud, or whatever one perceives to be based on deceit—all that should be annulled."
Yoga is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Thus ends the section on "Non-delivery of what has been given" (Dattāpradānika). 2.176.

Thus ends the section on the non-delivery of what has been given (*dattāpradānika*) in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, who was born in the lineage of the illustrious King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the line of the illustrious Vidyādharas. Section 12.
Now begins the section on rescission of purchase in the Yājñavalkya-smṛti with its commentary. (13) He states the specific time limits for those who examine particular types of goods:
The examination of seeds, iron, draft animals, gems, women, milch cattle, and men shall take ten days, one day, five days, seven days, one month, three days, and half a month respectively. (2.177)

The word *ahaḥ* (day), which precedes the word *māsa* (month), is connected individually with each of the words beginning with *daśa* (ten). During these seven periods of time—beginning with ten days—one must examine the seven types of goods, starting with seeds, according to their respective order. Among them: for a seed, in ten days; for iron, in one day; for draft animals such as oxen, in five days; for gems such as rubies (*padmarāga*), in seven days; for a female slave, in a month; for milch cattle such as cows, in three days; and for a male slave, in half a month. The meaning is that once one has purchased seeds and other such items after they have been examined in this manner, no rescission of the sale (*anuśaya*) should be made. (2.177)
In connection with this, he states the method for examining other substances:
"Gold is not diminished when [melted] in fire; silver [loses] two palas per hundred;
tin and lead [lose] eight; copper [loses] five; and iron [loses] ten. (2.178)

When gold is being smelted, there is no loss at all; that which appears to diminish is merely mixed with other substances, for pure gold does not diminish at all. When silver weighing one hundred *pala*s is being liquefied, two *pala*s are lost. In the case of tin (*trapu*), when one hundred *pala*s are liquefied, eight *pala*s are lost. The same applies to lead (*sīsaka*). In the case of copper (*tāmra*), when one hundred *pala*s are being smelted, five *pala*s are lost. Likewise, in the case of iron (*ayasa*), ten [are lost]. (2.178)
Regarding woven cloth, he says: "In the case of woolen and cotton cloth weighing one hundred [palas], the increase is ten palas;
for medium quality, the increase is five palas; but for fine quality, it is considered to be three palas. (2.179)

In the Sūtra, it is stated that when there are one hundred *pala*s of cotton or wool, whatever cloth is produced from them increases by ten *pala*s. This should be understood to apply to cloth made of coarse thread; however, for cloth made of fine or very fine thread, the increase would be five *pala*s and three *pala*s respectively. (2.179)
Having stated [the rules for] increase, he now states [the rules for] decrease:
"In the case of manufactured cloth and that woven with hair, a one-thirtieth part is considered the decrease;
there shall be neither decrease nor increase in the case of silk and garments made of bark. (2.180)

That [cloth] in which forms such as those of women or men are produced in the woven fabric by the power of the work is *kārmika*. That in which the fibers are bound together is *romabaddha*. In both types of cloth, one-thirtieth part of the measure is lost. In the case of silk (*kauśeya*) and flax (*atasīmaya*), as well as bark-fiber cloth (*vālkala*) and linen (*kṣauma*) and the like, there is neither loss nor increase. Regarding this, Nārada says: "In the processing of woven cloth, however, loss and increase are declared;
therein, for cotton and wool, the increase is ten palas per hundred."
For these middle-sized threads that are like coarse yarns, the loss is five per hundred;
however, for very fine threads, it is three palas—thus the loss has been declared.
The loss of woven hair-cloth and of items produced by manual labor is one-thirtieth;
however, for silk, bark garments, and the like, there is neither increase nor loss.
If there is a greater reduction than what was stated, the artisan shall be fined. (2.180)
Regarding that, he states the measure of the fine:

"Having ascertained the place, the time, and the use, as well as the relative strength or weakness in the case of loss, those who are experts in matters of property shall declare what [the value] is; that must undoubtedly be made to be paid. (2.181)

[Thus ends the section on regret over what has been purchased (krītānuśaya-prakaraṇa) || 13 ||] In cases where gold, copper, boundary markers, or materials such as silk thread or cotton are being fashioned by their makers—such as goldsmiths and others—and gold or thread is stolen from them before it reaches the owner, the artisans, including the goldsmiths, should be made to pay the value of the loss without hesitation by the king. This determination must be made after carefully considering the time and place of the theft, the owner’s enjoyment of the item, and its quality or lack thereof, by those who possess true knowledge of the value of goods. As Manu says: "A weaver shall give ten palas of thread and receive one pala more in return."
If he acts otherwise than that, he shall be made to pay a fine of twelve [paṇas].
A fine amount measured at twelve *kārsāpaṇas* is called "twelvefold. Nārada says:
One-eighth of the value shall be deducted for a garment washed once;
for one washed twice, one-fourth; for three times, one-third; and for four times, exactly one-half.

But beyond the point when half has been destroyed, there is a gradual reduction by one-quarter at each stage, until the cloth reaches a state where ten parts are worn away; for that which is decayed, destruction is indefinite.

Thus ends the section on rescission of purchase in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, who was born in the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the glorious Vidyādhara clan. Section 13.
Now begins the section on service after having entered [into it] (*abhyupetyāśuśrūṣā*) in the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* with its commentary. (14) Now he speaks concerning the subject of slaves (*dāsa*).
One who has been forcibly enslaved by thieves, or even one who has been sold, is liberated by providing for his master’s life, by serving him with devotion, or by paying his ransom. [2.182]

One who has been made a slave by force or by fraud—even if he was not previously a slave—and one who has been sold by thieves, shall be released; that is to say, he must be set free. If [the purchaser] does not release him, then he must be released by the king. Regarding this, Nārada says: "Those who have been seized by thieves and sold, or those who have been made slaves by force, must be released by the king; servitude is not recognized in their case."

A slave who, having accepted his own death, out of devotion delivers his master from death; one who has been released from slavery by his master; and one who pays the ransom-money for the sake of being liberated from his own slavery—all these must be released by the master. Alternatively, the meaning of the phrase "from that ransom" (*tanniṣkrayāt*) is this: a slave who has been given as a pledge to a creditor is released by the repayment of the debt or by the delivery of another pledge. Manu says: "Even if released by his master, a Śūdra is not released from slavery."
For that [nature] is innate to him; who can remove it from him?
Nārada says:

One born in the house, one purchased, one obtained as a gift, one who has come as an heir, one supported during a time of distress, and likewise one who has been placed there by the master; [these are the types of slaves].
One who has been released from a great debt, one won in battle as a prize,
one who has approached saying "I am yours," one made over by means of renunciation,
and likewise one brought [as a slave] by a mare— these are to be known as slaves for food (*bhaktadāsa*).
And one who sells himself; in the treatise, fifteen types of slaves are recorded.

One born of one’s own female slave is a *gṛhadāsa* (house-slave). One acquired for a price is a *krīta* (bought). One obtained through acceptance as a gift or similar means is a *labdha* (received). One who has come from an inheritance is a *rikthalabdha* (obtained by inheritance). One supported during a famine or in times of distress is an *anākālabhṛta*. One made a pledge (*ādhi*) against a creditor by the master is an *āhita*. One defeated at a wager is a *dyūtajita* (won at gambling). One who has fallen away from the life of a renunciant is a *pravrajyāvasita*. One who has agreed, saying "I shall be your slave for this much time," is a *kṛta* (contracted). A *bhaktadāsa* is one of the form: "As long as you give me food, I am your slave. A *vaḍavāhṛta* is one brought by a female slave—that is, having married her upon obtaining her, he enters into slavery. The others are well-known.
In this regard, the first four classes are not released from slavery except through the favor of their master; for them, servitude is hereditary.
That lowest of men who, being independent, sells himself—
he is the most wretched of them all, and even he is not released from servitude.
And whoever shall liberate their master from a life-threatening danger shall be released from servitude and receive a share equal to that of a son.
One who has been maintained at an improper time is released from slavery by giving a pair of cattle;
however, that which was consumed during a time of distress is not purified by ritual action.
Even if he has been adopted, if the owner should recover him after having given him wealth, then the adoptive father may take him back;
he too ranks immediately after the purchased son.

But if one should cause a slave to approach [the master] through conciliation, making him accept [the status] by saying "I am a slave," then he is "next after the purchased," meaning equal to one who was purchased. Regarding the case of a slave for debt, that same author says: "By paying the debt along with interest, the debtor is released from slavery;
and the one made a slave [for service] is also released upon the completion of the work for which the debt was contracted."
One who has approached saying "I am yours," one who has been captured under a banner,
or one won at a stake, is released by the giving of a counter-slave as an equivalent act.

"Acquired through a banner" means won in battle. "Giving a counter-head" means giving another slave. Regarding the qualification "of equal labor": the meaning is that by giving a slave who performs work equal to the work performed by the former slave, the former slave is released from slavery. (2.182)
Regarding one who has fallen from the religious life (*pravrajyā*), it is said:
"One who has fallen from the religious life is the king’s slave for as long as life lasts.
Having turned back from the religious life, he remains the king’s slave for the rest of his life. Thus says Nārada.
But a man who has fallen from the religious life shall become the slave of the king alone;
for him there is no release, nor purification by any means whatsoever.
There are only two outcastes by their actions in this world, utterly excluded from society:
one who has returned from the life of renunciation, and one who has entered it in vain.
Kātyāyana states:
In a kingdom where the three twice-born castes are established in the life of renunciation,
the king shall cause the Brāhmaṇa to be banished and the Kṣatriya or Vaiśya to enter into servitude.
Dakṣa says:
But the king should swiftly banish from his realm that man who, having taken up the life of a wandering mendicant, does not abide by his own duty, marking him with the sign of a dog's foot.
He describes the manner of releasing a slave other than one who has completed his period of probationary ordination (*pravrajyāvasita*):
"One who, with a joyful mind, desires to make his own slave no longer a slave,
should take from the slave's shoulder a water-pot filled with water and break it."
One should sprinkle water mixed with raw rice grains and flowers upon his head;
then, having said "He is no slave," one should release him facing the east three times.
There is another distinction between one enslaved for food (*bhaktadāsa*) and one captured by a mare (*vaḍavāhṛta*):
by the release of the one enslaved for food, he is immediately liberated;
by the restraint of the mare, the one captured by a mare is released.

"Food" (*bhakta*) refers to cooked rice; "offering" (*pratipādana*) means providing it to him. A "mare" (*vaḍavā*) is a female slave. "Restraint" (*nigraha*) means confinement; that is to say, non-enjoyment [of sexual intercourse]. Likewise: "But she who should have union with her own male slave and subsequently give birth—without regard for the seed—the child, along with its progeny, shall not be a slave."
Whatever wealth a slave may possess, it is traditionally held that the master has authority over it;
however, in the case of those who have been sold openly, the master does not deserve that wealth.
But she who was not a slave and is married by a slave shall acquire ownership through that slave,
because her husband is her master, since the lord of a wife is dependent upon her owner.

Regarding the reading *dāsāt sattvam*, "sattva" means a living being; if that [child] is obtained from the slave of her husband while she herself is not a slave, then it should be understood that he enters into the state of slavery belonging to the owner of that slave. This is the meaning.
Slavery among the castes occurs through the natural order (*ānulomya*), not through the inverse order (*pratiloma*). (2.183)
A person of lower caste becomes a slave to one of higher caste; however, the reverse is not the case—this is the meaning. Nārada states:
"Slavery is not ordained through the inverse order of castes;
except for those who have abandoned their own duty, slavery is considered to be like marriage."

One who abandons his own duty (*svadharma*) and has fallen from the state of renunciation (*pravrajyā*) is subject to being branded on the foot with the sign of a dog and banished, provided he was a Brāhmaṇa. However, in the case of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, it is stated that they must become slaves to the king. By this [present rule], however, servitude to the King is ordained for the Śūdra, while servitude to the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya is ordained for the Brāhmaṇa. Kātyāyana says:
"Bhṛgu states that through the gift of one's own self by one who is independent, servitude is established just as in the case of a wife;
yet servitude toward the three [higher] castes is to be understood as never applying to a Brāhmaṇa."
Servitude for the castes occurs according to the natural order and not in the inverse order;
for Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras lose their independence by [entering] it.
[789] Even one of equal caste must never compel a Brāhmaṇa to servitude; however, if he is deficient in virtue or Vedic study, he may perform such labor at his own will.
Even there, the best of the twice-born should not perform any unwholesome act;
for by becoming a slave to a Brāhmaṇa, the royal splendor is destroyed.
Nārada said: Action is also declared to be of two kinds—unwholesome and indeed wholesome.
Unwholesome action is said to be that performed by slaves, while wholesome action is remembered as that performed by those who act with mastery.
The cleaning of house doors, impure places, streets, and refuse heaps;
the touching of private parts, the handling of food remnants, and the removal of feces, urine, and mounds [of earth].
Furthermore, serving the master with one's own limbs when he so desires should be understood as inauspicious action; any other [action] beyond this is auspicious.
Manu says: One captured under a banner, one who is a slave for food, one born in the house, one purchased, one given,
one inherited from a father, and one enslaved as punishment— these seven are the origins of slavery.

This is intended as an illustration, for servitude is declared even for those other than Nārada and the rest. A "slave by way of fine" (*daṇḍadāsa*) is one who becomes a slave for the purpose of paying off a fine. Likewise: "A Brāhmaṇa, out of compassion, should support a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who are distressed for a livelihood, making them perform his own works."
If a Brāhmaṇa, out of delusion, should compel initiated twice-born men to perform servitude against their will by virtue of his superior power,
he shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king.
*Prābhavyam* is the state of being a master (*prabhavataḥ bhāvaḥ*); that is to say, mastery. [The fine shall be] six hundred *paṇas*.
However, he may compel a Śūdra to perform service, whether he was purchased or not purchased;
for he was created by the Self-existent One solely for the service of the Brāhmaṇa.
Viṣṇu: "He who employs a man of the highest caste in servitude shall be punished with the highest amercement. Kātyāyana:
"If anyone should seize or likewise sell a Brāhmaṇa woman, that act must be declared null and void by the king, and all of them shall be punished."

But he who, out of lust, should make a woman of good family a slave by force, or should transfer her to another, shall be punished; and that [marriage] shall be considered as never having taken place.
He who enjoys the service of a nurse for an infant or a chief female slave as if she were a common maidservant,
or the wife of an attendant, shall incur the first amercement.
He who, being capable and not in a state of distress, desires to sell a bonded slave woman who is crying out [in protest], shall incur a fine of two hundred [paṇas]. (2.183)

Even when he has mastered the craft, the apprentice shall remain in the teacher's house for the prescribed period; having received his food from the teacher, he shall offer the fruits of his labor to him. [2.184]

[Thus ends the section on Service by Contract. || 14 || A pupil seeking the knowledge of a craft, having obtained his food from the teacher, shall present to the teacher the fruit of the craft-work he has performed himself. Even after he has acquired the craft, he shall remain in the teacher’s household for as long as the period he had agreed upon for residing in the teacher’s house. This pertains to the legal title (*vyavahārapada*) characterized by service by contract. In that very context, other Smṛti texts concerning this subject are shown. Nārada says:
But when one has undertaken service and does not perform it,
this is called the legal dispute concerning the failure to perform service after having undertaken it.
The meaning is "failure to serve after having undertaken [the service].
According to the treatise, the wise have observed five kinds of servants:
four types are laborers (*karmakara*), while the remaining fifteen are slaves (*dāsa*).
Likewise:
"Disciples, resident pupils, and hired servants—the fourth being the laborer for extra tasks—these are to be known as laborers; slaves, however, are those born in the house and so forth."

The wise have declared that their lack of independence is their common characteristic; however, the distinction among them is said to arise from their genus, their actions, and likewise from their livelihoods.
Until he has mastered the knowledge, the student should serve his teacher with self-restraint;
he should adopt the same conduct toward the teacher’s wives and likewise toward the teacher’s son.
But having completed his studies and having presented the teacher's fee to the guru, he should return to his own home; this is declared to be the proper conduct of a student.
He should go forth—
that is, he should depart— desiring to acquire his own craft with the permission of his kinsmen; having made a firm determination regarding the duration, he should dwell in the presence of a teacher.
The teacher should instruct him in his own home, providing him with food;
he should not make him perform any other work and should treat him like a son.

The science of arts (*śilpavidyā*) is a science other than the fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*). It has been stated that "craft" (*śilpa*) refers to manual labor; with reference to this, a pupil should dwell together with a teacher, saying, "I shall reside in your presence for such a length of time. Kātyāyana says: "But he who does not teach the craft and instead makes him perform other tasks shall incur the first *sāhasa* fine; from that, the pupil withdraws. [791]

The meaning is that if a student abandons a teacher who is teaching him [the Vedas] and making him perform his own duties, the student shall be abandoned by the teacher, and the king shall impose upon him the first amercement as a fine. Nārada says:
"He who abandons a teacher who is faultless and is teaching him must be forced to stay [with him] by means of physical restraint; he deserves both corporal punishment and imprisonment."
In this context, "killing" means beating, not the severing of life.
Even if he has been trained, the pupil must complete the task within the allotted time;
whatever work he performs therein, the fruit thereof belongs to the teacher alone.

The meaning is that he should complete the time agreed upon while living there; for the teacher, the fruit and gain of the work performed by the pupil residing there belongs to him. Having mastered the craft, at the proper time, having circumambulated the teacher from left to right and having honored him according to his ability, the apprentice departs.
A hired servant is to be known as being of three kinds: superior, inferior, and middling;
their wages shall be appropriate to their capacity and depend upon the calves they tend.
Among these, the one armed with weapons is the highest, the cultivator is the middling, and the porter is the lowest; thus is the hired laborer of three kinds.
He who is authorized over all [the members] and likewise stands at the head of the family should be known as a *karmakara* (servant), and he is also remembered as a *kauṭumbika* (householder).
For these four are proclaimed as performers of auspicious deeds;
however, the remaining fifteen servants are partakers of inferior karma.
Among all types of laborers, the one appointed, placed in authority, or—in other words—the supervisor is the subject here. Bṛhaspati says:
"The sharecropper is recorded as being of two kinds among those who live by agriculture and cattle-rearing;
he shall receive [a portion] from the harvested grain and likewise from the milk, without a doubt."
Thus ends the section on rescission of purchase and sale (and breach of service after entering into an agreement). 2.184.

Thus ends the section on "Service after Having Entered into an Agreement" in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, who was born in the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the lineage of the glorious Vidyādharas. Section 14.

Now begins the section on the Breach of Agreement (*saṃvidvyatikrama*) in the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* with its commentary. First, he states the matter relevant to the legal title (*vyavahārapada*) characterized by the breach of agreement.

[792] Having established a residence in the city and appointed there the Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the three Vedas, the king should provide them with a livelihood and say: "Let your own dharma be protected. 2.185.

The king, having established a site in his own city—a plot of land endowed with excellent dwellings and other amenities—making that place "possessed of a livelihood" (vṛttimat), meaning equipped with both immovable and movable wealth sufficient for the maintenance of a family; and having settled there Brāhmaṇas "versed in the three Vedas" (traividyān), those possessed of the three branches of knowledge consisting of the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman, and having assigned them houses, means of subsistence, and so forth as is appropriate, he should say to those Brāhmaṇas: "Let your own duty (svadharma)—the duty pertaining to caste, stage of life, and so forth—be observed and performed. Some read the text as *traividyaṃ vṛttimat*; in that case, the meaning is that he should act so that the group of those learned in the three Vedas is provided with a livelihood. The term *traividyam* is a collective compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) denoting the aggregate of the three sciences beginning with the Ṛgveda. And the excellence of the site consists in its being inhabited by such Brāhmaṇas. Thus, since the arrangement of a community of Brāhmaṇas is mentioned, it follows by implication that the establishment of a convention (*saṃketa-samaya-kriyā*), which is expressed by the word *saṃvit*, must be performed. For without that [convention], it is impossible to ward off disturbances to the community, such as thieves and the like, nor can one accomplish religious duties such as sacrifices (*iṣṭa*) and public works (*pūrta*). Therefore, Bṛhaspati says: [He should establish] a settlement (*sthāna*) provided with a livelihood (*vṛttimat*), and having settled there those who know the three Vedas, he should say to them: "Let your own duty be protected. || 1.26 || (Note: The verse cited corresponds to Bṛhaspati Smṛti 1.26.)
Having summoned Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas, well-versed in the scriptures, and maintainers of the sacred fire-offering,
he should establish them there and provide for their livelihood.
The king should grant them house-sites with non-confiscable taxes,
and having recorded it in his own edicts, he should ensure they are made freehold.

They shall perform the daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), desire-based (kāmya), pacificatory (śāntika), and nourishing (pauṣṭika) rites according to the Purāṇas, as well as provide a definitive decision in cases of doubt.
However, for the sake of a village, a guild, or a corporation, an agreement and the performance of its terms should be made;
it should likewise be done at a time of distress or for a religious purpose.
Fear of thieves and wild beasts, as well as affliction, is known as the "support of all" (sarva-saṃdhāraṇā).
In that situation, peace must be brought about by everyone collectively, and not by any single individual alone.
Having first established mutual trust through a sealed deposit, a written contract, or by means of guarantors standing below them, they should thereafter carry out their business affairs.
Those who are hostile, addicted to vices, modest, lazy, or timid;
those who are greedy, excessively aged, or children—these should not be appointed as counselors for state affairs.
Those who are pure, knowers of the Vedic dharma, skillful, self-controlled, of noble birth, and proficient in all undertakings—such persons should be appointed as the most eminent officials. (2.185)
[793] It has been stated that Brahmins should be settled by the king in appropriate places; now he describes what must be done once they have been settled:
"That which is conventional (*sāmayika*) provided it does not conflict with one's own duty (*nijadharma*)."
Even that dharma established by the king must be protected with effort. (2.186)

That which is not in conflict with one's own Vedic and other duties (*śrauta-ādi-dharma*), yet is beneficial to the community, is a conventional duty (*sāmayika-dharma*)—a duty established by convention and the like. For example: in times of affliction such as disease, a specific amount of wealth must be given at every field or every house for the sake of performing propitiatory rites (*śāntika*) such as the *gṛhayajña*; or, all the inhabitants of a district, setting aside their own occupations, must assemble at a particular place on such-and-such an occasion, and whoever does not come shall be subject to this punishment; or, the restoration of assembly halls, water-stations, temples, tanks, and so forth when they have fallen into decay, the maintenance of the poor and the helpless, and the distribution of gifts for the purpose of sacrifices and alms-giving—all this must be performed according to this arrangement using common funds; or, whatever customary duty has been established by the king, such as "whosoever among you recites or knows more [of the scriptures] shall receive such-and-such honor," and so on. Both these types of duties must be diligently protected. On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
The construction of assembly halls, water-stations, temples, tanks, gardens, and parks,
as well as the rehabilitation of the destitute and the poor, and the performance of beneficial works.
Those who are capable must protect [the agreements]; however, for one who is capable but violates [them], the punishment shall be the confiscation of all his property and banishment from the city.
In that case, whatever man creates a division or shows indifference [toward the teacher], a fine of four suvarṇas and six niṣkas is ordained for him. (2.186)
He states what should be done toward one who violates the religious duties established by convention and toward one who misappropriates the property of a corporation:
"But he who takes the property of a corporation, and he who transgresses an agreement—having confiscated all his possessions, the king shall banish him from the realm. (2.187)
A compact is a covenant. This is a grave offense. Regarding this, Manu says elsewhere:
"That man who, having entered into a covenant by oath with a village, a district, or a corporation, should break it out of greed, the king shall banish from his realm."
Having restrained him, the king should compel that violator of the compact to pay four suvarṇas, six niṣkas, and one śatamāna of silver.

In this case as well, four types of punishment—such as banishment from the country and so forth—are to be determined according to the nature of the offense. Kātyāyana states: "The perpetrator of violence, the one who causes division, and the destroyer of the community's property—all these must be executed after being publicly proclaimed in this manner before the king," says Bhṛgu. [794]
Bṛhaspati:
But he who would injure what is common property, or revile those learned in the three Vedas, or obstruct an agreement or a ritual act, must be banished from that city.
The phrase "having cast aside the threefold knowledge and so forth" means that one should expel or remove them. Furthermore:

"One who inflicts pain on others, a slanderer, a creator of dissension, as well as one who acts with reckless violence, and one who hates a guild, a corporation, or the king—these shall be swiftly banished from there."

An *aruṃtuda* is one who wounds the vitals; a *sūcaka* is one who makes known faults; a *bhedakṛt* is one who causes dissension among those bound by affection. The heads of families, guilds, and assemblies, as well as the inhabitants of cities and fortresses, shall impose verbal censure, fines, or banishment upon evildoers.
The punishment and favor toward men performed by them according to their own duty must also be approved by the king, for they are traditionally considered to have been delegated with full authority.

The *adhyakṣas* are the highest-ranking officials. They shall impose restraint of speech or restraint of mind according to the nature of the offense. In the reading *vāgviśrama*, "cessation of speech" means being unfit for conversation; "exclusion" means being unfit for social intercourse.
