Those who have been granted full authority (*nisṛṣṭārtha*) are those whose actions have been authorized. If they should cause harm—having become embroiled in mutual hatred toward one another—they must be restrained by the king and punished along with their associates.
"Anubandha" means persistence.
When a conflict arises between the assemblies and their leaders,
the king should then deliberate and establish them upon his own path.
Nārada said: The king shall not tolerate their forming secret conspiracies, their bearing of weapons without cause, or their mutual injury.

He should neither tolerate nor forgive it. Kātyāyana says: If someone should eat from the same vessel or in the same row as another, and he does not report that person's fault, he should be punished in the same manner as that person.
Bṛhaspati: Those who, having formed a corporation and made a single entity of themselves, misappropriate what is due to the king, shall be made to pay eightfold; and so too shall merchants who flee.
The king’s share is the tax. Nārada says:
Whatever is contrary to the king’s interests, whatever is despised by the subjects, and whatever is detrimental to wealth—these he should cause to be withdrawn from them.
Whatever cause should be defective and not established by sacred tradition, even if it has been set in motion, a king who desires his own welfare should cause it to be abolished. (2.187)
Furthermore:
"The words of those who speak for the welfare of the community must be carried out by all."
Whoever therein acts contrary [to the truth] shall be compelled to pay the first fine. 2.188.

What those who belong to an assembly say for the benefit of the group must be carried out by all the members of that assembly. But he who is antagonistic toward those who speak for the common good shall be punished by the assembly with the first amercement. Kātyāyana states: "He who destroys what is reasonable, he who gives no opportunity to the speaker, and he who speaks what is unreasonable, shall incur the first amercement. (2.188)
The lord of the earth, having honored those who have come for the sake of the collective task with gifts, respect, and hospitality once their business is accomplished, should dismiss them. (2.189)

The king, having honored with gifts, respect, and hospitality those leaders of the corporation who have come for the sake of the corporation's business and have accomplished their task, should dismiss them. (2.189)
One who has been dispatched for the business of a group shall hand over whatever he may obtain;
if he does not hand it over himself, he shall be made to pay eleven times that amount. (2.190)

When someone has been dispatched by a corporation toward a king or other authority for the sake of accomplishing the corporation’s own business, whatever he may receive from that person must be given back to the corporation by him personally. Otherwise, the corporation shall take eleven times that amount from him. Bṛhaspati states:
"Whatever is obtained by force from them all belongs equally to everyone;
it should be distributed according to their respective shares, whether for a six-month period or a month."
One should give to the destitute, the elderly, the blind, women, children, the afflicted, and the sick; likewise to those seeking offspring and others—for this is the eternal law.
Whatever has been acquired through efforts, or preserved, or staked for the sake of the community,
or obtained through the favor of the king— all that belongs equally to everyone.

If what has been obtained by those sent out by the community, when divided, is sufficient for the maintenance of the members for a period from one month up to six months, then it should be distributed according to their respective shares. If it is small, it should be given to those who are destitute and so forth. Kātyāyana says: Whatever debt may have been consumed by anyone on behalf of the community, or whatever was expended for personal purposes, that must be paid back by those very individuals.
Those who have joined the midst of guilds, corporations,
or associations shall all receive equal shares of the previous wealth or debts.

In the same way, food, property to be divided, and wealth for religious acts should be shared by one who remains within the community; however, one who has departed is not entitled to a share. [2.190]
Those who know the Vedas, who are pure and free from greed, should be the thinkers of affairs;
the word of those who speak for the welfare of the community must be carried out. (2.191)

Those who recite the Veda and understand its meaning are "knowers of the Veda" (*vedajña*); "pure" (*śuci*) means those of pure intention; "not greedy" (*alubdha*) means those free from covetousness. Persons of such a character should be the deliberators regarding what is beneficial or detrimental to the affairs of the community. While the role of being deliberators on affairs is prescribed for those distinguished by their knowledge of the Veda and other qualities, other [qualities] are merely restated. Bṛhaspati: Two, three, or five persons should be appointed who speak for the welfare of the community.
Their word must be carried out by the village, the guilds, the assemblies, and so forth. (2.191)
He states the extension of the rules for the customary laws (*sāmayika-dharma*) prescribed for Brahmins to other groups:
"This same rule applies to guilds, merchant associations, heretical sects, and corporations;
the king shall protect them from internal dissension and preserve their traditional livelihood. (2.192)
Thus ends the section on the violation of agreements. || 15 ||

A guild (*śreṇi*) is a group of those belonging to the same caste who subsist by a common occupation, such as a guild of washermen. Those of various castes who travel together for the purpose of trade in foreign lands are *naigamas*; those established in non-Vedic asceticism are *pāṣaṇḍins*; and others who share a common livelihood distinct from Brāhmaṇas are *gaṇas* here. For these as well, this very same law applies—that which was stated previously as being "without contradicting their own specific duties" and so forth. Likewise, the king should protect and prevent mutual division or dissension of mind among the guilds and other groups; he should also maintain their traditional mode of livelihood. Thus ends the section on the violation of conventions (2.192).

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, concerning the performance of legal procedures (*saṃvidyatikarma*), in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, who was born in the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the family of the glorious Vidyādharas.

Now begins the section on the non-payment of wages in the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* with its commentary. (16) Now he commences the title of legal dispute known as *vetanānapākarma* (the non-payment of wages).

One who abandons work after having received wages shall pay double; if he has not received wages, he shall be made to pay an equal amount. The tools and implements must be protected by the servants. [2.193]

Wages (*bhṛti*) mean remuneration (*vetana*). Having received that, if a hired laborer abandons his master’s work and fails to perform it, he shall pay double that amount; that is, he shall give it to the master. If he abandons the work after having agreed to it, even though the wages have not been received, the master may claim as much of the wages as was agreed upon by him to be paid, and the draft-animals, plow-teams, and so forth must be protected [by the laborer]. Nārada says: "The sequence of rules for the giving and receiving of wages for servants has been stated; the non-payment of wages is recorded as a title of dispute (*vivādapada*)."
Just as a master should give wages to a servant according to the work performed—
whether determined at the beginning, the middle, or the end of the task.
Bṛhaspati says: A hired servant must not commit even the slightest act of deception against his master;
he incurs a loss of wages, and from that, a legal dispute arises.
When a hired laborer, having received his wages, does not perform the work,
he shall, if capable, be made to pay a fine of twice that amount as well as the wages.
Nārada says: One who, having promised to perform work, does not do it; or one who, having received wages, does not perform the work by force, shall pay double the wages.
But he who, having undertaken an enterprise, does not bring it to completion, should be compelled by force; if he still does not act, he deserves punishment.
Vṛddha-Manu:
He who, having given his promise, does not perform [the work], should be compelled to do so even by force;
if he still does not perform that task, he shall incur a fine of two hundred [paṇas].
Manu:
A servant who, though not afflicted by illness, fails out of pride to perform his work as prescribed,
shall be fined eight *kṛṣṇalas*, and his wages for that period shall not be paid.
The phrase "even for one who has performed the work" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
As it has been said: "Whether he is distressed or healthy, if one does not cause that work to be done, his wages must not be paid;
however, wages must be paid even for work that is slightly deficient."
As it has been said:
"One who was distressed should, once restored to health, perform [the work] from the beginning exactly as promised;
even after a very long time, he shall certainly receive his wages. (2.193)
He who employs laborers without having fixed their wages must be made by the king to pay them a tenth part of the profits from trade, cattle, or grain. (2.194)

If a master causes work to be done without having determined, "I shall give you such an amount as wages," then the master shall give to the laborer a tenth part of the wealth produced from that trade or other activity for which the labor was performed. If he does not give it, the master must be compelled by the king to pay it. Vṛddha Manu says:
"Those who are skilled in sea-voyages and who perceive the requirements of place, time, and profit shall determine the wages, provided that no agreement has been made beforehand."
Bṛhaspati says:
The plowman should take either one-third or one-fifth [of the produce].
One who is maintained by food should take a fifth part from the plow.
Furthermore, from a field where crops have grown, he may take one-third, provided he has not been supported by them.
Nārada says:
One who abandons his work before the term is completed shall forfeit his wages;
however, if he departs due to a fault of the master, he shall receive payment for the work actually performed.

Viṣṇu: "A hired servant who abandons his wages before the term is completed shall forfeit the entire value of his labor and pay a hundred *paṇas* to the king. Whatever is lost through his fault must be made good to the master, except in the case of an act of God. If the master dismisses the hired servant before the term is completed, he shall pay him the full value of his wages and a hundred *paṇas* to the king, except for faults on the part of the servant. (2.198)

If one should transgress the place and time, or should effect a gain in an improper manner, in that case it shall be at the pleasure of the owner; if more work has been done, more should be given. (2.195)

If the master, acting independently, should cause the servant to miss the place and time at which agricultural work or similar tasks yield fruit, or should cause a profit to turn into loss by incurring excessive expenditure, then the master may, according to his own will and intention, pay the servant wages; he cannot independently give less than what is due. If the servant obtains a greater amount of time [or fruit], the master must give him a reward consisting of wealth exceeding the price already received. (2.195)
Whatever work one performs, for that much is his wages;
provided there is no deceit on the part of either party, but in case of deceit, one should act according to what has been heard.

When a single master’s work is to be accomplished by many laborers, a wage corresponding to the amount of work performed should be given to whichever servant performs it, provided that deceit is avoided. If one person should perform work that requires two people to accomplish, double the wages should be given there. If the work is less, a reduction in the share should be calculated. However, in the case of deceit, it should be understood that the master may give according to his own will, as heard or as stated. This should be understood to apply when the work is to be accomplished by many laborers or when the wages have been stipulated. Here, the mention of both cases is for the sake of illustration; therefore, it is established that even where many laborers perform the work without deceit, the payment of the price should be according to the work done. (2.196)
The carrier shall be made to pay for goods lost through no fault of the king or fate;
likewise, one who causes an obstruction to the journey shall be made to pay double the wages. (2.197)

If one who has been hired to transport goods destroys the merchandise or the goods to be carried due to his own negligence—excluding acts of the king or providence—he shall be made to pay its value. However, he who creates an obstacle to the journey shall be made to pay double the wages. Vṛddha-Manu says:
"He shall be made to pay for what is destroyed through negligence; for what is destroyed by delusion, twice as much.
But he shall not be made to pay for what is stolen by thieves, or burnt, or carried away by water."

The meaning is that it is double, twice as much. Bṛhaspati says: "Whatever work a hired servant performs when commissioned by his master, for that [work], even if it be an inauspicious task, the master shall incur the blame."
"For that purpose" means for the sake of the master. "Inauspicious" refers to theft and so forth. "He would offend" means he would become subject to punishment and the like. (2.197)

If he has set out on the journey, he shall abandon a seventh part of the fare at the fourth stage; however, if he abandons him halfway, he must be made to pay the entire fee, and the one who causes the abandonment shall be liable as well. M 198.
Thus ends the section on the non-payment of wages. 16.

When the journey has commenced, prior to reaching the royal highway, if the driver abandons his work, he shall be made to pay a seventh part of the wages; this is to be understood as applying when there is no obstacle to the departure and another driver can be obtained. However, if there is such an obstacle, it is stated that double the amount must be paid. But if he abandons the work after reaching the road, then he shall be made to pay a fourth part of the wages. If he abandons it halfway, however, he shall pay the full wages. The same applies if the owner, having hired a driver, causes him to abandon the task or does not have him drive. (Manu).
If one who has undertaken the work fails to perform it when the time for action has arrived, another person of similar conduct should be employed; he shall be made to pay double the wages.

Nārada says: Having hired carriers for goods by means of vehicles and draft animals, if one abandons them before reaching the destination, he shall be made to pay a fourth part of the wages; if he abandons them halfway, he shall pay the full amount. [800]
Vṛddha-Manu: If a merchant abandons a servant after having sold that merchandise on the road, then [the goods] must also be given to him;
he shall receive half of the wages.
If that merchandise is obstructed or stolen on the road,
he shall receive as much wages as corresponds to the distance he has traveled.
Nārada says: Having agreed upon a wage consisting of a sixth part of the produce, one may abandon a beast of burden on the road;
but if he does not pay the wage, he must provide it along with interest after having caused the work to be done.

The meaning is as follows: when one who has hired a beast of burden—such as a horse or an ox—for the purpose of transporting goods does not pay the wage, having promised it as a sixth part of the goods to be carried, and instead abandons him, then the owner must give that person the wage along with interest. Bṛhaspati says:
"If an employer does not pay the wages to a laborer after the work has been completed, he shall be compelled by the king to pay it, along with a proportional fine."
Kātyāyana says:

He who abandons a companion on the road when he is exhausted or afflicted by illness shall incur the first amercement; if he fails to provide protection for three days within a village, he shall incur the same.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"He who, having received payment, does not impart knowledge or a craft,
shall be made to pay the full amount as a fine by the king who knows the Dharma."
Nārada says: Having accepted the bride-price, a courtesan who does not wish to perform her service shall pay double;
likewise, the giver of the bride-price who does not wish to enjoy her service shall suffer the loss of that price.
Likewise, a man who enjoys a woman without paying the bride-price,
or who has intercourse with her out of order, striking her with blows, teeth, nails, and so forth, [is liable for punishment].
He who approaches a woman in a place other than the womb, or causes her to dwell with many men,
shall be made to pay eightfold the nuptial fee (śulka) and an equal amount as a fine.
Those courtesans who are preeminent therein, and the lovers who reside in their houses,
are known to provide a decision in cases of doubt regarding matters arising from them.

In the *Matsya Purāṇa*: "If a courtesan, having accepted her fee, goes elsewhere out of greed, the king shall compel her to pay that money; he shall also cause her to pay the hire even for one who has not yet had intercourse with her."
If one should lead a courtesan away from another for the sake of someone else,
his punishment from the king shall be one māṣaka of gold.
He who, having taken up work, does not provide the labor, shall be compelled to pay double wages;
he shall also pay a fine of double that amount to the king, so that the law is not violated.
[801] When many people go together to commit a single offense, they shall all pay double the fine individually to the king; furthermore, they shall each pay an additional double penalty.
According to the Smṛti: "One who is ill, one who is distressed by fatigue, one intent on royal duties,
or one who has been invited but does not come— such a woman is declared to be a barren mare (vaḍavā)."
Nārada says: He who, having built a house on another's land and provided a sacrificial fee (stoma), should dwell there,
must take with him when departing the grass, wood, bricks, and so forth belonging to that house.
Having clothed himself with the *stoma* and other [garments], yet not yet certain of the higher stage,
he must by no means take up grass or wood while departing.
Whatever grass, wood, or bricks have been placed there,
all that which is being removed shall be reported to the owner of the land.
The word *svāminī* is used in the locative case with the sense of the dative. *Stoma* means rent or wages. Vyāsa says:
"If one constructs a temple after obtaining a plot of ground out of affection, the timber belongs to him as he departs, provided that rent has been paid; it is not otherwise."
Kātyāyana states: He who, having taken a house, a cow-pen, a shop, or the like on lease,
does not return it to the owner, must be made to pay that rent for as long as he retains possession.
Vṛddhamanu:
He who, having hired a cart and taken it elsewhere, departs,
shall deliver the goods capable of being carried by the draught-animals when the full time has elapsed.
To the perceiver, it would appear as broken or destroyed, except in the case of its convergence with another.

Those earthen vessels which are brought for the purpose of obtaining other substances such as clarified butter or oil by means of a *stoma*—that is, a rental fee—are called *stomavāhīni*. When the period of the full rental has expired, one should return them to their owner. Among those, whatever is broken or destroyed through negligence shall belong to the one who took the *stoma*; the meaning is that it need not be paid for by the other. And this applies except in the case of a collision (*saṃplava*). In the event of a collision, however, the value of the broken or damaged vessel must be paid to the owner of the goods. A *saṃplava* is the striking against another substance. Thus ends the section on the non-payment of wages (Chapter 2, Verse 198).

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, on the Non-payment of Wages, in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, born of the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the line of the glorious Vidyādharas.
[802] Now begins the section on gambling and betting in the Yājñavalkya-smṛti with its commentary. (17)
Now, the legal title known as gambling and betting is introduced. Regarding this, Nārada says:

"Gambling (dyūta) consists of playing with dice, fists, sticks, and so forth, conducted with deceit; betting (samāhvaya) consists of games of chance with animals and the like. This is the legal title of gambling and betting."

*Akṣāḥ* are dice; *vadhraḥ* is the piercing of leather rings and the like; *śalākā* (sticks) are to be understood as belonging to gamblers. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), other items such as rags (*karpaṭaka*) and the like are included. *Devanam* means play or the desire for victory. *Jihmam* means crooked. That wealth which is taken from one who has been defeated is the *paṇa* (stake). *Vayāṃsi* are birds. Gambling (*dyūta*) is playing with inanimate objects such as dice, and with animate beings such as birds, by means of a crooked disposition. Manu says: "That which is performed with non-living things is called gambling (*dyūta*) in the world."
That which is carried out by means of living beings is to be known as *samāhvaya* (gambling).
Kākinyas, vadhrikās, aśalākās, bhauryas,
akṣas with seeds, and kuhakas— these are the six types of gaming equipment.
Bṛhaspati says: When birds, rams, bulls, and the like, having made a wager, fight while being held by one another, they call that *samāhvaya* (betting-fight). 2.198.
Regarding that, the text states what the increase is and from whom it should be taken by the master of the gambling hall:
"The master of the hall may take five percent from a gambler who stakes one hundred, but from another, he may take ten percent. (2.199)

He who, having established a gambling hall and prepared the implements for play, provides money at an interest rate to gamblers so they may gamble, is the *sabhika* (the master of the gaming house). He is a sharper than the fraudulent gambler, or a victorious gambler himself; he is the one who conducts the game. From that fraudulent gambler—referring to the one who has won the interest when the wager or stake consists of a hundred coins—one should take five percent (*pañcakaṃ śatam*) from that "hundred-interest" (*śatikavṛddhi*). As for the one who is defeated, the other [the *sabhika*] shall take ten percent (*daśakaṃ śatam*) from him. (2.199)
Having protected it properly, he should give the share to the king as prescribed by tradition;
he should cause the victor to take what was won and, being patient, should speak the truth to the winner.

The previously mentioned *sabhika* (master of the gaming house), properly protected by the king and well-guarded from gamblers, shall give a share from his own wealth according to what was agreed upon as heard from the king. He shall cause the won wealth to be collected or recovered from the defeated gambler. Likewise, being patient for the sake of inspiring confidence, he shall give the true word to the winner, saying, "At such a time, I will give you this much wealth. Kātyāyana says:
The *sabhika* shall conduct the gambling and shall pay to the king whatever is due;
and he may take a ten percent interest on the losses incurred.
The winner shall give his own wealth; the stake won shall be recovered from the gambler either after three fortnights or immediately by the keeper of the gambling house—of this there is no doubt.
Nārada says: The master of the gambling house shall conduct the game and shall pay whatever is owed therein;
his fee for conducting the gambling shall be ten percent of a hundred.
Alternatively, a gambler, having given the king his appropriate share, may engage in open gambling; in this way, no fault is found.

Alternatively, even in the absence of a master of the gaming house (*sabhika*), the gambler himself may conduct an open game after paying the king’s share. The singular number in the word "gambler" (*kitava*) is used with reference to the class as a whole. Bṛhaspati states: "If anyone should suffer a loss in a duel, the stake that was agreed upon therein must be paid by his owner."
This refers to the subject of a formal challenge. *Avasāda* means loss of strength. Nārada says:
"An impure gambler shall not resort to another gambling circle;
nor shall one obstruct a gambler who is paying his winnings according to his own will."
If a gambler wins his own wealth—which was not to be given away and was impure—the king shall not restrain him. (2.200)
When the share has been won in a well-known circle of gamblers, the king shall cause the winner to receive it in a place presided over by court officials; otherwise, he shall not do so.

Deceitful gamblers, in that gambling circle which includes the keeper of the hall, shall be made by the king to pay what has been won when the agreed-upon share has been received, provided it is well-known and according to the stipulated rules; otherwise, he shall not do so. Nārada says:
"But that man who engages in gambling without being authorized by the king shall not obtain his desired object [of winning], and he deserves punishment."

If one who has been appointed by the king as the master of the gaming hall (*sabhika*) should engage in gambling without being specifically authorized, he shall not receive the share due to the master of the hall, and he shall incur punishment. [804] Kātyāyana states:
One should compel the payment of what is owed in that place, and not otherwise;
for in that case, the victory belongs to the master of the hall, and the legal proceeding depends upon his authority.

One who is ignorant and defeated should be released; one who is knowledgeable and defeated should not be released. Even when all one's property has been won, if the opponent is knowledgeable, one should not compel him to surrender his entire wealth.

Bṛhaspati says: One who has lost in secret, one who is ignorant of the game, or one who uses false dice or deceit, must be released—even if he is knowledgeable; even if he has lost everything, he shall not be made to pay the entire stake. (2.201)
For they alone are the observers and witnesses of these transactions.
Indeed, those same gamblers are the observers, the adjudicators, and the witnesses of the transactions involving gamblers. Nārada says:
"Regarding matters of doubt, gamblers should remain among gamblers themselves."
They alone are the observers therein, and they alone are the witnesses for these.
Bṛhaspati, in his *Sabhikānuvṛtti*, states:
"In a doubtful case, that very person shall be the witness, provided he is approved by the members of the court and by three others.
Kātyāyana says:
In disputes over victory, gain, or the fraudulent gambling of cheats,
the keeper of the gaming house is the authority there, provided that the keeper of the gaming house is himself pure.
There is no certainty regarding Mlecchas, dog-cookers, rogues, gamblers, ascetics, or those who adopt the conduct established by them; however, there is certainty regarding the king.

The term *rājanīti* (the science of statecraft) is intended as an illustration for all the previously mentioned members of the court. Consequently, those members of the court described as "endowed with learning and study of the Vedas," and so forth, are not to be relied upon in disputes involving barbarians (*mleccha*) and the like. Bṛhaspati states:
"When there is doubt regarding both parties, gamblers are the investigators;
but when they are hostile, then the king himself should deliberate."
Those who play with fraudulent dice or by means of deception should be banished by the king, branded with a mark.

Viṣṇu states: "In gambling, those who play with fraudulent dice shall have their hands cut off; those who play with fraudulent devices shall have the joints of their fingers cut off. Fraud (*upadhi*) consists of mutual agreement for the sake of another's statement, such as the skillful manipulation of the hand or causing the dice to fall according to one's desire. "Cutting the joints" (*saṃdaṃśacchedaḥ*) means the cutting off of the thumb and finger. (2.202)
Gambling should be conducted with a single entrance for the purpose of identifying thieves.

"With a single entrance" means having one primary [entrance] and being supervised by a single royal official; it should be carried out for the sake of discovering thieves. As for that which was stated by Manu:
"He who engages in gambling or betting, or causes them to be done..."
"The king shall cause all of them to be executed, as well as Śūdras who assume the marks of the twice-born.
[805] And so forth; this refers to gambling that is not supervised by royal officers. Bṛhaspati states: "Gambling, which destroys grain, purity, and wealth, was forbidden by Manu."
But that which was established by others, however, is accompanied by the king's share.

The meaning is that [the game] should not be played if deprived of the king's share. This same rule is to be understood as applying to gambling with living creatures and to betting on animal fights. 2.203.
Thus ends the section on gambling and betting. 17.

This rule and method has been declared by me regarding gambling known as *samāhvaya*, which is to be understood as being accomplished with living creatures such as rams, buffaloes, and the like. Thus ends the section on Gambling and Betting (*dyūtasamāhvayaprakaraṇa*). 2.203.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, on Gambling and Betting, in the *Aparārka*— a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, born of the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the noble Vidyādhara race.
Now begins the section on verbal abuse (*vākpāruṣya*) in the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* with its commentary. Regarding its nature, Nārada says:
Speech that reviles others based on their country, birth, family, and so forth— known as "exposing vulnerabilities"— and speech whose meaning is disagreeable, is called verbal abuse (*vākpāruṣya*).

Screaming, reviling, and abuse constitute verbal assault (*vākpāruṣya*). Among these, *deśākṣepa* (abuse of place) is, for example: "The Gauḍas are fond of quarreling" directed against a Gauḍa. *Jātyākṣepa* (abuse of caste) is, for example: "Brahmins are excessively greedy" directed against a Brahmin. *Kulākṣepa* (abuse of family) is, for example: "The descendants of Viśvāmitra are of cruel conduct. *Nyaṅga* is indecorous speech. Kātyāyana says:
"To mimic or to repeat a 'hum' sound, a cough, or anything else that is censured in the world—that is called verbal assault."
Because of its harshness, vulgarity, and intensity, that [abusive speech] is also remembered as being threefold:
censure (*ākṣepa*) is to be known as the harsh, while the vulgar is designated as *nyaṅga*.

The wise say that verbal abuse involving offenses leading to expulsion is a grave matter; yet, when someone occasionally reviles another using limbs [of speech] designated as improper, it is even more severe.
Whether based on what is untrue or true, that speech which is harsh and uttered with malice,
or which, through verbal abuse, seeks to strike at another's vulnerabilities— that is indeed *svṛtā* (malicious speech).
[806] But that which is indecorous for those of good conduct, country, and family is considered by the wise to be a bond of great sin and a cause of enmity toward the king.
Furthermore, that intense speech which causes loss of caste is well known.
"Nyaṅgāvagūraṇa" is the act of insulting by exposing a person's inferior limbs. Bṛhaspati states:
"Harshness is recorded as being of two kinds: speaking unpleasantly and striking."
Each one, moreover, is divided into three types; thus, self-control (dama) is said to have three characteristics.

The disparagement of the laws of the land, the dharma, one's family, and so forth, as well as the incitement of others to sin— this, occurring first and without the use of physical force, is called verbal abuse (*vākpāruṣya*).
The verbal abuse of those related to one's sister or brother, as well as the proclamation of their secondary sins (upapātaka),
is declared by those learned in the scriptures to be "middling" verbal [abuse].
The discourse on forbidden foods and drinks, the defilement by mortal sins,
and the infliction of severe injury to vital organs are declared to be the highest forms of verbal abuse.

In the phrase "without substance" (*dravyaṃ vinā*), the word *dravya* refers to the object denoted. Thus, the meaning is that verbal abuse consists in such a designation that is distinct from the actual object being described.
Regarding the specific punishments for particular types of verbal abuse, he says:
"For those with deficient limbs or senses, or who are diseased, [one who uses] true, false, or otherwise distorted praises..."
If he causes delay, he shall be fined twelve and a half paṇas. || 2.204 ||

The *aṅgas* are the organs of action (*karmendriyas*), such as the tongue and so forth; the *indriyas*, moreover, are the organs of cognition (*jñānendriyas*), such as the ear and so forth. "Diseases" refers to leprosy and the like. He who—whether by truth, by falsehood, or by perverse praise—insults those whose limbs or organs are deficient, or those who suffer from diseases, shall be fined twelve and a half *paṇas*. In this regard, an insult regarding the deficiency of a limb by truth is, for example, saying "You are lame" to one who lacks a foot. By falsehood, for example, saying "You are deformed" to one with all his limbs intact, or "You are complete in limb" to one who is deformed. By perverse praise, for example, saying "You have beautiful arms" or "You have great arms" to one who lacks a hand. The same applies to insults regarding the deficiency of an organ. "Twelve and a half *paṇas*" means those *paṇas* of which the thirteenth is a half. As for that which was stated by Manu:
Whether one is one-eyed, lame, or otherwise similarly deformed,
even if speaking the truth, one shall be made to pay a fine of at least one kārṣāpaṇa.

Therefore, this should be accepted when the accuser possesses extreme excellence or when the fault in his disposition is very slight. Bṛhaspati states: "In cases of verbal abuse between persons of equal caste and qualities, the punishment prescribed in the treatise is a fine of twelve and a half paṇas. [807]

Viṣṇu: "In the case of insulting someone of equal caste, one shall be fined twelve *paṇas*; but for insulting someone of a lower caste, six. For an insult involving a false accusation regarding the highest caste at an appropriate time, the fine shall be of that same measure, or three *kārṣāpaṇas*. The same applies to uttering false words regarding a toll (*śulka*). This refers to cases involving those of little wealth. For members of the twice-born of equal caste, the fine is exactly twelve [paṇas] in the event of a transgression;
in disputes where speech is improper, that same fine shall be doubled.

The mention of "equal caste" (*samavarṇa*) is for the purpose of establishing equality between the accuser and the accused in terms of both birth (*jāti*) and qualities (*guṇa*). Therefore, when there is equality in all respects, the fine for verbal abuse (*vākpāruṣya*) consisting of an offense is twelve *paṇas*. When there is equality in birth alone, if one of inferior quality insults one of superior quality, the fine is double. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "In the case of an offense against one of equal caste, the fine is twelve *kārṣāpaṇas*. For insulting one who is distinguished by his appearance while being undistinguished oneself, the fine is twenty-four; and likewise, for one who is distinguished insulting one who is undistinguished, the amount is the same. (2.204)
The punishment for the first degree of verbal abuse has been stated; now he declares the punishment for the middle degree of verbal abuse:
"If one swears, 'I shall violate your sister or your mother,' the king shall compel him to pay a fine of twenty-five [paṇas]. (2.205)

The king shall cause a fine of twenty-five *paṇas* to be imposed on one who insults another by saying, "I shall approach your sister as if she were your mother. Regarding verbal abuse, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "For one who reviles authorized Brahmins or gurus, the punishment is shaving the head, smearing with cow dung, mounting a donkey, or a fine that strips away pride (*darpahāra*). Viṣṇu, continuing from the term "fine," states: "One who insults [them], such as a sister and so forth, shall pay a fine of fifty *paṇas*. This refers to cases involving those of small means. (2.205)

The punishment for verbal abuse among those of equal caste has been stated for both the first and middle degrees. Now he states the distinction based on the presence or absence of qualities that make one subject to punishment:
"Half [the fine] in the case of inferior persons, double in the case of the wives of others and of superior persons."

When those possessed of qualities such as learning and religious practice revile others who are inferior and possess inferior qualities, the punishment for the one so addressed shall be only half. In that regard, for the first degree of verbal abuse, the fine is six *paṇas*, and a fourth part of a *paṇa* is to be paid as a penalty; however, for the middle degree, it is twelve and a half. But he who reviles another’s wife, or one who is himself of low character yet addresses a woman of superior character, the aforementioned fine is doubled. In that case, for the first degree of verbal abuse, it is twenty-five. Bṛhaspati says: "The fine is equal for equals; for one who is inferior, it is double."
In the case of mutual verbal abuse, it is declared that the fine for the superior person shall be half [of that prescribed].
Now, he states that the king must determine the punishment when members of the various castes, such as Brahmins and others, or twice-born Mūrdhāvasiktas, engage in mutual verbal abuse:
"The infliction of punishment must be carried out according to the higher or lower status of the castes and birth-classes. (2.206)

When an insult is committed by those of higher castes against those of lower castes, or by those of lower castes against others, the king, having himself deliberated upon it, shall determine the infliction of punishment. In this regard, the *mūrdhāvasikta*, the *ambaṣṭha*, and so forth—those born in the direct order (*anuloma*)—possess a caste equal to that of their mothers; consequently, they are subject to punishment just like *kṣatriyas* and the other [higher-caste] classes. (2.206)
Now he states the specific fines for insults involving the inverse order of castes:
"In cases of insult involving the inverse order of castes, the fines are double and triple; in the direct order of castes, they decrease by half and half again from that. (2.207)

When a lower caste reviles a higher caste, it is an *apavāda* (insult) in the inverse order (*pratiloma*). In that case, for one who reviles the caste immediately following [one's own], the fine shall be double the previously mentioned amount of fifty, namely a fine of one hundred. However, in the case of an insult across an intervening caste, the fine shall be triple that same amount, making it one hundred and fifty. Consequently, for a Kṣatriya insulting a Brāhmaṇa, or a Vaiśya insulting a Kṣatriya, the fine is one hundred; for a Vaiśya insulting a Brāhmaṇa, it is one hundred and fifty; for a Śūdra insulting a Vaiśya, it is one hundred; and for insulting a Kṣatriya, it is one hundred and fifty. As for insulting a Brāhmaṇa, other Smṛti texts providing different punishments will be cited later. When a higher caste insults a lower caste, it is an *apavāda* in the direct order (*anuloma*). In that regard, the punishment for a Kṣatriya insulting a Brāhmaṇa has been stated to consist of one hundred *paṇas*. For insulting a Kṣatriya, the Brāhmaṇa’s fine is half of that, fifty *paṇas*. For insulting a Vaiśya, it is twenty-five *paṇas*; for insulting a Śūdra, it is twelve and a half *paṇas*. And regarding this interpretation:
A Brahmin shall be fined fifty [paṇas] for defaming a Kṣatriya;
for a Vaiśya, the fine is forty-five; and for a Śūdra, the punishment is twelve.

This statement of Manu is the source. Likewise, a Kṣatriya reviling a Vaiśya shall be fined fifty; but for reviling a Śūdra, twenty-five. For a Vaiśya reviling a Śūdra, it is likewise fifty. Regarding a Śūdra reviling a Brāhmaṇa, Manu says:
"A Kṣatriya, having reviled a Brāhmaṇa, deserves a fine of one hundred;
a Vaiśya, one hundred less half (fifty) or two hundred; but a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment. [809]
In this context, "killing" means the cutting off of the tongue. As that same author says:
"If one of low birth should revile a twice-born person with harsh words, he shall suffer the cutting off of his tongue, for he is of inferior origin."
For one who maliciously utters the names or the caste of others,
a glowing iron spike ten fingers long shall be thrust into his mouth.
This is the result of extreme habitual practice:
for one who, out of pride, imparts instruction on dharma to the twice-born,
the king shall cause heated oil to be poured into his mouth and his ears.
"Of this [it is said]" refers to the Śūdra. Bṛhaspati says:
"A Śūdra who slanders a Vaiśya should be made to pay the first amercement;
for a Kṣatriya, the middle amercement; and for a Brāhmaṇa, the highest fine."
One who gives false instruction on the Dharma, one who cites the Vedas for improper purposes, and one who reviles Brahmins deserve the cutting off of their tongues.

Gautama: "If a Śūdra, having maliciously intended against a twice-born man and having struck him with verbal or physical abuse, should not have a limb severed, then his ears shall be filled with molten tin and lac while he listens to the Veda; for reciting it, his tongue shall be cut out; for retaining it, his body shall be torn asunder. Viṣṇu: "One who speaks falsely regarding what has been heard, or regarding country, caste, or deeds, shall be fined one hundred kārṣāpaṇas. Nārada: "One should not defame with false accusations a person who has been purified according to the scriptures. Nor should one defame a king who has already imposed a punishment, for by doing so one becomes liable to that same punishment. (2.207)
In the case of injury to the arms, neck, eyes, or thighs, the punishment shall be verbal;
for the feet, nose, ears, hands, and so forth, it shall be half of that. (2.208)

For one who performs an act of destruction against the arms or other limbs without verbal provocation—such as saying, "I shall cut off your arms"—a fine of one hundred *paṇas* should be imposed. For one who inflicts a verbal injury to the feet, nose, or other such parts, a fine of fifty *paṇas* (half of a hundred) should be levied. (2.208)
He states the specific application of what was stated in general terms:
"But one who is incapable, if he speaks thus, shall be punished with a fine of ten paṇas;
likewise, one who is capable shall be made to provide a surety for his security. (2.209)

If he is capable of cutting off the arms or other limbs [of the offender], and should say so, then, having taken the aforementioned fine, he shall be made to provide a surety for the safety and protection of the person who has been thrown down. But if he is incapable of cutting off the arms or other limbs, he shall be made to pay only ten *paṇas*. (2.209)
For an accusation made regarding an offense involving loss of caste (pātitya), the punishment is the middle amercement;
but for one associated with a minor offense (upapātaka), he shall be made to pay the first amercement. (2.210)

When an accusation is made using grounds for loss of caste (*patanīya*), such as the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) and so forth—saying, "You are a killer of a Brahmin"—the middle amercement (*madhyama-sāhasa*) shall be the punishment. One who accuses another by means of causes for minor offenses (*upapātaka*), such as the killing of a cow and so forth, shall be made to pay the first amercement (*prathama-sāhasa*). Vyāsa states:
"Those who speak of minor or secondary sins, and those who proclaim a great sin (*mahāpātaka*), shall pay the first, middle, and highest fines respectively."

Whatever is not specified among the group of minor offenses (*upapātaka*) in the scriptures, yet is prohibited, is designated here by the term "sin" (*pāpa*). Viṣṇu states: "If an accusation regarding a cause for loss of caste (*patanīya*) is made against another, the highest fine (*uttamasāhasa*) is prescribed; if it concerns a minor offense (*upapātaka*), the middle fine (*madhyama*) is prescribed. This refers to the case of making an accusation against someone of a higher caste. (2.210)

The fine for insulting those learned in the three Vedas, a king, or a deity is the highest amercement; that for insulting a caste or a guild is the middle amercement; and that for insulting a village or a district is the lowest amercement. (2.211)
Thus ends the section on verbal abuse. 18.

For one who insults a reciter of the Ṛg, Yajur, or Sāma Vedas, or a king, or Brāhmaṇas and other deities, the punishment of the highest amercement (uttama-sāhasa) shall be imposed. For one who insults groups of learned men belonging to the Brāhmaṇa and other castes, such as assemblies (pariṣad) and others who perform a single common task like the adjudication of legal disputes, the punishment is the middle amercement (madhyama-sāhasa). For one who insults a village or a district, the punishment is the first amercement (prathama-sāhasa). Viṣṇu states: "The first [amercement] for those learned in the three Vedas, for groups of castes, and for villages and districts. This refers to cases involving minor intentions or faults. Bṛhaspati says:
One who defames another regarding their country or other such matters shall be made to pay thirteen and a half paṇas;
one who, out of arrogance, falsely accuses another of a crime shall be made to pay the first amercement.
Uśanas says: If one says, "I spoke thus out of delusion, negligence, excitement, or affection," and declares,
"I shall not speak so again," the judge should impose half of the prescribed punishment upon him.
Bṛhaspati said:
This punishment has been fully declared by me with reference to the individual;
it should be determined by the wise according to whether the offense is equal, less, or greater.
Thus ends the section on verbal abuse (vākpāruṣya). 2.211.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, on Verbal Abuse, in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, born of the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the family of the glorious Vidyādharas.
[811] Now begins the section on assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*) in the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* with its commentary. (19)

Now follows the rule regarding punishment for assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*). Assault is defined as causing pain to another person by striking their body, by defiling it with impure substances, or by threatening to strike them. Regarding this, Nārada says: "Inflicting injury upon the limbs of another with hands, feet, weapons, and so forth—therefore, when harm is caused by these means, it is called assault."
Likewise, for him as well, three types [of results] are observed according to the sequence of inferior, middling, and superior:
through threats, through the sight of blood from a wound inflicted without attachment, and through the sight of blood from a wound.
But by transcending the distinctions of the low, middle, and high castes.
Bṛhaspati says:
Assault with violence is said to consist of striking with hands, stones, or clubs; with ashes, mud, or dust; or with weapons and missiles.
Regarding that, he first states the grounds for determination when there is doubt as to whether an offense has occurred or not:

"In a case where [the perpetrator] has been killed without witnesses, the legal proceeding must be investigated by means of physical marks, logical reasoning, and tradition—except in the case of one who has fabricated false marks. (2.212)

When someone reports to the king in a place where there are no witnesses, saying, "I have been struck by this man," the king and his court officials—having avoided false marks produced by hatred or other motives—must investigate and decide this dispute by means of other marks, logical reasoning (*yukti*), authoritative testimony (*āgama*), and, according to the word "and" (*ca*), by ordeals (*divya*). [They must determine: "This litigant is the victim; this one is the wrongdoer. A "mark" (*cihna*) refers to wounds and the like. "Logical reasoning" refers to such factors as the proximity of the killer and the victim, and the possibility of a cause for hatred. "Authoritative testimony" (*āgama*) refers to the words of a reliable person. Some read: "out of fear of forged marks" (*kūṭacihnakṛtād bhayāt*). Its meaning is: a decision should not be made merely by seeing a wound or similar mark without further investigation; for, under the influence of malice and the like, it is possible to create even a forged or artificial mark. (Nārada).
Someone, having marked themselves for destruction, might attack another out of malice;
in such a case, an investigation is appropriate by means of logical arguments, reasons, and the consistency of the facts.

*Yukti* is circumstantial implication (*arthāpatti*). *Hetu* is inference (*anumāna*). *Artha* is the purpose (*prayojana*). *Saṃbandha* is acquisition (*prāpti*), which is to say proximity (*saṃnidhi*), or it refers to a prior quarrel. Kātyāyana states: "If one does not perceive the cause of physical assault through reasons and the like, one should employ witnesses or divine ordeal (*divya*) in that case. [812]
"Realized" means made to stand as a witness. Nārada says:
"When there is verbal or physical abuse arising from a relationship between two agitated parties, he who endures it is honored; he who retaliates becomes liable for punishment."
If no distinction were seen between those two who are both shrouded by the fault of harshness and engaged simultaneously, then discipline would apply equally to both.
Bṛhaspati:
When two strike each other, the punishment is declared to be equal for both;
however, the initiator and the one who persists in the attack shall be made to pay a heavier fine.
Nārada says: He who, however, persists in a dispute between two parties who have fallen into equal distress,
incurs the punishment for both of them, whether he was the first or the latter.
He who first utters an accusation will certainly be the one to bear the fault;
he who does so later is likewise a wrongdoer, yet in the former case, the disciplinary penalty is more severe.
Kātyāyana says: "That man who strikes with a terrifying weapon,
whether he himself was previously unharmed or not, is declared to be liable for punishment."
Bṛhaspati:
A man who, having been previously insulted, returns the insult; or, having been struck, strikes back;
or, having slain an assassin—none of these becomes guilty of an offense.
If a base person should insult a virtuous man through verbal abuse and the like,
the king need not seek out the one who strikes him in retaliation.

The meaning is that if a virtuous person, having been insulted by a base individual through verbal abuse and the like, should strike that base person in return, he is not to be punished by the king. Nārada says:

"In the case of dog-cookers, eunuchs, Caṇḍālas, prostitutes, those who live by killing, elephant-keepers, those born of outcast marriages, and those who have transgressed against their gurus and teachers..."
If there is a transgression of the established rule, one should immediately inflict corporal punishment;
and the wise say that no fault lies in such severity of punishment.
For if these people among men should transgress against one who is virtuous, that very person should practice discipline; he should not be a partaker in their lack of discipline.
"For these are indeed the stains of men; their stain consists of wealth.
Therefore, the king should have them executed, but he should not punish them with a fine.
— Kātyāyana.
For untouchables, rogues, slaves, barbarians, evildoers, and those born of inverse unions, corporal punishment is not a fine in terms of its purpose. (2.212)
A fine of ten paṇas is prescribed for touching [another] with ashes, mud, or dust;
for touching [another] with impure matter, the heel, or spittle, the fine is double that amount.
In the case of other men's wives who are of equal status, the fine is the same; for those of superior status, it is double;
for those of inferior status, half the fine is prescribed; however, there is no punishment for acts committed through intoxication and the like.

For one who joins another person of equal birth or equal qualities with ashes, mud, or dust, the fine is ten *paṇas*. If, however, he joins them with impure substances such as excrement and the like, then the fine is twenty *paṇas*. In this context, if one commits the aforementioned offense against a mere woman belonging to another, or against men superior in birth or qualities, then a fine double the previously stated amount should be imposed, which would be twenty *paṇas*. In cases involving those inferior in birth or qualities, one should be fined half of what was stated. There is no punishment for one whose consciousness is lost due to intoxication and the like, because there is an absence of culpability. "Impure" (*amedhya*) refers to bodily waste consisting of fat, semen, and so forth. "Pārṣṇi" is the back part of the foot. "Niṣṭyūta" means spat out (saliva). — Bṛhaspati.
Throwing ashes and the like, as well as striking with the hand or other means, constitutes the first degree of assault; in this case, a fine of one *māṣa* shall be imposed.
This punishment has been declared for equal [women] and for the wives of others;
it should be understood by the wise as being double or triple, according to the relative superiority or inferiority of status.
The meaning is that the fine is double for the wives of others and triple for those of high status. Here, the *māṣa* is one of silver. Kātyāyana states:
"If [the semen] is discharged by means of vomit, urine, feces, and so forth, the fine shall be fourfold;
it shall be sixfold if it enters the middle of the body, and it is recorded as eightfold if it reaches the head. (2.213, 214)
Furthermore:
"But for one who is not a Brahmin, that limb which causes pain to a Brahmin shall be cut off;
if he merely raised his hand, the first amercement is the punishment, but if there was actual contact, it is half of that. (2.215)

The king shall cut off the hand, foot, or other limb of a Kṣatriya or others that has been used as an instrument for striking a Brahmin. For one who raises a weapon, a staff, or the like for the purpose of striking a Brahmin, the punishment is the first *sāhasa* fine. For one who touches a weapon or the like for the purpose of raising it, the punishment is half of the first *sāhasa*. This punishment applies to the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya; however, regarding a Śūdra, Manu has said: "Whatever limb of a low-caste person (*antyaja*) may injure a superior, that very limb of his shall be cut off—this is the instruction of Manu. (MDh 8.267)
And here, by the statement "one who is superior," even a limb of a Śūdra that causes pain to a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya may be amputated. Likewise:
"Raising his hand or a staff, he deserves the amputation of a hand;
striking with his foot out of anger, he deserves the amputation of a foot."
Regarding a Śūdra who spits or performs other such acts upon a twice-born man, that same author states another punishment:
"The king shall cause the two lips of one who spits out of arrogance to be cut off;
[he shall cut off] the penis of one who urinates [upon him], and the anus of one who passes wind [upon him]."
Likewise:
A person of lower birth who seeks to sit on the same seat as one of higher rank shall be branded on the hip and banished,
or else his buttocks shall be cut off.
If someone seizes him by the hair, he should cut off both hands without hesitation;
likewise for seizing him by the feet, the beard, the neck, or the testicles.
“Dāḍhikāyām” means on the beard; “vṛṣaṇeṣu” means on the testicles and so forth—the sense being that it is not otherwise possible for the plural number to be justified. (2.215)
If a hand or foot is raised [in a threatening manner], the fines shall be ten and twenty [paṇas] respectively;
but for all [offenses] involving a weapon against one another, the middle amercement applies.

When the hand is raised for the purpose of inflicting injury on another, the fine is ten *paṇas*. If it is the foot, the fine is twenty *paṇas*. If it is a weapon, it is the middle amercement (*madhyama-sāhasa*). This applies to the mere raising [of the limb] and not to the actual striking, because a different punishment is prescribed for the latter. Because of the expression "mutually" (*parasparam*), this refers to cases involving persons of the same caste; for a different punishment is prescribed for one of lower caste raising a limb against one of higher caste. Bṛhaspati says: "In the case of two agitated parties brandishing weapons, the middle amercement should be applied.
But when a blow has actually landed, the wise should impose a fine proportionate to the injury inflicted."
For striking with bricks, stones, or wood, the fine shall be two māṣas;
for drawing blood, the punishment prescribed by the wise shall be double that amount.
Furthermore:
For pulling at the feet, hair, or garment, or for seizing them by the hand, the fine shall be ten paṇas;
for causing pain, dragging, wrapping with a garment, or stepping upon [the feet], the punishment shall be one hundred [paṇas]. (2.217)

For pulling or dragging the hair, the garment, or the clothes of another man’s feet, or for pulling or dragging his hands—provided they are of the same caste—one shall be fined ten *paṇas*. For performing these acts together with *pīḍā* and the rest, the fine is five hundred *paṇas*. *Pīḍā* means squeezing; *ākrośa* means shouting; *ākarṣaṇa* means dragging; *aṃśukāveṣṭa* means binding with a cloth around the neck and so forth; and *pādādhyāsa* means placing the foot upon the head and so forth. (2.217)
Furthermore: A man who inflicts pain with wood or other materials without shedding blood—
He shall be made to pay thirty-two paṇas, and double that amount if he shows his blood. (2.218)
One who causes pain to another person of the same caste with wood or other implements, even without drawing blood, shall be made to pay thirty *paṇas*; but if blood is drawn, sixty-four. Manu says:
"The piercer of the skin shall be fined one hundred; the drawer of blood likewise;
the breaker of the flesh shall be fined six *niṣkas*, but the breaker of bone shall be banished."
When there is an excess of binding, the fine for one who causes blood to flow is one hundred [paṇas]; otherwise, it is sixty-four. Bṛhaspati states:
"For piercing the skin, the first amercement; for piercing the flesh, the middle; for piercing the bone, the highest; but for killing by striking, the death penalty."
This punishment applies to Kṣatriyas and others, but not to a Brāhmaṇa, because it is improper to put him to death. || 2.218 ||
In the case of breaking a hand, foot, or tooth; cutting off the ears or the nose;
piercing a wound; or likewise killing one who is as good as dead, the middle amercement is the punishment. (2.219)

For the severing or crushing of each of the hands, feet, or teeth; for the cutting off of an ear or a nose; for the reopening of a healed wound or its re-injury; and likewise, when a blow is struck such that the victim becomes nearly dead, motionless, as if dead—such an assault merits the middle amercement. Furthermore, in these cases, the adjustment of the penalty for equalizing an inequality must be determined according to the relative gravity of the consequences and other factors. "In the case of cutting off the ears, lips, nose, feet, eyes, tongue, penis, or hand, the highest amercement is prescribed; for piercing them, the middle amercement is heavy."
Viṣṇu: "The king shall not release from bondage for as long as he lives one who pierces both eyes; or he shall inflict exactly such [a punishment] upon him. (2.219)
Furthermore:
In cases of obstructing movement, food, or speech; piercing the eyes or other [sensitive parts];
or breaking the neck, arms, thighs, or feet, there is middle-level punishment (madhyama-sāhasa). (2.220)

"Movement" refers to going and coming, the voiding of urine and excrement, and so forth; "eating" refers to the act of consuming food; "speech" refers to verbal expression. If there is obstruction or restraint of any of these, or if there is the piercing of the seats of the organs of perception—such as the eyes—which results in the destruction of their functional capacity, or if there is a fracture of the neck, the many thighs, the hips, or the feet, the punishment shall be precisely the middle amercement (*madhyama-sāhasa*). This preceding statement and this present one prescribe the punishment for one who is not a Brāhmaṇa but belongs to an equal caste committing such an offense. Viṣṇu states: "In the case of obstructing movement, eating, or speech, or in striking [another], or in fracturing the eyes, neck, arms, or thighs, the highest [punishment] applies. "Highest" means the highest amercement (*uttama-sāhasa*); the word "punishment" is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence. Here, the jurisdiction of the middle and highest amercements is established respectively for a Kṣatriya offending against a Vaiśya, and for a Vaiśya offending against a Kṣatriya. Alternatively, the rule for the middle amercement applies to a Śūdra for an offense against one of his own caste, while the highest amercement applies to a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya for an offense against one of their own respective castes. (2.220)
Furthermore:
"For those who strike many people, the fine shall be double that which has been stated. Likewise, what was taken away during a quarrel must be restored, and the fine shall be double. (2.221)

Furthermore, when many persons become the assailants of one individual—inflicting physical violence, or applying ashes, mud, or dust—then for each of them, a fine double that which has been prescribed for that offense must be imposed. And while a quarrel is taking place, whoever has seized anything from another must restore it to him and then pay twice its value to the king. Viṣṇu states: "For many who strike one person, the fine for each is double that which is prescribed for the individual; the same applies to those standing nearby who do not run to the aid of one crying out. Kātyāyana says:

Those against whom verbal censure or physical beating has been prescribed for their offenses shall be made to restore what was stolen or broken; however, those who possess no wealth shall purify themselves through labor. 2.221
But he who causes pain involving the expenditure of effort and wealth shall be made to pay that fine which has been prescribed for that particular quarrel. (2.222)

He who causes pain to another by striking with a weapon or similar means shall pay the expenses incurred for the healing of wounds and other such matters; and he shall also pay to the king the fine prescribed for that specific instance of physical assault in the context of a quarrel. Bṛhaspati states: "In cases of breaking a limb, causing pain, or likewise cutting it off, the offender shall be made to pay the expenses for recovery and whatever was seized during the quarrel."

Kātyāyana says: But when the body or the sense organs are destroyed, the wise should inflict a punishment such that it provides satisfaction and ensures the restoration of the person to his former state.
He shall also provide for the expenses of treatment until the wound is healed. [817] Manu says:
A wife, a son, a slave, a pupil, and a uterine brother—
Those who have committed an offense should be beaten with a rope or a split bamboo cane.
But one must strike on the back of the body and never on the head;
for striking otherwise than this, one incurs the guilt of a thief.
"Offense" refers to punishment. Regarding the topic of the religious student (*brahmacārin*), Nārada states:
"If he does not comply with the instructions of his teachers, he should be disciplined without [physical] violence, or else he may be struck with a rope or a split bamboo cane."
One should not strike him excessively, nor on the head, nor on the chest;
having instructed him and inspired confidence, he should be disciplined by the king, otherwise like a teacher.
A father does not incur punishment for the offense of his son, nor does a dog-owner for that of his dog,
nor a monkey-owner for that of his monkey, provided he did not strike with that very [weapon] himself.
By non-injury, that is, by non-violence. || 2.222 ||
In cases of striking, cutting, piercing, or causing a wall to collapse,
one shall be made to pay five, ten, or twenty paṇas, as well as the cost of repair.

One who steals from a wall shall be made to pay five paṇas; one who cuts it, ten; one who breaks it, twenty; but one who causes it to fall shall be made to pay the cost of repairing the wall to the owner. (2.223)

One who throws into a house property that causes suffering, or likewise something life-threatening, shall be made to pay sixteen paṇas for the first offense, and the middle amercement for the second. (2.224)

He who throws a scorpion or similar creature that causes pain into another's house shall be made to pay a fine of sixteen paṇas; but he who throws a snake or similar creature that takes life shall be made to pay the middle amercement. (2.224)
In the case of causing pain, drawing blood, or likewise cutting off a branch or a limb, the fine for small animals shall start from two paṇas and increase progressively. (2.225)
In the case of cutting off the male organ or death, the middle amercement and the price [of the organ] itself [must be paid].

Regarding small animals such as goats and the like, when pain is inflicted, blood is shed, a horn or a limb (such as a foot) is severed, or a member is cut off, the fine shall be two *paṇas* and so forth, respectively. Each subsequent penalty is double the preceding one. Among these, for causing pain, the fine is two *paṇas*; for shedding blood, four *paṇas*; for cutting a horn, eight *paṇas*; and for severing a limb, sixteen *paṇas*. For the cutting of the genitals (*liṅga*)—that is, the male organ—or the crushing of the testicles of these same animals, the middle amercement (*madhyama-sāhasa*) applies. However, if death is caused, he shall pay the value of the animal to its owner and the middle amercement to the king. (2.225)
In these cases involving large cattle, the fine shall be double. || 2.226 ||

Those causes for punishment mentioned in connection with small livestock, when they apply to large livestock such as cows and the like, should be understood to carry double the fine. While the rule "one should be fined one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*" is being followed, Viṣṇu states: "One who destroys the virility of animals, as well as one who kills a horse, a camel, or a cow, shall have one foot amputated. One who sells meat that is not [properly] slaughtered, and one who kills village livestock, shall be fined one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*. He shall also pay the value of that [animal] to the owner of the livestock. One who kills wild livestock shall be fined five hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*. One who kills birds or fish shall be fined ten *kārṣāpaṇas*. One who destroys insects shall be fined one *kārṣāpaṇa*. Manu says:
One who drives away young cows, sacred animals, bulls, or oxen, shall first incur a fine of one thousand paṇas; for killing them, he shall incur the highest penalty.

Kātyāyana says: A man who yokes animals such as donkeys, cows, buffaloes, or camels when they are exhausted, afflicted by thirst, or hungry, or at an improper time, shall incur the first amercement. (2.226)

For the cutting of branches, trunks, or the entire body of trees that are growing and spreading, as well as for trees that provide livelihood, the fines shall be double those prescribed for twenty [smaller trees]. (2.227)

For cutting branches, trunks, or entire trees—namely, growing trees such as the *nyagrodha* and other useful trees such as the *ṭaṅkāmraka*—there are three penalties respectively: for cutting a branch, twenty [paṇas]; for a trunk, double that, forty; and for an entire tree, double again, eighty. In this context, "growing" refers to the *nyagrodha*; a "trunk" (*skandha*) is the root of the main branch. (2.227)
In the vicinity of a shrine, a cemetery, a boundary, a sacred site, or a temple, the fines for trees that have grown there are doubled; the same applies to a tree of renown.

In the case of trees growing at sacred sites (*caitya*) and the like—referring to those renowned trees whose branches and trunks are completely cut down—the previously mentioned twenty and other units of punishment (*dama*) should be understood as being doubled. A *caitya* is a place that is captivating to the mind. (2.228)

For the cutting of shrubs, clusters, bushes, creepers, spreading plants, medicinal herbs, and climbing vines in the places previously mentioned, the fine shall be half of that prescribed for trees. 2.229.

[819] Shrubs (*gulma*) such as the *kuruvaka* and others, which arise from the soil, are smaller in size than trees. Smaller still are clusters (*guccha*). Even shorter than those are shrubs (*kṣupa*). Creepers (*latā*) and vines (*vallī*) are the same; when they are thick, they are called spreading creepers (*pratāna*). Grasses (*oṣadhi*) such as rice and barley, which perish at the ripening of their fruit, are distinct. Creepers (*vīrudh*) are those that grow from seeds or from cuttings. For these, one should take half of the previously mentioned fines in accordance with the previously mentioned grounds for punishment. As Manu says: "In proportion as the utility of all forest-trees..."
In whatever way injury occurs, discipline must be applied accordingly; such is the settled rule.

Viṣṇu: "One who cuts down a tree that provides fruit for enjoyment shall be punished with the highest amercement; one who cuts down one providing flowers, with the middle amercement; one who cuts down a creeper, shrub, or climbing vine, with one hundred kārṣāpaṇas; and one who cuts down grass, with one [kārṣāpaṇa]. Furthermore, for all these cases, the owner of the trees shall receive compensation for their loss and a fine for the violence. (2.229)

Thus ends the twelfth section, on Assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*), in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, who was born in the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the glorious Vidyādhara race.
Now begins the section on Violence (*sāhasa-prakaraṇa*) in the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* with its commentary. Regarding violence, he says:

The forcible seizure of common property is recorded as *sāhasa* (violence). The forcible seizure—that is, the taking by force and by means of an act of will (*haṭha*) while disregarding them—of the property belonging to several persons, such as brothers and others, in the presence of the owners, is *sāhasa*. And this is not the definition of *sāhasa*, but rather an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). Nārada, however, states its true definition: "Whatever action is performed through violence by those arrogant because of their power is *sāhasa*."
That is called *sāhasa* (rashness); here, *saha* is said to mean strength (*bala*).
Killing a human being, theft, violating another's wife,
and the two kinds of verbal and physical cruelty— these are recorded as the five types of *sāhasa* (heinous acts).
Malice, the use of poison, weapons, and the like; violating another's wife;
and whatever else obstructs life—these are declared to be the highest amercement (uttama-sāhasa).
The destruction of domestic animals, vehicles, and household utensils—
by this very same method, the middle amercement is prescribed.
Bṛhaspati says:
That [fine] is proclaimed to be of three kinds—low, middling, and high.
In this context, the fine depends on the nature of the object, whether it be low, middling, or high.
Regarding the theft of property belonging to the Madhyamaka, he states the punishment:
"The fine shall be double its value; however, if there is denial, it shall be fourfold. (2.230)

The punishment for the thief shall be double the value of the stolen property. However, if he denies the theft—that is, makes a false claim—then it shall be four times that value. Bṛhaspati states: "One who destroys or steals the implements of a field, an irrigation channel, or roots, flowers, and fruits, shall be fined one hundred [paṇas] according to the gravity of the offense."
One who steals livestock, clothing, food, drink,
or household utensils should be made to pay a fine of two hundred panas, as well as a penalty for violence, like a thief.
For women, men, gold, gems, as well as the property of gods or Brahmins,
and for silk or other excellent articles, the fine shall be equal to their value.
Or rather, kings should impose double the fine in consideration of the person;
or the killer should be executed in order to prevent a recurrence of such incidents.
Nārada says:
The punishment for the first [offense] depends on the nature of the act and shall not be less than one hundred;
however, for the middle [offense], it is observed by those learned in the scriptures to be no less than five hundred.
In the case of the highest degree of violence, a fine of at least one thousand [paṇas] is prescribed;
[the punishments may include] death, confiscation of all property, banishment from the city, and branding.
In the case of the highest violence (uttama-sāhasa), the punishment is declared to be the amputation of a limb;
however, the two preceding punishments, when duly inflicted, render the offenders fit for social intercourse.
Even one who has been punished with a fine of clarified butter is to be known as unapproachable for conversation in the case of the highest violence.
Manu:
"He who damages the goods of another, whether intentionally or unintentionally,
shall restore their satisfaction and pay an equivalent amount to the king."
For leather goods, leather articles, and items made of wood or clay,
as well as for flowers, roots, and fruits, the fine shall be five times their value.
Kātyāyana says: A man who causes injury, breaking, or crushing to goods shall incur the first amercement; the owner is declared to be the one who possesses the value of the goods. 2.230.
He who causes a rash act to be committed shall be made to pay double the fine;
and he who, having said "I will give," causes it to be done, shall pay four times the amount. [2.231]

The punishment prescribed for the perpetrator of a violent act (*sāhasa*) shall be doubled for one who instigates it. However, for one who causes such an act to be committed by saying, "If you commit this violent act against my property, I will give you the wealth," the punishment is fourfold. Kātyāyana states: "The initiator, the accomplice, the one who points out the way, the one who provides shelter, the one who supplies weapons, and the one who provides food to those engaged in illegal acts [are all liable]."
One who instructs in war, one who demonstrates its destruction,
one who is intent on indifference toward what ought to be done, and one who speaks of faults while giving approval [for such acts].
Those who are capable and do not prevent [an offense] shall all be made to perform that same task;
however, the king should impose upon them a punishment appropriate to their respective capacities. (2.231)

One who offers water for honor to the wrong person, one who utters abuse, one who transgresses [a command], one who strikes his brother's wife, one who fails to deliver what has been entrusted, and one who breaks down a house situated by the sea. (2.232)
For those who cause harm to neighbors, guildsmen, and others, the settled rule is that their fine shall be fifty paṇas. (2.233)

One who utters unpleasant words or insults those worthy of honor (*arghya*), one who strikes the wife of a brother, one who fails to give what has been promised, one who breaks the seal of a house, and one who harms neighbors—those who own houses, fields, and so forth in the vicinity—as well as clan-elders (*kulika*) born of noble lineage and other virtuous persons; for each of these, a fine of fifty *paṇas* is determined in the legal treatises. Manu says:
"A twice-born man who eats forbidden food or drinks forbidden drink from a Vaiśya or others shall deserve the lowest, middle, or highest fines respectively."
The fine for a Śūdra shall be five paṇas;
however, those who have swallowed [the food] should themselves be expelled from the realm by the king.
Viṣṇu: "One who eats food that causes loss of caste or is otherwise unfit to be eaten shall be banished. Manu:
"In all cases of malevolent magic (abhicāra), a fine of two hundred [paṇas] shall be imposed;
likewise for root-rites (mūlakarman), acts of enmity (vidveṣa), and various kinds of sorcery (kṛtyā)."
For the adulteration of unadulterated goods,
as well as for their breaking or the false piercing of gems, the punishment is the first amercement.
If one who is low by birth should live by superior occupations out of greed,
the king, having deprived him of his wealth, should banish him immediately.
Likewise:
"One who destroys bridges, flagstaffs,
or images shall repair all of that and pay five hundred [paṇas]."
Kātyāyana states: "If one should carry away, break, or burn an image of the gods,
or likewise destroy its temple, he shall incur the first amercement."

Viṣṇu: "The seller of that which is unfit for consumption or forbidden to be sold, as well as those who destroy images of the gods, shall be punished with the highest amercement. Nārada: "A Brāhmaṇa who sells items that ought not to be sold has fallen from his path;
he must be restored to the right path by the king through severe punishment."
Yama:
But he who takes the water of a tank that was previously prohibited,
or who destroys the inlet for the waters, shall be made to pay the first amercement.
One who destroys a tank should be executed by drowning in water or by some other form of pure execution;
or he may repair that very tank, or pay the highest fine.
In this case, the killing of a Śūdra and others [is the offense]; for a twice-born man, there is another punishment. (2.232, 233)
