One who approaches a widow against her will, one who does not run to help when a cry for aid is raised, one who raises a false alarm, and a Caṇḍāla who touches members of the highest castes; 2.234.
One who feeds Śūdras or renunciants at rites for the gods or the ancestors; one who takes an improper oath; and one who performs the duties of an unfit person—[these are excluded]. (2.235)
One who obstructs the virility of bulls or small animals, one who denies a common property, and one who causes the destruction of a maidservant's fetus; 2.336.

Father and son, sister and brother, husband and wife, teacher and pupil: he who abandons any one of these, provided they have not fallen from their caste, shall be subject to a fine of one hundred [paṇas]. (2.237)

One who approaches a widow out of his own will or desire, rather than under the authority of the scriptures; one who does not run toward a person being attacked by thieves and the like when they cry out in distress, shouting "Run! Run!", nor toward the one crying out; one who cries out falsely even in the absence of an affliction such as thieves; a *caṇḍāla* who intentionally touches superior twice-born men (*dvijāti*); one who feeds Śūdras, renunciants (*pravrajita*), or those dedicated to the gods or ancestors; a Brāhmaṇa who performs improper and unworthy acts such as the drinking of the *kośa* (oath-water); one who is unfit—meaning one who is uninitiated (*anupanīta*) or has not performed penance—who performs the rites of one who is fit, such as one who is initiated; one who causes the destruction of virility in a bull, a steer, or small animals such as goats and sheep by crushing their testicles; one who denies common property belonging to both himself and another; one who destroys the fetus of a female slave; and one who abandons his father and others who have not fallen from caste, shall each receive a fine of one hundred *paṇas*. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "The mother, the father, and virtuous *sapiṇḍa* relatives are all not to be abandoned. He who, out of lust, abandons them while they have not fallen from caste, shall incur a fine of two hundred [paṇas]. One must not transgress against mother or father, nor against a teacher (*guru*). For transgression against these three, there shall be the amputation of a limb. Here, the "teacher" refers to the preceptor (*ācārya*) and not the father, because the father is mentioned separately. The meaning is that whichever limb one uses to commit the transgression, that limb shall be cut off. (Manu).
Neither a mother, nor a father, nor a wife, nor a son deserves to be abandoned.
If one abandons these who have not fallen from their status, he shall be made to pay six hundred [paṇas] by the king.
The renunciation of these accumulated [sins] is this. Thus ends the section on rash acts (sāhasa). 2.234, 235, 236, 237.
A laundryman who wears another's garment must be made to pay three paṇas;
however, for selling, bartering, pledging, or borrowing it, he shall pay ten paṇas. (2.238)

If a washerman himself wears or puts on another's garment that was brought for washing, he shall be made to pay three *paṇas*. If he sells or otherwise disposes of that very garment, he shall be made to pay ten *paṇas*. *Avakraya* means giving by way of rent; *ādhāna* means giving as a pledge to a creditor; *yācita* means a borrowed item. Manu says:
"A washerman shall wash garments on a smooth board made of *śālmali* wood;
he shall not exchange garments for garments, nor shall he wear them."

"Having bound [the debtor] with clothes, one should not take away his garments. This means that one should neither clothe him in one's own house nor keep him there; or alternatively, it means that one should not give him money for the purpose of clothing. || 2.238 ||
In a dispute between a father and a son, the fine for witnesses is three paṇas;
but for anyone who stands as an intermediary between the two, the fine shall be eightfold. (2.239)

In a dispute between father and son, those witnesses who—though capable of resolving their conflicting testimonies—do not do so, shall be fined three *paṇas*. But he who stands between them as a surety for the delivery of the winnings shall be punished with a fine eight times that amount. Viṣṇu states: "For witnesses in a dispute between father and son, the fine is ten *paṇas*; for one who stands between them, it is the highest amercement (*uttama-sāhasa*). This refers to a case of extreme persistence. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "In a dispute between father and son, no witness should stand by. He who does stand by shall be fined three *kārṣāpaṇas*, and he who stands between them shall also be made to pay one hundred and eight. This pertains to the category of middling offenses. (2.239)
One who forges scales, royal edicts, measures, or coins, as well as anyone who deals with such forged items, shall be made to pay the highest fine. (2.240)

One who manufactures false scales and the like, as well as one who knowingly deals with such counterfeit scales and so forth, shall be made to pay the highest fine (*uttamasāhasa*). A *tulā* is the standard measure for things weighed by balance; a *śāsana* is the royal edict, as stated in the verse beginning, "Having granted land and a title-deed" (*datvā bhūmiṃ nibandhaṃ ca*). This is intended as an illustration; *māna* refers to measures such as the *kuḍava*, and *nāṇaka* refers to coins such as the *dramma*. (2.240)
He who declares a counterfeit coin to be genuine, or a genuine coin to be counterfeit—that examiner of currency shall be made to pay the highest fine. (2.241)

If one who lives by examining coins, such as *drammas* and the like, should declare a genuine coin to be counterfeit or an improper one to be proper, and conversely, a counterfeit coin to be genuine, he shall be punished with the highest amercement at that very moment. This is the rule for punishment regarding one who knows the truth but speaks otherwise due to the influence of passion, hatred, or other such motives. (2.241)
A man who behaves falsely toward animals shall be made to pay the first fine;
toward humans, the middle fine; but toward those of royal status, the highest fine. (2.242)

A physician who practices false medical treatment on animals such as cows and the like shall be made to pay the first amercement; for a human being, the middle amercement; but for a human being related to the king, he shall again be made to pay the highest amercement. "False" means contrary to the scriptures. Vyāsa says: "Physicians cause men to suffer for a long time by the administration of liquid decoctions;
having provoked the aggravation of diseases, they seize the wealth of the patient."
Bṛhaspati: A physician who prescribes medicine without knowing the medical treatise, and who does not understand the treatment for a disease,
yet takes wealth from patients, should be punished like a thief.

Tantra means a treatise. Viṣṇu states: "A physician who practices deceitfully toward persons of the highest class shall be punished with the highest amercement; toward those of the middle class, with the middle amercement; and toward animals, with the first amercement. (2.242)
He who binds one who should not be bound, or releases one who has been bound, and he who obstructs legal proceedings, shall be made to pay the highest fine. (2.243)

[825] He who, out of arrogance, imprisons one who is not liable to imprisonment and is free from fault; or he who, out of arrogance, releases one who has been imprisoned and fettered by the king; or he who releases a litigant who has not yet reached the age of legal majority—he shall be made to pay the highest amercement. Viṣṇu: One who releases a person from punishment shall incur a fine double that of the punishment itself.
And even when appointed, he who inflicts punishment upon those who should not be punished is the lowest of men.

If one appointed by the king to inflict punishment releases a person deserving of punishment from it, or punishes one who does not deserve it, his fine shall be double [the prescribed penalty]. (2.243)
Whoever should take an eighth part [of the produce] by means of a measure or a scale, shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred; this is ordained for both increase and decrease. 2.244.

Whoever, by means of a false measure such as a *kuḍava* or a scale, should defraud another of one-eighth part of merchandise in buying or selling, shall be made to pay two hundred *paṇas*. If the fraud exceeds one-eighth part, he shall be made to pay a fine determined in accordance with the amount defrauded; if it is less, he shall be made to pay a fine proportionate to that. Manu says: "But he who deals unequally with equals, whether by weight or by price, that man shall incur the first or indeed the middlemost amercement."
He who sells seed that is unfit for sowing, and likewise he who uproots seed-crops;

He who transacts business with "equals"—that is, with those who pay equal prices—by giving goods of superior or inferior quality, incurs the first *sāhasa* fine. The meaning is that if he takes a large amount of price for an equal-quality good, or a small amount [for one of superior quality], he incurs the middle *sāhasa* fine. An "seller of non-seed" (*abījavikrayī*) is one who sells what is not seed as if it were seed. A "stealer of seed" (*bījotkraṣṭā*) is one who takes up the sown seed by digging it out. Likewise: "And by breaking a boundary, one shall incur a modified fine. Likewise:
All scales, measures, and weights shall be well-protected;
they must be re-examined every six months.
Bṛhaspati:

One who sells again a refined commodity that was previously mixed with concealed defects shall be made to pay double its value as a fine, and the merchant shall pay an equal amount as a penalty. 2.244.
For one who sells inferior goods—such as medicines, oils, salts, perfumes, grains, molasses, and so forth—the fine shall be sixteen paṇas. (2.245)
For one who throws away or discards inferior merchandise—such as medicines and the like—that is of low value, the fine shall be sixteen paṇas. "Medicine" (bheṣaja) means an herbal remedy. (2.245)
[826] For one who fakes the origin of clay, leather, gems, thread, iron, wood, bark, or cloth by representing them as something else, the fine for selling them is eightfold. 2.246.

Among clay and other such substances, if someone takes the price of a good article by giving an inferior one—having rendered it similar to that superior substance through some means and thereby inducing the buyer to believe, out of delusion, "this is a good one"—he shall be fined eight times that very price. For example, as when clay is made to fetch a higher price by being mixed with musk, creating the illusion that it is musk; this is likewise possible in the case of leather and other materials. *Valkala* refers to tree bark. Thus says Bṛhaspati.
Those who, by means of processing, turn an article of small value into one of great value,
and those who deceive women and children, shall be punished in proportion to the value of the object.
Those who manufacture artificial gold, pearls, coral, and so forth, shall be made to pay the value to the purchaser and a fine of double that amount by the king. (2.246)
For one who brings back from the ocean either counterfeit merchandise or artificial goods, whether for deposit or sale, a legal penalty shall be prescribed. (2.247)
If the amount is one paṇa, the fine is fifty; for one paṇa, it is said to be one hundred;
for two paṇas, the fine is two hundred; thus, as the principal increases, the fine increases accordingly. (2.248)

"Samudra" means that which exists together with a seal (*mudrā*) and the closing of the door. Having displayed one thing as something excellent, he skillfully creates a delusion for the buyer or the creditor by handing over another thing that is inferior to it. For one who, for the sake of deception, brings or sells to another worthless, low-value items such as clay and the like, representing them as valuable goods such as musk and other precious commodities—the determination of his punishment is stated as follows: If a counterfeit coin (*bhinna-paṇa*)—that is, a coin of less value—is introduced or sold, the fine is fifty *paṇas*. If the counterfeit coin is equal in value to one *paṇa*, the fine is one hundred *paṇas*. If its value is double, the fine is two hundred *paṇas*. In this manner, for every increase of one *paṇa* in the value, the fine shall be increased by one hundred *paṇas*. (2.247, 248)

For artisans and craftsmen who, having come together, act for their own profit by causing congestion [in the market], a fine of one thousand [paṇas] is prescribed when the price of goods either falls or rises. (2.249)

Having ascertained the price fixed by the king for commodities, if one causes distress and suffering to those who live by trade—such as artisans and craftsmen—by setting a price that is otherwise than that [official price], whether through a decrease or an increase relative to the royal fixed price, a fine of one thousand *paṇas* shall be imposed. (2.249)

[827] For merchants who, having banded together, obstruct the sale of their merchandise by fixing an excessive price, or for those who sell it [in such a manner], the prescribed fine is the highest amercement (uttama-sāhasa). || 2.250 ||

For those who, disregarding the price fixed by the king, obstruct the merchandise brought by fellow merchants among those assembled for trade by offering a high price of their own choosing, or who engage in illegal sale; and likewise, for those who export their own goods by establishing a lower price than that fixed by the king—the punishment shall be the highest amercement. Manu (2.250):
"The king shall confiscate the entire property of one who, out of greed, conceals royal merchandise or items that have been prohibited."
He states that price by means of which merchants should conduct their business:
"The sale or purchase [of goods] should be carried out daily at the price fixed by kings; from that [price], the surplus is traditionally held to be the profit of the merchants. (2.251)

The price established and determined by kings must be used daily by merchants for both selling and buying. Whatever surplus or increase in wealth results from that price is alone considered the commendable profit for merchants; not otherwise. Manu says:
"Having deliberated upon the source, the market, the location, as well as both the increase and decrease [of value], one should carry out the buying and selling of all commodities."
When five nights, seven nights, a fortnight, or a month has passed,
the king should establish the determination of their case in person.
A merchant who buys and sells immediately may take five percent on goods from his own country, but ten percent on those from a foreign land. (2.252)

A merchant who sells merchandise at the very price for which he purchased it shall take five percent when the goods come from his own country, but ten percent when they come from another country. (2.252)

Regarding the sale on a subsequent day after a purchase, he says: Having calculated the expenses arising from the merchandise, the price should be fixed so as to be favorable to both the buyer and the seller. (2.253)

[Thus ends the section on rash acts, || 20 ||] Having established the expenses incurred in connection with merchandise brought from one's own country or another country, the king, for the sake of granting equal favor to both the buyer and the seller, should determine a price after deducting all those expenses based upon the merchandise itself. (2.253)

Thus ends the section on Sāhasa (Violent Crimes) in the Aparārka, a commentary on the Yājñavalkya-smṛti composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, born in the lineage of the glorious King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the family of the glorious Vidyādharas. Section 12.
Now begins the section on "Non-delivery after Sale" (*vikrīyāsaṃpradāna*) in the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* with its commentary.
(21) He now commences the title of dispute known as "Non-delivery after Sale. Nārada states its essential nature:
When, after having sold a commodity for its price, it is not delivered to the buyer,
that is called the legal subject of dispute known as "non-delivery after sale."
The legal subject of dispute concerning one who neither pays the price nor delivers the merchandise for the purpose of sale has been stated by him [Manu]. Likewise:
"In this world, there are two kinds of property, namely immovable and movable;
all of that is called 'merchandise' (paṇya) in the context of the laws of purchase and sale."
The wise have recorded its method of giving and taking as being of six kinds:
by counting, by weighing, by measuring, by action, by form, and by splendor.

*Gaṇima* refers to betel nuts and the like; *tulima*, gold and the like; *meyam*, rice and the like; by action, such as milking or carrying, cows, horses, and the like; by form, courtesans and the like; by wealth (*śrī*), villages, gardens, and the like; or by beauty (*śrī*), gems and the like.
Regarding this, he states the punishment for one who takes the price but does not deliver the merchandise:
"He who, having received the price, does not at all deliver the merchandise to the purchaser..."
This [debt] shall be made to be paid by him with interest, or the profit from trade if he has come from abroad. (2.254)

If a seller does not deliver to the buyer a commodity for which the price has been received, he must restore that commodity to the buyer together with its *udaya*—that is, accompanied by the profit (*dhanalābha*) derived from it. Furthermore, if the commodity was taken to another region to be sold, then it must be given to him together with whatever profit is realized from that sale in that other region; this is what is called *upacaya*. Here, *udaya* does not consist of the regional profit alone; rather, it refers to every increase in value of the price. The commodity must be delivered along with both of these: the increase in value and the profit obtained from selling the commodity at that specific time. This applies when the seller fails to deliver the commodity due to a lack of repentance (*anuśaya*) after having sold it. However, if he fails to deliver it because of actual repentance, that constitutes a different legal dispute. (Nārada).
If, after selling a commodity for its price, one does not deliver it to the buyer,
they shall be made to pay the loss of the immovable property and the profit from the use of the movable property.
If the profit margin should diminish, one should bring back the merchandise with interest;
this is the rule for stationary traders, while those who travel to various regions may take the local profit of their respective directions.

"Regarding the destruction of immovable property," this refers to matters concerning immovable things; the meaning is that the purchaser must be made to pay for the loss resulting from the deterioration of his enjoyment. "Use" (*kriyā*) refers to activities such as carrying loads and the like. "Fruit" (*phala*) refers to milk and so forth. Viṣṇu states: "If one who has received the price does not deliver the merchandise to the purchaser, he shall be compelled by the king to pay it with interest, and he shall be fined one hundred *paṇas*. Nārada says:
"If the merchandise is destroyed, burnt, or stolen, that loss falls upon the seller himself if he fails to deliver what was sold. (NSm 2.254)
Even if the sale has been completed, the goods may be returned to the seller if the previous buyer does not accept them;
for if the loss is due to the fault of the buyer, that loss shall indeed belong to the buyer alone. (2.255)

But when, having paid the price, one does not take the merchandise, then it may be sold elsewhere by the seller. If it is lost in the meantime, that loss falls upon the buyer alone; the meaning is that the price need not be refunded to him. Nārada says: "If a buyer does not accept the purchased merchandise when it is being delivered, that same fault shall belong to the seller for not delivering it."
The fault of the seller has been stated in the passage beginning with, "or the merchandise may be spoiled," and so forth. (2.255)
He states an exception to what was previously said:
"If a defect in the merchandise arises due to injury caused by the king or fate, the loss belongs solely to the seller who does not deliver it when requested. (2.256)

But when the seller, even though requested by the buyer, does not deliver the merchandise for which the price has been paid, then any loss of it caused by the king, fate, or other such factors falls upon the seller alone. Consequently, he must restore either the full value of the merchandise or an equivalent item to satisfy the buyer. (2.256)
[830] And if one sells what has been sold into another's hand, or if he sells what is defective as if it were non-defective, the fine in that case shall be double the value. M 2.257.

When a seller has sold a commodity to one person and sells that same commodity again to another hand—that is, sells it to someone else—likewise, when one who knows a commodity to be defective nevertheless sells it as if it were defect-free by concealing its faults, a fine of double the price shall be imposed upon that seller. By the use of the word "and" (ca), the double of the price itself must be returned to the buyer. Nārada says: "But he who, having sold a thing to one hand, delivers it to another, shall be made to pay double the value of that object, and an equal amount as a fine."
One should pay back double the value of any property that was acquired through a formal oath of truth.
Thus ends the section titled "Non-delivery of what has been given. (2.257)
Regarding the remorse of the purchaser, he says something:
"A merchant who has purchased goods without knowing their depreciation or increase in value should not exercise remorse; if he does so, he shall be subject to a fine of one-sixth. (2.258)
[Thus ends Chapter 21: On Non-delivery after Sale.

One who has purchased a commodity should not exercise *anuśaya*—that is, repentance—without having properly considered its depreciation or appreciation; for one who knows its depreciation and appreciation may repent immediately. Nārada says:
"A purchaser who, having bought a commodity for a price, considers it a bad purchase..."
That [article] must be returned by the seller to the buyer on that very same day, provided it is undamaged.
On the second day, the buyer, while returning it, shall pay a thirtieth part of the price;
on the third day, double that amount; after that, it belongs to the buyer alone.
And this refers to the case of merchandise that has not been examined; as he himself says: "The buyer should personally examine the merchandise beforehand for its qualities and defects.
Once it has been purchased with the understanding that it has been examined, it cannot be returned to the seller."

The period for rescission has also been stated: "ten, one, seven, or five days," and so forth. This being the case, when the examination has taken place within the stated period, the fine for the one who effects the rescission is one-sixth of the price. (Even if the examination has not taken place, the fine for the one who effects the rescission is that same one-sixth of the price. Furthermore, when a person, having purchased an article that is not defective, becomes desirous of rescission at the very time of rescission, Kātyāyana says:
"If a man, having purchased a milch cow or other such article, should abandon it because he regrets the purchase... [831]
But if it is not defective, he shall carry ten parts out of the price at the proper time.

If one has purchased an item and is departing after the transaction is complete, Bhr̥gu says that if a flaw in the purchase is discovered upon taking possession, one may abandon the purchased object by paying a sixth part of its value.
This [period] begins after the time of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). Bṛhaspati says:
One should examine the merchandise oneself and show it to others;
having accepted what is considered excellent after examination, one should not reject it again.
Manu:
Having purchased or sold anything, if one should experience regret in this matter,
he may give back or take back that article within ten days.
But after ten days have passed, one should neither give nor cause [the gift] to be given;
both he who takes it and he who gives it shall be made to pay six hundred [paṇas] by the king.
Thus ends the section on rescission of purchase and sale (2.258).

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Non-Delivery of What Has Been Sold," in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, born in the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the glorious Vidyādhara clan.
Now begins the section on Partnership (Saṃbhūyasamutthāna), the twenty-second title of legal dispute, within the Yājñavalkya Smṛti along with its commentary.
It commences the title of legal dispute known as Partnership.
When merchants perform work for the sake of profit through a partnership, the gain and loss shall be according to their respective capital or as determined by their agreement. (2.159)

*Samavāya* means a meeting or an association—that is to say, a collective body. For those merchants, such as traders and the like, who perform activities such as commerce for the sake of profit, that is, for the sake of acquiring additional wealth, the gain and loss shall be divided in accordance with the capital invested and the agreement made; specifically, in proportion to how the capital was pooled and how the contract was established. Nārada states: "Where merchants and others perform work collectively, that is recorded in the legal treatises as *saṃbhūyasamutthāna*, the title of law concerning partnerships."
Bṛhaspati:
The wise should not perform ritual acts together with those who are powerless, lazy, afflicted by disease, unfortunate, or without support, nor with merchants and the like. [832]
The basis is the principal capital.

One should carry out business activities together with those who are of noble birth, skillful yet not indolent, wise, knowledgeable in coinage, experts in income and expenditure, pure, and courageous.
Nārada says:
When those who act together through a means for the sake of a reward perform a work,
the contributions that serve as the basis [of the enterprise] shall arise from their respective shares.

For those performing work in partnership, the capital investment is the foundation and the basis; having regard for that, they shall emerge with separate wealth. Whatever share belongs to anyone—whether equal, excessive, or deficient—in accordance with that, such shall be his loss, non-loss, and profit.
Whether a share is equal, less, or more, he by whom it was cast [into the dice] shall likewise give the inheritance,
perform the labor, and indeed receive the profit.
Kātyāyana says: Whatever craftsmen or even merchants may be assembled together,
the fruit obtained therein by those who have not separated from one another shall be shared equally.
This is the meaning: whatever profit has been acquired by the brothers while they remain undivided, that should be divided equally among them, not unequally.
Established by a formal agreement, they should manage the goods, the capital, the expenses, the deductions, the labor, and the assessment of value without deviation.
*Bhāṇḍa* refers to goods for sale; *piṇḍa* refers to provisions for a journey. Vyāsa says:
Whether in the presence of others or in private, those who deceive one another should conduct their buying and selling in accordance with the various commodities involved.
Bṛhaspati says: Those same persons who are examiners are declared to be witnesses for one another in a disputed matter,
provided they are not subject to deception and are not possessed by enmity.
If anyone among them is known to be a cheat in buying or selling, he shall be cleared by means of oaths; this rule applies to all disputes.
Kātyāyana says: But for those who carry out the investment with gold, grain, liquids, and so forth,
their profit shall be of a corresponding kind, according to shares that are equal, less, or more.
If a single man, approved by many, should give wealth or even cause a debt to be incurred, it shall be considered as contracted by all of them.
A debt to kinsmen, relatives, and friends may be paid even when secured by a pledge;
for others, it must likewise be accompanied by a guarantor and supported by a written document as well as witnesses.
Gold may be given at one's own will; however, liquids and grain must be given with a time-limit. They should be given and likewise received in accordance with the local custom of the region.
But that which is given by those assembled together must likewise be requested;
whoever does not ask for it is deprived of his gain. (2.259)

If anything forbidden or not specifically prescribed is destroyed through negligence, he shall restore it; and the guardian who has preserved the property from loss shall receive a tenth part as his fee. (2.160)

If one who is engaged in a collective undertaking acts in a manner forbidden by the rule "this must be done in this way," or performs work not so commanded or instructed, and thereby, through negligence or intellectual error, causes the destruction of wealth while remaining within that group, he alone must restore that wealth to the others. However, he who has preserved the wealth from ruin caused by the king or by fate (such as natural calamities) shall receive an additional tenth part of it. Bṛhaspati says: "But he who, though unappointed, prevents [the loss] yet destroys [the property] through negligence..."
By that very person it should be given to all those who are assembled together.
But he who protects [the property] by his own power out of fear of the king or the gods, they shall give him a tenth part as his share and take the remainder from that portion. (2.260)
The king shall take a twentieth part as toll from the act of half-immersion;
that which is established by experts, fit for the king, and sold, belongs to the king. (2.261)

The king shall take the twentieth part of the price of merchandise as a tax known as *śulka* (customs duty), by adding it to the value. However, that which is prohibited from sale by the king with the command "this must not be sold here," and that which is fit for the king such as elephants, horses, and so forth—even if its sale is not otherwise prohibited—both of these, once sold, go to the king and do not belong to the purchaser. Manu says: "Those skilled in the places of trade and expert in all kinds of merchandise shall fix the price according to the goods; from that, the king shall take the twentieth part."

Following the word "of the king," Gautama states: "A twentieth part is the toll (*śulka*) on merchandise; for roots, fruits, flowers, medicinal herbs, honey, meat, grass, and fuel, it is a sixth part. Because it is his duty to protect these, he should be constantly intent upon them. Baudhāyana says: "Regarding maritime toll, having set aside the best portion, one hundred and ten *paṇas* [should be taken]; for other goods as well, one should determine the toll according to their value without violating justice. The meaning is: whatever is the best portion of a maritime commodity, that alone is the toll; having set that aside, one hundred and ten [paṇas] should be collected. For other items as well, the toll should be fixed according to their value without violating justice. Vasiṣṭha: [834]
"There is no customs duty on a broken kārṣāpaṇa coin, nor on artisan's goods, nor on an infant, nor on a messenger;
nor on what is obtained as alms, nor on the remnants of an oblation, nor on a *śrotriya*, nor on a wandering ascetic, nor at a sacrifice. Thus says Manu.
Whatever goods have been prohibited by the king as being of notorious quality,
the king shall confiscate the entire property of anyone who exports them out of greed.

Viṣṇu states: "For one who sells what is prohibited by the king, there shall be the forfeiture of that [article]. From this statement it is understood that the seller of a prohibited item must restore the price to the previous buyer, and the king shall confiscate the article purchased in violation of the prohibition even without compensation. (2.261)

One who speaks falsely regarding the quantity [of goods] while departing from a customs station, as well as one who engages in fraudulent buying or selling, shall be made to pay eight times the amount. (2.262)

A merchant who, for the purpose of evading customs duty, falsely declares the quantity of his merchandise, or who departs from the place where duties are collected, shall be fined eight times the amount of the duty. Furthermore, he who conducts buying or selling through fraudulent means or by deceiving the customs officials shall also be fined eight times the duty. Nārada states:

"One who bypasses the customs station, one who buys or sells at an improper time, and one who makes a false statement regarding the enumeration [of goods], shall be made to pay eight times the excess [duty]."
*Atyaya* is a punishment occasioned by transgression. Bṛhaspati says:
A merchant who arrives at a customs station (*śulkasthāna*) shall pay the duty (*śulka*) as is appropriate;
he must not deviate from that, for this is proclaimed to be the tribute (*bali*) due to kings.
Viṣṇu: "One who evades a place where tolls are collected shall suffer the confiscation of his entire property. (2.262)
A ferryman who collects a land toll shall be made to pay ten paṇas;
this same penalty applies to a Brāhmaṇa for failing to invite those who are entitled to be invited.

A ferry official who collects land-based tolls shall be fined ten *paṇas* by the king. When a meal for Brahmins is to be prepared, a Brahmin who fails to invite his neighbors—the owners of adjacent houses—shall likewise be fined ten *paṇas*. Regarding the water-toll, Manu says:
"A vehicle should be made to pay one *paṇa* at the ferry;
a man, half a *paṇa*; an animal and a woman, a quarter; and a man with two hands (a laborer), half a quarter."
Vehicles filled with goods shall be made to pay a ferry-toll according to their value;
those with empty vessels, as well as men without belongings, shall pay whatever little they have. [835]

The meaning of this is as follows: for crossing a river (*tara*), a vehicle such as a palanquin and the like should be made to pay one *paṇa*; a man should be made to pay half a *paṇa*. An animal and a woman should each be made to pay a fourth part of a *paṇa*, while a man with empty hands should pay two *kārṣāpaṇas*. Vehicles filled with goods should each be made to pay a toll according to their value for the purpose of crossing rivers and so forth. Those same vehicles, when their goods are empty, should be made to pay a small amount of toll for the purpose of crossing rivers and so forth. Men who are without belongings or attendants should also be made to pay. Regarding an exception to this, the same author states:
A pregnant woman in her second month or beyond, as well as an ascetic,
a sage, a Brahmin, and those bearing religious emblems, shall not be made to pay a ferry-toll when crossing.
Likewise: "If a Brahmin does not feed his immediate neighbor and next-door neighbor— who are worthy— at a virtuous rite for twenty Brahmins, he deserves a fine of one māṣaka."

A *muni* is one who performs the *cāndrāyaṇa* and other such penances; *liṅginaḥ* refers to those such as celibate students (*brahmacārin*) and others; an *anuveśya* is a neighbor who visits one's house. A ceremony where twenty twice-born men are present is called "twenty-twice-born" (*viṃśatidvija*); "auspicious" (*kalyāṇa*) means beautiful or excellent. One who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) is a virtuous man; he must not be fed at rites for prosperity (*bhūtikṛtya*). If such a person is fed, that food must be made double [in compensation], and he shall also be made to pay a *māṣaka* of gold.

Rituals for prosperity (*bhūtikṛtyāni*), such as feeding Brāhmaṇas and other ceremonies primarily characterized by auspiciousness, are to be accomplished with abundant wealth. Viṣṇu states: "He who gives a wrong path to those for whom a path ought to be given shall be fined twenty-five *kārṣāpaṇas*. He who fails to give a seat to one worthy of a seat, or fails to honor one worthy of honor, or bypasses a neighboring Brāhmaṇa [when passing], or having invited someone does not provide food, or eats without having accepted an invitation saying 'so be it,' shall pay one *māṣaka* of gold; and for the host, double the amount of food. This is also stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*.

A twice-born man who has been invited but is currently engaged in receiving gifts should not go [to the ceremony] without a valid reason; he shall be made to pay a fine of eight hundred [paṇas]. (2.263)
He states the order of succession for those entitled to the estate of one who has died while engaged in a joint enterprise:
"When a man has died in a foreign land, his heirs, kinsmen, or cognates shall take his property upon their arrival; in their absence, the king shall take it. (2.264)

If a partner in a joint enterprise has gone to another country or has died, his heirs—the sons—shall take that wealth. In their absence, kinsmen and relatives, the wife, daughters, and so forth; in their absence, cognates (*jñātayaḥ*) who are *samānodaka* (sapindas up to the seventh degree); in their absence, those who were partners in the joint enterprise and came along with him; and in their absence, the king. This statement is intended to establish the entitlement of the joint partners to the property. Others, however, merely restate what was said regarding the wife, daughters, and so forth. Nārada says: "If one of them should meet with misfortune, his heir shall obtain it."
Or if another heir resides there, whether he is attached to it or all [the heirs] are so.
Calamity is death; "attached" means bound together; all act in concert.
If any one, while traveling through various regions, should die as a merchant who has arrived, the king shall protect his merchandise until an heir is found.
If there is no heir, one should entrust that property to relatives or kinsmen;
in their absence, one should keep it well-guarded for ten years.
Property that has no owner and no heir, which has remained for ten years, the king may take for himself; in this way, the law is not violated.
An heir is a son. Bṛhaspati says:
When anyone among those engaged in a single undertaking passes away, the rite must be performed by his relative or by all the collaborators together. (2.164)
Those who act crookedly should be deprived of their share; one who is unable should have the work done by another.

Among those acting in partnership, he who is crooked—that is, deceitful, meaning one who performs his individual task improperly—others should exclude him from the group by depriving him of his share, rendering him profitless. However, if he does not act crookedly but fails to perform the work due to incapacity, then one should have that work performed by someone else.
Extending the stated principle to the officiating priests and others, he says:
"By this, the rule for officiating priests, cultivators, and laborers has been declared. (2.265)

By this rule regarding officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the legal procedure for priests and others should be understood as declared. Consequently, if a priest who has been chosen is unable to perform the ritual due to illness or other causes, another person must have that work performed by him. If he does not do so out of deceit, he should indeed be dismissed. On this point Vasiṣṭha says: "A priest or a teacher who fails to officiate or teach should be abandoned; otherwise, one falls [from his status] upon such abandonment. Nārada says:
"In the event of a calamity befalling the priests, another shall likewise complete that rite;
he shall receive the portion of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) duly assigned from that [original allotment]."
Manu:
If a priest chosen for a sacrifice should abandon his own duty,
the deity’s share [of the offering] shall go to the other performers together with them, in proportion to that person's work.
If, after the sacrificial fees have been given, he should abandon his own work,
he shall receive his entire share and have it performed by another.

All [the priests] are entitled to shares; the principal ones are the *ardhins*, those entitled to half-shares; next, the *ardhina-ardhins* receive half of that; the *tṛtīyins* receive one-third shares, and the *pādins* receive one-fourth shares.

If the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) were to perform all the ritual acts, they would then take the entire share from the patron (*yajamāna*). Among all those priests, those who are the principal ones—the great priests (*mahartvij*), namely the Hotṛ, Brahman, Adhvaryu, and Udgātṛ—are called "Halfers" (*ardhin*); even though they receive slightly less than half, by virtue of their proximity, they are the masters of the half-share of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Those who are the second-tier priests—the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, Praśāstṛ, Prastotṛ, and Pratiprasthātṛ—are also "Halfers," meaning they should be made to receive half of the share of the great priests. Those who are entitled to a third part—the Āgnīdhra, Acchāvāka, Pratihartṛ, and Neṣṭṛ—receive a third share of the great priests' sacrificial fee. Furthermore, those who are entitled to a quarter—the Grāvastut, Potṛ, Subrahmaṇya, and Unnetṛ—receive a fourth share of the great priests' sacrificial fee.
Whatever specific fees for individual parts of the ritual have been prescribed for a particular act, he alone shall receive them; or alternatively, all [the priests] may share them together.

Regarding the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) prescribed in connection with specific officiants for each respective part of the ritual: should they be received by each individual with whom they are connected? For example, in the *Abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice, it is stated, "He gives two golden mirrors to the Adhvaryu. Is it to be taken by that very Adhvaryu, or is the Adhvaryu merely the recipient, and all [the priests] should take them after dividing them? This is the doubt. [The answer is: Manu and Bṛhaspati [state]: "The Adhvaryu shall take the chariot, and the Brahman the horse at the *Āghāra* offering;
the Hotṛ shall take the horse, and the Udgātṛ the cart at the purchase [of the Soma]."

This is the resolution regarding the doubt previously stated: For certain reciters of the Vedic branches (*śākhins*), a chariot is prescribed for the *adhvaryu* at the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*); a swift horse for the *brahman*; and for the *hotṛ*, a horse, while for the *udgātṛ*, it is a cart for carrying the *soma* during the purchase of the *soma*. In this arrangement, the verb "to give" (*dadāti*) retains its primary meaning, and the connection with human agents does not result in an unseen spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭa*). As stated by Manu: "If a sacrificer should abandon a priest, or if a priest should abandon a sacrificer—provided both are capable of the task and free from fault—the punishment for each of them shall be one hundred [paṇas]."

Thus, this should be understood to apply to officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who have been selected by the patron himself according to the traditional order. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Now, if after an officiating priest has been chosen, one should choose another, the latter receives a small portion of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) belonging to the previously chosen one. If he should go abroad, he should wait for that time while observing the specific occasion; he must not perform the sacrifice in the interim. Or, if there should be an urgent matter, he should complete that sacrifice [with another priest]. Having returned from his journey, he should receive a small portion [of the fee]. Furthermore, if one who has been forbidden goes abroad out of desire and returns to the *savana* (sacrificial session), that officiating priest shall be fined one hundred [paṇas]; the same applies to the family preceptor (*kulopādhyāya*) who is not at fault. Likewise, in the case of officiating priests who are diseased, fallen, insane, abandoned, or deceased, there is no obligation to provide the gift. If an officiating priest should abandon a patron (*yājya*) who has not fallen [from his status] out of desire, he shall incur a fine of two hundred [paṇas]; and if the patron should abandon him, he shall incur the same. This is the rule regarding the abandonment of an officiating priest whose patron has not fallen. One may, however, abandon a patron who is fallen through desire, or one who lacks Vedic learning (*aśrotriya*), or one who is accused (*abhiśasta*), or one who does not give. *Kāla* refers to the period beginning with the month of Prauṣṭhapada (Bhādrapada). *Nimitta* refers to occasions such as marriage and so forth. Regarding the phrase "there should be an urgent matter" (*syād ātyayika*): *ātyayika* means an emergency (*atyaya*). Therefore, the meaning is that if, upon waiting for that time, a failure or obstruction of the sacrifice is likely to occur, then one should complete that sacrifice with another officiating priest. *Prahīṇa* means one who has been cast off due to a curse or similar reason. *Pradhvasta* means one who is very old. Bṛhaspati [states]: [text follows]
The preliminary ritual has been previously explained in brief;
now listen as this procedure for the cultivators and others is being described.
"Application" refers to the lending of wealth to priests and others.
A wise man should carry out agricultural work together with those who are equal to him in external means, such as farmers, seeds, and the equipment for the field.
Where a loss of the field occurs due to the failure of external seeds,
that [loss] must be borne by all those who live by agriculture.
This ancient law has been fully declared for plowmen regarding gold,
base metals, thread, wood, stone, and leather.
The wise have declared that a *saṃskartā* is an artisan (*śilpī*) skilled in the arts;
this applies where goldsmiths and others perform their craft collectively.
May they receive their reward in accordance with their actions, each according to their respective share.
"Kīnāśas" are farmers. "Kātyāyana" refers to artisans—namely, those who are instructors, experts, and skilled craftsmen—and teachers;
these shall take one, two, three, or four shares respectively, in ascending order.
Bṛhaspati says: Among those who, having come together, construct a mansion, a temple, or even the household utensils of a righteous person, the leader deserves two shares.
[839] This indeed is the duty of dancers proclaimed by the virtuous:
one who knows the rhythm receives one and a half shares, while the singers receive equal shares.
But those who, by the king's command, recover from a foreign land what was stolen by thieves,
shall give a sixth part to the king and divide the remainder among themselves according to their shares;
of these, the leader shall receive four parts, while the hero shall obtain three parts.
But the capable one shall take two shares; all the rest shall have equal shares. (2.265)

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, on Partnership, in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, born of the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the noble Vidyādhara race.
Now begins the section on theft (*steya*) in the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* with its commentary.
(23) He states the means for identifying a thief for the purpose of inflicting punishment upon him.
A thief is apprehended by the pursuers either by means of the stolen goods or by his tracks;
likewise, one who has committed a previous offense and one who resides in an impure place [is apprehended]. (2.266)

A thief is apprehended—that is, identified—by the seizers, namely those authorized to capture thieves, through such items as stolen property (*loptra*). *Loptra* refers to a portion of the stolen goods. A footprint (*pada*) is a mark on the dust or mud consisting of the impression of a person's foot; he whose house is reached by a continuous trail of such footprints starting from the place where the theft occurred is also a thief. Likewise, he at whose house a continuous trail of footprints of the stolen cow or other animal has proceeded is also a thief. This is intended to illustrate the class of characteristics that are invariably concomitant with theft. Therefore, when rice or similar items remaining after a loss are seen in each other's houses, if they are of a single type, it is declared that they are mutual thieves. Furthermore, one who is known to be an offender due to a prior act of theft, and one who is an "impure dweller" (*aśuddhavāsaka*)—meaning one whose dwelling place is not pure, not proper, or not clean—he too is a thief. (2.266)
The causes for apprehension in the form of a definitive conclusion have been stated. Now he states the causes for that very same apprehension in the form of doubt:
"Others also should be apprehended with suspicion through the concealment of name, caste, and so forth;
as well as those addicted to gambling, women, and drink, and those whose faces and voices are parched and altered. (2.267)

Those who inquire about the property and houses of others while moving about in secret, those who have no income yet have many expenditures, and those who sell goods that do not exist—[these are signs of a thief]. || 2.268 ||

Those other than those already mentioned who are suspected of being thieves due to their denial or concealment of names, caste, group, place of origin, and so forth—this means they are to be regarded as potential thieves—are to be apprehended on suspicion of theft. Likewise, those addicted to gambling and the like; those accused of theft whose mouths become parched and whose voices become broken; those who inquire about the belongings or houses of others, asking "Whose are these goods? or "Whose house is this?"; those who wander about in secret or concealed fashion, being habituated to such behavior; those who have no income yet possess wealth that has not been seen coming in, yet spend lavishly; and those who sell ornaments such as neck-chains that have been stripped away—all these are to be apprehended on suspicion of being thieves. Thus says Nārada.
Theft is established by the seizure of stolen goods; when there is stolen property, it is proven by its consumption.
Suspicion arises from association with wicked persons, as well as from a lack of income and expenditure.
One should interrogate captured thieves who have not confessed by means of enumeration,
using various forms of intimidation and stratagems, so that they may speak the truth.

Having confronted them, one should interrogate them regarding their country, village, direction, name, caste, or place of refuge, as well as the nature of the task they have performed and their accomplices.
Because of differences in complexion, voice, and form; because of reporting with uncertainty;
because of being a witness at an improper place and time; and because of the purification of the deposition.
On account of the disappearance of property, prior theft, and association with the wicked,
one should be pursued for these faults even beyond the mere discovery of the stolen goods.

*Hoḍha* means stolen property. *Upabhoga* (enjoyment) refers to the acquisition of the stolen goods, since there is no other way for them to be possessed except through such acquisition. *Aikārthya* means having a single purpose. *Bhayopadhā* refers to afflictions and stratagems that cause fear. Likewise:
"When cattle and other such things have been lost or stolen, those who know [the matter] should conduct an investigation by following the tracks back to the source."
From the root down to the place where it was taken—
whether in a village, a cow-pen, or a pasture— wherever that footprint falls,
the owner must bear the cost; unless he carries it elsewhere.
If he is confused or broken by the unevenness of the ground near people,
he should discharge it toward whichever village or herd is closer. On a level path, where there are two [options], he should aim at the place where the people are mostly thieves and impure.
Whether he be corrupt due to past offenses or associated with evil-minded persons.
The Dasyus do not emerge from the atmosphere, nor from heaven, nor from the ocean, nor from anywhere else; therefore, one should arrange it in this manner.
Caṇḍālas, executioners, and others should conduct searches within the villages,
while those who roam outside at night should conduct them outside.
On the same path, on an identical route, between two villages. And "abounding in thieves" means full of many robbers. Manu and Nārada [state]:
"Assembly halls, water-stations, bakeries, brothels, taverns, and food-sellers; crossroads, sacred trees, public gatherings, and spectacles."
Gardens in ruins, forests, and the workshops of artisans;
empty houses, as well as woods and groves.
The king should cause such regions to be patrolled by both stationary and mobile military units, as well as by spies, for the purpose of suppressing thieves.
Likewise:
"One should recognize and incite them by means of clever former thieves who follow as companions and advocate for various criminal acts."
Under the pretext of providing food and drink, by means of visiting Brahmins,
and under the guise of discussing heroic deeds, they should bring about their meeting.
Even those who would not approach him even by means of dispatched spies—
those, along with their friends, kinsmen, and relatives, should also be won over.
Those thieves whom they may capture there, having beaten and humiliated them,
and having proclaimed their crime everywhere, the king shall put them to death by various methods of execution.
Even those who are not thieves may be seen in the company of thieves;
however, the king should not touch them with punishment unless it is based on his own certain conviction.
Kātyāyana says: One should carefully examine an object that has fallen from another's hand, been picked up unintentionally on the ground, or been dropped by a thief.

The meaning of this is as follows: "Is this seen in his hand because it fell from another's hand, or was it taken out by him without any desire for theft, or was it thrown out and then picked up by a thief?"—because such a doubt or uncertainty may arise, the stolen property (*loptra*) must be investigated with great care. || 2.268 ||
If one accused of theft on suspicion does not clear himself,
he shall be made to pay the stolen property and be punished with the penalty for a thief. [2.269]

If one who has been seized and accused on suspicion—that is, on account of a doubt regarding theft—does not clear himself by means of either a divine (*divya*) or human (*mānuṣa*) proof, such that he does not remove the suspicion of theft, then, after being made to pay the stolen property, he is to be punished with the punishment for a thief as will be described hereafter. Nor should it be argued here that one suspected of theft is unfit for proof because of his status as a false speaker; for it is not merely the state of being a false speaker that renders one unfit for evidence. Rather, it is when the first party is an obstinate accuser. Therefore, it is appropriate in this case that one under suspicion should employ proof. Furthermore, it is not the case that there is an absence of proof regarding the non-existence of theft and the like. For if that were so, statements such as "In cases of great accusation these [oaths] are used," "Either party may act according to their own inclination," and "And for those suspected by kings," would never have been composed. Nor should it be said that the absence of human proofs is not established; because those who establish a particular positive state (*bhāva-viśeṣa*) which is invariably concomitant with the absence of theft and the like, necessarily establish the absence as well. For example, when someone's property was stolen at a certain time, if one establishes—by reflecting that "I was situated very far from the place of the theft at that time, exhausted by a great illness, etc."—one indeed proves the absence of theft in oneself. For this very reason, Śaṅkha, having stated, "When no witnesses are produced, there is an ordeal," further said: "Or else, he should not clear himself even through friends or virtuous men; if he [fails], he is to be punished and made to pay the property to the claimants. (2.269)
Having compelled the thief to restore what was stolen, he should execute him by various methods of death;
however, having branded a Brāhmaṇa, he should banish him from his own kingdom.

Having caused the thief—whose guilt has been established by evidence—to restore the stolen property to the owner, either in its original form or by its value, the king shall have him executed by various means of capital punishment or cause him to be harmed. However, in the case of a Brāhmaṇa thief, the king, having branded him with the mark of a dog's foot, shall banish him from his kingdom; he must not, however, put him to death. Regarding this, Manu says:
"He shall never kill a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is found guilty of every possible crime;
he should expel him from the kingdom, leaving him with all his wealth and his body unharmed."
This refers to offenses other than the great sins (*mahāpātaka*). Regarding those, it has been stated by that same author:
"In the case of violating the Guru’s bed, the mark of a vulva should be made; for drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern flag;
for theft, the footprint of a dog; and for killing a Brahmin, the figure of a headless man. [843]
And they—
neither to be shared meals with, nor to be sacrificed for, nor to be taught the marriage rites—
shall wander the earth in misery, excluded from all religious duties.

And branding should be carried out for those who refuse to perform penance; for it is said: "But the three castes performing their appropriate penance should not be branded on the forehead by the king; rather, they should be made to pay the highest fine."

And from this, the combination of punishment and penance is understood. Furthermore, regarding the non-performance of penance, the same author has stated that there is a combination of corporal punishment and the highest fine (*uttamasāhasa*):
"For all four of these who do not perform penance, a lawful punishment involving both body and wealth is ordained."

This means: for the four who have committed the great sins (*mahāpātaka*). Nārada says: "For a Brāhmaṇa, there shall be execution, shaving the head, banishment from the city, branding on the forehead, or being paraded on a donkey."

Gautama states: "For a Brāhmaṇa, there is no corporal punishment; [the penalties are] loss of specific rights, public proclamation of the offense, banishment, branding, and so forth. Corporal punishment consists of the amputation of limbs and the like. Āpastamba says: "In the case of killing a person, theft, or seizing land, one who has taken these [goods] is subject to death; however, for a Brāhmaṇa among them, the penalty is blinding. Bṛhaspati says:
"One who possesses good conduct and Vedic study, even if caught in the act of theft, shall not be subjected to long-term imprisonment;
he should be made to pay that wealth to the owner and perform penance. (2.270)
When the thief has been apprehended, it has been stated; now he declares what must be done when he has not been apprehended:

"If [the property] has been killed or stolen, the guilt falls on the village headman if the thief has not departed; but on the superintendent of the pasture-lands if it was on the road, and on the one who protects the forest if it was outside the forest. (2.271)

If a human being or the like is killed, or if cattle, horses, or the like are stolen, and the thief is not seen and has not gone outside the village, then the fault of the theft falls upon the owner of the village; the essential meaning is that he must either deliver the thief or the stolen property. However, if killing or theft occurs in a *vivīta* (pasture land) and the thief is not seen outside the *vivīta* on the path, the fault lies with the master of the *vivīta*. But if the killing or theft occurs elsewhere than in a *vivīta*, the fault lies with the official appointed to apprehend thieves. A *vivīta* is a plot of land intended for grass and similar purposes. Thus says Nārada.
If a thief is robbed within his own jurisdiction, he must be apprehended with effort by that [ruler],
or else made to pay the value of the theft, provided the tracks of the robbery have not vanished.
If, however, that footprint has not fallen elsewhere after it has gone forth,
one should cause the neighboring kings, the guardians of the roads, and the guardians of the directions to pay tribute.

If a theft occurs on a path leading out from that village, and the stolen property was not dropped by the thief within another village, then the king shall cause the neighboring lords and others to pay for it. Kātyāyana states: "But if a house is robbed, the king shall cause those who apprehend thieves to pay, as well as the boundary guardians who failed to provide protection, provided that the thief is not recovered."
Property stolen within a village shall be made good by the village headman;
in a pasture-land, it must be restored by the owner, and in a royal preserve, by the officer in charge of the preserve.
Likewise: Whatever ghee belongs to anyone in his own country should be given by the king;
the king himself should take that which has been lost and recovered after searching for it.
If property has been stolen by thieves, the king should diligently restore its original form;
in its absence, however, he should provide its value, otherwise the king becomes guilty of sin.
Even if the thief has been apprehended, if the stolen property is not recovered from him, he shall be made to pay it;
or else, he shall be handed over as a thief at the king's pleasure.
If, however, there should be doubt regarding the guilt of those being compelled to pay,
the one who has been robbed shall be made to swear an oath, or he may be cleared by his kinsmen.
The meaning is: by kinsmen who are residents nearby and are not corrupt, acting as witnesses;
because the owner has recovered from the stolen property only a small portion, he shall receive the remainder of that [property] once the owner has established his claim. (2.271)
The village shall provide land within its own boundaries, or wherever the path leads;
or else, five villages beyond the *krośa*, or even ten villages. (2.272)

If the robbery occurs right at the village boundary, then that very village shall make restitution for what was stolen. But if the track of the thieves—the path taken—should lead from outside the village boundary toward some other village, then that [other] village alone shall pay. However, when a theft occurs among several villages situated within a distance of one *krośa* from one another, then five villages situated on equal distances shall collectively provide the stolen goods. Furthermore, when ten villages are at equal intervals from the place of the robbery, then all ten, combined, shall make restitution for what was taken. (2.272)
It has been stated in general that one should put a thief to death by various modes of execution. In this regard, he specifies particular types of theft:
"Those who capture prisoners, as well as those who steal horses and elephants, and those who commit violent assaults—such men the king shall impale upon a stake. (2.273)
And the healing of a wound includes even execution. Manu says:
"Those who break into a fire-sanctuary, an armory, or a temple, as well as those who steal elephants, horses, or chariots, one should indeed put to death without hesitation."
Those who kill by force in the presence of people are killers of humans and the like. Vyāsa states: "The thief of a horse shall be executed after having his hands, feet, and hips cut off;
and the thief of livestock shall have half a foot severed with a sharp weapon."
Manu says: Those thieves who commit robbery at night by breaking through a wall,
the king, having cut off their hands, should impale them on a sharp stake.
The meaning is that one whose hand has been severed should be impaled there on two stakes. Bṛhaspati says:
"Those who cut through a joint [of a wall] or those who steal should be made to abandon their property and then impaled on a stake;
likewise, those who rob travelers should be tied by the neck to a tree and suspended."
Kātyāyana says: Those who are destroyers of their own country, as well as those who obstruct the highways—the king, having confiscated all their property, shall impale them on a stake. (2.273)
For the first offense, those who commit acts of expulsion or the breaking of a sealed knot shall have their hands and feet mutilated;
for a second offense, they shall be deprived of one hand and one foot respectively.

He who lifts and steals another's property with his thumb and fingers, and he who breaks a knot [of a bundle], both shall be deprived of their thumbs and fingers—the very hands and digits that were the instruments of the offense. For a second offense, they are to be deprived of one hand and one foot. Manu says:
"In the first seizure of a knotted bundle, one should cause the fingers of the thief to be amputated;
for a second, his hand and foot; for a third, he deserves the death penalty."
Kātyāyana says: For whatever part by which a thief commits an injury against another, the king shall cut off that limb from him so that he does not do it again. (2.274)

It was stated without qualification that "having made the thief restore what was stolen, one should have him executed by various forms of death"; now, in order to specify the scope of that rule, he says:

"In cases of seizing small, middling, or large property, the punishment shall be according to the value; in the administration of punishment, one must consider the place, time, age, and physical capacity. (2.275)

Minor items include earthenware and the like; middling items include clothing and the like; and major items include gold and the like. Punishment for thieves should be determined according to the value of these items, consisting of the confiscation of wealth, branding, mutilation of limbs, or execution. Place, time, age, and power constitute "place, time, age, and power"; all of this must be considered by the king, together with the Brahmins, when the matter of punishment arises. Regarding the threefold classification of property, Nārada says: "Earthenware, seats, swords, and so forth, as well as beautiful skins, grass, and the like..."
Pulses, prepared food, and small articles are declared to be minor property.
Pulses such as beans and mung beans; prepared food and cooked food; clothing, excluding silk; likewise cattle, excluding cows;
metal, excluding gold; and rice and barley—these constitute the middling [gift].
Gold, jewels, silk garments, women, guñjā seeds (or groups of men), elephants, and horses,
as well as the property of gods, brahmins, and kings, should be known as the highest category of wealth.

Silk is that which has eight borders. Gold refers to both gold and silver. Regarding the theft of these three types [of property], the same author states the extension of the threefold fines for violence:
"Whatever punishment has been prescribed by the wise for the three degrees of violence, that same punishment applies to theft as well, according to the sequence of the three kinds of goods."
Regarding that, Manu states a specific rule concerning grain:
"For one who steals more than ten *kumbhas* of grain, the punishment is death;
for stealing less than that, he should be made to pay eleven times the value, and that property must be returned to its owner."
A *kumbha* is two *droṇas*. This has been stated: "Two *palas* are considered a *prasṛta*; twice that is a *kuḍava*.
Four *kuḍavas* make a *prastha*, and four *prasthas* make an *āḍhaka*."
"Four *āḍhakas* are declared by the wise to be one *droṇa*;
two *droṇas* are a *kumbha*; a *śūrpa* is [the same]; and sixteen *droṇas* are a *khārī*.

For one who steals more than ten *kumbhas* of grain, there is the death penalty. In cases where less than that has been stolen, the thief shall be made to pay eleven times the fine that is prescribed for the theft of that specific quantity of grain, as well as an amount equal to what was stolen, to the owner.
Likewise, for goods measured by weight, there is the death penalty for stealing more than one hundred [palas],
as well as for gold, silver, and the like, and for the finest garments.

“Dharmameyāni” means those things which are measured by weight (*dharama*); these are specifically qualified by the phrase “of gold, silver, and so forth. If only the words “of gold, silver, and so forth” were used, then only metals would be included. If, on the other hand, only “measured by weight” were said, then molasses and the like would also be included. By employing both terms, however, there is the inclusion of pearls, coral, and so forth—which, though distinct from metals, are measured by weight—because they belong to the category of gold and silver due to their high value. This word “and so forth” (*ādi*) expresses a category. For this very reason, there is an exclusion of molasses and the like, even though they are measured by weight, because they lack the quality of being equal to gold due to their low value. Consequently, base metals such as tin and lead are not included here. Furthermore, “excellent garments” refers to those made of *pattra*, wool, silk, fine cloth, and so on. Likewise:
If the value exceeds fifty [paṇas], the cutting off of the hand is prescribed;
for the remainder, however, one should determine a fine eleven times the value.
One deserves death for the abduction of men of noble birth, especially women, and also for the theft of the most precious gems.
Upon seizing large cattle, weapons, or medicinal herbs,
the king shall determine the punishment after considering the time and the specific circumstances of the act.
Large animals such as cows and others; [the theft of] thread, cotton, fermenting agents, cow dung, molasses,
curd, milk, buttermilk, water, and grass.
In the case of stealing bamboo, articles made of bamboo, salts,
as well as earthenware, earth, and ashes;
Of fish, of birds, of oil, of clarified butter,
of meat, of honey, and whatever else originates from animals.
For other such kinds of liquor, for cooked rice,
and for all types of prepared food, the fine shall be double their value.
Where the fine for an ordinary person would be one kārṣāpaṇa, there a Brahmin should be fined one thousand; this is the established rule.
But for a Śūdra, the guilt in the case of theft becomes eightfold;
for a Vaiśya, it is sixteenfold, and for a Kṣatriya, it is thirty-twofold.
For a Brahmin, it may be sixty-four, or even a full hundred;
or twice sixty-four, for he is indeed one who knows the virtues and faults of those [qualities].

This statement refers to a learned person (*vidvat*), because the reason provided is "for he knows their defects and virtues. Therefore, the punishment that applies to theft for one who is ignorant—such as a child—who does not know the defects and virtues of theft and non-theft pertaining to this world and the next, shall be eightfold for a *śūdra* who does know them. Thus it has been said: "But for a *śūdra*, the offense is eightfold" (*aṣṭāpādyaṃ tu śūdrasya kilbiṣam*). That by which an offense of theft is incurred such that eight punishments are to be imposed is called "eightfold" (*aṣṭāpādyam*). [Furthermore: "A man who steals goods prepared for the sake of a sacrifice..."
The king shall fine him one hundred [paṇas] who steals fire from a house.
But he who takes a rope or a water-jar from a well, or who destroys a public water-shed,
shall receive a fine of one māṣa and shall restore that very thing to its place.
For one who steals large animals, the punishment is the highest amercement;
for stealing medium-sized animals, the middle amercement; and when small animals are stolen, the first amercement.
For one who steals the hands of a man, the punishment is the highest fine;
for one who steals his entire property, it is the same; but for one who abducts a woman or a maiden, the punishment is death.
For goods measured by weight, those measured by volume, and those counted by number— in all such cases,
for items of superior value, the fine shall be ten times their price.
Of wooden vessels, grass, and the like, as well as those made of clay;
of bamboo, articles made of bamboo, and likewise of sinews, bones, and skins.
In the case of stealing vegetables with their roots still moist, as well as fruits and flowers, products derived from milk or sugarcane, and likewise salt and oil;
For cooked grains, prepared foods, honey, and meat—
as well as for all items of small value— the fine shall be five times their price.
Smṛti:
"Whether it be grass or wood, or whether it be a flower or a fruit—
one who takes them without asking deserves the amputation of the hand."

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "If a non-Brāhmaṇa forcibly or secretly steals from a Brāhmaṇa sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, wood for the fire, grass, *ulapa* reeds, awns, flowers, incense, or fruit, he shall suffer the amputation of his hand. For one who steals articles made of *kuśa* grass or leather, a water-pot (*karaka*), or materials for the *agnihotra*, there shall be the amputation of a limb in the presence of witnesses; if it is done in the absence of witnesses, once this offender is identified, the Brāhmaṇa shall ride a donkey-cart. He shall have his head shaved with a thread. For others, however, there is only the donkey-cart. Viṣṇu states: "All thieves must be made to restore the stolen property to the owner; thereafter, the prescribed punishment shall be applied to them. Manu states: [849]
A righteous king shall not execute a thief without proof of the stolen goods;
however, he may execute one caught with the goods along with the implements of theft, without hesitation.

*Hoḍha* means stolen property; *upakaraṇa* refers to the implements of theft. Kātyāyana states: "Whether caught in the act (*sahoḍha*) or not caught in the act (*asahoḍha*), once the gravity of the crime has been established, the king should seize the stolen goods, have them returned, and deprive the offender of all his possessions."

The meaning is that even without physical evidence (*hoḍha*)—such as being determined through reality, proof, or the commission of a violent act—one should, having made it known to all people that "this man is a perpetrator of violence," carry out execution by confiscating all property, amputation of limbs, or other such punishments according to the prescribed rule. Kauśika states: "But those who are loyal to the king, protected by iron armor, and endowed with strength, may perform the king's tasks until death."
The joining of iron refers to an iron fetter for the feet. "Those with meager provisions" means those who have little food.
When property has been seized from a foreign land by a foreigner, having taken that [property] back from him, one should release him without punishment.
A foreigner is one who is living abroad. || 2.275 ||
In connection with the topic of theft, he says something else as well:
"If one knowingly provides food, shelter, fire, water, mantras, or implements to a thief or a robber, the highest fine shall be imposed. (2.276)

Even if one knows, "This man is a thief" or "This man is an armed robber," yet provides him with food, space, or lodging; fire for the purpose of cooking and so forth; water for the removal of cold or for bathing and drinking; spells consisting of instructions on the means of stealing; tools such as spades and weapons; or expenses such as provisions for the journey—one who thus renders assistance favorable to the thief or the armed robber shall be subject to the highest fine. Manu says:
"And those in villages who provide food to thieves, as well as those who give them space for their goods—all of them, too, he shall cause to be executed."
The lord should punish like thieves those who provide fire, food, or shelter to robbers, as well as those who act as their storekeepers.
Nārada says: Those who purchase goods, those who receive them as gifts, and all those who conceal them, are declared by law to be subject to equal punishment. [850]

Gautama says: "A minister who intentionally accepts what is connected with unrighteousness is equal to a thief. On this very point, Manu cites a Brāhmaṇa passage: "If a Brāhmaṇa should seek wealth from the hand of one who takes what is not given, even by means of officiating at sacrifices or teaching, he is just like a thief."

In the various kingdoms, he swiftly punished the provincial governors and vassal chiefs who had been incited [to rebellion], as well as those who remained neutral during the attacks, treating them like thieves.
In the event of a village raid, the destruction of a *hiḍa* (a watch-station), or the sighting of a robbery on the road,
those who do not come to the rescue to the best of their ability shall be banished along with their belongings.
For the destruction of a crop sown in a field is like the breaking of a dam. Nārada says:
"When a person is being carried off while people are crying out, those who hear it but do not run to the rescue are also partakers of that guilt. (2.276)
For causing the miscarriage of a fetus by the application of a weapon, the highest fine shall be imposed;
likewise for the killing of a man or a woman, either the highest or the lowest fine may be applied.

"Inflicting a weapon" means striking with a weapon; when this is done against another, as well as in the case of causing an abortion, the punishment is the highest amercement (*uttama-sāhasa*). Since a fine of one hundred *paṇas* has been prescribed for causing an abortion of a female slave, it should be understood that the abortion referred to here is other than that. However, regarding the abortion of a Brāhmaṇī's fetus, [it is stated]:
"Having destroyed an unknown fetus, one should perform this very same vow."

Thus, since only the atonement (*prāyaścitta*) has been extended by analogy, the punishment (*daṇḍa*), which was not previously established, is indeed ordained by this [text]. In the case of killing a man and a woman respectively, the highest and lowest [fines] are to be understood; the "lowest" is the first *sāhasa* (fine). Because of the two occurrences of the word "or" (*vā*), another alternative punishment is also to be understood in consideration of qualities and other factors. Uśanas says: "By causing suffering, the first [fine] shall apply; by administering medicine [to cause an abortion], the middle; but for striking so as to cause the miscarriage of the fetus, the highest fine is the penalty."

Baudhāyana states: "For the killing of a Brāhmaṇa by Kṣatriyas and others, there shall be death and the confiscation of all their property. For the killing of an equal or an inferior among those same classes, one should release to the king a thousand cows with an additional bull. For the sake of avenging enmity, one hundred [cows] for a Vaiśya, and ten for a Śūdra, with a bull added here as well.
