By the rule for the killing of a Śūdra, the killing of a woman and the killing of a cow are explained. Except in the case of an Ātreyī, a milch-cow, or a bull, at the end of these [penances] one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa. The killing of an Ātreyī is explained by the rule for the killing of a Kṣatriya. An Ātreyī is a woman in her menses. "For the killing of swans, cranes, peacocks, ruddy geese, herons, ravens, owls, mongooses, frogs, *hiṇḍikā* snakes, *bherīka* snakes, dogs, brown-colored animals, mongooses, and so forth, [the penance is] like that for a Śūdra."—Bṛhaspati.
Those who kill openly as well as those who kill by secret means—
having identified them correctly and seized their wealth— they should be executed by various methods of killing.
Whether for the sake of gaining allies or acquiring wealth, a king who desires the welfare of the world must not release those who act with reckless violence, for they bring fear to all people.
If a king, out of greed or fear, does not punish those who act unjustly,
his kingdom becomes agitated and he is deprived of his sovereignty.
Where many, filled with rage, strike at one person,
he who delivers the blow to the vital organ is designated as the slayer.
But he who actually strikes them shall be made to pay the fine as previously stated;
the one who incites the attack and the accomplice are sharers in the guilt, each liable for half of that amount.

Having ascertained through signs the smallness or greatness of the wound, the location of vital points (marmans), the effort required, the patient's capacity, and the complications, one should treat the condition with care.
Nārada said:
This rule of punishment is ordained for all without distinction, except for the case of a Brāhmaṇa; a Brāhmaṇa does not deserve death.
Shaving the head is his punishment, as is banishment from the city;
furthermore, he shall have a mark of infamy branded upon his forehead and be made to travel on a donkey.
Yama is the authority over rashness and valor.
Never shall there be corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa;
rather, having bound him in secret confinement, the king should cause food to be provided for him.
Alternatively, the king may bind him with a rope or compel him to perform labor;
having ascertained the facts of the case in truth, he should carry out this work for half a month or a full month.
But according to the offense, he may even compel a Brahmin to perform tasks that are outside his prescribed duties.
A woman who has committed a grievous offense— such as being a killer of a fetus or a man, or one who is not pregnant but has breached a dam—
he shall cause to be cast into water after binding a stone to her.

One should bind a stone to a woman who is not pregnant and cause her to drown in water—she who is excessively and variously wicked and sinful, as well as a killer of an embryo (a fetus) or a man, and a destroyer of a bridge that is beneficial to many worlds. (2.278)

[852] Having deprived her of her ears, hands, nose, and lips— whoever has given poison or set fire, or has caused the death of her husband, her elders, or her own children— one should banish her from the land with cattle. 2.279.

But she who gives poison for the death of a human being, or fire for the burning of a village and so forth, or likewise kills her husband, teacher, father, father-in-law, or her own child—having cut off her ears, hands, nose, and lips, one should place her upon a bull and banish her from the country. If the reading is *pramāpayet* (one should cause her to be killed), then one should act in such a way that oxen, having bound her by the neck with a rope to their yoke, drag her along until they kill her. (2.279)
Regarding the means of identifying the murderer when the cause of death is unknown, he says:
"The sons and kinsmen of one who has been suddenly killed should be questioned, as well as his women who were devoted to other men, individually. (2.280)
Or, desiring [to know about] a woman, wealth, or livelihood, with whom did he go?
Or he should also slowly question people near that location. (2.281)

One should quickly ask those who do not know him specifically, as well as those who do not know him, such as his sons and relatives: "With whom could he have had a quarrel? Likewise, one should ask each of his women—specifically those who are unchaste—whoever's wife, property, or livelihood he might desire, and with whom he was last seen. Furthermore, one should discreetly question the people living near the place where he died in the manner previously described. Thus says Bṛhaspati: "When a person is seen killed but the slayer is not seen..."
He should be recognized by the king according to his former enmity.
His neighbors, both immediate and distant, as well as his friends, enemies, and kinsmen, should be interrogated by the king’s officers through methods such as monthly inquiries.
He is to be identified by men through association with the wicked, or by means of signs and stolen goods;
Vyāsa says:
"Having thoroughly ascertained the murderer, along with his accomplices and kinsmen..."
The king should slay [his enemies] by various means of execution that cause them terror.

Bṛhaspati: One who has been purified by divine ordeals shall be deemed pure; one who is not pure deserves execution. Through such restraint and favor, the king's fame and righteousness increase. (2.280, 281)
Those who set fire to fields, houses, forests, villages, pastures, or threshing floors,
as well as one who has sexual intercourse with the king's wife, shall be burned in a fire of straw mats.

[853] Those who set fire to a field containing crops, a large building belonging to the king or others, a forest, a grove, a village, a cluster of houses, a pasture (vivīta)—that is, land serving as a support for grass and the like—or a threshing floor (khala), which is a place for processing grain; and one who approaches the wife of a king: each of these is to be burned with a *kaṭāgni*, a fire of a mat (*kaṭa*). A *kaṭa* is a specific material used for sitting, made of *vīraṇa* grass. Manu says:
"One who breaks down a wall and one who fills in moats..."
And one should swiftly put to death the breaker of gates.
He should have executed with various punishments those who steal from the king's treasury, those who stand in opposition to him, and those who instigate enemies.

The word "of the king" is connected with each [clause]. By means of that punishment being prescribed, the execution of even those who commit acts of violence (*sāhasika*) is incidentally ordained within this very section. Thus ends the section on theft (*steya*). 2.282.

Thus ends the section on theft in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, who was born in the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the noble Vidyādhara race. Chapter 23.

Now begins the section on adultery (*strī-saṃgrahaṇa-prakaraṇa*) in the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* with its commentary. (24) Next, regarding the occasion of adultery consisting of sexual intercourse with another's wife, he states the grounds for the apprehension of the man.
A man shall be apprehended for adultery by seizing each other by the hair with a woman who is another's wife;
or immediately by signs born of passion, as well as when both parties admit it. (2.283)

A man is to be seized for punishment on the occasion of *saṃgrahaṇa*—that is, sexual union with another's wife. When the question arises as to by what means he is to be seized, it is stated: "by *keśākeśi*"; the construction is that the man is to be seized by means of the game of mutual hair-grasping with another's wife. *Keśākeśi* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) formed from a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in the third case, with the suffix *īc*. Not only is this the sole reason; rather, he is also to be seized by means of the marks produced immediately after—the wounds from teeth and nails and so forth—which arise from the mutual desire for sexual union and are indicative of illicit intercourse. Furthermore, even in the absence of the aforementioned reasons, he is to be seized when there is an admission (*saṃpratipatti*) in the form of the two, man and woman, saying, "Our sexual union has been accomplished. (Manu).
When those who violate the wives of others persist in their conduct, the lord of the earth,
having branded them with terrifying punishments, shall banish them.
For from that arises the confusion of castes among the people,
by which unrighteousness, which destroys the very root, leads to total ruin.
Bṛhaspati says: Harshness is declared to be of two kinds, and violence is of two characteristics;
understand that adultery, which has its root in sin, is of three types.
Two types [of love] are produced by the condition of physical strength, while the third is born of passion;
that, moreover, is said to be of three kinds: inferior, middling, and superior.
That which is done against her will by one who is asleep, intoxicated, or distracted,
or while she is prattling in secret— that indeed is considered an act committed by force.
When a union is brought about by leading a woman into one's house under a pretext or by administering intoxicants or magical charms,
that is known as "induced" (upādhikṛta).

It should be understood that [the act] born of mutual passion is performed through mutual longing of the eyes and by sending messengers from afar, out of greed for the beauty and wealth [of the other].
Greed for forms and objects is "greed for forms and objects" (rūpārthalobha). The "magical" (kārmaṇa) [power] is the power of subjugation (vaśīkaraṇa). || 2.283 ||
Touching her girdle, breasts, upper garment, or thighs;
conversing with her at an improper place or time; and even staying together in one place. (2.284)

The term "to be apprehended for adultery" (*saṃgrahaṇe grāhyaḥ*) carries over [from the previous rule]. He who touches the *nīvī* (the knot of the lower garment) or other parts of another man's wife; and as for place and time, those other than that place and time where conversing with another man's wife is not censured by the learned are "improper place and time" (*adeśakāla*). In such cases, he who engages in conversation with another man's wife, and he who stays together with another man's wife on the same bed or seat—that man is to be apprehended for adultery. *Nīvī* is the knot of the lower garment (*paridhāna*). *Stanaprāvaraṇa* is the covering of the breasts. *Sakthi* is the hip/thigh. Vyāsa says: [as follows].
Gathering is to be known as threefold— the first, the middling,
and likewise the superior— and its characteristics have been explained separately in the treatises.

Conversing with another's wife at an improper place or time in a forest, looking at her with sidelong glances, laughing with her, and prior intimacy— these are recorded as the preliminary stages of sexual union.
Manu:
A man who, having been previously accused of offenses, engages in conversation with another's wife,
shall incur the first amercement.
"But he who, being unaccused of faults, should speak for a valid reason,
would incur no fault whatsoever, for there is no transgression on his part. [855] By 'faults' are meant disreputable things such as soliciting her woman and so forth."
The sending of perfumes, garlands, incense, ornaments, and garments,
as well as the enticing with food and drink, is recorded as the middling means of winning over.
In a secluded place, on a bed or seat, mutual reliance and even seizing each other by the hair should be known as the highest form of sexual union.
"Secluded" means uninhabited. Bṛhaspati says:
"Of these three types [of offenders], the first, middle, and highest fines shall be prescribed;
the fine should be greater when the wealth is greater."
Vyāsa states: "Assistance, performing services, play, touching her ornaments and garments, and sharing a bed or seat— all this is recorded as *saṃgrahaṇa* (adultery)."
If a man touches a woman in an improper place, or if he, being touched by her, tolerates it,
all such acts when done with mutual consent are recorded in the legal tradition as *saṃgrahaṇa* (adultery).
Nārada says: If one should say of his own accord, out of pride, delusion, or self-praise,
"This woman was enjoyed by me previously," that is recorded as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse).
If one should seize another by the hand, or by the braid of hair, or even by the hem of the garment, or should say "Stay! Stay!", all such acts are recorded as *saṃgrahaṇa* (seduction).

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "A young man who, though adorned, enters another's wife or seduces an unmarried girl unintentionally, should be fined; but if he does so intentionally with a wicked disposition, he shall be punished. (2.284)
In the case of a prohibition against a woman, she shall pay one hundred; but for a man, the fine shall be two hundred.
In the case of their mutual prohibition, the punishment shall be the same as in the case of adultery.

If a woman engages in conversation with a man with whom she has been forbidden by her husband or others to speak, she shall be fined one hundred *paṇas*. Likewise, the man shall be fined two hundred *paṇas*. When both engage in mutual conversation that has been forbidden for them, the same fine as that which will be declared for *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse) should be understood to apply. Manu says: "The wives of men of all four castes must always be most carefully guarded;
likewise [the wives of] mendicants, bards, those initiated for sacrifice, and artisans."
One who is not forbidden may engage in conversation with women;
however, one who has been forbidden must not carry on a conversation with women.
But one who speaks after having been forbidden deserves a fine of one suvarṇa;
this rule does not apply to the wives of wandering performers (cāraṇas) nor to those who subsist on their own labor.
For they prepare a woman for him and send her about in secret;
he who engages in conversation with them should be made to pay a small fine.
And they should eat only one meal among female servants and female renunciants in private.

Beggars and the like, being unforbidden and not prohibited from speaking, may converse with women; it follows by implication that those who are forbidden must not converse. Consequently, the prohibition "one shall not converse with women" refers to men other than beggars and the like. And the injunction regarding punishment—"he deserves a fine of one *suvarṇa*"—refers to that same category. This word *suvarṇa* denotes a specific measure. For if this is the case, there is a mention of both genus (*jāti*) and measure (*parimāṇa*); otherwise, there would be a mention of genus alone. Furthermore, a genus that lacks a measure cannot serve as a subordinate member of a compound. Therefore, the status of the fine as either two hundred *paṇas* or one *suvarṇa* is to be determined according to the [man's] capacity. "Servants" refers to female slaves and the like. "Devoted" means faithful wives. And this rule does not apply to women who have taken religious vows—this is the syntactical connection. (From the *Matsyapurāṇa*).
Whether it be a mendicant, a woman,
or even an actor who enters [the assembly] when forbidden, he shall incur a fine of two hundred [paṇas].
The man who acts as a go-between there shall be punished in that same manner; and he who provides a place of refuge for an adulterer shall be punished like an adulterer himself. (2.285)

In the case of persons of equal caste, the highest fine shall be imposed; in the case of a lower caste man approaching a woman of a higher caste, the middle fine; but in the case of a man of a higher caste approaching a woman of a lower caste, the man shall suffer death and the woman shall have her ears and other [limbs] cut off. (2.286)

For all castes, when there is sexual intercourse with a woman of the same caste within her own kin-group (*sajāti*), the punishment is the highest fine (*uttama-sāhasa*). However, in the case of *ānulomya*—that is, when a Brāhmaṇa or another higher-caste man approaches a woman of the Kṣatriya or other lower caste—the punishment is the middle fine (*madhyama-sāhasa*). This applies specifically to one who approaches a protected woman by force. As Manu says:
"A Brāhmaṇa approaching protected women of those [castes] should be made to pay a fine of one thousand;
for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya approaching a Śūdra woman, the fine shall indeed be one thousand."

Those [penalties apply] to a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya. Likewise: "A Brāhmaṇa who approaches an unprotected Vaiśya woman or a Rājanya woman, or even a Śūdra woman, shall be made to pay five hundred [paṇas]; but for approaching a woman of the lowest castes (antyaja), he shall pay a thousand."

In the case of *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse) where a man of lower caste approaches a woman of higher caste—such as this form of offense—the man shall be executed. As for the woman, however, her ears, hands, nose, and lips are to be cut off; this applies when the woman is protected (*guptā*). As Manu says: "If a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya should have intercourse with an unprotected Brāhmaṇī woman, he should fine the Vaiśya five hundred [paṇas] and the Kṣatriya one thousand."
But both of them, having violated that very Brahmin woman while she was protected,
should be punished like Shudras or burned in a fire of straw.

A Śūdra who dwells with a member of the twice-born caste, whether protected or unprotected, shall lose one limb if she was unprotected and his entire property if she was protected; in the case of a protected woman, he is deprived of everything.

"One limb" refers to the penis; the meaning is that it shall be removed along with his entire property and life. Thus, Gautama states in the section concerning Śūdras: "In the case of approaching an Ārya woman, there shall be the excision of the penis and the confiscation of all property. Manu says: "If a Vaiśya should approach a guarded Kṣatriya woman, or a Kṣatriya should approach a guarded Vaiśya woman, both of them deserve the same punishment as one who approaches an unguarded Brāhmaṇa woman."

This fine of five hundred [paṇas] applies to a Vaiśya who has intercourse with an unprotected Kṣatriya woman who is utterly corrupt. For an uncorrupted protected woman, the punishment is death, as stated by the specific rule: "In the case of [intercourse] against the natural order, there is death. Generally, for one of the same caste, the punishment is the highest amercement. To provide an exception to that, Nārada states another punishment for specific women:

"The mother, the mother’s sister, the mother-in-law, the maternal uncle’s wife, the father’s sister, the paternal uncle’s wife, the female friend of a teacher, the pupil’s wife, the sister, her female friend, and the daughter-in-law..."
A daughter, a teacher’s wife, one of the same lineage, one who has sought refuge,
a queen, one who has gone forth, a nurse, a virtuous woman, and one of the highest caste.
Having approached any one of these women, one is called a violator of the Guru's bed;
for that offense, no punishment other than the excision of the penis is ordained.
Manu says: "A man shall cause the sinner to be burned on a heated iron bed;
they shall set fire to the logs there, and the evildoer shall be consumed by the flames."
This refers to cases involving those other than Brāhmaṇas who violate the teacher’s bed. Regarding such a Brāhmaṇa, Bṛhaspati says:
"But he who should lust after her through deception shall suffer a fine that takes away everything;
having been branded with the mark of a female organ, he should then be banished from the city."
One who desires the wealth of another should seize it all;
having cut off that person's penis and testicles, he should cause him to be paraded on a donkey.
[858] Incidentally, he speaks regarding the case of a maiden:
"For abducting a decorated maiden, the punishment is the highest; otherwise, it is the lowest."
He should pay a fine [if he violates] a woman of his own caste; however, in the case of violating one of a higher caste, death is ordained by tradition.

There is no offense when [the girl] is of equal status and of marriageable age; otherwise, it is base. One who carries off a maiden of the same caste (*savarṇā*) while she is adorned shall pay the highest fine (*uttamasāhasa*); but if she is unadorned, he shall pay the first fine (*prathamasāhasa*). For one of lower caste who carries off a maiden of higher caste, the punishment is death. When a maiden of lower caste is carried off by one of higher caste with her consent, there is no offense for the abductor. Otherwise, if she is unwilling, it is base—the first fine. This is the prescription of punishment for the mere act of abduction. (2.287)
Now he states the punishment for one who defiles a maiden: "But for defilement, there shall be the cutting off of the hand; likewise, for a maiden of the highest caste, there shall be death. (2.288)

But he who causes defilement by making a wound in the vulva with his finger shall suffer the punishment of having his hand cut off. In this offense, regarding a maiden of the highest caste (*uttamavarṇa*), the punisher shall face execution. Here, the word "hand" (*kara*) refers to the finger; for this very reason, Manu says: "But that man who, out of arrogance, violates a maiden by force, his two fingers shall be immediately cut off, and he deserves a fine of six hundred [paṇas]."

"Having overcome by force," means that he should defile the maiden by violating her virginity; for that, his two fingers, which were the instruments of the defilement, are to be cut off without delay. Likewise:
"One who defiles a willing maiden deserves no cutting off of fingers;
however, he shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas] to prevent a recurrence."
"Equal" means of the same caste (*savarṇa*). "Occurrence" refers to an excessive occurrence. Regarding one who defiles a maiden through sexual intercourse, Manu himself says:
"A man who defiles a maiden against her will deserves immediate execution;
but a man defiling one who is willing does not deserve execution, provided he is of equal status."

He who violates an unwilling, unconsenting maiden—one who has not been married and whose virginity remains intact—deserves death, whether he be of the same caste as a Brāhmaṇa or of a different caste; however, for a Brāhmaṇa, a different punishment must be prescribed. If he approaches a willing maiden of equal status and the same caste, there is no death penalty for him, but rather the punishment of the highest fine (uttama-sāhasa).

One should not compel a maiden to pay anything at all if she consents to union with a man of superior status; however, if she consorts with one of inferior status, she should be kept confined in her home.
"Superior" means of superior caste; "inferior" means of inferior caste. One of the same caste is indicated by the term "superior.
However, an inferior man who has intercourse with a superior woman deserves corporal punishment.
If the father desires it, one having intercourse with a woman of equal caste shall pay a nuptial fee (śulka).

If one approaches a woman of equal caste who is of the same age, he should pay the bride-price (*śulka*) to her father. Nārada says: "But when a girl is willing, there is no transgression in approaching a man of equal caste; rather, having adorned and consecrated her, that very man shall marry her."

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "If the maiden is unwilling, the punishment for [the man] is the cutting off of two fingers and the highest fine; if she is of low status, there is death. But if she is of equal status and willing, he may take back his own daughter after paying her nuptial fee (śulka), her ornaments, and double her woman's property (strīdhana). Manu states: "If a maiden herself should defile another maiden, she shall be fined two hundred [paṇas];
she shall also pay triple the nuptial fee and receive ten lashes with a rod."

This is the meaning: if a maiden, for any reason, should cause her virginity to be violated by means of a finger or other such instrument, she shall pay two hundred *paṇas* to the king; likewise, having given three times the *śulka* (bride-price) or value which that defiled maiden deserves to her, she shall receive ten lashes with a whip—a *śiphā* being a blow with a rope or a creeper. But a woman who should commit [this act] herself immediately deserves shaving of the head, as well as the amputation of two fingers and being led away on a donkey.
And here, the "woman" should be understood as distinct from a maiden, because the maiden has already been mentioned previously. (2.288)
Furthermore: "One who defames a woman shall pay one hundred; but he who makes a false accusation shall pay two hundred.
One who has sexual intercourse with a low-caste woman shall be made to pay one hundred, and for a cow, the middle amercement. (2.289)

The "defiling of a woman" (*striyā dūṣaṇam*) refers to falsely declaring a maiden to be non-virgin by means of such grounds as her having had her hymen torn. The fine for one who commits this is one hundred *paṇas*. If he should speak falsely regarding that very matter, he is to be fined two hundred *paṇas*. One who has sexual intercourse with an animal other than a cow shall be made to pay one hundred *paṇas*. For one who has intercourse with a woman of the lowest castes (*antyajā*) or with a cow, the punishment is the middle amercement (*madhyama-sāhasa*). This punishment applies to anyone other than a Brāhmaṇa who has intercourse with a woman of inferior status; however, for a Brāhmaṇa, the fine is one thousand, according to the statement: "But [the fine is] one thousand for [intercourse with] a woman of the lowest castes. Nārada describes the defects of a maiden:
A girl who is tall, loathsome, afflicted by disease, deformed, who has had sexual intercourse, is forward, or whose affection is directed toward another—these are proclaimed as defects in a maiden.
As for what was stated, "But he who falsely defiles [a maiden] shall pay a hundred," that refers to the case of one with little wealth. (2.289)
A man who has sexual intercourse with female slaves, female servants, or likewise with women kept as concubines—even if they are legally accessible—shall be made to pay a fine of fifty paṇas. (2.290)

Those female slaves who have been kept by their master and whose service to other men is forbidden, as well as those *bhujiṣyā* women who are enjoyed exclusively by their master—even though they may be approached in accordance with the natural order (*ānulomya*) because they are in a state of slavery—the man who approaches them shall be made to pay a fine of fifty *paṇas*. This designation of them as "approachable" (*gamya*) is not intended to imply an absence of sin (*pratyavāya*), but rather an absence of punishment (*daṇḍa*). Consequently, there is no penalty for one who approaches a *bhujiṣyā* woman or a slave-girl who has not been kept [by a master]. Nārada says: "A wanton woman (*svairiṇī*), a non-Brahmin woman, a courtesan, a slave-girl, and one who lives out of her own house..."
Women may be approached in the direct order [of castes], but not in the inverse order.
But with these very female slaves, there would be a fault similar to that regarding the wives of others;
for even though they are approachable, one should not have intercourse with them, since they are under the protection of another.
Vyāsa states:
For approaching a woman who has been restrained by another, the fine is fifty paṇas;
for approaching a prostitute by force, the punishment is recorded as ten paṇas.

The fine for the twelve [offenses] is twelve paṇas. Vyāsa says: "If that lowest of men should approach a woman who has previously been enjoyed by many, they desire his punishment to be like that of a prostitute, and not like that of a wife."

Kātyāyana says: A wanton woman who, afflicted by desire, seeks [a man] of her own accord, may be enjoyed with the king’s permission after she has been publicly proclaimed in the presence of people. (2.290)
For approaching a slave woman by force, a fine of ten paṇas is prescribed;
if she is unwilling and there are many men, the fine is twenty-four paṇas for each individually.

For one who forcibly approaches the wife of another, the fine is ten paṇas; for those who approach a woman against her will while she belongs to many [men], the fine is twenty-four paṇas for each individual. (2.291)

[861] For one who has sexual intercourse with a woman in a non-vaginal opening, or who urinates over a man, the fine is twenty-four [paṇas]; the same applies to one approaching a female renunciant. 2.292.

Furthermore, he who has sexual intercourse with a woman in a non-vaginal opening such as the mouth, he who discharges urine and feces upon a man, or he who approaches a female ascetic such as a *śramaṇikā*—for him the fine is twenty-four *paṇas*. Or, according to the reading "the fine is forty *paṇas*," it consists of forty *paṇas*. (2.292)
But for approaching a woman of the lowest caste, he shall be branded with the mark of a headless trunk and banished;
likewise, a Śūdra who approaches a woman of the higher castes shall be branded, while for a man of the lowest caste approaching a woman of the higher castes, there is death.
Thus ends the section on adultery with women (strīsaṃgrahaṇa), [chapter] 24.

The women of the lowest castes are those of the Caṇḍāla, Kṣattri, and Āyogava classes. A twice-born man who has sexual intercourse with such women, if he does not perform penance, shall be branded on the forehead with the mark of a headless torso (kabandha) and banished from his own kingdom. A Śūdra, however, even if performing penance, must still be branded. For one of the lowest caste who approaches a woman of a higher caste, there is only death. Thus ends the section on adultery with women. 2.293.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, on the seduction of women, in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, born of the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the noble Vidyādhara race.
Now begins the section on miscellaneous matters (*prakīrṇaka-prakaraṇa*) in the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* with its commentary.
(25) He now introduces the title of dispute known as the "Miscellaneous" (*prakīrṇaka*).
Whoever writes a royal edict with either omissions or additions, or who releases an adulterer or a thief, shall receive the highest punishment. (2.294)

If one who is authorized to draft the royal edict writes down a measurement for land or other property granted by the king that is either less or more than what was actually specified, he shall be punished. Furthermore, whoever is authorized to apprehend thieves and the like, having seized a thief, an adulterer, or anyone else deserving of punishment, and releases them without the king’s permission, shall be punished with the highest amercement. [862] Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "For the employment of a forged edict, for obstructing a royal edict, or for dealing with forged weights, measures, and balances, there shall be corporal punishment or the amputation of a limb. Kātyāyana says:
Whoever should accomplish a legal matter by means of a false measure, a forged seal, or even a counterfeit stamp, shall be made to pay the highest fine.
Manu:
"The king shall put to death those who forge royal edicts, those who corrupt the subjects,
those who kill women, children, or Brahmins, and likewise those who serve his enemies."

The constituent elements (*prakṛti*) are the components of the kingdom, beginning with the sovereign; those who serve the enemy are those who serve one hostile to the king. Viṣṇu states: "The king shall punish those who forge edicts and those who forge documents. (2.294)
Having defiled a twice-born man with forbidden food, he shall be fined the highest amercement;
for a Kṣatriya, the middle amercement; for a Vaiśya, the first amercement; and for a Śūdra, half of that. (2.295)

Having defiled a Brāhmaṇa with forbidden food such as garlic and the like, one shall be punished with the highest amercement; having defiled a Kṣatriya, with the middle amercement; having defiled a Vaiśya, with the first amercement; and for defiling a Śūdra, half of that. Regarding the phrase "shall be punished," Viṣṇu states: "One who defiles a Brāhmaṇa with forbidden food shall be fined sixteen *suvarṇas*; if it is food that causes loss of caste, the fine is one hundred. For defiling [a Brāhmaṇa] with liquor, he shall be put to death. For defiling a Kṣatriya, the fine is half of that; for defiling a Vaiśya, half of that again; and for defiling a Śūdra, the first amercement. One who eats forbidden food that causes loss of caste shall be banished. (2.295)
One who deals in counterfeit gold and one who sells forbidden meat shall have three limbs mutilated and be made to pay the highest fine. (2.296)

He who deals with another by creating the perception of gold where there is no gold, and he who sells forbidden meat—such as that of a village pig or the like—by creating the perception that it is wholesome meat, shall be deprived of three limbs—the nose, the ear, and a hand—and shall be fined the highest amercement. As for that which was stated by Manu:
"But the king shall cause the goldsmith, who is the most wicked of all thorns and who acts unjustly, to be cut into pieces with razors."
That refers to the case of a goldsmith who steals the gold of a Brahmin. (2.296)
He states an exception to the punishment regarding specific circumstances:
"There is no fault caused by quadrupeds when one cries out, 'Do not go!
nor likewise for [damage] caused by wood, clods of earth, stones, or draft animals yoked to a cart. (2.297)

[863] An offense such as the killing of a human being committed by four-footed animals, such as goats or horses, becomes a ground for punishment for their driver. However, if he should say to the other, "Move aside! while employing wood or other implements, the offense caused by the wood or other implements does not become a ground for punishment for him who is speaking loudly, "Move aside! A *loṣṭa* is a clod of earth; an *iṣu* is an arrow; a *yugya* is a vehicle. (2.297)
If injury occurs by means of a vehicle with a broken nose-rope, or one with a broken yoke and so forth, or if it retreats backward, the owner incurs the blame for the harm. (2.298)

A rope tied to the nose of a bull is called *nasyā*; that vehicle on which such a rope has been severed is a "vehicle with a severed nose-rope" (*chinnanasya-yāna*). Likewise, that whose yoke and so forth are broken is described in that manner. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), other parts of the vehicle such as the wheels and axles are included. When injury to living beings is caused by a vehicle retreating backwards in the manner described, the owner does not incur guilt. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), other modes of movement for the vehicle besides retreating backwards are also included. The mention of the "owner" is for the sake of illustration; therefore, the charioteer and others are also not liable for the fault. (Manu).
When the nose-rope is severed, when the yoke is broken, when the vehicle turns sideways or comes face-to-face, or likewise when there is an absence of the axle or the wheels;
Manu has declared that there is no punishment for the breaking of a yoke, nor likewise for the snapping of the traces or the reins, nor when one cries out "Get away! while being struck.
If a vehicle turns off course due to the negligence of the driver,
the owner shall be liable for the damage and must pay a fine of two hundred panas.

The driver is the charioteer; the owner is the rider. If the driver be trustworthy, the driver alone deserves the punishment; if the driver be untrustworthy, all those seated in the vehicle shall each be fined one hundred [paṇas].

A trustworthy person is one capable of preventing [an accident]. But if that person is untrustworthy, then all those standing on the carriage or riding in it shall each be fined one hundred [paṇas]. Likewise:
"But if, being obstructed by cattle or by a chariot, he should cause a living being to perish, the punishment in that case shall be determined after due consideration."
In the case of killing a human being, one quickly incurs guilt equal to that of a thief;
for large living beings such as cows, elephants, camels, and horses, the guilt is half.
For the killing of small animals, the fine shall be two hundred;
but for auspicious beasts and birds, the punishment shall be fifty.
For donkeys, goats, and sheep, the fine shall be five māṣakas;
for the killing of a dog or a pig, the fine shall be one māṣaka.

Even if capable of doing so, a master who fails to rescue [his dependents] from fanged or horned animals shall pay the first amercement; likewise, if they have cried out for help, he shall pay double.

The owner of fanged animals such as elephants or of horned animals such as bulls, being capable of preventing them, incurs a fine of the first *sāhasa* if he fails to restrain them while they are engaged in killing living beings. However, for one who does not restrain them even when the victim cries out, "Save me!", the fine is double that which was previously mentioned. (2.299)
One who calls his paramour a thief shall be made to pay a fine of five hundred;
but one who releases him after having lived off his wealth shall pay that same amount multiplied eightfold.

But he who, desiring to conceal the fault of his own wives, accuses their lover of being a thief, shall be fined five hundred [paṇas]. But he who, having received property from a paramour, releases him without reporting it to the king, shall be made to pay eightfold the value of the property taken. 2.300.
Furthermore: Having cut out the tongue of one who speaks what is undesirable to the king, of one who reviles him, and of one who divulges his secret counsel, he should banish him. (2.301)

One who speaks excessively of what is undesirable and unpleasant to the king—the protector of the realm and so forth—such as praise for his enemies; likewise, one who utters abuse or curses directed at the king; and one who reveals or divulges his secret counsel concerning peace, war, and other matters: having cut out their tongues, the king shall banish them. (Manu) Furthermore, those who steal from the king’s treasury, those who stand in opposition to him, and those who instigate his enemies, he shall cause to be executed by various forms of punishment. (Manu)

"Sowers of discord" and "encouragers" [are those who incite others]. "By various punishments" means that all forms of punishment should be applied according to the offense. Regarding this, Nārada states that when one's entire property is to be confiscated, the means of livelihood must not be seized:
"The weapons of those who live by arms; the oxen and other tools of those who live by external labor;
the ornaments of courtesans; and the musical instruments of those skilled in them."
Whatever is the tool of anyone, by which artisans live their lives—even when all one's property is being seized, the king ought not to take that away. [2.301]
The punishment for one who sells the body of a dead person, for one who strikes a teacher, and likewise for one who mounts a king's vehicle or throne, is the middle amercement. (2.302)

For one who sells clothing or other items attached to the body for the purpose of decorating a corpse, for one who strikes a teacher with the aforementioned characteristics, or for one who mounts the king’s vehicle or seat without his permission, the punishment is the middle amercement. (2.302)
For one who pierces two eyes, for one who acts against the king's enemies, for one who issues royal commands on his own authority,
and for a Śūdra living by the profession of a Brāhmaṇa, the fine shall be eight hundred.

He who, out of anger, plucks out both eyes of another, he who carries out the commands of one hated by the king, and he who, being a Śūdra, lives by assuming the marks of a higher caste—these shall each be fined eight hundred [paṇas]. If a Śūdra living by the status of a Brāhmaṇa enters into a matrimonial alliance with twice-born men or through the womb, he is certainly to be put to death.
"The king shall cause all those to be executed, as well as Śūdras who bear the marks of the twice-born."

Thus says the *Manu* [Smṛti]. As for the statement from another Smṛti: "In the case of a Śūdra who assumes the dress of a Brāhmaṇa, one should give him a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) with a red-hot iron pin and likewise brand his body," that is to be understood as referring to one who performs for others Smārta rites such as the Śrāddha meal or the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice. Manu [says]: "The king, having deprived of wealth that lowest-born person who, out of greed, lives by the actions of the superior castes, should immediately banish him."
This refers to the case of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. (2.303)
To conclude all legal proceedings, he says something:
"But when the king has correctly scrutinized ill-scrutinized legal proceedings, the members of the court, together with the winner, shall each be fined double the amount of the dispute. (2.304)

Those legal proceedings which were wrongly perceived due to the influence of greed and other such motives, and thus conducted contrary to the scriptures—having reviewed them again correctly, the king, together with the victorious litigant from the previous court, shall punish the members of that assembly individually with a fine double the penalty prescribed for the defeated party.
Each member of the assembly shall be punished separately with a fine double that of the dispute itself.

Thus it has been stated; that [previous rule] concerns the subject of a dispute over a gift (*dāna-vivāda*), whereas this [present rule] concerns a subject distinct from that, and therefore there is no tautology. However, when a legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) becomes tainted by the defects of the witnesses, then the punishment of the members of the court (*sabhyas*) does not apply, because they are not the cause in that case. But when a legal proceeding becomes improper due to the influence of the litigants, the members of the court, the presiding judge, or the witnesses, then there would be a slight accumulation of demerit (*pratyavāya*) for all of them. As it has been said: "One quarter of the unrighteousness falls upon the perpetrator, one quarter falls upon the witness."
One quarter falls upon all the members of the court, and one quarter reaches the king. || 2.304 ||
He states the means for the judge to discern the truth regarding a litigant who has been defeated according to justice, yet believes himself not defeated:

"If one should think, 'I am not defeated,' even though he has been defeated by justice, the judge, having defeated him again as he approaches [the court], shall cause him to pay double the fine. (2.305)

If a litigant, though defeated according to the treatises (*śāstra*), thinks "I am not defeated," and returns for a further examination of the case, the judge, having won him over again through that renewed examination, shall cause him to pay double the fine. The essential meaning is that the case is to be examined again only upon his acceptance of the double fine, and not otherwise. For this very reason, Nārada states:
"If one considers a case to have been decided or adjudicated contrary to the law (*vidharma*), the judge, having imposed a double fine, shall reopen that matter."

The meaning is as follows: if one considers that both that which was written down as the cause of his defeat and adjudicated (*tīrita*), and that which was his punishment and ordained (*anuśiṣṭa*), have arisen contrary to the law—that is, in opposition to the *dharmaśāstra*—then he shall accept double the fine and have the judicial proceeding conducted again. However, if the litigant does not accept the double fine, then what was previously determined must not be overturned; thus he says:
"Wherever a case exists that has been adjudicated and ordained..."
"That which has been done should be known as being in accordance with the Dharma; a wise person should not turn back from it. (2.305)
Whatever fine has been unjustly taken by a king, he should report it to Varuṇa and himself give it to the Brahmins multiplied thirtyfold.
Thus ends the miscellaneous section (prakīrṇa-prakaraṇa), [number] 25.

But when a king has taken a fine from anyone through injustice or by transgressing the law, he should give that fine-money back to him, then announce thirty times its value to Varuṇa, and having himself relinquished it for the sake of Varuṇa, he should give it to Brāhmaṇas; the meaning is that he should bestow it upon Brāhmaṇas. (2.306)

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, the Section on Miscellaneous Topics (*prakīrṇa-prakaraṇam*), in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, who was born in the lineage of the royal Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the glorious Vidyādhara clan.
This second chapter on legal procedure is completed.
